title: Hesekê Asayish Command: Two of our members killed in bomb attack
content:
A security centre belonging to the Internal Security Forces, located in the Mişêrfê neighbourhood of Hesekê, was targeted in an attack involving a bomb-laden motorcycle.

In a statement on the attack, the Internal Security Forces (Asayish) Command said that ISIS cells had targeted the security centre using three motorcycles rigged with explosives.

The Asayish Command confirmed that two of its members had been killed, and five others wounded in the attack.

title: Peoples’ Climate Summit: COP31 has failed to deliver climate justice
content:
The Peoples’ Climate Summit, held in Antalya from November 14 to 18, has published a statement on the outcomes of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). After more than two weeks of negotiations, the global climate conference ended without an overarching final agreement or a consensus on phasing out fossil fuels. The Peoples’ Climate Summit also sees this as a structural failure of the international climate regime and questions its democratic foundations.




Global power imbalances in climate policy




In the statement, the organizations criticized the lack of transparency in the decision-making processes at COP31, stating that the presentation of draft negotiating texts in the middle of the night made it difficult for participating countries to engage effectively in the deliberations. The Peoples’ Climate Summit highlighted an incident during the closing session as particularly revealing: “COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister, Murat Kurum, cut off Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who was speaking on behalf of 54 African countries. The fact that representatives of African peoples, who have contributed the least to causing the climate crisis but face its most severe consequences, are silenced reflects the power imbalances within the international climate regime. There can be no climate justice without democracy.”




False technological solutions serving the interests of the fossil fuel industry




The statement said: “While references to fossil fuels disappeared from the draft decisions over the course of the negotiations, the COP31 presidency maintained its targets for carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) technologies, despite opposition from a coalition of 126 countries. The Peoples’ Climate Summit views the political promotion of technologies whose viability on a large scale has yet to be demonstrated as a means for polluting corporations to evade their responsibility to reduce emissions.




“Forests and ecosystems must not be reduced to carbon credits that companies can purchase to continue polluting the environment. Technology cannot replace actual emissions reductions.”




Half a billion dollars to host COP31




According to the organizations, the demand by countries of the Global South to provide $120 billion annually by 2035 for adaptation to the impacts of the climate crisis went unmet in Antalya. The Peoples’ Climate Summit illustrated the priorities that were set instead by pointing to the costs of hosting COP31. Citing data from the Electronic Public Procurement Platform (EKAP), the organizations estimate that the total value of tenders awarded and contracts signed by Turkey as part of the summit preparations up to September 2026 exceeded 25 billion lira, equivalent to approximately $500 million. According to the statement, this contrasts with just $50.2 million in new funding pledges to the international Adaptation Fund.




The total value of contracts for preparing the UN Climate Change Conference was therefore approximately ten times the amount of new pledges to the Adaptation Fund. The Peoples’ Climate Summit demanded that the Turkish government provide a detailed disclosure of all expenditures.




The hypocrisy of fossil fuel policy




 




Among the fundamental contradictions of COP31 is the continued investment in fossil fuels by Turkey and Australia, which jointly assumed leadership of the UN Climate Change Conference. On November 9, the very day COP31 began, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced the discovery of two new oil fields in the Gabar region of Northern Kurdistan, with an estimated potential of 135 million barrels. “The fact that a government which, in its capacity as COP31 president, brings countries together in Antalya presents increased fossil fuel production as a success exposed the hypocrisy of its climate policy on the very first day,” the statement said.




Five concrete demands to the Turkish government




The Peoples’ Climate Summit expects concrete political action from Turkey, which will hold the COP presidency until COP32: “Coal-fired power plants must be shut down, and a binding timetable for phasing out coal must be presented. New oil, natural gas and coal projects must be halted, and fossil fuel subsidies must be abolished. Ecocide must be established as a criminal offense under national law; Turkey must accede to the Rome Statute and the Aarhus Convention. Legal provisions that leave nature at the mercy of capital’s interests, particularly the Mining Law and Law No. 7554, must be repealed. Just transition plans must be developed for workers and local communities in coal-producing regions, with the participation of trade unions.”




For a democratic international climate council




In view of the influence of fossil fuel corporations and lobbying groups representing polluting industries on the COP mechanism, the Peoples’ Climate Summit proposes an alternative institutional framework: a democratic International Climate Council should be established under the auspices of the United Nations, without veto privileges and with the authority to impose sanctions. The organizations from the environmental, trade union, women’s and youth movements that gathered in Antalya intend to further strengthen their cross-border solidarity and continue their joint struggle for climate justice, including at COP32, which will take place in the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, in 2027.

title: DEM Party Imrali delegation meets with MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli
content:
The Imrali delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) met with Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) Chair Devlet Bahçeli in Ankara on Thursday.




The meeting, held in Bahçeli’s office in the MHP parliamentary group section of the Turkish Parliament, was attended by DEM Party deputies Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, as well as lawyer Faik Özgür Erol. The meeting, which lasted approximately one hour, focused on the current state of the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the legal and political requirements of the present phase. The Imrali delegation had last met with Bahçeli on October 9.




The Imrali delegation had also held talks with Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek on Wednesday. According to the DEM Party’s press office, the meeting focused on the legal aspects of the ongoing process to resolve the Kurdish question, as well as conditions in prisons. Particular attention was given to the situation of sick prisoners and problems related to the execution of sentences.

title: Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court strengthens Baghdad’s control over the Kurdistan Region
content:
The dispute between the Iraqi central government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) over control of border crossings, energy resources and public revenues is intensifying. On Wednesday, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court issued a ruling on the constitutional division of powers between Baghdad and Hewlêr (Erbil), largely upholding the central government’s recent decisions. Meanwhile, Iraqi border guard forces have begun implementing the first measures.




On November 24, the government in Baghdad announced a series of decisions aimed at strengthening federal control over border crossings and the energy sector. These include closing officially unrecognized border crossings, transferring control of oil fields in territories disputed between Baghdad and Erbil to the federal Oil Ministry, and tightening oversight of oil transportation and exports.




The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) subsequently warned in a joint statement against interference with the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, describing any violation of those rights as a red line.




Baghdad rejects allegations of foreign interference




Amid the dispute, the media office of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi rejected allegations that the decisions had been made at the behest of other countries. It stated that all measures taken within Iraq’s internationally recognized borders were based on the country’s sovereign decision-making authority, constitutional powers and legal obligations.




“Our decisions are Iraq’s own, our will is national, and our points of reference are the Constitution and the law. Iraq’s overriding interests are the guiding principle for our positions and actions,” the Prime Minister’s office stated.




Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council also intervened in the dispute. It called on the central government, the regional government and all political forces to abide by the 2005 Constitution. At the same time, the council reiterated that the authority to interpret the Constitution rests exclusively with the Federal Supreme Court.




Regional government rejects the language of weapons and threats




The Kurdistan Regional Government discussed Baghdad’s decisions at a meeting. In a statement issued afterward, it emphasized its willingness to cooperate in combating corruption, oil smuggling and other illegal activities, but rejected the central government’s approach.




“We have always acted jointly and in coordination with the federal government to prevent and put an end to all illegal activities. However, we reject the language of weapons and threats,” the regional government stated.




the Kurdistan Regional Government stated that efforts to combat corruption and oil smuggling must extend across the entire territory of Iraq. At the same time, it announced legal action against individuals who undermine the constitutional status and interests of the Kurdistan Region and incite the population to conflict.




Federal Supreme Court reaffirms Baghdad’s extensive powers




In its ruling announced during a public session on November 25, the Federal Supreme Court clarified the constitutional powers of the central and regional governments in several key areas. The ruling is final and binding on all state institutions.




Citing Articles 109 and 110 of the Iraqi Constitution, the court ruled that the protection of international borders falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the central government. Accordingly, Baghdad has the authority to deploy federal security forces along the external borders of the Kurdistan Region and take appropriate security measures.




Furthermore, under Law No. 30 of 2016, federal authorities have extensive supervisory and regulatory powers over all border crossings in Iraq. However, customs inspections at border crossings in the Kurdistan Region must be carried out in coordination with the regional government. According to the court, the introduction of a unified nationwide electronic monitoring system for border crossings and customs offices also falls within Baghdad’s jurisdiction.




In customs and fiscal policy, the court also reaffirmed the central government’s authority to introduce uniform regulations nationwide, monitor compliance with them, and ensure that public revenues generated from taxes, fees and other non-oil sources are transferred to the state treasury.




Joint management of oil and natural gas resources




The ruling takes a more nuanced approach to the energy sector. Referring to Article 112 of the Constitution, the court ruled that the management of extracted oil and natural gas must be carried out jointly by the federal government, the Kurdistan Regional Government and the respective oil- and gas-producing provinces.




However, the federal Oil Ministry and the relevant regulatory authorities have supervisory and oversight powers covering all aspects of oil and natural gas production, marketing and export. These powers also extend to the relevant contracts and production processes.




At the same time, the court emphasized that the cooperation between the central and regional governments stipulated by the Constitution must not be interrupted or undermined.




Disputed territories remain a central issue of contention




The ruling on the territorial scope of the regional government’s jurisdiction is of particular political significance. In this context, the Federal Supreme Court referred to Article 53(A) of the Transitional Administrative Law and Article 143 of the Iraqi Constitution.




Accordingly, the relevant territories are those in the provinces of Duhok, Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Kirkuk, Diyala and Nineveh that were administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government up to March 19, 2003.




According to the court, the exercise of regional powers beyond these boundaries must be assessed in light of the constitutional provisions governing disputed territories. Outside the recognized jurisdiction of the Kurdistan Region, administrative and executive powers rest with the federal government. The court thus ruled that de facto administration by the regional government does not, in itself, establish constitutional rights or powers.




The ruling therefore also touches on the still-unresolved issue of the disputed territories, whose status is to be determined in accordance with Article 140 of the Iraqi Constitution.




Iraq begins closing border crossings




While the political and constitutional dispute continues, the implementation of Baghdad’s initial decisions has already begun. Mohammed Abdulwahab Said, Commander of the Iraqi Border Guard Forces, confirmed to Iraqi media that his units had begun closing officially unrecognized border crossings and implementing measures to combat oil smuggling.




According to Said, efforts are also underway to integrate the administrative structures of border crossings in the Kurdistan Region with those in the rest of Iraq. While securing the external borders falls under the responsibility of the border guard forces, the control and management of border crossings are the responsibility of the federal Border Crossings Authority.




The statements issued so far do not specify which border crossings have already been affected by the measures or to what extent the central government’s other decisions are being implemented.

title: KDP forces detain journalist and two civilians in Soran
content:
In a statement, a relative of journalist Ebdo Rostayî reported that KDP security forces had detained Rostayî and two other civilians. The detentions were reportedly carried out because the civilians had been asked to share their views on the situation in the region and the decisions made by Elî Zeydî.




In a statement, VAR Media Institution reported that its Soran correspondent, Ebdo Rostayî, had been abducted by security forces while carrying out his journalistic duties.




The statement said: “The Soran Autonomous Administration Security Forces are responsible for the safety and well-being of our colleague Ebdo Rostayî.”

title: MP Cengiz Çiçek: Targeting ill prisoners is an ideological attack
content:
The vigil launched outside the Ministry of Justice to demand the medical treatment and release of ill prisoners entered its 10th day. The vigil is led by the MED Federation of Legal Solidarity Associations of Prisoners’ Families (MED TUHAD-FED), with the support of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) and the Free Lawyers Association (ÖHD).




DEM Party MP for Istanbul Cengiz Çiçek addressed the vigil on Wednesday, saying that the action was not only a political but also a moral responsibility. Çiçek said that the action represented an insistence on upholding all human values and that human values, law, justice and peace were necessary for everyone.




Çiçek said that a former minister had been released on health grounds after 18 days, while thousands of political prisoners had been held in prison for decades, describing this as a political choice by the government.




Çiçek emphasized that the Peace and Democratic Society Process was not merely about ending armed conflict but also encompassed the struggle against systemic and structural inequalities.




Çiçek said that the Kurdish question could not be reduced to weapons and must be addressed as a question of democracy and law. He added that the issue of ill prisoners was not limited to the individuals whose names had been made public.

title: KNK calls on Southern Kurdistan’s political parties to protect national gains
content:
The Executive Council of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) issued a statement concerning the protection of the constitutional rights and powers of the Kurdistan Region.




The KNK said it had been closely following the Iraqi Prime Minister’s recent remarks, and drew attention to statements and initiatives aimed at restricting the management of oil, natural resources and other revenues.




Emphasising the need for political and economic stability in both federal Iraq and the Kurdistan Region, the statement said that Iraq’s strength and the continuation of its democratic system depend on respecting the will of the people and protecting everyone's constitutional rights.




Pointing out that the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) is the result of the Kurdish people's struggle and the sacrifices made by the people of Kurdistan, the statement said: "Any attempt to undermine the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region regarding oil and non-oil revenues contradicts the principles of federalism and cooperation and will weaken the understanding and trust between Erbil and Baghdad.




We also emphasise that the Kurdistan Region's share of the Iraqi budget, as well as the salaries and financial entitlements of employees and citizens in Kurdistan, must not be entangled in political disputes. These must be guaranteed as fundamental constitutional rights."

title: Gülderen Varlı: Women's freedom is a fundamental condition for peace
content:
Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP for Van (Wan) Gülderen Varlı spoke to ANF on International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. She talked about the Peace and Democratic Society Process, women's freedom, violence against women, ecological problems and women's role in decision-making mechanisms, saying that a democratic society could only be built if women had an equal and free say in every sphere of life.




Gülderen Varlı emphasized that the Peace and Democratic Society Process, initiated by Abdullah Öcalan's call, must be addressed in conjunction with women's freedom, saying that women had established an important tradition of struggle within the Kurdish freedom struggle.







 







'The women's struggle is rooted in a historical legacy'




Varlı said that the women's struggle was rooted in a historical legacy: "Our struggle is a women's struggle. Within the Kurdish freedom struggle, we come from a 50-year tradition of struggle. The women's struggle extends from the Mirabal sisters to the present day and has grown through the struggle waged by women like Sakine and many other women comrades."




Varlı added that 25 November was not only a day of struggle against violence against women but also an occasion to discuss how a democratic society should be built. She drew attention to women's role in establishing a shared, equal and free life, saying that "women are struggling to ensure that both they and those around them can live freely. Women will also play their part in creating a democratic and free country."




'Women's right to speak and decide is the foundation of democratic society'




Varlı said that systematic violence against women was the result of a system shaped by the male-dominated mentality and the state. She said that women's participation in social life and decision-making mechanisms was decisive for democratization and continued: "Women have been subjected to systematic violence for centuries. This violence is the result of a system shaped by the male-dominated mentality and the state. Women's participation in social life, their ability to have a say, take part in governance and express their consciousness and ideas will ensure that the process develops in a democratic direction."




Varlı emphasized that women must not merely voice their demands but also act as subjects directly involved in decision-making and governance processes. She said, "If we all live together in this world and in this country, we must have a collective voice. We, as women, must also be represented in decision-making mechanisms, governance and every sphere of life." She added that women would play a leading role in building social peace during the democratic society process and that the demand for peace voiced by the Peace Mothers and women in every sphere of life for years was an important part of this struggle. She continued: "Despite all the exploitation, torture and violence we have experienced, our demand is peace. Once peace is achieved, it will once again be women who build the social fabric of peace between the two sides. Women will also actively participate in this process."




'Peace is possible through a life where women are not killed'




Varlı said that the Peace and Democratic Society Process could not be assessed solely in terms of silencing the weapons and ending deaths, drawing attention to the continuing femicides and violence against women. She said that discussions on peace must be accompanied by concrete steps to guarantee women's right to life and that genuine peace could not exist in an environment where women disappear and are killed: "We have been discussing the democratic society and peace process for two years. Many politicians and people from different sections of society are expressing their views on this issue. However, as we discuss peace today, we must also bring the violence experienced by women onto the agenda on the occasion of 25 November. Women are being killed today. Women are falling from the balconies of their homes, disappearing or being murdered. First, there are reports of missing women, and then it emerges that these women have been killed."




Varlı underlined that mothers had endured immense suffering for years because of the children they had lost in the conflict and that peace was therefore extremely valuable. However, she emphasized that peace must be addressed alongside the resolution of social problems, saying, "If we want peace and democracy, we must also build a life where women are not killed and no woman is lost. The foundations of peace must be laid with such an understanding. We must pursue this process by addressing numerous issues together, with women's freedom foremost among them."




'The weapons have fallen silent, but social problems remain'




Varlı said that silencing the weapons was an important development in the peace process but was not sufficient on its own. Varlı said: "The weapons have fallen silent during this process, but most social problems remain unchanged. There has been no concrete progress in areas such as women's rights, children's rights, healthcare and agriculture. We cannot say that peace has been achieved in terms of ecology either. We are now facing different problems in the areas where the weapons have fallen silent."




Varlı pointed to ecological problems caused by hydroelectric power plant (HPP) and solar power plant (SPP) projects in Kurdistan and emphasized that peace must be established with nature and all sections of society. She said, "HPP and SPP projects are being implemented in many mountainous areas of Kurdistan. But have we made peace with nature? There are still serious problems that need to be resolved in this regard. The necessary negotiations have yet to take place and the necessary steps have yet to be taken to prevent violence against women."




Varlı stressed that the concept of democratic society must encompass all these problems and emphasized the importance of translating verbal statements into concrete action: "If we are to make peace, we must also make peace with all sections of society and with nature. Concrete steps must therefore be taken beyond verbal statements, and the necessary arrangements must be put in writing and given legal guarantees. Peace is valuable, but it is not sufficient on its own."




'

Society must first make peace within itself'




Varlı said that Abdullah Öcalan's assessments of women's freedom were important for building a democratic society. She recalled Abdullah Öcalan's words, "Society cannot be free unless women are free," and said that genuine democracy and equality could not be achieved in a society where women were not free. She added that women had struggled against the male-dominated system from the time of the Mirabal sisters to the present day and that important gains had been achieved through this struggle, but these remained insufficient. She said, "If a woman in this country does not feel free on the street, at home, in the fields or at her workplace, we cannot speak of a democratic life. Peace cannot be achieved under such circumstances either. Society must first make peace within itself."




Varlı emphasized that women were struggling against men making decisions about their lives, adding that "a man has no right to decide what I wear, what I eat, where I walk, where I go, how I spend my money or what role I play in economic life. This mentality is incompatible with a democratic, free, equal and peaceful life." She also said that women's equal representation in mechanisms where opinions are expressed and decisions are made must be guaranteed. She referred to Abdullah Öcalan's assessments on this issue and said: "Mr. Öcalan has made numerous assessments and written extensively on this issue. He says that society cannot be free unless women are free. This is a very accurate assessment. We cannot speak of democracy, freedom or equality unless women are free, have a say and decision-making power, and participate on an equal footing in areas dominated by the male-dominated system."




Varlı said that assessments of women's freedom must not remain merely conceptual but must find concrete expression in every sphere of life to build a democratic society.




Call for the establishment of a Ministry of Women




Varlı also discussed the parliamentary inquiry motion they had submitted, saying that a dedicated institution was needed to address the problems faced by women. She said that femicides, violence, the failure to identify perpetrators and the continuing search for justice demonstrated the inadequacy of existing mechanisms. She called for the establishment of a Ministry of Women and said: "There are many women who have been killed or subjected to violence, whose perpetrators have yet to be identified and who are still awaiting justice. We submit various parliamentary questions to bring these problems onto the agenda. When a woman is killed, we submit questions to the relevant ministries, the Ministry of Interior or the Ministry of Family and Social Services. The responses we receive clearly demonstrate the need for a dedicated institution to address these problems.




We believe that a dedicated institution is needed to resolve the problems women face in society. Based on this need, we submitted a parliamentary inquiry motion and called for the establishment of a Ministry of Women. We also maintain that this ministry should be headed by a woman, because it is another woman who can best understand a woman. I hope that all women in parliament will support the parliamentary inquiry motion we have submitted without imposing any conditions and that the motion will be adopted. This awareness must also be reflected in parliament if we are to establish a democratic, free and equal life and eliminate violence against women."




'Trustees appointed men to women's policy departments'




Varlı drew attention to the fact that women's institutions and women's policy departments within municipalities had been rendered ineffective following the appointment of state-appointed trustees. She said: "We had established women's institutions and departments within municipalities. However, after the appointment of trustees, we were removed from these departments and men were appointed to our women's policy departments. It is unacceptable for men to be appointed to head departments responsible for implementing women's policies."




'May no woman have been killed by next 25 November'




Varlı expressed her hope that the next 25 November would be marked at a time when no femicides had occurred and the problems faced by women had been resolved. Varlı concluded: "I hope that by next 25 November, we will come together in an environment where no woman has been killed and solutions have been found to the problems women face. Perhaps then we will even change the name of 25 November. We will celebrate 25 November together in a democratic, free and equal country, where we no longer have to struggle and can share the happiness of living together."

title: KCK on the 48th anniversary of the PKK’s founding: A new beginning in the freedom struggle
content:
The Co-Presidency of the Executive Council of the Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) issued a statement on the occasion of the 48th anniversary of the founding of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). In the statement, the KCK reviewed the historical achievements of the movement led by the PKK and placed the party’s dissolution and the transition to a new political strategy of struggle within the continuity of the Kurdish freedom struggle.




The KCK statement on Thursday reads as follows:




“We congratulate Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan], our people, their friends, and all forces engaged in the struggle on the 48th anniversary of the founding of the PKK. We commemorate with gratitude and respect our martyrs, who made the emergence of the PKK and its 52-year struggle possible.




Leader Apo initiated the efforts to establish the party in memory of our esteemed martyr Haki Karer. On November 27, 1978, he convened the first congress and founded the PKK, which would go on to lead the struggle of the Kurdish people.




The PKK has led the longest-running freedom struggle in the history of the Kurdish people. Under its leadership, profound transformations have taken place among the Kurdish people, the likes of which have not been seen anywhere else in the world. The Kurdish people were raised from their deathbed and became the most dynamic force for freedom in the Middle East. The Kurds, once regarded as backward, have now become a shining example not only for the Middle East but for the entire world.




Our homeland, once regarded as a buried, imaginary Kurdistan, is now a region where an exceptionally vibrant freedom struggle is being waged. All the achievements and the strength of resistance in Northern, Southern, Eastern, and Western Kurdistan are owed to the freedom struggle led by the PKK.




The Kurdish people’s freedom struggle has faced attacks on a scale unprecedented anywhere in the world. We have lost tens of thousands of martyrs, while hundreds of thousands of Kurds have been subjected to severe torture and thrown into prison. The Kurds have set a record in world history for political imprisonment. Thousands of villages were burned down and destroyed, and Kurdistan was depopulated. Nevertheless, the freedom struggle led by the PKK continued uninterrupted for 52 years and achieved tremendous gains.




As the freedom struggle repelled all attacks aimed at its annihilation, the Turkish state found itself facing serious problems both domestically and internationally. Under conditions of non-conflict, it entered into a process of political discussions with our freedom movement. State representatives held dozens of talks with Leader Apo on Imrali. Delegations from the Kurdish side also participated in these talks.




The fact that the Turkish state, which has long denied the existence of the Kurdish people and sought to subject them to physical and cultural genocide, recognizes Leader Apo and our movement as interlocutors is a significant political development. All the talks on Imrali are also being conducted as a form of political struggle.




The Peace and Democratic Society Process, which has been underway for two years, and the new strategy of political struggle have also developed on the foundations of the 52-year struggle. The values created over these 52 years and the reality of our people struggling for their freedom are our greatest source of strength. Today, the Kurds are neither without advocates nor without leadership or strength of their own. We now have a leader who guides not only the Kurdish people but also the pursuit of a free and democratic life in the Middle East and throughout the world. We have a leader who is supported by women because he has developed a path toward women’s liberation. We have a leader who has developed a new social science. Today, we have a leader who enables the Kurdish people to raise their heads as high as the stars.




As Leader Apo said, the PKK is an unfinished novel, a folk song, a poem. The dissolution of the PKK marks a new beginning in the freedom struggle. Just as the Kurdish people entered the struggle alongside the PKK with youthful spirit and enthusiasm and achieved great gains, they will also achieve great gains through the Peace and Democratic Society Process. By attaining a free and democratic life, the Kurds will also pave the way for all peoples of the Middle East to achieve a free and democratic life. This is the dialectic of the Kurdish freedom movement; this is its inherent law of development.




The Kurdish people express their recognition of the PKK’s great achievements through their unwavering commitment to our leadership. By preserving the memory of their martyrs, the Kurdish people demonstrate their commitment to what the PKK has created. All our martyrs said during their lifetimes: “If I were born again, I would join the PKK again.” Every militant member of the PKK says: “If I came into this world again, I would join the PKK again.”




Our people, who have chanted “The PKK is the people, and the people are here” for decades, also express at every opportunity that they will remain committed to the PKK forever. The response of our people when the deaths of our martyrs are announced is a clear expression of this. By standing by their children, they also stand by the PKK and the struggle it has led.




Our people celebrate the anniversary of the founding of the PKK everywhere and will continue to do so in the future. We also call on all our people and their friends to participate in large numbers and with enthusiasm in the celebrations marking the anniversary of the PKK’s founding.




The path of Leader Apo and the PKK, which has embarked on a new beginning, will continue to bring achievements to our people and all humanity. On this basis, we congratulate all our people and their friends on the Day of Resurrection and wish them success in their ongoing struggles for freedom and democracy.”

title: HPG: Our determination to carry our people’s struggle to victory is stronger than ever
content:
The HPG (People’s Defense Forces) Press Liaison Center released a statement marking the 48th anniversary of the founding of the PKK (Kurdistan Workers’ Party)




The HPG statement on Thursday includes the following:




“Happy National Resistance Day and the 48th anniversary of the founding of the PKK to Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan], the leader, founder, first self-sacrificing militant, and greatest contributor to our Freedom Movement; to the families of our martyrs, our patriotic people, the valued friends of our people, the prison resistance fighters, and all our comrades struggling in every sphere!




The PKK is a Party of Martyrs that emerged on the basis of keeping alive the memory of Comrade Haki Karer and fulfilling his goals, and has pursued this cause without interruption for half a century.




The Army of Martyrs, which pioneered the PKK, has, throughout 48 years of struggle, created great values, honorable principles, profound human virtues, high moral and spiritual values, the Apoist spirit of self-sacrifice, and a life so meaningful that it is worth dying for. These sacred values of ours have taken concrete form in the path of the martyrs as our most fundamental source of strength. We commemorate with respect, love, and gratitude all our revered martyrs who created this reality through their sweat, lives, and blood, represented by our great Party Martyr, Comrade Haki Karer.




Forty-eight years ago, the Kurdish people were on the brink of extinction. They faced a reality marked by policies of denial, annihilation, and genocide, in which their very existence had become a matter of debate and even imagining independence and freedom was out of the question. Rescuing the Kurdish people from this situation, shaking off the dust of death that had settled over them, raising them to their feet, breathing life into them, giving them the will to act, enabling them to struggle, proving their existence, and leading them toward freedom required an extremely arduous resistance.




At the same time, there was a need for courageous cadres with an iron will and a spirit of self-sacrifice who could lead this historic resistance, shoulder the burden of the oppressed Kurdish people who had been left without support and of the Kurdistan Freedom Struggle, assume this responsibility, and carry the struggle forward.




Recognizing this historical reality, Leader Apo made a historic breakthrough alongside the Apoists he had organized around him. On November 27, 1978, in the village of Fis in the Lice district of Amed, he made the decision for the Kurdish people’s National Resistance and founded the PKK, which would lead our national resistance.




Every year, every month, every day, and even every hour of this half-century-long epic National Resistance Struggle has been etched into history through magnificent acts of resistance and heroism. Apoists who joined this struggle from all parts of Kurdistan, from abroad, and from other peoples demonstrated unprecedented resistance and heroism, creating an entirely new history and a new reality for the people. Leader Apo’s emergence marked a turning point in Kurdistan. The PKK’s struggle said “stop” to the policies of denial, annihilation, and genocide. Through its relentless resistance, it proved the existence of the Kurdish nation and compelled everyone to acknowledge it.




It brought about a profound revolution in understanding, conscience, and mentality in Kurdistan. It created an entirely new language, culture, discourse, style, and pace. It established the ethics and principles of a free life. Through the intellectual and social revolution it fostered among the Kurdish people, the National Resistance Struggle led by the PKK completely changed and transformed society. By carrying out a revolution within the revolution, it brought forth the reality of free women. This reality took shape as a guerrilla force, developed into an army and a party, and became a guiding philosophy, a set of principles, and a science.




Throughout our 48-year National Resistance Struggle, we have lost nearly 50,000 martyrs, including the PKK’s founding leadership cadres, pioneers, guerrillas, fighters, militia members, friends, and civilians. Each of our martyrs demonstrated extraordinary courage and became a monument of honor in whom we take eternal pride, our most sacred value, and an immortal pioneer who continues to guide us. On the foundation of the legacy of the martyrs, a powerful national spirit and unity among the Kurdish people emerged.




The Apoist ideology paved the way for and spearheaded a new internationalist understanding, spirit, and struggle that influenced Kurdistan, the region, and the world, giving rise to the Democratic Nation Paradigm. Undoubtedly, all these achievements are the result of Leader Apo’s tireless efforts above all, as well as the self-sacrificing struggle waged by our people and fallen comrades, who wholeheartedly believed in Apoist ideology. On this occasion, we once again respectfully commemorate our martyrs, to whom we will always remain grateful.




As the Kurdistan People’s Defense Forces, which have never compromised on following the path of the martyrs, our determination to carry our people’s struggle for existence and freedom to victory through different means and methods is stronger than ever. As Apoist self-sacrificing fighters who are fully committed to securing Leader Apo’s freedom and ready to pay any price for it, we declare that we will enter the 49th year of struggle with greater effort, performance, and a faster pace of achievement, determined to fulfill our historic duties. We once again congratulate all our people and comrades on National Resistance Day and wish them outstanding success in the new year of struggle.”

title: Nine intact skulls and hundreds of bone fragments recovered from cave in Silvan
content:
Following the discovery of numerous human remains in a cave in the Silvan district of Amed (Diyarbakır) province, initial findings have emerged from the crime scene investigation ordered by the prosecutor’s office. Nine intact skulls, 36 skull fragments, and hundreds of other bone fragments were recovered from the cave. The identities of the deceased, as well as the dates and circumstances of their deaths, remain unknown.




The Human Rights Association (IHD), the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), and the Amed Bar Association provided information on the progress of the investigation at a joint press conference held at the IHD offices. Given the history of state violence and enforced disappearances in the region, the organizations consider the discovery particularly significant for efforts to address the past.




Prosecutor’s office notified following tip-off from local residents




Zeynep Karayılan, Co-Chair of the ÖHD in Amed, reported that a delegation from the three organizations had conducted an initial on-site investigation on November 19 following a tip-off from local residents received by the IHD. During the investigation, numerous human bones and skulls were discovered and documented on different levels of the three-story cave.




On November 23, the organizations contacted the prosecutor’s office in Silvan and requested the launch of a comprehensive investigation. That same evening, the Turkish gendarmerie informed the organizations that a crime scene investigation had been scheduled for the following day. An eleven-member delegation from the IHD, ÖHD, and the Amed and Mardin bar associations subsequently went to the Bayrampaşa Gendarmerie Station on November 24. However, only one representative from each organization was permitted to participate in the investigation.




Recovery operation under difficult conditions




The cave is located in a rural area known locally as Qesra Fila, according to the bar association. The area is accessible by off-road vehicles and is also frequented by people engaged in livestock farming in the surrounding area. After the site was secured and searched for possible explosive devices, ventilation measures were initiated.




The entrance to the cave is extremely narrow, and its three levels extend deep underground. Due to these conditions, representatives of the legal organizations were unable to enter the cave themselves and observed the operation from outside. Under the supervision of two prosecutors, four forensic crime scene investigators and two members of the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) descended into the cave. The low oxygen levels, particularly on the third level, made the recovery operation difficult.




Nine skulls, hundreds of bone fragments, and a blue button




Human remains were found on all three levels of the cave. In addition to nine intact skulls, 36 skull fragments, and hundreds of other bone fragments, a blue button was also recovered. Soil samples were also collected from all three levels. The recovery operation was documented through photographs and video recordings.




The work at the site ended at approximately 5:15 p.m. The recovered items, secured in a total of seven bags, were then taken to the central gendarmerie station in Silvan. There, the human remains were counted, sorted, and documented in the presence of prosecutors and representatives of the legal organizations.




Müslüm Dalar, a board member of the Amed Bar Association, announced at the press conference that the human remains have since been transferred to the state-run Forensic Medicine Institute (ATK) in Istanbul. The forensic examinations conducted there are expected to shed light on the age of the bones, the identities of the deceased, and the circumstances of their deaths.




The history of enforced disappearances in Silvan




For the human rights and lawyers’ organizations, it is crucial that the investigation not be limited to the forensic identification of the deceased.




Karayılan stated: “At present, it is, of course, not yet known to whom the bones belong, what period they date from, or under what circumstances these people lost their lives. However, the fact that such remains have been discovered in Silvan, where enforced disappearances, unsolved murders, and serious human rights violations occurred on a large scale, particularly in the 1990s, is of extraordinary significance for investigating past events that still remain unresolved.”




“In addition to determining the causes of death, the investigation must therefore also examine how the cave was used in the past and whether there is any connection to serious human rights violations. We consider this process important for uncovering the truth, ensuring the right to truth of the relatives of those who may have been forcibly disappeared, identifying any individuals responsible, and confronting the past. We demand an effective, impartial, transparent investigation conducted in accordance with scientific methods. We reaffirm that we will continue to monitor the investigation,” Karayılan added.




IHD: At least 303 unopened mass graves in Kurdistan




Ercan Yılmaz, Co-Chair of the IHD in Amed, positively assessed the evidence collection conducted so far. He said that soil samples had been collected and evidence items secured separately in accordance with proper procedures. Yılmaz expressed his belief that the people whose remains were found in the cave had not died of natural causes. The forensic examinations must now shed light on the circumstances of their deaths, he stated.




“Even if this incident took place a hundred years ago, we want it to be investigated and clarified. If the remains turn out to belong to people who were victims of unsolved murders in the 1990s, DNA comparisons and blood samples would at least provide us with an opportunity to confront the past.”




According to the IHD’s findings, there are at least 303 mass graves in Kurdistan that have yet to be opened. The recent discovery in Silvan is not included in this figure. “We emphasize that this is a minimum figure and that the actual number is much higher. We call on members of the public to contact us if they have any relevant information,” Yılmaz said.




Forensic examination in Istanbul




It remains unclear when the first results of the forensic examination can be expected. Yılmaz referred to a similar discovery in the Lice district last year. At that time, the examination results concerning the remains of three people were available within three months. Given the considerably larger number of bone fragments found in Silvan, it is not yet possible to estimate how long the examinations will take.

title: Iraq begins closing “unofficial” border crossings amid deployment to Kirkuk and some other provinces
content:
Iraqi Border Guard Forces Commander Mohammed Abdulwahab Said told the Iraqi press that his forces had begun implementing the Iraqi Prime Minister’s decisions on “combating oil smuggling” and closing “unofficial” border crossings.




Mohammed Abdulwahab Said added that efforts were underway to merge the administrative centers of the Kurdistan Region’s border crossings with those of other border crossings in Iraq.




The Iraqi Border Guard Forces Commander stated that their duty was to protect the border, while the control and management of border crossings fell under the authority of the Border Crossings Authority.




Mohammed Abdulwahab Said provided the following details about the measures being implemented: “Our command has divided all of Iraq’s borders into six regions, and our forces are responsible for border security. Behind the borderline, within the country’s territory, are army units, the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), police forces, and border guards. The customs police also operate under our command.”




On the other hand, Iraqi Defense Ministry Spokesperson Yahya Rasoul announced on Wednesday evening that military forces have been deployed to Kirkuk and several other provinces on the orders of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.

title: Fidan Ataselim: Repression and violence rise as democracy is eroded
content:
The We Will Stop Femicide Platform (KCDP) took to the streets across the country ahead of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, to protest the cover-up of the growing number of suspicious deaths of women under the slogan, "Stop the cover-ups, shed light on suspicious deaths of women." Families of women killed by male violence stood at the forefront of demonstrations in Istanbul's Kadıköy district, demanding an end to systematic impunity and the effective implementation of Law No. 6284. We Will Stop Femicide Platform Secretary General Fidan Ataselim spoke to ANF and said that the increase in femicides and suspicious deaths of women cannot be separated from the policies of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), adding, "Violence increases as democracy is eroded."




'Women's deaths are being concealed in the name of protecting the family'




KCDP Secretary General Fidan Ataselim, who has been fighting against femicide for years, said that they took to the streets on this year's International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women to draw particular attention to the growing number of suspicious deaths of women. Fidan Ataselim said that the increase in male violence against women cannot be considered independently of the AKP's policies: "This is a consequence of the government's 'Decade of Family and Population' policies. We repeatedly warned against this, but they did not listen. Women are most often killed within the family by the men closest to them. If you say that 'the family is important,' not only are women killed, but their deaths also begin to be concealed. Indeed, femicides and suspicious deaths of women have increased as a result of these family-centered policies."




'A strong response to rights violations can prevent further violations'




Fidan Ataselim said that 247 femicides and 289 suspicious deaths of women were recorded in the first ten months of 2026 alone, pointing out that suspicious deaths of women have increased significantly, just like femicides. Fidan Ataselim said that violence against women cannot be explained solely through family policies and must be considered in conjunction with the restriction of democratic rights and freedoms in the country: "Everything is so interconnected and forms part of a whole. Those who support the appointment of trustees, those who support the annulment of elections and those who profiteer from funding, when you consider them all together, you see that once you begin to undermine democracy, you also undermine every relationship in which democracy plays a role. For example, the family is promoted as the smallest unit of society and the foundation of property ownership, creating conditions in which women are disregarded within the family and subjected to treatment that goes even beyond slavery. The AKP's definition of the family is limited to families that resemble them and conform to their mindset and interests. They want a uniform family model. We already see this in their overall policies. Repression and violence increase as democracy is eroded. This repression and violence increase not only against women but against society as a whole. However, the first targets of this repression and violence are women, who are relegated to the very bottom of all inequalities. Beyond women, we also see what LGBTQ+ people are experiencing today. They said, 'My family is safe,' and shelved the entire issue of freedom of association. That is why we always say that no one can disregard equal citizenship. There is such a thing as equal citizenship, the right to organize and freedom of expression. When were these rights of ours shelved? Yet they are able to do this in practice through repression. That is why I say that repression and violence increase as democracy is undermined. This repression and violence are not only increasing but are also being concealed, as we see in suspicious deaths of women. This situation cannot be separated from the struggle for democracy. If a strong response is mounted when such rights violations occur, further violations can be prevented. However, when no response is possible, these violations spread, as they do today. The attitude of saying, 'This person is not one of us, that person is not one of us,' ultimately leaves everyone in the same situation, with trustees being appointed everywhere."




'The Gülistan Doku case exposed the state's mechanism for covering up murder'




Fidan Ataselim said that both the extent of repression and violence and the mechanisms used to conceal them were particularly evident in the case of Gülistan Doku: "We saw this clearly in the murder of Gülistan Doku. In cases of suspicious deaths of women, quite apart from connections to MPs close to the government, we saw that the state apparatus, consisting of prosecutors, law enforcement agencies and governor's offices, operated not to conduct a proper investigation but, on the contrary, to conceal the truth. We read in the press the testimonies of police officers suspected of involvement in the Gülistan Doku case. One says, 'They brought me a screenshot, and my superior ordered me to include it.' Another says, 'They told me not to inform the family about the items recovered from the water.' We see that all the resources of the state are mobilized to cover up a murder. Male perpetrators of violence draw encouragement from this mechanism. They believe they have something very powerful backing them. Worse still, perpetrators who commit violence or plan murders believe they are justified. I think this is even more dangerous. Why? Because they believe they can do it. Just recently, a woman was attacked in a crowded supermarket in Bursa. After the incident, the male perpetrator had the audacity to tell the court, referring to the woman he attacked, 'If I had wanted to kill her, I would have done it somewhere dark, where there were no witnesses or cameras.' They learn these blind spots all too well. Whenever we observe such cases, we analyze them and share our findings. Measures can be taken, from collecting evidence to redesigning the entire system so that nothing remains concealed in those blind spots. Both the means and the resources are available, but they are not being used. However, this situation cannot continue indefinitely. There used to be a very common saying: 'There is no such thing as a perfect murder.' Even that sentence offers a degree of hope. It means that no murder is perfect and that the truth will eventually come to light. Yet given the situation we are currently facing regarding certain deaths of women, even a statement like that is no longer being made."




'The commission would not have been established if we had not struggled'




Fidan Ataselim said that the establishment of the Department for the Investigation of Unsolved Crimes within the Ministry of Justice was the result of years of struggle and the persistent efforts of families: "The establishment of this department initially offered some hope. Developments in the Gülistan Doku murder case gave hope to the families of women who had died under suspicious circumstances. However, a month has passed since we submitted an application to this department as the KCDP, and nothing has happened. We submitted an application concerning the Aysun Yıldırım case. However, the department consulted the very authority that had twice decided not to prosecute the case. What is that authority going to say? It will say, 'I did what was necessary.' Where is the examination here? Where is the investigation? If you establish a department, are you not also required to develop its working methods? What we see here is a lack of political will. The Minister of Justice turned the establishment of this commission into a means of self-praise and propaganda. Yet would they have established such a commission if we had not struggled for years and if Gülistan Doku's sister and mother had not fought tirelessly for six years? Of course they would not have."




'We will not give up'




Fidan Ataselim said that all struggles, including the women's struggle, must be pursued with concrete objectives: "Struggle requires patience. It requires us not to give up when we fail on our first attempt and to put forward a political idea and an objective. We cannot get anywhere if we keep repeating generic statements. That is why we decided to address suspicious deaths of women this 25 November and focused on this issue, because suspicious deaths of women have increased. We also repeatedly explain what needs to be done in this regard. There is no alternative in this respect. It requires patience, continuity and organization. Just because none of these things are happening to us does not mean they never will. We see how organized the patriarchal capitalist system we are confronting is, along with its government and representatives. We must be just as organized in the face of it. The AKP used to say, 'We stand with those who have no one.' Now they have declared the Decade of the Family. They have not healed a single wound and have squandered all the resources of this country. We are now struggling to claim what is rightfully ours in the face of all this. First and foremost, we are fighting for our right to live, to receive fair compensation for our labor and to live in democracy and peace as equal citizens. We will continue to struggle. We will not give up."

title: Applications for violence and rights violations in Amed increase by 36%
content:
The Amed Network Against Violence has published its 2026 Violence Report, covering the period from 23 November 2025 to 23 November 2026.




Speaking at the presentation, held at the Tahir Elçi Conference Hall of the Amed Bar Association, lawyer Zilan Esen stated that, according to the network’s shared database, 7,145 applications had been recorded in the city. This represents a 36% increase compared with the previous year, when 5,253 applications were registered.




According to the report, applications relating to psychological violence increased by 34.4%, economic violence by 58.7%, physical violence by 43.7% and sexual violence by 27.2%.




Cases of intentional homicide rose from 4 to 17, an increase of 325%, while attempted intentional homicide cases increased from 14 to 18. In addition, five suspicious deaths were recorded.




Reports of torture and ill-treatment increased from 9 to 80, cases of pressure by law enforcement from 3 to 22, and incidents of ill-treatment in prisons from 4 to 14.




The report also stated that four assaults and one murder targeting LGBTI+ people had been recorded.




The network called for the Istanbul Convention to be reinstated, the effective implementation of Law No. 6284, effective investigations into cases of violence against women, and the expansion of free legal assistance and shelter services.

title: MSD: Protecting women’s rights requires explicit constitutional and legal guarantees
content:
The Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) released a statement marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women as Syrian women look toward a future that ends decades of systemic abuse.




This moment calls for a new chapter built on justice, full equality, and human dignity, said the MSD statement on November 25, which included the following:




“Violence against women extends far beyond murder, abduction, exploitation, and overt discrimination. It includes systematic marginalization and exclusion from leadership roles. Denying women an active voice in political decision-making and public governance is a direct form of violence that must be confronted.




Despite the political transition following December 8, 2024, conditions for Syrian women have deteriorated due to ongoing discriminatory policies. The transitional government and society at large must urgently reassess their approach to women’s rights. We need genuine gender justice in practice—not merely symbolic gestures for the media.




Protecting and sustaining women’s rights requires explicit constitutional and legal guarantees. These frameworks must ensure full equality and safeguard the hard-won gains of Syrian women against any rollback, regardless of the pretext.

Yet, in its most blatant manifestation as state violence, it imposes itself through policies of elimination and denial, intimidation, censorship, repression, and detention, reaching its peak in execution. Meanwhile, through economic pressure, the shrinking of people’s means of subsistence, and under the shadow of war and its consequences, those in power have effectively placed a noose around the neck of society as a whole. I see the issuance of a death sentence for the second time as an attempt to turn time into an instrument of subjugation, replacing the “possibility of living” with the “anticipation of death.” Yet those in power fail to realize that the foundations of my commitment, and ours, to our historical and intellectual choices are so firmly established that no polic

title: Kurdistan Regional Government: We reject the use of military rhetoric and threats
content:
Kurdistan Region’s Prime Minister Masrour Barzani chaired the KRG Council of Ministers’ meeting today. The meeting focused primarily on the KRG’s position regarding measures taken yesterday by the federal government of Iraq.




The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region is committed to fulfilling all its constitutional obligations and demands the full provision of its constitutional rights: “The KRG has consistently expressed its readiness to resolve outstanding issues with the federal government within the framework of the Constitution. Consequently, the KRG expresses its deep concern and strong protest regarding the statement issued on behalf of the spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, which violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region. This statement is a dangerous indication of a lack of belief in the federal system and represents an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime, which contradicts the Iraqi Constitution. The KRG rejects the use of military rhetoric and threats, which appear to stem from a premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.”




The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region has consistently supported measures to combat corruption and illegal activities, and has cooperated and coordinated with the federal government and will continue to do so to eliminate illicit practices. It called for the comprehensive eradication of corruption and oil smuggling across all of Iraq.




The Council of Ministers stressed that the Kurdistan Region is the product of the sacrifices of the heroic Peshmerga and thousands of martyrs; it is not a gift bestowed upon the people of Kurdistan: “The Kurdistan Region has played an active and influential role in establishing the current federal system in Iraq, regards itself as a co-owner of that system, and will never relinquish its constitutional rights, which extend far beyond salaries, budgets, and financial entitlements. They also encompass political rights and the legitimate cause of the people of Kurdistan.”




The KRG Council of Ministers stressed that issues between the Kurdistan Region and the federal government must be resolved through dialogue, negotiations, and mutual understanding within the constitutional framework, calling for the full implementation of the permanent Iraqi Constitution.




“The primary reason these issues remain unresolved is the failure to implement the Constitution, particularly Article 140, which has been neglected for years, with no steps taken to normalize the situation in the disputed Kurdish territories. In accordance with the Constitution, the Federal Council of Iraq should be established, and the Federal Supreme Court reconstituted on a constitutional basis that reflects all components of Iraq.”




The Council of Ministers expressed its gratitude to the Kurdistani people, as well as to all political parties, forces, and components, urging them to maintain their national stance, unity, and solidarity in defense of the constitutional rights of the people of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Region's constitutional framework. It also called upon the Kurdistan Region's representatives in the Iraqi Parliament and the federal government to continue their national role in defending the rights of the Kurdistani people.




The Council of Ministers reaffirmed its support for freedom of opinion and expression. However, it emphasized that anyone who acts against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region, constitutional principles, or Kurdistan’s national interests and incites people to create chaos and oppose the rights of the Kurdistani people should face appropriate legal action.

title: “Let’s Talk Manifesto”: Internationalist women in Rojava launch podcast
content:
With “Let’s Talk Manifesto,” young women from the Internationalist Commune in Rojava have launched a new podcast project. The initiative is rooted in a collective engagement with the Manifesto of Democratic Communal Society by Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. The internationalist women aim to connect the perspectives developed in the manifesto with their own experiences of the Rojava Revolution and the realities of women’s lives in different parts of the world.




In each episode, the young women focus on a chapter of the manifesto, discuss its theoretical approaches, and explore how these can be translated into social practice. The aim is to create a shared space for learning, reflection, and political discussion across national borders.




In the tradition of the international women’s struggle




The publication date was deliberately chosen. On November 25, 1960, the Mirabal sisters were murdered in the Dominican Republic for their resistance to the dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo. In 1981, feminist movements from the Caribbean and Abya Yala declared the anniversary of their murder a day of struggle against violence against women. Today, women around the world take to the streets to protest patriarchal violence, commemorate murdered women, and carry on their struggles.




The young internationalist women also situate their project within this tradition. In their statement
