title: Invisible violence: Psychological violence
content:
How do people come to hate themselves, reject their own identities and feel ashamed of who they are? To get to the root of this question, I would like to address a form of violence that often remains invisible: psychological violence.




Psychological violence targets our existence, our sense of self, our differences and, above all, our connections with one another. By psychological violence, we mean violence directed against our experiences, self-esteem, emotions, thoughts, perceptions and all our internal processes. This violence does not consist of a single action or word. Rather, it is a continuous process of humiliation that takes effect through repetition. This makes it difficult to recognize and equally difficult to find the words to describe what is actually happening to us. Psychological violence can take the form of bullying and stalking, as well as isolation and control. Psychological violence is not simply perpetrated by an individual but stems from a system of violence that creates the conditions for people to be humiliated because of their identities, characteristics and personalities. People are not born with a tendency towards violence; they learn such violence from their surroundings. As long as we live within a patriarchal, state-centered system, no sphere of life is safe from psychological violence, whether family relationships, schools, workplaces, neighborhoods, cities or even interactions on social media. Within these systems, people are devalued, and their identities, cultures and characteristics are portrayed as weak, stupid and ugly. They are declared unacceptable by the system, their identities and personalities are rejected, and they are not allowed to be themselves. This reaches a point where those subjected to violence begin to ask themselves: Which of these things actually belong to me, and which have been instilled in me? Those affected begin to see themselves through the eyes of those who humiliate them. The devaluation imposed by others becomes their own internal standard. This leads to a rupture with one's own self, accompanied by a breakdown of trust in one's surroundings. This rupture lays the foundations for exploitative dynamics of dependence through hierarchical relationships or systems. People's perceptions of themselves and their surroundings are increasingly determined by others. Ultimately, this violence is internalized and leads to a loss of self-confidence.




Human beings exist through their relationships




Human beings are highly complex. Their souls, bodies, thoughts and emotions constitute a form of existence capable of producing both incredibly beautiful and meaningful actions and cruel and meaningless ones. One phenomenon that we constantly experience today, and whose consequences have an enormous impact on our existence, is the separation of our bodies from our souls. We separate ourselves from our surroundings, society and nature. The fragmentation of human existence and the world deprives us of the connections necessary to better understand ourselves and our circumstances. If we want to understand who we are today, we must recognize that thousands of years of development are also embodied within us. The experiences of our ancestors continue to shape our worldview and identity today. For example, we cannot understand what it means to be a woman or a man without examining how identity has been constructed and transformed over thousands of years. Similarly, we cannot understand illnesses without considering environmental factors such as stress, pollution and their effects on the body.




Symptoms such as coughing may be signs of an illness. However, if we merely treat the symptoms without addressing their causes, they may intensify and occur more frequently. We then find ourselves primarily occupied with combating these symptoms rather than resolving the underlying problem.




Human beings can only be healthy when they are in harmony with nature and themselves. This is because human beings constitute a unity of body and mind or soul. This means that we must understand our psychological condition in relation to our bodies and surroundings. Anxiety, fear, stress and psychological problems, for example, can lead to sleep disorders, heart palpitations and even heart attacks. The expression "broken heart" is used when people in romantic relationships experience separation or another form of rupture. Those affected describe a pain as though their hearts have been broken, as though someone has plunged a knife into their hearts. All of this clearly demonstrates that the close connection between mind and body must not be overlooked when discussing psychological violence. Unlike physical violence, psychological violence often remains invisible and continues unnoticed, which can have particularly profound and long-lasting consequences for those affected. Physical violence and attacks on our bodies are always attacks on our existence. This existence encompasses our entire being, including our bodies, souls, minds and psychological selves. When we speak of sexual abuse and rape, it is Xwebûn (being oneself), our sense of self, that suffers the deepest wounds in this process. Being subjected to another person's domination deprives our sense of self of its meaning. Such profound disregard for a person's will creates a rupture between the survivor and their own will, body and self. Violence is essentially a demonstration of power. Its purpose is to show the victim that they cannot make decisions independently and must be directed by others. This is the foundation of establishing domination in order to subjugate people and deprive them of their will. Therefore, when discussing psychological violence, we must also address the consequences of these attacks. For thousands of years, such attacks have sought to break the will of women and society.




The fragmentation of life




Why are women the most affected by these attacks? Why does it now seem normal that almost all women experience attacks throughout their lives?




To understand women and their role in society, we can look at our surroundings. We often see that it is women who bring people together and maintain connections between different groups. Women act as ambassadors of peace throughout the world. They continue to maintain a special connection with life. We cannot say with absolute certainty whether this connection ultimately stems from the experience of fertility, menstrual cycles or acquired skills. However, it is clear that women, through their particular characteristics, experience a connection that directly binds them to their surroundings and other people. Being separated from people, their surroundings and nature is therefore a painful process for women. Women often defend the values of humanity because their connections with others allow them to feel the consequences of violence themselves.




This connection with life has a healing effect on human beings. It is the exact opposite of the toxic effects of the fragmentation and isolation of life that we experience today under capitalist, neoliberal and fascist systems. It is a source of healing for society but acts like poison to the logic of the state. This is why women and their connection with life are among the first targets of attacks worldwide. Attacks and humiliation are intended to sever women's ties with their people and surroundings, thereby making them easier to control.




Attacks on the mother tongue are also psychological violence




Women's connection with language and culture also makes them the guardians of identity and language. This poses a significant threat to states that seek to impose a single culture, language and identity on their citizens. People are deprived of their right to exist through the prohibition and humiliation of their languages and cultures. This constitutes a systematic form of psychological violence, since one of the most serious elements and consequences of psychological violence is the erosion of one's sense of self. This is inevitably also an attack on women and their existence because women are deeply intertwined with language. The language a mother teaches her child when teaching them to speak is their mother tongue. When this language is prohibited, women are deprived of their means of self-expression and their connection with their surroundings. Children attending state schools are taught another language, and their entire identity is devalued through the devaluation of their mother tongue. Children can thus be alienated from their parents and turned into instruments of the state against their own cultures and identities.




All this devaluation, which takes place within and through state, capitalist and patriarchal systems, paves the way for violent relationships within society, whether within families, romantic relationships, marriages or friendships between women. Violence has been internalized within our society, and a profound and sustained struggle is necessary to overcome these dynamics of violence.




Turning violence against ourselves




Resisting such dynamics and attacks becomes particularly difficult when we are exposed to them from childhood. When young girls are taught that they belong to the "weaker sex," and sexual assaults are normalized and become part of everyday life, girls are made to believe from an early age that their female identity is something bad and shameful. Their bodies become objects of sexual fantasies, are forced into unnatural forms and are thereby alienated from themselves. They are driven towards behaviors that do not originate from their own will or sense of self. Through sexualization, their bodies become objects of desire and public consumption. Insecurity is created, and anything that deviates from prevailing beauty standards becomes a point of vulnerability in their self-perception. The violence inflicted on women by their male partners or the patriarchal system is thus internalized. Women take hold of the violence directed at them like a knife and turn it against themselves. This manifests itself in self-destructive behaviors such as eating disorders or cosmetic surgery. It is an expression of the enormous violence inflicted through their own thoughts, driven by shame and low self-esteem. This violence alienates girls and women from themselves and strips their identities of meaning because women are denied the right to exist as they truly are. The effects of psychological violence are so powerful that women may even come to believe that they themselves are to blame.




Violence that spreads insidiously within relationships




The problem with psychological violence lies in its insidious nature. Its consequences become particularly severe when the patriarchal system is internalized by family members. Those subjected to violence often realize that they are trapped in such a relationship only after many painful years, if they recognize it at all, because psychological violence frequently takes place under the guise of intimacy and affection. It is concealed in the name of "love." Violence becomes more visible when psychological violence escalates into physical violence. By that point, however, the situation has often progressed so far, and psychological, emotional and financial dependence has become so strong, that those affected can no longer imagine their lives without the dominant person. This occurs through the merging of one's identity with that of the perpetrator, sometimes to such an extent that the person subjected to violence appears to have ceased to exist. An existence outside this reality then seems impossible to them. They are forced to adapt themselves entirely to the dominant person and conform to their expectations. Men are raised to believe that they must control their relationships and surroundings. If a woman's personality becomes too prominent, it is perceived as an attack on the man's status and the patriarchal system, and something that must be eliminated. Although the state and intimate relationships may appear to be very different, striking similarities emerge in practice, particularly in situations of dependence. Psychological pressure and manipulation operate in similar ways across all hierarchical relationships, whether it is a father seeking to shape his daughter, a man seeking to shape his wife or a state seeking to make its citizens obedient. In all these cases, we can observe the near-total erasure of the identities of those subjected to violence.




Whether through the prohibition of one's language, the denial of one's right to live according to one's identity or the deprivation of a woman's ability to make her own decisions, psychological violence seeks to make people malleable and controllable. Psychological violence feeds on isolation. It is therefore vital that we, as women, do not become separated from one another or leave anyone isolated. Instead, we must strengthen our self-defense and Xwebûn by connecting with one another and organizing together.




Breaking free from the system of violence...




If this system has pushed those subjected to violence to the point where they believe they have no value, breaking free from such a violent system requires a profound and long-term struggle. When speaking of those subjected to violence, it is important to recognize that victimization is not limited to individuals. Rather, a collective identity is attacked through individuals. The first step towards overcoming this violence is to understand these systems of violence and recognize how many allies around the world struggle against and resist this violence every day. To restore meaning to our own existence, we need, above all, a new form of social life based on the connections we establish with other people, nature and, consequently, ourselves. It is only through community that we can discover ourselves. Our relationships are like mirrors that allow us to become aware of ourselves. How we conduct our relationships and whom we establish them with reveal an extraordinary amount about our personalities. We need positive experiences of social life to once again perceive ourselves as active participants in history and life. We must build our relationships on human values such as respect. Only in this way can we gradually and steadily return to ourselves.




To struggle against such a deeply rooted system of psychological violence, we first need one thing: ourselves, our awareness of who we are. As women who cherish freedom, our sense of self is an identity founded on fundamental values such as freedom, justice and solidarity, encompassing all our colors, languages, cultures and genders. The world and the universe thrive through these differences. Xwebûn, being ourselves, means being able to resist psychological violence. It means being aware of ourselves and not losing our identities within relations of power established with the state or individuals. If we know ourselves, our language, our culture and our identity, we will not become subjects or people under domination. Instead, we can consciously defend ourselves through a shared identity. We need one another as a whole: unity in diversity rather than homogenization.

title: Women in Southern Kurdistan face violence, impunity and social pressure
content:
Femicide, domestic violence, forced marriage, economic dependence and gender inequality continue to threaten women's lives in Southern Kurdistan (Başûr). The March 8 Network, which reported that 69 women were killed in 2025, recorded 46 femicides as of October 2026. Women journalists and activists face political repression and digital violence, while Yazidi women continue their struggle for justice, overcoming displacement and rebuilding their lives following ISIS attacks.




Women's lives in Southern Kurdistan are shaped by interconnected social, economic, political and legal inequalities. Femicide, domestic violence, child and forced marriage, female genital mutilation, discrimination in employment, economic dependence and repression in the public sphere are among the fundamental problems threatening women's right to life and freedom.




Various legal reforms have been introduced in the field of women's rights, but their failure to translate into everyday life demonstrates the seriousness of the problem. Significant shortcomings remain in protecting women from violence, enabling them to achieve economic independence, ensuring their equal participation in political and social life and allowing them to organize independently.




Statements issued by women's rights organizations and reports published by international institutions in 2026 also indicate that this situation remains unchanged. Data on femicide, digital violence and women's access to justice particularly demonstrate the need to reassess existing protection mechanisms.




Legal regulations remain only on paper




The Southern Kurdistan Region adopted Law No. 8 on Combating Domestic Violence in 2011. The law established an important legal framework for preventing domestic violence and protecting survivors.




However, the adoption of the law does not mean that women have access to safety and justice in practice. Significant shortcomings remain in the effective handling of women's complaints, the prosecution of perpetrators, the implementation of protection orders and the provision of adequate living conditions for women.




Research published by Amnesty International in 2024 pointed to serious difficulties in holding perpetrators of domestic violence accountable. A report published by the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) in November 2026 also draws attention to the inadequacy of shelters in the Southern Kurdistan Region and the legal and institutional barriers to independent accommodation services for survivors of violence.




Women forced to leave abusive households struggle to rebuild their lives due to economic and social circumstances. This demonstrates that protection mechanisms must go beyond providing temporary accommodation. Conditions must be created in which women can live safely, work, receive an education and make their own decisions.




Child and forced marriages threaten the future of girls




Child and forced marriages are among the major problems restricting women's freedom in Southern Kurdistan. These practices directly affect girls' right to education, physical and psychological development, economic independence and ability to make decisions about their future.




Data from the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) show that 27.9 percent of women aged 20 to 24 in Iraq were married before the age of 18. Although this figure applies to Iraq as a whole, it reveals the extent of child marriage in the country.




Poverty, unequal access to education, family pressure and traditional social norms are among the factors behind early marriage. Forced marriages deprive women and children of the right to make decisions about their own lives.




Female genital mutilation: A violation of bodily integrity




Female genital mutilation (FGM) is another major problem that must be addressed in Southern Kurdistan. The practice affects the bodily integrity and physical and psychological health of women and girls, constituting a violation of fundamental human rights.




UNFPA data indicated that the prevalence of female genital mutilation across Iraq stood at 7.4 percent, while the figure reached 37.5 percent in the Southern Kurdistan Region.




Economic dependence is a barrier to women's freedom




Women's limited participation in economic life constitutes a significant dimension of gender inequality in Southern Kurdistan. Unemployment, precarious employment, low wages and the disproportionate burden of unpaid care work placed on women deepen economic dependence.




The Kurdistan Region Statistics Office's labor force data for 2021 showed that women's labor force participation rate stood at 16.5 percent, compared with 73.5 percent for men. The same data put women's unemployment rate at 29.6 percent and men's unemployment rate at 13.6 percent.




Childcare, care for the elderly, domestic work and other family responsibilities fall largely on women's shoulders. This reduces the time women can devote to education, employment and participation in social life.




Data on Iraq from the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women) indicate that women spend 24.1 percent of their time on unpaid care and domestic work, compared with 4.2 percent for men.




Economic dependence also makes it more difficult for women to leave abusive relationships. Women without their own income, access to housing or social security may be forced to remain in environments where they experience violence.




Women journalists and activists face political and social pressure




The problems women face in Southern Kurdistan are not confined to the domestic sphere. Women journalists, human rights defenders and activists also face restrictions on freedom of expression, political repression, threats and digital violence.




Violations against journalists and media workers also affect women's participation in the public sphere. A country assessment on the Kurdistan Region published by the United Kingdom government in September 2026 states that journalists and activists may face detention and physical attacks over their online content, while women journalists are particularly vulnerable to discrimination, harassment and blackmail.




Women journalists face censorship, threats and obstruction of their reporting because of their professional activities, while also having to confront sexist attacks because they are women.




Digital violence is emerging as another form of repression restricting women's presence in the public sphere. Threats, insults, blackmail, the unauthorized disclosure of personal information and coordinated smear campaigns through digital media directly affect women's freedom of expression.




A study on digital violence against women in the Kurdistan Region, published by the SecDev Foundation in February 2026, reveals that the problem is not limited to isolated incidents but constitutes a structural issue linked to shortcomings in legal and institutional frameworks, education and digital governance.




Digital violence affects not only women's online safety but also their participation in social and political life. Threats and blackmail can force women to refrain from expressing their opinions, continuing their journalistic activities or participating in social struggles.




Yazidi women continue their struggle for justice and life




The ISIS attack on Shengal on 3 August 2014 marked the beginning of a devastating genocide and widespread social destruction for the Yazidi people. Thousands of people were massacred, and thousands of women and children were abducted. Yazidi women were subjected to systematic sexual violence, enslavement, torture and forced marriage.




Twelve years after the genocide, the problems faced by Yazidi women and their families persist. The unknown fate of abducted women and children, displacement, housing, healthcare, education, employment and access to justice remain central issues in their ongoing struggle.




Independent women's organization is a force in the struggle for freedom




Strengthening women's rights in Southern Kurdistan cannot be achieved through the implementation of existing laws alone. Opportunities for women to organize independently must also be expanded, and women must actively participate in social decision-making processes.




Women's organizations are important actors that support survivors of violence, combat gender inequality, demand legal reforms and strengthen women's participation in political life. Organizations and initiatives such as the March 8 Network, Asuda for Combating Violence against Women, the Emma Organization, the Kurdish Women's Relations Organization (REPAK), the Kurdistan Women's Union and the Yazidi Women's Freedom Movement (TAJÊ) struggle against femicide, domestic violence, impunity and gender inequality.




These organizations work to protect women's legal and social rights, support survivors of violence, strengthen women's economic independence and ensure their equal participation in political life. Their work constitutes important examples of women's solidarity and independent organization.

title: Mehmet Uçum cannot distort the facts
content:
Mehmet Uçum has once again written an article distorting the facts. It appears that Mehmet Uçum has been assigned such a task. He reflects the views of the state side in the Peace and Democratic Society Process. He is being made to write these views. In this respect, what Mehmet Uçum writes reveals the approach of those who instruct him to write.




He criticized the language used by the movement's leadership and members of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party). He is thus attempting to prevent the movement's leadership and DEM Party members from explaining the facts to the public. One purpose of this article is also to exert pressure on the movement's leadership and DEM Party members.




The difficulties in securing broad social support for the process are entirely the responsibility of the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government. The pro-AKP media does not speak of a peace and democratic resolution process. It speaks of eliminating terrorism and disarmament. The attacks and attempts at liquidation that have continued for decades are now presented as being pursued through different means. The AKP government has not prepared its own political base for this process and is trying every possible means and method to turn opposition political circles against it. It is attempting to turn a significant portion of society against the process through provocative practices. Mehmet Uçum makes baseless accusations against the movement's leadership and DEM Party members to conceal this reality.




If there is a Peace and Democratic Society Process today, it is thanks to the approach of Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan and the unprecedented steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement in the context of such conflicts. The process continues today because of the Kurdish side's flexible approach and its efforts to encourage the AKP government to take steps. There is a widespread public perception that the Kurdish side is taking steps while the government is doing nothing. Mehmet Uçum is also attempting to conceal this public perception and the reaction against the government.




The Kurdish Freedom Movement has taken steps to eliminate all risks of confrontation with the Turkish military. It has left no armed forces inside Turkey and has withdrawn its armed forces from areas close to the Turkish border and the Turkish army. Downplaying these steps could result in the sabotage of the process. According to Mehmet Uçum, these steps are not particularly significant. He suggests that they should be unarmed wherever they are. He is almost suggesting that they should be left at the mercy of predators. The leadership and cadres of this movement must protect themselves until they return to Turkey. Otherwise, they could be eliminated in various ways. The movement's leadership has already stated that no one should expect them to seek refuge elsewhere. However, they insist that they will return to Turkey if a legal and judicial environment conducive to democratic politics is established. Devlet Bahçeli said after the weapons-burning initiative on 11 July 2025 that he wished the necessary laws had been enacted so that they could return.




Have laws enabling democratic politics been enacted, only for the Kurdish side to say that it will not lay down its arms or return to Turkey? If Turkey's existing laws and judicial system remain in place, those returning to Turkey will eventually be imprisoned for violating one law or another. Would anyone in their right mind take a step that would lead to their arrest? In fact, the issue of disarmament has already been resolved. Its implementation requires facilitating returns to Turkey. It is the AKP government's responsibility to make this possible. The Anti-Terror Law remains in force. This law should have been amended so that it no longer constitutes an obstacle to democratic political struggle. We have given just one example, because there are laws under which those engaged in democratic political struggle can immediately be arrested.




All the steps taken by the Kurdish side to date have been aimed at laying down arms and returning to Turkey. No one has said that they would refuse to lay down arms. On the contrary, the criticism has been that Turkey is failing to create the political and legal conditions necessary for complete disarmament. Is the AKP government planning to launch another war once the guerrilla forces have withdrawn completely? How else can its failure to take steps that would accelerate the process be explained? Perhaps there are other reasons for its failure to act. Some circles suggest that the AKP government wants to prolong the process and enter the election period under these conditions.




We cannot know exactly why the AKP is not taking steps. The AKP government may have different calculations. It may instrumentalize the process, as it has done in the past. However, there is one thing that both we and the public know: despite the significant steps taken by the movement's leadership, the AKP has not taken any substantial steps. It has yet to fulfill many of the promises it made during the meetings on Imralı.




Mehmet Uçum reveals his true intentions by telling people not to speak too much about Abdullah Öcalan. In a sense, he is asking them to bury their leader alive there. A people or an organization that fails to stand by its leader cannot defend its existence or its right to a free and democratic life. The Kurds continue their struggle for a free and democratic life by standing by their leader. Mehmet Uçum knows the sensitivities of the Kurdish people and therefore says that the question cannot be resolved without Abdullah Öcalan. This rhetoric merely serves to conceal efforts to make people forget the Kurdish People's Leader. Mehmet Uçum also knows that this people and this movement will do everything necessary and will not take a single step back from standing by their leader and keeping his situation on the agenda.




Mehmet Uçum accuses the DEM Party. Yet DEM Party officials have adopted an approach suggesting that positive steps have been taken, even though the AKP government has taken no significant steps. Slightly expanding the living quarters on Imralı and allowing two or three people to visit does not constitute a substantial improvement. The new accommodation had already been built a year ago, but Abdullah Öcalan had not moved there until now to avoid misunderstandings. However, meetings have reportedly been held there. Mehmet Uçum's criticism of the DEM Party, even as its officials seek to create a positive atmosphere, constitutes a method of exerting pressure through special warfare.




Mehmet Uçum must not forget that he is dealing with a movement that has been engaged in political struggle for 53 years. Those who fail to take this movement seriously and approach it through special warfare methods, schemes and tactics will be disappointed.




Source: Yeni Yaşam Newspaper

title: YRK reports Iranian airstrikes in Pêncewîn region
content:
Iranian regime forces once again attacked positions of the Eastern Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) in the border area of Pêncewîn in Southern Kurdistan on Tuesday evening. According to the YRK Press Center, four consecutive airstrikes were carried out within an hour, beginning at 9 p.m. on November 24.




“Our forces suffered neither casualties nor material damage in these attacks. All our units are safe,” the organization stated.




The YRK described the bombardment as part of a series of Iranian attacks on various areas of Kurdistan in recent days. “The attacks are an expression of the Iranian regime’s ongoing policy of war, which targets not only the YRK but also the people and nature of Kurdistan.”




In its statement, the guerrilla organization characterized the repeated attacks as a sign of weakness on the part of the Iranian regime, which it said was attempting to compensate for its limitations and military shortcomings through airstrikes. “Such attacks not only fail to change the actual situation on the ground but also reveal the regime’s fear and helplessness in the face of the peoples’ demands,” the statement concluded.

title: Parliamentary Monitoring Committee to consist of 19 members
content:
In a letter signed by Numan Kurtulmuş and sent to political parties by the Parliament Speaker’s Office, the parties were asked to submit the names of their members for the Monitoring Commission, to be established pursuant to Article 7, Paragraph 5 of the “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion,” by 5 p.m. on Monday, November 30, 2026.




The distribution of seats among political parties on the committee has also been finalized. Accordingly, the AKP will be represented by nine MPs, the YENİ Party by three, the DEM Party by two, the MHP by two, the CHP by one, the İYİ Party by one, and the YENİ YOL Party by one. The committee will thus consist of 19 members.




The seats allocated to political parties that do not participate in the committee are expected to be redistributed among the other political parties.

title: Gelawêj Ewrîn: Jin Jiyan Azadî is a philosophy beyond borders - Part Two
content:
Gelawêj Ewrîn, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), spoke to ANF about state repression against women in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat), the struggle for women's freedom, the philosophy of Jin Jiyan Azadî (Woman, Life, Freedom) and the impact of war on women.




The first part of this interview can be read 

here

. 




How have the attacks by the United States and Israel against Iran affected the lives of women and children?




The consequences of war for women are multifaceted. Losing loved ones, forced displacement, economic insecurity, deprivation of healthcare, the growing burden of childcare and having to sustain life under the constant threat of death leave deep wounds in women's lives. Since the beginning of Iran's war with the United States and Israel, we have witnessed the killing and massacre of women on an extremely horrifying scale. On the one hand, the state keeps women under constant repression through arrests, killings and severe punishments.




On the other hand, the difficulties created by wartime conditions in present-day Iran are further deepening and intensifying social problems. Domestic violence has increased significantly. When men cannot draw strength from the state and feel powerless in the face of it, they direct all their anger and hatred towards women and children. Over the past few months, more than 20 women have been murdered by men using brutal and fascistic methods.




One of the greatest dangers of war for Eastern Kurdistan is that the democratic and national demands of the Kurdish people will once again be overshadowed by security policies. During wars, states seek to place their security and existence above everything else and create a political atmosphere around this understanding. Under these conditions, the demands of different peoples for identity, freedom, equality and equal democratic representation can easily be defined as threats. This creates a dual uncertainty for Kurdish women. On the one hand, there is repression by the Iranian state; on the other, there is the instability and uncertainty of war brought about by external military interventions.




The trauma that war leaves in society's collective memory also causes immense devastation. Women are forced to live with the consequences of war not only during attacks but also long after the fighting has ended. The loss of loved ones, destruction of homes, economic poverty, trauma experienced by children and uncertainty about society's future can persist for years. Therefore, women's security in Eastern Kurdistan is not simply a matter of protecting them from military attacks. The fundamental issue is building a democratic life in which women can feel secure politically, economically, culturally and socially.




How might war affect national rights, democratic representation and the Kurdish people's demands to determine their own future?




It is wrong to assume that war will automatically produce positive results for peoples' struggles for freedom. The military weakening of a state does not mean that the peoples living within that country will automatically become free. Similarly, a change of regime does not guarantee the establishment of a democratic society. In discussions about Iran's future, the fundamental question is not merely how the current government will be replaced. The real question is what kind of political and social system will be established in its place. The future of the Kurdish people cannot be tied solely to the military and political calculations of external powers. The Kurdish people's national rights, democratic representation and demand to determine their own future cannot be defined according to the interests of any state. Nor can they be shaped according to the interests of capital.




A political system must be established in Eastern Kurdistan in which people can live freely with their own identities, languages and democratic will. For this reason, it is important to consider the solution within the perspective of a democratic republic and democratic federation. From our perspective, the issue is neither the fragmentation of Iran nor the continuation of the existing centralised structure under another name. The issue is building a political system in which different peoples and faiths can live together on the basis of equality, freedom and democracy. Women's will must be decisive in the construction of this system. A genuinely democratic system cannot be established without women's freedom.




How is the Iranian government using wartime conditions to intensify repression against opposition groups and women's rights defenders?




The Iranian government's use of wartime conditions to intensify political repression and maintain security policies is a characteristic of the state's historical nature. In an atmosphere of war, it becomes easier to silence opposition voices, unite society around a single ideology under the pretext of so-called national security and portray different political demands as acts of hostility. The portrayal of social movements as terrorist threats and the legitimisation of the state's brutal practices pave the way for fascism. The Islamic Republic is also laying the groundwork for civil war by organising various radical and extremist groups. In this way, the state seeks to portray criticism of its policies as unacceptable under wartime conditions.




Women's rights defenders, human rights activists, journalists, Kurdish political circles and other opposition groups are directly affected by this repression. The state seeks to prevent uprisings in the streets through repression. Yet social struggle in the streets can be considered one of the most effective ways of transforming authoritarian and repressive systems. The massacres last winter showed us that this regime can kill thousands of people in a single night to maintain its power and then attempt to cover it up. It is also possible to describe this massacre as the largest massacre of women in Iran's recent history.




Such massacres remind people of the Middle Ages. In those periods, thousands of women were also massacred within a few nights under pretexts legitimised by the male-dominated state to strengthen its own existence. The massacre last winter, in which more than 50,000 people were reportedly killed, including women and children, left an extremely disturbing image in the collective memory of all of us and Iranian society. Those black bags! Those who were massacred were people at the forefront of the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution and all the social and political movements in Iran. Among them were women students, teachers, intellectuals, workers and artists. The intellectual life and collective memory of Iranian society were massacred on such a dark night. An entire sea of the country's most knowledgeable, valuable and pioneering people was destroyed.




How can women's right to speak out and resist both external military intervention and the Iranian regime's repressive policies be guaranteed?




Women's struggle for freedom must not be tied to the political interests of any military power or state. Women have the right to speak out against both the repressive policies of the Iranian government and the devastation caused by external military interventions. Women must be able to express themselves through their independent political will, organise and make decisions about their own future. The current war has emerged as a result of the Iranian regime's policies. Iran is fighting to maintain its hegemony in the region. It appears that this war, the conflicts and the chaos will continue for many years. What will determine the outcome and save society from collapse is the social struggle that Iranian women can lead. This reality has been demonstrated.




For this reason, it is important for women to organise in every sphere from now on. The state regards wartime conditions as a pretext and is organising everywhere, both openly and covertly. So to speak, an entirely militaristic system that also makes extensive use of women is coming to dominate every sphere. It is forcibly accustoming young people, even young girls, to the use of weapons and dragging society down an irreversible path. Organisational, cultural, social and artistic activities can therefore lift the shadow of this fascism from Iranian society, particularly women. If society remains silent, the state will seek to organise in every sphere and impose its policies on everyone under the pretext of war and a state of emergency. The determination and spirit of the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution will once again lift this veil of death from Iranian society as a whole.




Is the nationalist and militaristic atmosphere created by war pushing women's demands for freedom into the background? How can the Jin Jiyan Azadî perspective be preserved under these conditions?




During wars, nationalism and militarism grow stronger, while social issues are pushed into the background. Women's demands for freedom are often presented as secondary matters that must be postponed. Women are told that the war must end, state security must be ensured and national unity must be established before anything else. However, history has shown us that no political system that continually postpones women's freedom to the future has brought genuine freedom. This is precisely where the importance of the Jin Jiyan Azadî philosophy becomes clear. This philosophy treats women's freedom as a demand that cannot be postponed or left for the future. Women's freedom must be regarded as the starting point of social transformation.




We now all know very well that life cannot be free without women's freedom, and that a democratic society cannot be built without a free life. Therefore, preserving the spirit of the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution under wartime conditions is the responsibility of all women. This is possible by developing women's organisations, strengthening unity among women without discrimination, taking control of their economic and social lives and developing mechanisms of self-defence. Women's struggle for freedom must not disappear within the nationalist and militaristic atmosphere created by war. On the contrary, it must become the force that builds democratic life and social peace against the devastation of war.




Can regime change or the transformation of Iran's political system alone guarantee women's freedom? Why must women play a direct role and become the decisive actors in shaping their own future?




A change of the current regime in Iran could bring about major political developments. Iranian women would be the most affected by such a change. However, would regime change alone be sufficient to meet women's demands? When a regime changes, the patriarchal mentality, statist understanding and power relations on which that structure was built may continue to exist. Simply replacing those in power does not mean that society has become free. One of the greatest dangers for Iran's future is that the current authoritarian system could be replaced by another centralised and patriarchal system. In such a situation, the problems faced by women would continue in different forms. For us as women, freedom does not merely mean bringing an administration to an end, but removing relations of power and domination from social life.




Women must not be regarded as parties who join the process only after this transformation has begun. A democratic society cannot be built without women. Women must participate equally and decisively in political decision-making mechanisms, establish their own organisations and take responsibility for every sphere of social life. Women must make decisions about their own future. This is not merely a question of representation or quotas. Politics must be freed from male-state domination and become the politics of society as a whole. Those who make laws concerning women and take important decisions are representatives of the dominant male mentality that continually excludes women from these mechanisms. Change does not mean excluding women, but ensuring that they play a fundamental role in the transformation process. Of course, this can be achieved primarily through women's own struggle. A foundation for struggle must be established in which women can speak, make their own decisions and determine their future. Genuine freedom is not a solution imposed from outside; it is a way of life built through society's organised will.




What perspective do women's demands for freedom, equality and a democratic society in Eastern Kurdistan offer for the post-war future?




The women's struggle in Eastern Kurdistan also provides an answer to the question of what kind of society should be built after the war ends. From our perspective, what needs to be done after the war is not merely rebuilding buildings, improving economic conditions or establishing a new political administration. The fundamental issue is reorganising society on a democratic basis. Within this framework, women's demands for freedom and equality must form the foundation of a new social life. Iran's anti-women laws must be changed. The rights of all peoples, beginning with women's rights, must be guaranteed by law. Women's free and equal participation in education, healthcare, the economy, politics and culture must not be limited to guaranteeing individual rights. Women must also establish their own institutions and organisations. The development of a democratic society is possible through strengthening local people's assemblies, women's assemblies, communes and democratic decision-making mechanisms.




Women have a strong historical and cultural role within the social structure of Eastern Kurdistan. It is important to combine this social standing with a perspective for a democratic future. Iran is a rich country, and the traces of the mother-woman culture run very deep within it. Through the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution, it has therefore returned to its roots. Today, the sociological dimensions of this return need to be properly understood. Women's freedom is also a fundamental condition for society to take responsibility for itself and govern its own life. Therefore, our perspective for the post-war period is not merely the establishment of a new state system, but the construction of a democratic society. The more democratic society becomes, the less significant the existence of laws and the state in general becomes. It is a democratic society that makes a state democratic. A democratic society, in turn, consists of free individuals.




What perspective for transformation does the struggle of the Free Women’s Society of Eastern Kurdistan (KJAR offer in the face of state repression and gender inequality?




KJAR's approach to women's freedom does not regard women as a section of society seeking to obtain more rights within the existing system. It regards women as the founding force of social life, the pioneers of democratic transformation and a force that determines its own future. In this approach, women's freedom cannot be separated from the freedom of society. Women's self-organisation, the development of their economic and social independence, their participation in political decision-making mechanisms and their struggle against the patriarchal mentality are fundamental conditions for a democratic society. One of the important dimensions of the transformation developed by KJAR is the strengthening of women's autonomous organisations. Without the organisation of society, it is impossible to ensure the continuity of demands for freedom. Women's assemblies, academies, economic solidarity networks and women's self-defence mechanisms play an important role in the development of a democratic society.




How can women's movements in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan unite their struggles?




The unification of the struggles of women's movements in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan must also be considered on this basis. Kurdish, Persian, Baloch, Azeri, Turkmen, Gilaki, Lur and women from other peoples must establish common ground for freedom while preserving their different identities and experiences. This unity does not mean eliminating differences, but bringing them together on the basis of democratic unity. The aim must be a social system in which every people can freely live according to their own language, culture and identity, and in which women become the founding force of this democratic unity. The historical impact created by Jin Jiyan Azadî in Iran demonstrates that such a common struggle is possible. The unity developing among women is not merely a collective response to state repression, but also a search for a new social life. This struggle can be strengthened when women stand together in the face of one another's suffering and resistance. However, for it to become a sustained struggle, common organisational mechanisms, intellectual discussions and social solidarity must be developed.




What is your message to women struggling against violence, repression and inequality in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November?




Violence against women is not merely an individual problem; it is a consequence of the historical and institutionalised structure of the patriarchal system of power. Therefore, the struggle against violence must not be limited to opposing its consequences, but must aim to transform the mentality and social relations that produce it. Protecting women's right to life also means protecting their right to freedom. We must not be satisfied with simply saying that women should live; we must guarantee that they can live freely, organise themselves and exercise their own will. Today, women's struggle in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan continues despite all forms of repression. This struggle goes beyond opposition to a regime; it represents a new way of life that challenges thousands of years of patriarchal mentality.




The truth that Jin Jiyan Azadî has shown us is that society cannot become free without women's freedom. A democratic future cannot be built without women's will and organised strength. Therefore, we regard 25 November not merely as a day to condemn violence, but as a day to strengthen women's struggle for freedom, organisation and a democratic society. The freedom of women and society is not something that can be postponed or left to time. Freedom is a way of life that must be built starting today. Women everywhere, under all circumstances, must refuse to accept what is imposed upon them and turn every sphere of their lives into a field of struggle.

title: Karstarlı: HABAŞ has seen repeated workplace deaths
content:
The explosion at the HABAŞ Iron and Steel Factory in the Aliağa district of Izmir, which claimed the lives of 19 workers, has once again brought occupational health and safety measures in Turkey into focus. According to data from the Workers' Health and Workplace Safety Assembly (ISIG), at least 1,930 workers lost their lives in workplace killings during the first ten months of 2026. In 2025, at least 2,105 workers were recorded as having died in workplace killings.




The decision to release the company's owner under house arrest following the explosion at HABAŞ has also sparked debate over the judicial process.




Selçuk Karstarlı, a volunteer with the ISIG Assembly and a Class A occupational safety expert, spoke to ANF about the problems affecting occupational health and safety in Turkey.




'A massacre of the working class'




Karstarlı said that the figures published in ISIG Assembly reports and the worker deaths that can be documented reflect only part of the reality. He stressed that comparisons with Social Security Institution (SGK) records reveal that the scale of workplace killings is considerably greater than reported.




Karstarlı emphasised that ISIG Assembly reports cover only the worker deaths that can be identified: "Data on occupational safety can be found to a certain extent in the ISIG Assembly's reports on workplace killings. I say 'to a certain extent' because these reports cover only the deaths we can identify. However, comparisons with SGK data show that the reality is far worse than what is visible. Because we are aware of this, we publish all our reports using the phrase 'at least'. Looking at the deaths we have been able to document, we see at least 1,930 workers killed in the first ten months of 2026 alone, and at least 2,105 in 2025.




This clearly amounts to a massacre of the working class. Moreover, deaths caused by occupational diseases are not included in these reports because occupational diseases are almost never diagnosed in our country. The system has been structured in a way that prevents their identification. Yet various academic studies indicate that between 20,000 and 30,000 deaths from diseases, particularly cancer, can be attributed to occupational risks. What we are witnessing can, in fact, be described as outright class destruction and a massacre of workers."




'The metal industry has never seen a massacre of this scale'




Karstarlı addressed the workplace killings brought back into focus by the HABAŞ explosion, noting that the metal industry had never previously experienced a disaster of this magnitude. He stressed that what happened at HABAŞ was foreseeable: "We have witnessed many such massacres in the mining industry. The massacres in Hendek, Gayrettepe, Dilovası and Davutpaşa were also major disasters. However, the metal industry had never before witnessed a massacre of this scale at such a large industrial facility. The massacre at HABAŞ was neither unforeseeable nor unexpected. We already knew that this was a workplace where workers had repeatedly been killed.




There had been explosions before, even if they did not result in deaths. A worker had died just four days before the massacre. Even the company's own sustainability reports show an increase in workplace accidents. In other words, as with all the other massacres, this was a disaster that was clearly approaching.




According to our Assembly's records, we documented 19 workplace killings between 2013 and this massacre. Press reports also reveal seven workplace killings before 2013. This means that, in addition to the 19 workers killed in the latest massacre, there had already been 26 workplace killings and dozens of injured workers whose exact number we do not know. So what sanctions did HABAŞ face despite all these deaths? Not a single day's work was suspended, and the company faced no sanctions. To use the words of Minister of Labour and Social Security Vedat Işıkhan, inspections did not cause the company any difficulties. On the contrary, the company expanded while receiving substantial financial incentives. Mehmet Rüştü Başaran received a negligible sentence for previous workplace killings, and the announcement of the verdict was deferred, effectively ensuring that he faced no punishment.




What we see here is a recurring reality in Turkey: an employer who kills workers by failing to take precautions, a state that fails to inspect the employer, and a judicial system in which those truly responsible are not punished or, even when convicted, do not go to prison. This chain can be seen in every workplace killing.




We saw the same pattern after this massacre. While Başaran was effectively rewarded with house arrest in his waterfront mansion, he issued instructions from there banning workers from entering the factory with mobile phones. Workers who opposed this decision were beaten and detained by the police. This was a clear attempt to conceal evidence. That alone should have been grounds for his detention.




So what would we expect if normal legal standards were applied? All operations at HABAŞ should have been suspended and a thorough investigation launched at the facility. Given the seriousness of the offence and the risk of flight or evidence tampering, pre-trial detention should have been imposed. But whom does the judiciary detain instead of Mehmet Rüştü Başaran? It imprisons Can Atalay and Selçuk Kozağaçlı, lawyers involved in the Soma and Hendek workplace massacre cases. In short, this massacre is a systemic problem."




'Most workplace killings occur in construction, agriculture and transport'




Karstarlı said that the highest numbers of workplace killings over the past year had occurred in the construction, agriculture and transport sectors. He drew attention to the main causes of worker deaths and the structural problems underlying them: "If you examine the ISIG Assembly's data, you will see that most deaths occur in construction, agriculture and transport. Traffic accidents, including accidents involving workers' transport vehicles, crushing incidents, collapses and falls from heights are among the leading causes of death. But these are merely the visible technical causes. Looking at the underlying reality, we can say that what has made working life so dangerous is the chain I mentioned earlier: failure to take precautions, lack of inspections and impunity.




We must also consider the organisational problems facing the working class. Today, the unionisation rate in Turkey is around 14 percent, and trade unions are unable to move beyond wage bargaining. The absence of an organised working class fighting for safe working conditions allows a system in which workers' lives are left at the mercy of employers."




'We know the Palace regime for its harsh measures against workers'




Karstarlı said that the government had failed to take a position in favour of workers in cases of workplace killings and stressed that those responsible must be prosecuted: "Perhaps the most devastating consequence of this situation is the sheer number of workplace killings. But there is another side of the picture that remains largely unseen: lost limbs, occupational diseases and deteriorating health. In this grim situation, the Palace government, which effectively protects employers, particularly the Minister of Labour and Social Security and senior officials responsible for the inspection system, bears primary responsibility for these massacres. They must be prosecuted because their failure to fulfil their duties has caused these deaths.




We also know this same Palace regime for the harsh measures it takes against workers. It bans strikes, which are workers' legal right when seeking to secure their demands. It uses police violence against workers dismissed for union membership who then organise protests. It even imposes province-wide bans on demonstrations to prevent textile workers from protesting. I would say that this regime is, in every sense, a government serving capital."




'The situation may not change even if governments change'




Karstarlı stressed that organised struggle is the most important condition for preventing workplace killings. He said that workers must organise, occupational safety measures must be strengthened and inspection mechanisms must operate effectively to prevent further deaths.




Selçuk Karstarlı outlined the measures he believes are necessary: "First and foremost, the working class and oppressed people must organise. Organised struggle is essential to refuse unsafe work and improve safety measures in workplaces. Social opposition is also necessary to force the Ministry of Labour to carry out workplace inspections.




Otherwise, the situation may remain unchanged even if governments change. Judicial practice must also change. Although the law places responsibility on employers to take every necessary precaution, it is often engineers, occupational safety experts and other salaried employees who are prosecuted instead of employers, even though they have no influence over financial decisions or investments.




Yet, as the HABAŞ case demonstrates, these employees change repeatedly over the years while conditions at the workplace remain the same. That is because the real decisions within the company are made according to the employers' wishes, and safety is often sacrificed to reduce costs or increase production speed. Judicial practice must therefore change. But as you know, the judiciary has also become politicised. Genuine accountability requires organised social opposition."




Karstarlı also criticised trade unions and civil society organisations for failing to respond adequately to workplace massacres. He said, "I think there are two reasons for this. The first is that trade unions are largely controlled by pro-employer union bureaucrats. The second, I believe, is the failure to develop a practice of unity and collective struggle around common demands. Advancing this struggle is an important responsibility facing us."

title: Women must organize in communes against the male-dominated mentality
content:
The war unfolding in the 21st century is being waged by hegemonic powers that seek to suppress women's struggle for freedom in every possible way. Alongside the claim that the 21st century will be the century of women's liberation, women must further strengthen their systems of organization in order to respond to the attacks taking place today. Only in this way can women protect themselves and bring society around them together. Particularly in the Middle East, such organization and struggle are as essential to women as water and bread. This is because, in the Middle East, which has today become the centre of hegemonic warfare, women are subjected to violence, sexual assaults, massacres and every kind of attack. From Turkey to Iran, from Afghanistan to Sudan, Iraq, Syria and many other countries, women are becoming victims of both external and internal wars.




The war between Iran, the United States and Israel has been continuing for some time. As is well known, women are those most severely affected by this war, becoming victims of the hegemonic systems of states.




With the Taliban's rise to power in Afghanistan, women have been forced to prove their right to exist in every sphere of life. Although education and employment are their natural rights, securing these rights has itself become a major field of struggle. The Taliban, which seeks to surround women with a religiously fundamentalist mentality, is stripping them of their place in society through the laws it enacts and imposing its male-dominated system.




The situation of Sudanese women is similar. As is known, Sudan has been experiencing a civil war for approximately four years. Both the government and the armed forces known as the Rapid Support Forces are carrying out brutal acts against Sudanese women. As a result of the civil war, thousands of women have been subjected to mass sexual violence. While the two sides fight each other, both blame the people and women in pursuit of their own interests, attempting to legitimise their actions. These two forces, which provide no service or benefit to society, have forced tens of thousands of people to abandon their homes and flee.




In many different countries, women face oppression and tyranny. They are constantly forced to struggle to secure their most fundamental rights under the protection of law and to achieve further gains. State systems governed by men make no provision in their laws to protect women's interests. Laws, too, are drafted according to a male-dominated mentality. Many women are unable to access their rights because of laws designed in accordance with men's interests. They are deprived of numerous rights, from the right to divorce and children's rights to the right to work.




Today, in Tunisia, the Maghreb countries, Turkey and many other places, women are fighting to secure their legal rights. Of course, certain laws are being passed and referred to as 'family laws'. Yet even in these laws, women's rights are disregarded.




The male-dominated mentality does not consider the interests of society




Women are those most affected by the current war. Displacement, sexual assaults, unemployment and dire economic conditions are pushing women into profound distress. This is because it is women who organize society and create the conditions for life to flourish around them. However, the system of capitalist modernity, which constructs the mentality of the male-dominated state, has taken this natural role away from women and placed them at the service of its own policies. The dominant man, who gives no consideration to the interests of society, is plundering nature in order to escalate the current war, turning women into instruments of warfare and leaving society impoverished and helpless.




Of course, this picture is not limited to the countries of the Middle East. In many European countries, too, women are subjected to every form of attack and violence. Research shows that domestic violence has increased in Germany. The saying persistently repeated by reactionary men to confine women to their homes, 'The safest place is the home', has now lost its validity.




Unless there is strong organization and consciousness-raising, neither the home, the school, the workplace nor the street will be safe. This is because the mentality we are discussing is not simply the attitude of a few individuals; it is a culture. Moreover, it is a culture whose roots and foundations stretch back 30,000 years into history.




Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan]'s statement, 'The enslavement of society began with women,' makes this reality abundantly clear. When this mentality merged with state power, it became fully embedded within the system and intensified its violence against women and society.




This is also why the toll of femicides continues to grow. In many countries, the figures have reached horrific levels. In Iran, where the 

Jin, Jiyan, Azadî 

(Woman, Life, Freedom) uprising began under women's leadership, women rose up across the country; yet the existing violence has not disappeared. In Iran and Rojhilat, women continue to be killed and subjected to violence every day. Alongside social oppression, state repression is also extremely severe. Dozens of women in Iranian prisons are under the threat of execution, while dozens more have been sentenced to prison terms.




How and through which methods will women organize?




We can now say that violence has become an everyday practice throughout the world and that this violence is increasingly regarded as normal. This is precisely the most dangerous aspect. This is exactly what the system wants: to portray femicides, the destruction of nature, war, plunder, displacement and attacks against society and women as normal. Yet these practices, carried out by the hand of the male-dominated mentality, are neither normal nor ordinary. On the contrary, they run counter to the very nature of humanity and the universe.




Bakur, Shengal and Rojava are going through a process of integration. For this reason, these issues must be discussed extensively, and concrete steps must certainly be taken towards resolving them. Undoubtedly, Leader Apo has clearly outlined both the problem and its solution in his manifesto entitled 

Call for Peace and a Democratic Society

. Beginning with history, Leader Apo addresses the question of women, which is one of humanity's fundamental problems, and offers profound analyses of it. In this manifesto, he once again draws attention to the need for women and society to organize themselves.




So, how and through which methods will women organize themselves? First and foremost, women must organize in the form of communes wherever they are. Naturally, there must be a purpose behind bringing people together. What problems and needs exist? What do women want? What do they wish to offer, change and build? What should the path and method of transformation be? What kind of struggle should be waged, against whom, and in what way?




The answer to all these questions lies in the commune. Concrete steps must be taken in response to existing needs. Within these communes, economic, every day and organizational needs must all be institutionalized. In other words, these communes must develop into structures capable of meeting women's needs and supporting their work in every respect.




When we speak of communal organization, it is clear that such organisation must not be confined to its immediate surroundings. The structure we are referring to must encompass all women. Not a single woman should remain outside the commune. All women must see themselves as part of these communes, feel that they belong to them and develop an awareness that the commune is an indispensable, vital necessity for them. No matter how severe the attacks may be, it must also be recognized that women's consciousness and organization have developed much further than in the past.




Of course, the perspective for this has been put forward by Leader Apo and the Kurdistan Women's Movement. Women in all four parts of Kurdistan have now become a source of inspiration for women around the world through their struggle and organization. Kurdish women play a leading role in every field and have significantly strengthened their organizational structures. However, this organization must acquire a universal dimension, because the question of women is a universal one.




The male-dominated mentality has organized itself throughout the world and established itself as a system. For this reason, women's struggle and organization must not be confined to a single part of the world or a single country. Women must build their confederalism and wage a much stronger and more effective struggle. In this way, they can fight against darkness and make their world more beautiful and meaningful. At the same time, they can live in a free country as free individuals, with their own identities.




With the publication of the manifesto, we have once again seen that such a world is possible. What is needed to achieve it is a shared understanding and a common struggle.
