title: Displacement, poverty and violence: Women's endless war
content:
The war does not end for women who survive it. The real struggle begins afterwards. They lose access to housing, economic security, healthcare and food. The responsibility for keeping their children safe, finding food and water, caring for their families and earning a living often falls on their shoulders. Displacement, poverty and insecurity also expose women to new waves of violence. For decades, women across the Middle East have struggled to survive the devastating consequences of war.




Reports by the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women) and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) reveal how these conditions affect women in different ways across Palestine, Yemen, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon.




According to UNFPA's regional assessment published in April 2026, more than 18 million women and girls in these countries face heightened risks of gender-based violence. More than 101 safe spaces for women and girls reportedly closed over the previous 12 months, while funding for services addressing violence declined by more than 50 percent over the past two years. These figures demonstrate how war also destroys the mechanisms intended to protect women.




Palestine: Sexual violence, forced marriage and poverty




Gaza is one of the first places that comes to mind when discussing destruction, devastation, psychological and sexual violence, poverty and displacement. Conditions for women deteriorated further following the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war on 7 October 2023. The devastation experienced by women in Gaza is one of the starkest examples of how war affects every aspect of women's lives. Moreover, the situation of women and girls has not changed despite a year having passed since the announcement of the so-called ceasefire.




According to a UNFPA report published on 30 October 2026, covering the period from April to September 2026, the proportion of households headed by women rose from approximately 11 percent before the war to 25 percent. Women who have lost their husbands, been separated from their families or remain unaware of their relatives' fate are unable even to mourn. Instead, they must provide for their families and children.




Child marriage




A gender-based violence analysis covering the second quarter of 2026 recorded a 61 percent increase in cases of sexual violence. Even more alarming is the rise in forced and child marriages. According to UNFPA, reports of forced and child marriages increased by 123 percent between April and June compared with the January-March period.




Deteriorating health conditions




The severe damage to the healthcare system also exposes women to serious risks during pregnancy and childbirth. Miscarriages are increasing, access to safe abortion is unavailable, and maternal health is deteriorating. Hunger, malnutrition and the collapse of healthcare infrastructure make pregnancy particularly dangerous. The shortage of menstrual hygiene products and lack of access to clean water also represent serious violations of women's right to health.




A generation deprived of education




Disruption to education threatens the future of girls. The destruction of schools, the conversion of educational institutions into shelters and repeated displacement interrupt children's education. Girls who are forced out of school become more vulnerable to early marriage and economic exploitation.




92 percent experience psychological distress




According to a UNFPA field report published in July, 92 percent of the women surveyed experienced moderate or severe psychological distress, while the proportion displaying symptoms of post-traumatic stress rose from 55 to 62 percent. In the West Bank, war, destruction and restrictions have also severely worsened women's living conditions, leaving them with almost no freedom of movement. Access to healthcare, education, livelihoods and protection services is becoming increasingly difficult.




Yemen: Nowhere is safe




More than a decade of conflict in Yemen has once again demonstrated how economic collapse and humanitarian crisis can spread into every aspect of life. The conflict escalated in 2014 when the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The intervention of the Saudi Arabia-led coalition in 2015 transformed it into a complex war involving multiple actors.




Although the 2022 ceasefire temporarily halted the fighting, the war that began between the United States and Israel on one side and Iran on the other in 2026 drew Yemen back into regional conflict. Hostilities escalated again with reciprocal attacks involving the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. Women are once again bearing the heaviest consequences, particularly through the obstruction of their right to healthcare.




Women giving birth on the roads




According to a UNFPA field report published on 5 October, pregnant women displaced by the fighting have been forced to give birth on roads because they cannot reach safe healthcare facilities. More than 145,000 people were displaced from Yemen's western coast and the Taiz front, including over 3,200 pregnant women.




Displacement has been particularly widespread in Yemen. More than 300,000 people have been displaced since August, while 82,000 were forced to leave their homes in October alone. Women and children account for more than half of those displaced, including approximately 6,400 pregnant women. Road closures, insecurity and the closure of healthcare centres make it difficult for women to access prenatal check-ups and emergency medical services.




The nightmare women face every day in Yemen is the absence of safety. This also contributes to child and forced marriages and the interruption of education. Families often marry off their children as what they see as a means of "escape". Women who have lost their economic independence are particularly vulnerable to being pushed into marriage as a means of survival.




Syria: Millions of women displaced




The war that began in Syria in 2011 devastated women's lives through forced displacement, economic collapse, sexual violence and the breakdown of family structures. Women whose relatives were forcibly disappeared or whose whereabouts remain unknown have had to provide for their families and care for their children while waiting for news of their loved ones. Those forced to leave their homes have encountered new barriers to housing, employment, healthcare and education.




Disaster following HTS takeover




The takeover of power by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) in 2024, followed by attacks against Alawites, Druze, Kurds and other communities, triggered a humanitarian crisis. Alawite, Druze and Kurdish women faced threats of abduction, enforced disappearance, sexual violence and killing.




The massacres targeting Alawites in Syria's coastal regions in March 2025 and Druze communities in Suwayda in July 2025 became some of the most severe attacks carried out under the new regime.




The fate of abducted Alawite women remains unknown




Abductions targeting Alawite women were concentrated in Latakia and Tartus. The Alevi Bektashi Federation (ABF), the Syrian Human Rights Association (AHRS), Amnesty International and the United Nations reported that more than 100 women had been abducted. According to a Reuters investigation published on 27 June 2025, at least 33 Alawite women and girls disappeared or were abducted in the Tartus, Latakia and Hama regions. Families were reportedly subjected to ransom demands ranging from $1,500 to $100,000.




At least 1,500 Alawites were also massacred at 40 separate locations across Latakia, Tartus, Homs and Hama. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) drew attention to the killing of hundreds of women.




Druze women abducted




The clashes in Suwayda in July 2025 triggered a new wave of violence against Druze women. Attacks by HTS and various armed groups resulted in hundreds of deaths.




In a statement published on 21 August 2025, UN human rights experts reported that at least 105 Druze women and girls had been abducted and that the whereabouts of 80 remained unknown. The experts also drew attention to reports that some women had been sexually assaulted and that at least three women had been killed after being raped.




A report by the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria stated that some women had been used in "prisoner exchanges", while others had been abducted from their homes by armed groups.




Lebanon: Women in the shadow of the Hezbollah-Israel war




The humanitarian devastation experienced by women in Lebanon intensified with the renewed outbreak of war between Israel and Hezbollah in March. Reciprocal attacks forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes, particularly in southern Lebanon, the Bekaa Valley and Beirut's southern suburbs.




Between 2 March and 14 June, at least 3,783 people were killed and 11,699 injured in Lebanon. Those killed included 363 women and 247 children.




620,000 women and girls displaced




According to the United Nations, approximately 620,000 women and girls were displaced by the war, including around 16,000 pregnant women. More than 1,450 women and 1,036 children were also injured. Displaced people sought refuge in collective shelters, schools and relatives' homes in and around Beirut. However, temporary accommodation facilities failed to provide safe living conditions for women and girls.




A UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) safety assessment published in May 2026, which examined 180 collective shelters, identified severe overcrowding, inadequate lighting, doors that could not be locked and poor hygiene conditions. The shortage of dedicated safe spaces for women and girls also increased the risks of sexual harassment, exploitation and other forms of gender-based violence.




Between life and death




One of the most severe consequences of war for women has been the disruption of pregnancy and childbirth services. According to a Reuters investigation, 13,500 pregnant women were displaced in Lebanon during the first weeks of the war. A UNFPA report covering the period from 26 March to 1 April 2026 also stated that approximately 1.2 million people had been displaced, including 620,000 women and girls.




Growing economic and care burdens




The conditions created by displacement have also increased women's exposure to violence. The lack of privacy and hygiene in overcrowded shelters has further heightened women's vulnerability to harassment and exploitation.




Severe psychological scars




Losing their homes, living under the constant threat of attack, worrying about their children's safety and facing uncertainty about the future are also taking a heavy toll on women's mental health. A study published by UN Women in September examined the wartime experiences of Lebanese women from different generations.




Women's accounts highlighted separation from their families and social networks, anxiety about their children's future, constant fear of attacks and uncertainty about whether they would ever be able to rebuild their homes. Women who bear sole responsibility for caring for their children, in particular, are trying to keep their families together while putting their own fears and trauma aside.

title: ISIS attacks military bus in Deir ez-Zor
content:
The Islamic State (ISIS) militant group has attacked a bus carrying personnel from the Syrian Ministry of Defense in the eastern Syrian province of Deir ez-Zor. The attack took place in al-Baghouz, once ISIS’s last territorial stronghold in Syria.




According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the attack triggered armed clashes between ISIS militants and government forces. Both sides reportedly suffered casualties, with people killed and injured. No precise casualty figures were initially provided.

title: Gelawêj Ewrîn: Jin Jiyan Azadî is a philosophy beyond borders - Part One
content:
Gelawêj Ewrîn, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), spoke to ANF about state repression against women in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat), the struggle for women's freedom, the philosophy of Jin Jiyan Azadî (Woman, Life, Freedom) and the impact of war on women. Ewrîn also highlighted the significance of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November, saying that women's struggle for freedom in Iran goes beyond regime change and that women must directly determine their own future.




Gelawêj Ewrîn said that wartime conditions in Iran have further intensified state repression and violence against women in society, leaving women confronted with both the state's repressive policies and the devastation caused by war. Ewrîn stressed that the atmosphere of war must not be allowed to push women's demands for freedom into the background. She said that Kurdish women's struggle is not limited to national and cultural rights but represents the pursuit of a democratic life for all peoples and women in Iran. Gelawêj Ewrîn emphasised the importance of women's struggle for freedom, equality and the right to determine their own future in Eastern Kurdistan.




PJAK spokesperson Gelawêj Ewrîn shared the following assessments:




How do you assess the current extent of state repression against women in Iran?




Repression against women in Iran cannot be explained solely through the anti-women policies of the current government. Behind this repression lie the patriarchal mentality, power relations and the systematic deprivation of society's will that have been shaped over thousands of years within state-centred civilisation. The Islamic Republic has reproduced this historical mentality within its own ideological and political structure, turning women's bodies and identities into areas of its domination. The state believes it has the right to decide how women should dress, how they should live, whom they should have relationships with, which areas of life they should participate in and how they should present their identities in society. In essence, this is an attempt to eliminate women's will. The compulsory hijab policy is one of the most visible instruments of this system. The state seeks to subjugate society as a whole through control over women's bodies. A system that seeks to break women's will also seeks to break society's free will.




However, the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution that developed following the killing of Jina Amini shook this mentality and dealt it a historic blow. Women did not take to the streets merely to oppose compulsory hijab. They asserted their determination to have a say over their own lives, identities and futures. They made the struggle and demand for freedom, which had been accumulating in Iranian society for a long time and had developed enormous potential, much more visible. Today, the presence of women without headscarves in public spaces across many Iranian cities demonstrates that the social control imposed by the state for years has been significantly weakened. However, this cannot be interpreted as the end of state repression. Alongside direct interventions in the streets, the state seeks to maintain its control through pressure on workplaces and businesses, legal proceedings and financial penalties.




The important point here is that the state is not concerned because it can no longer control women's hair, clothing or lives, but because it fears women's struggle. It fears the possibility that women will establish a new social life through their own will and take the lead in society. This is the most significant change brought about by Jin Jiyan Azadî. Women no longer accept others making decisions on their behalf. They are asserting that they are the owners of their own lives and must govern them themselves. For this reason, the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution is not merely the name of a protest movement. It is a philosophy and method of struggle aimed at rebuilding society on the foundation of women's freedom. In other words, change is taking place in emotions, attitudes and ways of thinking.




What forms of repression do Kurdish women face because of both their gender and Kurdish identity? How are they resisting this repression?




The repression faced by Kurdish women should not be understood as problems arising from two separate identities, but as historical forms of domination that reinforce one another. Kurdish women are both subjected to patriarchal social relations and targeted by state policies aimed at denying their national identity. The banning of the Kurdish language, suppression of cultural identity and exposure to accusations on various grounds are among these policies. At the same time, the portrayal of demands for democratic rights in Eastern Kurdistan as hostility towards religion and threats to national security directly affects women's lives. However, Kurdish women have not merely been victims of this repression. The historical experience of the Kurdish women's movement has demonstrated that correctly defining one's own identity and will can play a decisive role in social transformation.




This is one of the main reasons why Jin Jiyan Azadî has found such a powerful response in Eastern Kurdistan. The resistance led by women in Sanandaj (Sine), Saqqez (Seqiz), Mahabad, Kermanshah (Kirmaşan) and other cities has brought the historical experience of Kurdish women's struggle together with the demands for freedom of other peoples in Iran. Kurdish women are struggling not only for their own national and cultural rights but also for a democratic society in which all women and peoples in Iran can live together. In this respect, the Kurdish women's movement goes beyond a local struggle for rights and presents a universal perspective of freedom. It also takes the issue of women's freedom beyond the local and national levels, giving it a universal dimension.




How do you assess the relationship between state violence against women and the violence perpetrated by men in society?




State violence and male violence cannot be considered separately. The statist system makes patriarchal social relations the foundation of its own power. The mentality that restricts women's will in many areas of life, from the family and education to the economy and politics, is also reflected in all state institutions and structures. Explaining violence against women solely through the individual attitudes of men conceals the historical and systemic dimensions of the problem. Of course, individual acts of violence also entail legal and social responsibility. However, this violence cannot be eliminated without changing the structures that make women economically dependent, exclude them from decision-making mechanisms and control their labour and bodies.




In Iran, state control over women and patriarchal relations within the family and society reinforce one another. Femicide, domestic violence, forced marriages and pressure on women's life choices are different dimensions of this structure. This is precisely where the Freedom Movement's approach to women's freedom differs. Women's freedom does not mean men granting women certain rights within the existing system or the system creating more space for women. Freedom means women developing their own will, organising themselves and having decision-making power in every area of life. Therefore, the struggle against the patriarchal mentality is not solely women's responsibility. Men must also question their own mentalities, habits and power relations and make efforts to change them. This is one of the fundamental conditions for building a democratic society.




What are the main reasons behind the arrests and prosecutions of Kurdish women activists?




The repression imposed by the Islamic Republic of Iran on Kurdish women activists is fundamentally rooted in its fear of the convergence of the women's freedom struggle with the national and democratic social struggle. Kurdish women's organising does not simply mean defending women's rights. It also means that Kurdish society is expressing its cultural identity, political will and democratic demands in an organised manner. For this reason, the state often targets women activists not merely because of their individual activities, but because of the possibility of social transformation they represent. It is deeply afraid of the changes their mobilisation and activities may bring about.




The association of women's political activities with accusations of hostility towards religion and God or threats to national security, and their prosecution on charges such as membership of an organisation or activities against the state, are part of this policy. The aim is to criminalise women's organised struggle, spread fear throughout society and prevent other women from joining the movement. However, these repressive policies can no longer stop the development of the women's movement. Women's demand for freedom has moved beyond the boundaries of particular organisations or political structures and has become a collective social consciousness.




How do detentions, executions, political arrests and the criminalisation of women's social demands, which continue even during wartime, affect women's ability to organise?




The fascistic and inhumane practices imposed on women in Iranian prisons are among the most severe forms of the state's policies aimed at breaking women's will for freedom. Arrest and detention, prolonged isolation, being held in undisclosed locations and enforced disappearance, denial of access to lawyers, restrictions on contact with families, psychological pressure, torture and all forms of sexual violence are major problems faced by women political prisoners. Women's bodies are constantly used as instruments of repression and the destruction of their will. The policy of executions is also one of the state's most severe methods of creating fear and suppressing social resistance. Death sentences imposed on women political prisoners are a direct attack on women's political will and organised struggle.




We must also draw attention to the available data. The United Nations Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran stated that at least nine women had been executed on security-related charges by August 2026. It was also reported that five women faced the threat of execution for participating in the 2025-2026 protests. These figures do not cover all executions of women. They refer only to documented cases and incidents involving specific charges within a particular period. What matters to the state now is no longer what an individual has done. What matters is that the state remains in a constant state of attack to preserve its own existence.




The Iranian authorities seek to intimidate the women's movement, fragment organised resistance and obstruct society's demands for freedom through death sentences. However, the history of women's struggle shows that repression does not always lead to submission. Sometimes it gives rise to much stronger solidarity. For the Kurdish women's movement, political prisoners are an important part of the culture of resistance and struggle and the will for freedom. Refusing to leave them alone is not merely a moral and humanitarian matter, but a political responsibility of the women's freedom struggle. The struggle carried out outside prisons must be creative and appropriate to the characteristics of the current period. The movement cannot be strengthened through certain old and repetitive methods.




How can solidarity with imprisoned women and the struggle against death sentences be strengthened?




The struggle must not be limited to bringing the voices of imprisoned women to international public attention through statements. Women's organisations, legal institutions, human rights organisations, intellectuals and democratic forces must establish a common platform for struggle. A continuous and organised social response against death sentences must be developed. The time has come to adopt a common position against execution policies worldwide. Most importantly, a strong connection must be established between the will for freedom of women in prison and the struggle of women outside. The struggle for freedom cannot be carried out independently either within prison walls or beyond them.

title: Zeynep Oduncu: Women must have a say in building peace
content:
Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP for Batman (Êlih) Zeynep Oduncu spoke to ANF about 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, and the role of women in building peace within the framework of the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan.




Zeynep Oduncu said that the women's freedom struggle developed alongside the Kurdish Freedom Movement and that building a democratic society and peace is essential to creating spaces where women can live freely. She stated that women are engaged in a twofold struggle for existence, both because of their Kurdish identity and because they are women.







 







'

Building a democratic society is extremely valuable for women'




Zeynep Oduncu said that building peace is something they have dreamed of for many years and want to see become a reality. She explained that the women's freedom struggle began alongside the Kurdish Freedom Movement: "The realization of peace is something we have dreamed of for a long time and want to see become a reality. The women's freedom struggle began with the emergence of the Kurdish Freedom Movement. We are at an important stage in enabling women to establish their presence in society, make their voices heard, rise up and stand against violence, denial and marginalization. The Kurdish Freedom Movement has created a foundation through which women can participate in every sphere of life, establish their own existence and assert themselves as individuals.




Building democracy and peace is the clearest indication that spaces can be created where women can have a say in their own lives and discover themselves. Today, building a democratic society in Turkey and the Middle East means creating spaces where women can participate alongside men in every sphere of life, express themselves and make their voices heard."




Zeynep Oduncu said that women face a twofold struggle because of both their Kurdish identity and their gender. She pointed out that women's struggle to establish their place in society is also a struggle for freedom.




Zeynep Oduncu stated that women around the world face massacres, oppression, enforced disappearances, harassment and rape. She said that building a democratic society is crucial to enabling women to live free from violence.




'Women's bodies are the first to be exploited in wars'




Zeynep Oduncu said that the patriarchal mentality turns wars into environments where violence against women and their exploitation intensify: "Today, as women, we find ourselves at the very center of war. The reality of war creates an environment in which the patriarchal mentality is prepared to subject women to harassment, rape and massacres in every sphere. Throughout history, whenever there has been war, women's bodies have been the first to be exploited. Unfortunately, in wars, the patriarchal mentality considers itself entitled to exploit women. Women are threatened and treated as spoils of war.




During the wars in Shengal and Kobanê in 2015 and 2016, women were sold in slave markets. Even in the 21st century, at a time when we believe we have made so much progress, women are unfortunately still treated as spoils of war. Women from Shengal were sold in slave markets. There was a mentality that targeted women first during war, seeking to massacre and destroy them."




Zeynep Oduncu pointed to the mentality behind ISIS attacks against women and said that women had never abandoned their struggle, even under the harshest conditions of war.




Jin, Jiyan, Azadî has spread across the world'




Zeynep Oduncu said that the struggle waged by women in Kobanê against the darkness of ISIS had become an example for women around the world. She emphasized that women asserted their existence on the battlefields through their songs and ululations: "In the victory of Kobanê, we witnessed women's victory, their existence and how they asserted themselves in the struggle. Women established their existence while fighting against ISIS barbarism. This struggle became an example for the entire world. Women's struggle, their existence and the way they asserted themselves on the battlefield through their songs and ululations truly became an example for the whole world. Today, the slogan 'Jin, Jiyan, Azadî (Woman, Life, Freedom)' has spread across the world.




Women demonstrated that they feared nothing in their struggle to participate in every sphere of life, even during war. They fought for their own existence while also waging the struggle for women's existence. In this sense, they powerfully embodied a struggle for existence that has been written in golden letters in the pages of history."




Zeynep Oduncu said that Kurdish women draw strength from this struggle and continue their struggle for existence through the strength they receive from one another. Oduncu said, "As Kurdish women, we have witnessed women who were reborn from their own ashes, even on the battlefields, and established their place in life through the philosophy of 'Jin, Jiyan, Azadî'. Today, we continue to carry forward that struggle. We draw strength from one another as we continue our struggle for existence."




'Society cannot be free unless women are free'




Zeynep Oduncu said that women's freedom is one of the fundamental areas of struggle within the Kurdish Freedom Movement. She recalled Abdullah Öcalan's words, "Society cannot be free unless women are free," and continued: "These words represent a perspective that has been presented to us and an idea that must be conveyed to all peoples. Mr. Öcalan has written numerous books on this subject, examining how society can be shaped, changed and transformed through women's freedom. He has developed an approach that evaluates the transformation of society through women's liberation.




Even today, when delegations visit Imralı, the first issues discussed are women's existence and their ability to assert themselves. In his most recent note to women, he once again expressed his belief that women can change and transform society through their own liberation. The women's freedom struggle is built upon this philosophy."




Zeynep Oduncu said that Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom would pave the way for both the Kurdish people and the women's freedom struggle.




Oduncu said, "Mr. Öcalan's physical freedom means not only the freedom of the Kurdish people but also the freedom of the ideas that open up the path, methods and spaces for the women's struggle. This will also bring about women's freedom."




Zeynep Oduncu stated that the perspective developed by Abdullah Öcalan must be passed on to future generations. She said that women attach great importance to the demand for his physical freedom and that this demand must be met as soon as possible.




'

Silencing the guns alone will not bring peace'




Zeynep Oduncu said that silencing the guns is an important step towards peace, but that women's right to life and their freedoms must be guaranteed to achieve lasting peace: "Today, silencing the guns alone cannot provide the foundation for peace. Silencing the guns is one of the greatest and most important steps towards peace. Today, there is no longer an environment of armed conflict because the guns have fallen silent. We are no longer receiving the bodies of those killed in conflict. However, the steps taken after the guns fall silent must also be capable of paving the way for the women's freedom struggle.




If women are still being murdered, if they are still trying to survive in conditions of insecurity and if they are living in situations where they need protection, this means that important issues remain unresolved. As we establish the foundations of peace, we must also create conditions that guarantee safe living spaces for women in our country."




Zeynep Oduncu said, "If women still cannot be protected in a country, if we wake up to news of a woman being raped, subjected to violence or murdered, then the foundations of peace have unfortunately not been fully established." She said that the state must abandon its policies of impunity and introduce legal measures to guarantee women's right to life.




'Women's rights must be legally guaranteed'




Zeynep Oduncu said that the call made by Abdullah Öcalan two years ago laid the foundations for building a democratic and peaceful society. She stated that the construction of a democratic society must be supported by legal guarantees.




Zeynep Oduncu said that women's ability to participate equally and freely in every sphere, from their right to life to employment, must be legally protected: "Building a democratic society means building democracy in every respect. Once the foundations of peace have been established in the country, they must also be legally guaranteed. Within a model of life protected by legal guarantees, all women's rights must be secured, from the right to life and participation in working life to every sphere in which they can establish their existence.




If we can build a democratic society today, we can truly achieve democracy and guarantee women's rights and freedoms through legal protections. This way, we will no longer wake up every day to news of women being murdered somewhere. Once the necessary legal arrangements are made and the laws are implemented, women will be able to participate in life without fear."




Zeynep Oduncu pointed out that the killing of women takes place within a political context. She said that the policies responsible for these killings must be changed, legal reforms must be introduced and existing laws must be effectively implemented.




'Women are the ones who will build peace'




Zeynep Oduncu said that women must have a say in building a democratic society and peace through the DEM Party Women's Assembly, the Free Women's Movement (TJA), the Democratic Regions Party (DBP) Women's Assembly and the parliamentary group. She stated that women are the driving force behind social change and transformation.




Zeynep Oduncu said that women's participation in decision-making mechanisms and their ability to express themselves without being marginalized would facilitate the construction of a democratic society.

title: Ayten Kordu: Men and states started wars, but women will bring peace
content:
Ayten Kordu, Dersim MP for the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), answered ANF's questions about the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan's call on 27 February 2025, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November, the relationship between women's freedom and peace, and women's expectations of the process.




Ayten Kordu said that the struggle against violence against women is not limited to 25 November, noting that the Kurdish women's movement and women's movements in Turkey have fought for many years against violence, massacres, harassment, rape, exploitation and policies of denial. Kordu said that Kurdish women have significant historical experience in this struggle and continue their activities under the slogan "We have a voice for a free and equal life, and we rebel against violence."







 







'The women's struggle aims for social transformation'




Ayten Kordu said that Kurdish women have fought for their identity, existence and freedom for many years, explaining that this struggle extends beyond gender-based demands. Kordu pointed out that women have challenged the patriarchal mentality established over thousands of years, as well as centralism and militarism: "For a long time, Kurdish women's struggle for identity, existence and their demands as women was not only a women's struggle but also a social struggle. When we speak of the patriarchal mentality, we are actually questioning the centralist and militarist mentality embodied in the state today. Women have approached their demands for equality and freedom in life as inseparable from social transformation."




Ayten Kordu said that one of the characteristics distinguishing the women's movement from other struggles is its aim of transforming society. Kordu added that the struggle carried out alongside women's movements in Turkey has gone through difficult periods.




'Violence against women targets society as a whole'




Ayten Kordu said that women are struggling against violence and massacres in almost every part of Turkey, adding that suspicious deaths of women, harassment, rape, impoverishment and labour exploitation also threaten women's lives.




Kordu said that special warfare policies have been implemented in Kurdistan for many years and that violence against women has developed into a mechanism affecting society as a whole. Kordu said, "Every form of violence against women has become a mechanism of violence that spreads throughout society and targets society as a whole."




Ayten Kordu argued that the patriarchal mentality has grown stronger, particularly under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government, pointing to Turkey's withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention and the failure to effectively implement Law No. 6284.




Kordu said that violence has increased despite official declarations of zero tolerance towards violence against women, adding that women have not abandoned their rights and continue their resistance in the streets and through organised struggle.




'Women's spaces of organisation have been targeted'




Ayten Kordu said that women have never abandoned their struggle or efforts to organise. Women's associations and cooperatives have been established, but these organisations have repeatedly been shut down.




Kordu also said that the appointment of government trustees to municipalities has targeted women's spaces of organisation: "This centralist mentality, this patriarchal state mentality, has always intervened first in places where women's spaces and organisations exist. This has always been the case. Women have established their own structures and developed an autonomous women's struggle in politics, workplaces, fields, streets, political parties and everywhere else. Through their own experiences, women have learned that organisation is their most essential means of self-defence."




Ayten Kordu said that women's labour is present in every aspect of life, yet women continue to be ignored and face attempts to confine them to their homes and restrict their living spaces. Kordu added that women in prisons also face various rights violations.




Kordu pointed out that women held in Sincan Women's Closed Prison have repeatedly had their release postponed through decisions by prison administrative and observation boards. Women prisoners also face difficulties accessing medical treatment.




'The patriarchal system fears women exercising their own will'




Ayten Kordu said that the patriarchal system fears women's organised struggle and that women exercising their own will in social life represents one of its greatest concerns.




Kordu described women as active participants who enrich life and promote justice and conscience throughout society. Kordu argued that those in power do not want a social order in which everyone can live equally, freely and with dignity.




Ayten Kordu also highlighted the importance of women's struggles with different identities and beliefs, identifying herself as a Kurdish and Alevi woman. Kordu said that being Kurdish and Alevi, as well as being a woman, means confronting different forms of exploitation and denial, adding that the women's movement is engaged in a multidimensional struggle.




'Men and states started wars, but women will bring peace'




Ayten Kordu said that women must play a leading role in the Peace and Democratic Society Process, stressing that the women's struggle cannot be separated from the struggle for peace.




Kordu said that a powerful freedom movement and women's struggle had emerged in response to a century of policies of denial, adding that women began organising in the areas where they experienced the greatest oppression.




Ayten Kordu said, "Men and states started wars, but women will bring peace," and emphasising that women have always stood at the forefront of the struggle for peace.




Kordu said that achieving peace requires abandoning militarist and centralist approaches: "We have said that the bloodshed in this country must end, peace must be achieved, and the militarist and centralist mentality must be abandoned. We have explained that these are directly connected to the patriarchal mentality and, in fact, represent the very same way of thinking. Therefore, every struggle we wage as women is also a struggle that brings us one step closer to peace."




Ayten Kordu said that women's organisation also means struggling against poverty, femicide, harassment, rape and suspicious deaths of women. Kordu added that the judiciary is not independent of the patriarchal system.




'Femicides are political'




Ayten Kordu said that femicides cannot be regarded as isolated incidents, arguing that systematic policies lie behind these killings.




Kordu said that the judicial mechanisms women encounter in their pursuit of justice are also influenced by the patriarchal mentality, explaining that this is why women raise the demand for "Real justice, not patriarchal justice."




Ayten Kordu drew attention to the cases of Gülistan Doku, Rojin Kabaiş and Rojwelat Kızmaz, saying that the women's struggle plays a decisive role in clarifying the circumstances of women's deaths and uncovering the truth.




Kordu said, "We say, 'Femicides are political.' This is because they are conscious and systematic policies carried out on a political basis."




Ayten Kordu said that women are struggling in every area of life, against economic exploitation, precarious employment, violence and femicide, describing 25 November as one of the symbolic days of this struggle.




'25 November is a day to demonstrate our determination to struggle'




Ayten Kordu recalled that 25 November is a day dedicated to all women through the struggle and resistance of the Mirabal sisters, adding that the women's movement has created new forms of resistance and experiences of struggle in many parts of the world.




Kordu said that the women's struggle is a long-term endeavour, noting that changing the patriarchal mentality is not easy and that the achievements secured so far have come at great cost and through sustained struggle.




Ayten Kordu said, "A beautiful, dignified life free from violence is possible for everyone, especially women. On days like this, we demonstrate our determination to struggle by taking to the streets and raising our voices even louder. Our struggle is not limited to a single day. However, this is a day when we demonstrate our determination to continue that struggle." Kordu added that women will continue struggling against states, the patriarchal mentality and inequalities in every aspect of life.




'We must build our own living spaces'




Ayten Kordu said that organisation, solidarity and women's ability to build their own living spaces form the foundation of the women's struggle. Kordu added that the Peace and Democratic Society Process offers an important perspective in this regard.




Ayten Kordu said that women must organise wherever they are, pointing out that the system continues attempting to suppress women's struggle and restrict their spaces of organisation: "The most fundamental principle is to organise, come together, develop solidarity and build our own living spaces. One of the most important perspectives offered by the Peace and Democratic Society Process is expanding organisations through which we can build our own living spaces. The women's struggle is not separate from this. On the contrary, it lies at the very centre of this process."




Kordu also said that the judiciary must be freed from patriarchal and male-dominated thinking, stressing that all institutions of the system are interconnected and that social transformation must be approached as a whole.




'The women's struggle is one of the freedom movement's greatest achievements'




Ayten Kordu drew attention to the historical experience of the Kurdish women's movement and Abdullah Öcalan's perspective on women's freedom, saying that the women's struggle has played a leading role in the development of the Freedom Movement.




Kordu said that the women's struggle had provided a foundation for examining identity, belief and gender, questioning established assumptions and advancing the struggle for freedom. Kordu added that the women's perspective also lies at the heart of the Peace and Democratic Society Process: "If the freedom movement has reached this point today, it has done so through its perspective, its ideas and the leadership of the women's struggle. We have all drawn strength from the different currents within the women's struggle. We have all looked at our own lives through that experience and questioned ourselves. It was through this struggle that we found the foundation for discovering our identity, understanding our beliefs, recognising our gender identity, questioning these issues and advancing our struggle."




Ayten Kordu said that the historical experience of the women's movement is rich in important lessons and achievements. Kordu added that women have insisted from the beginning that Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom must be secured as part of the ongoing process.




'Mr. Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom must be secured'




Ayten Kordu said that the isolation policies imposed on Abdullah Öcalan have affected not only Öcalan himself but also an entire people, including their women and children, and subsequently the peoples of Turkey. Kordu said that Öcalan's physical freedom must be secured for the Peace and Democratic Society Process to advance.




Ayten Kordu drew attention to the efforts Öcalan has made on Imralı to develop the process, explaining that women regard his physical freedom as important for building peace: "Mr. Öcalan's physical freedom must absolutely be secured. Isolation has been imposed not only on him but also on an entire people, their women, children and everyone else, extending from there to the peoples of Turkey. We women have always said that his physical freedom must be secured and that peace can only be built in this way. We will continue to say so."




'Mr. Öcalan has an important manifesto on women's freedom'




Ayten Kordu said that Abdullah Öcalan has developed important perspectives and a manifesto on women's freedom, recalling his argument that freedom and equality cannot exist in a world where women do not play a role in building life.




Kordu said that Öcalan continues to develop his perspective on women's leadership and their role in building social life. Kordu added that conditions must be created for these ideas to be discussed with all sections of society: "Mr. Öcalan has very important perspectives and a manifesto concerning the women's perspective. He has presented a vision that emphasises developing women's leadership, women's ability to build life, and the understanding that a free and equal world cannot exist unless women take part in building it. He continues to do this from Imralı. He still has messages for women and society as a whole on these issues."




Ayten Kordu also emphasised the importance of organisation, saying that conditions must be created for Abdullah Öcalan to meet and hold discussions with all sections of society, particularly women.




Kordu said, "It is now necessary to create conditions in which Mr. Öcalan can meet and engage in discussions with society, with all sections of society, especially women," and adding that they are struggling to ensure this does not remain merely a wish.




Ayten Kordu, DEM Party MP for Dersim, said that Öcalan's ideas must find practical expression and contribute to building society for the process to succeed.




Kordu said, "As an idea comes to life and finds expression in a person's own existence and daily life, it acquires greater meaning and value. We will achieve this through struggle as well."

title: Baghdad orders takeover of Kurdish border crossings and disputed oil fields
content:
The Iraqi central government has ordered sweeping measures to take control of border crossings and oil fields in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) and the disputed territories. The decisions announced on Tuesday by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi stipulate that all border crossings in the region be placed under the authority of the federal border crossings agency and that Baghdad’s powers over oil production and the export of petroleum products be expanded. The orders follow investigations into suspected oil smuggling and could exacerbate longstanding tensions between Baghdad and Hewlêr (Erbil).




According to Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the prime minister and commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, the Kurdistan Regional Government will henceforth be required to process export permits for crude oil and petroleum products exclusively through the Federal Ministry of Oil. Baghdad is thus asserting greater control over the region’s oil trade. Since oil exports via Turkey resumed in September 2025, they have already been subject to an agreement between the central government and the Kurdistan Regional Government.




Oil fields in disputed territories affected




The orders have particularly far-reaching implications for oil fields in the provinces of Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahaddin, and Nineveh. They affect facilities that Baghdad considers to fall under the authority of the Federal Ministry of Oil but that remain under the security control of the Kurdistan Regional Government. Their administration is to be placed directly under the Iraqi Ministry of Oil.




Control over oil production has been one of the central points of contention between Baghdad and Hewlêr for years. The dispute concerns both the distribution of revenues and political and administrative control over territories whose status remains contested between the central government and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.




Following the 2017 independence referendum, the Iraqi central government regained military control of Kirkuk and other disputed territories. Legal disputes over the independent production and marketing of Kurdish oil also remain unresolved.




Closure of unofficial border crossings ordered




In addition to interventions in the oil sector, the package of measures provides for tighter border controls. All unofficial crossing points along Iraq’s international borders are to be closed. This explicitly includes the Kurdistan Region. The Iraqi Ministry of Defense has also been instructed to block unauthorized routes connecting the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) with the provinces of Diyala, Salahaddin, Kirkuk, and Nineveh.




Personnel from the Ministry of Oil, the Energy Police, and national security agencies are to be stationed at entry points to Hewlêr, Sulaymaniyah, and Duhok. Newly established laboratories will inspect petroleum products transported into the region. At the same time, Iraq’s Commission of Integrity is to investigate possible irregularities in oil exports, supply contracts, and refinery supplies.




Additional technical measures are planned to strengthen oversight of the oil sector. All oil fields in Iraq are to be secured by the Energy Police and monitored by surveillance cameras. Electronic meters at production facilities and a nationwide digital pipeline monitoring system are intended to help detect unrecorded oil shipments.




Oil smuggling investigations lead to dismissals and suspensions




The decisions come amid investigations into suspected smuggling networks in Iraq’s oil sector. One of the main focuses is the state-owned North Oil Company, which is responsible for oil and gas fields in the north of the country. According to Iraqi authorities, substantial quantities of crude oil are believed to have been illegally diverted and sold over a period of several years.




The investigations have also led to allegations against the pro-Iranian militia Kataib Hezbollah, which is suspected of involvement in a smuggling network in the city of Jurf al-Sakhar, southwest of Baghdad. The organization denies the allegations.




Prime Minister al-Zaidi has ordered several personnel changes. The head of the Federal Border Crossings Authority was dismissed, while the Director General of the North Oil Company and his deputies were suspended pending further investigations. Senior police and security officials in Kirkuk were also removed from their posts.




Implementation of the decisions remains unclear




It is not yet known when the ordered transfer of border crossings and oil fields to federal authorities will take place. No information is currently available regarding any agreements between the central government in Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government in Hewlêr on the practical implementation of the measures.

title: Call for an independent investigation after the discovery of bones and skulls in Silvan
content:
Following the discovery of numerous human skulls and bones in a three-level cave near Silvan district, in the province of Amed (Diyarbakır), the Initiative for Respect for the Dead and Justice called for an independent investigation. The organization believes the remains may belong to people who were forcibly abducted or extrajudicially executed in the 1990s. This possibility must not be left uninvestigated, the initiative said in a statement on Tuesday.




The Mezopotamya News Agency (MA) reported the discovery on Monday and published footage of the human remains. It remains unknown how many individuals the bones belong to, or when and under what circumstances they died.




Indications of a possible clandestine burial site




The initiative recalled that Silvan and the surrounding areas were the scene of serious human rights violations, particularly in the 1990s. During the Turkish state’s dirty war against the Kurdish guerrillas, numerous cases of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial executions occurred in the region. “The fact that the remains belong to several individuals and are scattered across different levels of the cave raises the question of whether the site may have been used as a clandestine burial ground. Such a possibility must be examined through an independent and effective investigation.”

title: PJAK: There can be no social liberation without women’s freedom
content:
The Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) emphasized the central importance of women’s liberation for a democratic society on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25. In a statement released on Tuesday, the party described patriarchal violence as a manifestation of social and political power structures that cannot be overcome through legal reforms alone.




With regard to Iran and Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat), the PJAK pointed to the systematic oppression of women, political imprisonment, and executions. It called for strengthening recent protest campaigns led by women and continuing resistance until all imprisoned women are released. At the same time, it emphasized the international dimension of the struggle against patriarchal violence, exploitation, and war.




The PJAK statement, titled “Without the struggle for women’s freedom, neither a revolution nor a society is on the path to freedom,” reads as follows:




"November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, is a day on which we commemorate women’s historic struggle against all forms of violence, domination, discrimination, and patriarchal systems. It is a day when the voices of freedom-loving women grow louder in the face of oppressive structures, and the struggle for freedom, equality, and human dignity once again becomes a historic and social responsibility.




Women’s freedom is the foundation of social liberation




Violence against women is not an individual phenomenon that can be reduced to personal behavior. Rather, its roots lie in power structures, the patriarchal mentality, systems of domination, and social, political, and economic conditions. Therefore, the struggle against violence against women is also a struggle for the fundamental transformation of society and the liberation of humanity from all forms of domination.




In our philosophy of struggle, women’s freedom is neither a secondary issue nor merely a legal demand. Rather, it forms the foundation of social freedom and serves as the benchmark for the realization of genuine democracy. A society in which women are not free cannot be considered a free society.




The domination of women is the first and most deeply rooted form of domination in human social history. Through the continuous reproduction of power relations, sexist attitudes, and unequal structures, the patriarchal system restricts the freedom of both women and men. Women’s liberation therefore cannot be achieved through legislative changes or superficial reforms alone. Instead, it requires a revolution in mentality, the development of an independent consciousness, women’s autonomous organization based on freedom, and the restructuring of social relations on the basis of freedom, equality, and democratic coexistence.




“Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” is a vision for social transformation




The pioneering role of Kurdish women in the freedom struggle is one of the most remarkable expressions of women’s historic determination to break the chains of oppression and reclaim their identity, their will, and the right to determine their own destiny. Guided by the philosophy of “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom], Kurdish women have demonstrated through their struggle, organization, consciousness, and resistance that women are not passive victims of circumstances but a driving force in transforming society and building a free future.




This pioneering role is not limited to the struggle against gender-based discrimination. It also challenges the mentality of enslavement, authoritarianism, extreme nationalism, state domination, and all structures that subject life to subjugation. By linking women’s freedom, the right to life, and the freedom of society, the philosophy of “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” offers a new vision for human liberation and the establishment of a democratic, ethical, and free society in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan.




Resistance against the systematic oppression of women in Iran




In Iran, misogyny and the systematic oppression of women have become one of the main pillars sustaining the Islamic Republic’s regime. Through the enforcement of discriminatory laws, control over women’s bodies and clothing, restrictions on individual and social rights and freedoms, and the use of organized violence, the regime has taken patriarchal domination to its extreme.




Imprisonment, torture, threats, fabricated criminal proceedings, and executions are instruments through which the Islamic Republic seeks to silence the voices of freedom-loving women, social activists, political activists, and all those who oppose discrimination and despotism. Nevertheless, women in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan have not surrendered to this oppression. Through their resistance, courage, and tireless struggle, they have challenged the legitimacy of the misogynistic system and demonstrated that no power can imprison the will to freedom forever.




The “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” movement is the historic expression of this resistance and a call for liberation from despotism, patriarchy, and death. Therefore, we must make every day a November 25 and strengthen the campaigns of struggle that women have launched recently. We must stand against the recent executions and maintain our presence in the streets and public squares until all imprisoned women are fully free.




Women’s liberation and the struggle against capitalist exploitation




In today’s world, amid the deepening crisis of the capitalist system, women in various countries are increasingly confronted with poverty, unemployment, precarious employment, exploitation of their labor, war, displacement, racism, domestic violence, and the deprivation of fundamental rights. By turning human beings and life itself into instruments for maximizing profits and accumulating wealth, the capitalist system exacerbates class and gender inequalities. The heavy burden of economic crises, wars, and social disintegration is placed on women, particularly working-class women, migrant women, refugee women, and women in war zones.




In many societies, women continue to be denied equal pay, security, the right to determine the course of their own lives, and the freedom to participate in political and social life. Therefore, the struggle against violence against women must be inseparably linked to the struggle against exploitation, war, poverty, racism, and all systems that perpetuate inequality.




As long as women are not free, society will not be free




The Kurdistan Free Life Party commemorates all women who have fought and all those who lost their lives on the path to freedom and gave meaning to our people’s revolution. We emphasize the need for worldwide solidarity among women, the strengthening of organized struggle, the defense of political prisoners and oppressed women, and the promotion of a culture of freedom, equality, and free life.




We firmly believe that no society can achieve genuine freedom without women’s freedom, and that no struggle for justice can achieve its goal unless it also challenges patriarchy and systems of domination. As long as violence against women exists, the struggle for freedom will continue. As long as women are not free, society will not be free."

title: Three mass graves discovered in Shengal
content:
Three mass graves containing human remains have been discovered in the Yazidi region of Shengal. The graves are located in the Geliyê Hecî area and near the villages of Girzerik and Kersê. According to available information, the body of an as-yet unidentified man was found in a grave near Girzerik. The other two graves contain additional human remains, but the number of those buried has yet to be determined.




Iraqi forensic teams have traveled to Shengal to prepare for the exhumation of the graves and begin examinations aimed at identifying the deceased. The search in the affected areas is ongoing. It has not yet been confirmed whether the graves date back to the genocide perpetrated against the Yazidis by the Islamic State (ISIS) in August 2014.




Hundreds of victims remain unidentified




Twelve years after the genocide, numerous mass graves in Shengal remain unopened. According to recent data from Shengal, 97 mass graves have been documented so far, of which 78 have been exhumed. More than 900 sets of human remains have reportedly been transferred to Baghdad for forensic examination. Only 301 victims have so far been identified and their remains returned to their families.




These figures differ from those published by Iraq’s Martyrs Foundation earlier this month. According to the foundation, 90 mass graves have been discovered so far. Of these, 85 have been fully excavated, with the recovery of human remains and documentation completed. In total, the remains of around 700 people have been recovered.




In late October, Iraqi authorities and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) announced preparations to exhume another 18 mass graves. Victims are identified primarily through DNA analysis and comparison with samples provided by their relatives.




Background




In the summer of 2014, ISIS overran large parts of Iraq. On August 3 of that year, the jihadist militia committed genocide and femicide in the Yazidi main settlement area of Shengal (Sinjar), west of Mosul. Through systematic massacres, rape, torture, expulsion, enslavement of girls and women, and the forced recruitment of boys as child soldiers, the Yazidi community experienced the 74th genocide in its history.




According to recent estimates, around 10,000 people fell victim to the ISIS massacres, and more than 400,000 others were driven from their homes. Over 7,000 women and children were abducted, and around 2,500 of them are still missing today.




Only with the help of a dozen guerrilla fighters from the PKK were hundreds of thousands of people saved from certain death or enslavement. Reinforcements from the HPG (People’s Defense Forces) and YJA Star (Free Women’s Troops) then moved out of the Kurdistan mountains. Together with the YPG (People’s Defense Units) and YPJ (Women’s Defense Units), a corridor of escape to Rojava was created. Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Shengal Women's Units (YJŞ) were formed, and the region was liberated step by step. In January 2015, an autonomous council was proclaimed. On 31 October 2015, an offensive began to liberate the villages in the west of the city of Shengal, and on 13 November 2015, ISIS was completely driven out of the region.




After the liberation of the city, the HPG and YPG/YPJ subsequently withdrew in 2017. People who returned to their land after Shengal's independence reformed, established defensive units and built their institutions.




The fate of thousands of Yazidis, especially women, remains unknown. Many were sold in slave markets established by ISIS in cities such as Raqqa, Mosul, Deir ez-Zor, and Al-Bukamal. SDF forces have successfully liberated thousands of them, reuniting them to their families in Shengal.




Countless victims of the ISIS massacres in the city were buried in mass graves. Although the Iraqi government began opening mass graves in 2019, many have yet to be opened. Several families are still waiting for the work to begin so they can get back the remains of their loved ones.




According to a recent statement by Iraq’s Ministry of Migration and Displacement, more than 30,000 people have returned to Shengal so far. Around 19,000 families, the majority of them Yazidi citizens, are still living in a total of 16 camps in Hewlêr (Erbil) and Duhok.

title: Demirtaş: One does not demand peace when peaceful conditions already exist
content:
Selahattin Demirtaş, the former Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), who has been imprisoned since 2016, has responded to criticism of the ongoing peace process in Turkey. In a statement published through his account on the social media platform X, he recalled that the Kurdish movement had maintained its demand for a peaceful solution even during periods of severe state repression, armed conflict, and political persecution.




Demirtaş, who is being held in Edirne High-Security Prison, described the current stage of the process as historic. He acknowledged that ongoing violations of rights could not be denied. Precisely for this reason, he stressed the importance of not squandering the opportunity to bring the conflict to a lasting end. His statement reads in full:




“When villages were engulfed in flames, we demanded a peaceful solution. Even when people were shot from behind in broad daylight and we had to bury young people day after day, we wanted peace.




When bombs exploded in cities and waves of mass arrests took place, we continued to defend peace. When our parties were banned, when people were beaten with batons, attacked with tear gas, and dragged along the ground, we did not give up on peace.




Neither in prison cells nor in public squares have we ever stopped defending peace.

title: KDP and PUK: Any infringement of Kurdistan Region’s rights and achievements constitutes a red line
content:
The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) have issued a joint statement expressing concern over recent developments in Iraq, stressing the need to respect the Kurdistan Region's constitutional rights and warning against unilateral decisions.




The full statement by the KDP and PUK reads as follows:




“The statement issued by the Spokesperson for the Iraqi Armed Forces, together with the developments and measures taken in Iraq over the past few days, has come as an unexpected development and caused considerable surprise among the citizens of the Kurdistan Region.




All parties are fully aware that the Kurdistan Region has never sought anything beyond the rights guaranteed to it under the Iraqi Constitution. However, its constitutional rights have been violated over the years. We stress that all parties must abide by the Constitution and that, should any dispute arise between the Kurdistan Region and the Federal Government, the Constitution must serve as the ultimate point of reference. Any measure or decision taken against the Kurdistan Region outside the constitutional framework is therefore unconstitutional.




It must be clear to all parties that the Kurdistan Region is the result of the bloodshed and decades-long struggle of the people of Kurdistan, and that any infringement of its rights and achievements constitutes a red line.

author: Unknown
title: Hatimoğulları: Women will bring both peace and democracy to this country
content:
Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), emphasized the central role of women in combating violence and building lasting peace during the weekly parliamentary group meeting in the Turkish Parliament. The meeting was held as a women’s parliamentary group meeting to mark the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.




Hatimoğulları extended a special welcome to the Peace Mothers in attendance, who have continued to advocate for peace even during the most difficult periods of war and despite the loss of their loved ones. “I especially welcome the esteemed Peace Mothers, who have always paved the way for us in this struggle and have never stopped calling for peace, even during the most intense periods of war and conflict.”













Women’s struggles across borders




At the beginning of her speech, Hatimoğulları commemorated women who were killed in the freedom struggle, including Sakine Cansız, Seve Demir, Nagihan Akarsel, Deniz Poyraz, and Kader Ortakaya. She stated that women’s struggle knows no borders. “The uprising of women in one region is connected to the resistance of women in another.” She highlighted the struggle of women in Rojava for recognition of their identity, language, and political participation in a new Syrian constitution. She also paid tribute to the resistance of Yazidi women in Shengal, who continue to demand that the fate of abducted women be clarified. “The struggle for the missing Yazidi women is also our struggle,” she underlined.




Hatimoğulları also commemorated Alawite women killed in Syria and expressed solidarity with imprisoned women and LGBTIQ+ activists in Turkey. She specifically mentioned Janset Kalan and Nedime Erdoğan, who were detained as part of the “My Family Is Safe” operation, as well as Figen Yüksekdağ, Leyla Güven, Ayşe Gökkan, and Deniz Aktaş.




“This is femicide”




Addressing violence against women in Turkey, Hatimoğulları criticized the government’s family policies and restrictions on women’s rights. She demanded a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths of Gülistan Doku, Rojin Kabaiş, Rojwelat Kızmaz, İpek Er, and Narin Güran. She stressed that the DEM Party would continue to follow all the cases: “In October alone, 20 women were killed by men. The deaths of another 39 women remain unexplained. In the first ten months of 2026, 245 women were killed, excluding unexplained deaths. This is femicide.”




The DEM Party Co-Chair emphasized that the state was obliged to protect the right to life. Instead, she said, the government had withdrawn from the Istanbul Convention and was attacking further gains made by the women’s movement. “We will not give up the Istanbul Convention, Law No. 6284, or our right to alimony.”




Criticism of the budget: “Women are once again left out this year”




Hatimoğulları also sharply criticized the 2027 budget currently under discussion in Parliament. She pointed out that women’s economic needs were being neglected while the government placed family and population growth at the center of its policies. “Once again this year, we women have no place in the budget. We demand the share to which we are entitled,” she said.




Hatimoğulları said she spoke with farmers and producers and once again witnessed the extent of poverty during a visit to Kızıltepe on Sunday. “Society is already poor, but women are the poorest of the poor,” she added.




DEM Party Co-Chair noted that the draft budget allocates approximately 30 billion lira to family policy measures, while around 11 billion lira is earmarked for women’s economic and social empowerment. She said the government constantly talked about family but ignored the realities faced by women suffering from poverty and economic dependence. The DEM Party, she said, therefore advocated a gender-responsive budget that takes women’s needs into account across all ministries. Hatimoğulları also called for the establishment of a separate Ministry of Women: “We want our own ministry. As the DEM Party, we will establish this ministry.”













Serious allegations concerning women’s prison conditions




Another major focus of Hatimoğulları’s speech was the situation of women in Turkish prisons. She referred to reports by human rights organizations and visits by members of parliament that had documented a deterioration in prison conditions. She remarked that at least four female prisoners had died under unexplained circumstances at Sincan Women’s Prison within six months. “Women there are facing institutional pressure, violence, and severe psychological distress. Political prisoners are experiencing serious difficulties accessing medical care,” she added.




Hatimoğulları was particularly critical of the situation of seriously ill prisoners. She said Newroz Bozkurt had not received timely medical examinations and treatment and was now suffering from advanced cancer. Nevertheless, she has not been released, she noted. In the case of Evin Zapsu, who is imprisoned in Kayseri-Bünyan Prison and has stage-four cancer, transfers to hospital and medical treatment are being systematically delayed, she added.




“Are you waiting for her to die in prison?” Hatimoğulları asked, addressing the authorities. She also criticized the practices of the Administrative and Observation Boards, which repeatedly postpone prisoners’ release despite having served their sentences. Pınar Tikit’s release was blocked three times, Nedime Yaklav’s seven times, and Sermin Demirdağ’s eight times, while, nine women are still awaiting release at Sincan Prison alone, she said.




“Even if stones rain down on us, we will not leave”




Hatimoğulları praised the protest that families of sick prisoners have been holding for days outside the Turkish Ministry of Justice in Ankara. She recounted visiting the protesters during heavy rain. One mother told her: “You speak of a peace process, but our children are sick, imprisoned, and not being released. Even if stones rain down on us instead of rain, we will not leave the Ministry of Justice until we achieve a result.”




“The government must finally listen to these voices. Sick prisoners must not be kept in prison for even one more minute, without exception. The arbitrary postponement of releases by the Administrative and Observation Boards must also come to an end. You cannot leave sick prisoners to die. We will not allow it,” Hatimoğulları underlined.













Remove obstacles to the implementation of the peace law




In the subsequent part of her speech, Hatimoğulları turned to the peace process. She emphasized that women’s experiences and organized struggle were indispensable to building lasting peace. At the same time, the remaining obstacles to implementing the legal framework have to be removed, she said.




“Women reiterate their demand in this process: The obstacle posed by the verification and determination procedure must finally be removed,” Hatimoğulları said, referring to the pending procedure for confirming the steps taken by the Kurdish movement.




She continued: “The National Security Council must convene as soon as possible and clear the way for the implementation of the framework law. Society expects that the regulations adopted by Parliament will no longer be obstructed by the verification and determination procedure.”




Legally define Öcalan’s status and expand talks




Hatimoğulları also called for a legal regulation defining the status of Abdullah Öcalan, whom she described as the chief negotiator in the process. “Mr. Öcalan’s status must be defined by law. The Commission for Peace and Political Participation, which is to operate under his coordination, must begin its work and travel to Imrali as soon as possible,” she stated.




Hatimoğulları also advocated expanding contacts with Öcalan, stating that female journalists, lawyers, politicians, and academics must be given the opportunity to meet him personally on Imrali and conduct interviews with him.




She recalled the DEM Party’s Imrali delegation’s visit on Sunday and conveyed Öcalan’s greetings to the women’s parliamentary group. “Mr. Abdullah Öcalan has sent you his greetings. We also send him our greetings from here.”













Women as independent actors in the peace process




Shaping peace must not be left solely to political and state bodies, Hatimoğulları said, stressing that women would not leave either the process or the mechanisms established for it to the initiative of men. In this context, she welcomed the independent women’s commission announced on November 20 to monitor and oversee the peace process. She said its work could strengthen women’s direct participation and help establish the peace process within society.




“Lasting peace will be built by women. Lasting peace and democracy will come to this country through the will of women. We women will bring both peace and democracy to this country,” she said.




Call for protests on November 25




In closing, Hatimoğulları called on women to participate in demonstrations and protests across the country on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. She said the DEM Party would also take part in the feminist night marches: “We will intensify our resistance against male and state violence, inequality, and exploitation. Women will continue their struggle for a free and equal life. Women will be free. Society will be free. Peace will be firmly rooted in society, built, and permanently secured by women. We women were here, we are here, and we will be here.”




Hatimoğulları concluded her speech with the slogans: “Long live women’s solidarity! Mara, Hayya, Hurriya!* Jin, Jiyan, Azadî!”




*“Mara, Hayya, Hurriya” is the Levantine Arabic version of “Woman, Life, Freedom.”
