title: Ecological destruction driven by profit in west, security in Kurdistan
content:
The environmental destruction caused by the climate crisis is deepening across Turkey. According to data from the Agriculture and Forestry Workers' Union (Tarım Orman-Iş), 257,000 hectares of forestland have been destroyed in Turkey over the past decade.




The drying up of numerous natural lakes and the transformation of Turkey into a dumping ground for waste are further disrupting the ecological balance. Seasonal differences are becoming less pronounced, temperatures are rising and drought is becoming increasingly widespread.




Academic Metin V. Bayrak, a member of the Climate Justice Coalition and a volunteer with the Peoples' Climate Summit, spoke to ANF about environmental destruction in Turkey and the consequences of the climate crisis.




Bayrak described the climate crisis as the visible manifestation of a crisis of civilisation in nature. He said that humanity's relationship with nature has historically been shaped by domination.




Bayrak said: "What we call the 'climate crisis' is actually the crisis of civilisation becoming visible in nature. Since the Industrial Revolution, we have understood humanity's relationship with nature in terms of domination. Since Francis Bacon, we have regarded knowledge as a tool for controlling nature and nature itself as a resource. This perspective emerged because humanity positioned itself outside nature. Yet we coexist with all living and non-living beings. We are fellow inhabitants of this planet.




We are now reaping the consequences of this way of thinking. We encounter these consequences in every aspect of our lives, from the air we breathe and the water we drink to our food and shelter. However, just as our contributions to creating this crisis are unequal, so too are the ways in which we experience its consequences. The climate crisis is therefore also a question of justice."




'We opened agricultural land to construction'




Bayrak said that Turkey faces environmental problems exacerbated by public policies, in addition to the effects of the global climate crisis: "The global causes of climate change and the problems Turkey has created through its own actions are different. Turkey is located in the Mediterranean basin, a region highly vulnerable to climate change. So what have public authorities done with this knowledge? For decades, we have reduced development to growth, and growth largely to construction, extraction, consumption and, so to speak, plunder. We opened agricultural land to construction, altered riverbeds, drained wetlands and opened forests to mining activities.




How rational is it to measure a country's wealth by the income it generates from consuming its own assets? We claim to create economic value by destroying forests. But is the value of the destroyed forest included in this 'accounting'? What we leave out of these calculations returns to us as ecological debt."




'Destruction in Kurdish regions is justified on security grounds'




Bayrak said that ecological destruction justified on economic grounds in western Turkey is carried out through security policies in Kurdish regions, drawing attention to forest clearing in Şırnak (Şirnex). He said that tree felling in Cudi, Gabar and Besta demonstrates the relationship between security policies and ecological destruction, adding that documents emerging during judicial proceedings also revealed requests for tree felling on security grounds.




Bayrak asked, "We need to question the very concept of 'security' here. Whose security are we talking about, and what are we trying to protect? Whose security are we ensuring by destroying the geography and living spaces of a people?" and added: "We are talking about a region where dams are being built on 'security' grounds, even though dams are known to cause permanent ecological destruction. Security cannot be used as a justification for removing public decisions from public scrutiny. Peace also has an ecological dimension. Can we establish social peace without repairing a people's relationship with the land they inhabit, for example, without reopening pastures?"




'People's relationship with the land has changed'




Bayrak said that the industrialisation of agriculture in Turkey has transformed people's relationship with the land: "With the industrialisation of agriculture, it is not only the mode of production that has changed, but also humanity's relationship with the soil. Farmers were once the bearers of knowledge about life passed down through generations, but they have increasingly become replaceable or expendable links in the industrial production chain.




We confuse soil fertility with soil productivity. In pursuit of higher yields per unit of land, we are exhausting the soil's capacity to regenerate itself. Excessive use of fertilisers and pesticides, monoculture and production that disregards available water resources have become instruments of this process.




The issue is not abandoning technology, but determining what knowledge and values guide its use. The existing model of production and consumption, which disregards the conditions that make production possible, namely nature, is unsustainable. We must consider food sovereignty, biodiversity and farmers' autonomy together."




'

The ecological struggle is a long-term struggle'




Bayrak described the ecological struggle as a long-term endeavour and said that local movements form one of its most important foundations. He stressed the importance of bringing together the experiences of local struggles: "Social struggle is a long-term process. Local struggles are its most important driving force. However, we can achieve the results we seek only to the extent that we create forms of organisation that enable these struggles to learn from one another and share their experiences.




An environmentalist perspective and an ecological perspective are different. When we speak of the environment, we place humanity at the centre and other beings around it. Ecological thinking calls on us to recognise and understand the interdependence of all beings, the concept of coexistence.




The ecological struggle is a struggle to save trees and rivers, but it goes beyond that. It is also a struggle to transform the ways we work, produce, consume, govern and live together. It means discovering what different struggles have in common."




'Climate policies are too important to leave to governments and corporations'




Metin V. Bayrak said that the ecological struggle cannot be separated from society's political and cultural environment, noting that the ecological movement in Turkey is also influenced by nationalism, discrimination and habits of state-centred thinking.




Bayrak said that thousands of activists from different countries had gathered in Antalya for the Peoples' Climate Summit, organised as an alternative to the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31). He emphasised the importance of consistency in the principles guiding the ecological struggle: "The ecological movement in Turkey is not free from the political and cultural baggage of the society in which we live. We cannot claim that nationalism, discrimination and habits of state-centred thinking have not permeated the ecological struggle.




Look, thousands of activists from dozens of countries around the world are now in Antalya for the Peoples' Climate Summit, which we organised as an alternative to COP31, to internationalise the struggle. If we object to the cutting down of a tree in Akbelen but can excuse the felling of a tree in Cudi on security grounds, or if we ignore the genocide in Gaza and the relentless bombing of Yemen in one way or another, we must reconsider the values on which our objections are based. One of the things that distinguishes an ethical position from an opinion is that its underlying principles do not change according to individuals, identities or geographical locations. The ecological struggle can be liberating only to the extent that it challenges all relations of domination established between human beings, nature and peoples."




Bayrak also addressed the possible consequences of the climate crisis, warning that if current policies continue, difficulties in accessing water and food, agricultural production losses, forest fires, internal migration and the resulting social inequalities could increase. He stressed that the future is not defined solely by the negative developments that may occur: "This is also why I attach importance to the Peoples' Climate Summit, which we organised as an alternative to COP31. The formulation of climate policies is far too vital to be left to negotiations between governments and corporations. Lasting solutions cannot be developed unless those whose lives are affected by these decisions become active participants in the decision-making process. After all, we are the ones who will implement these decisions. What we need cannot be reduced to 'renewable energy'. We must develop a renewed political, economic and ethical understanding and create an awareness of our shared existence.




At what cost are we living this life, which is a gift? I do not believe we can build an ecological future without asking this question and confronting our answers. But I believe that our optimism in the will to live is, and will remain, our guide. Because the will to live is real."

author: Unknown
title: Zilan Oktay: Impunity has serious social consequences
content:
In the first ten months of 2026, at least 247 women were killed by men in cities across Kurdistan and Turkey, while 286 women died under suspicious circumstances. Investigations and trials concerning femicides are ongoing, but perpetrators in four femicide cases heard during the year received reductions in their sentences for good conduct. There are no official figures on how many cases in previous years resulted in decisions not to prosecute or were closed without punishment. Despite requests from women's organisations and MPs, up-to-date data has not been made public.




Six women killed and four died suspiciously in Amed




Six women were killed by men in Amed (Diyarbakır) in 2026, while four others died under suspicious circumstances. Most recently, Rojda Odabaşı was shot by her downstairs neighbour, Mazlum Çelebi. Çelebi was arrested following the attack but released two months later.




Women in the city began a justice vigil in response to the rise in femicides and judicial decisions concerning perpetrators. Lawyer Zilan Oktay, a board member of the Women's Rights Centre of the Amed Bar Association, said that decisions reflecting a policy of impunity have consequences that extend beyond courtrooms and affect society as a whole.




Zilan Oktay stressed that such decisions should not be considered solely in relation to individual cases or perpetrators. She said: "These decisions have a profound impact on women's lives and on society."




1,500 applications received in ten months




Zilan Oktay said that the centre had received a total of 1,500 applications since January 2026, with psychological violence accounting for the largest proportion. She explained that while applications concerning physical violence had previously been more common, psychological violence had become increasingly visible in recent years. She attributed this change partly to awareness-raising activities.




Zilan Oktay discussed the distribution of applications and the different forms of violence reported to the centre. Oktay said: "In previous years, applications concerning physical violence were more common, but today we see that psychological violence has become more visible. We believe that the training programmes organised by our centre, local administrations and civil society organisations have contributed to this change.




Women are now better able to identify the forms of violence they experience. The low number of applications concerning sexual violence is related to the fact that this form of violence is not always recognised. Sexual coercion within marriage, in particular, can be normalised. We therefore believe that the number of applications does not fully reflect the actual situation."




'Policies are encouraging perpetrators'




Zilan Oktay said that the perception of impunity is a major problem in combating violence against women. She explained that ineffective investigations, shortcomings in the assessment of evidence, lengthy judicial proceedings and sentence reductions granted in certain cases reinforce this perception. She noted that women seeking justice are repeatedly forced to recount and prove what they have experienced, undermining their confidence in the judiciary.




Oktay emphasised that impunity is not merely a problem confined to judicial proceedings but also influences how perpetrators commit acts of violence. She said that perpetrators calculate the sentences they might receive and the legal reductions they could benefit from before committing their crimes.




Zilan Oktay explained how the perception of impunity develops and how it affects perpetrators. She said: "Even before committing an act, the perpetrator investigates how to receive a lighter sentence and which legal avenues might reduce the punishment. This is because judicial practice sends perpetrators the message that such opportunities exist. Acting with this confidence, perpetrators carry out more planned, coordinated and extensive acts of violence. They make calculations such as, 'I will receive this much punishment, serve some time and then be released, or benefit from supervised release.' In this way, they can anticipate the consequences of their actions and believe that they may somehow escape punishment.




In fact, the state's pursuit of policies that pave the way for perpetrators and encourage them means that they do not fear the consequences of their actions and can commit violence with considerable ease. Even after the act, there is often no fundamental change in the perpetrator's life, and they can simply continue living as before."




'Judicial decisions do not remain within courtrooms'




Zilan Oktay also drew attention to the social consequences of impunity, stressing that a decision in one case does not affect only that particular trial but also the lives and safety of other women. She said that impunity can become an encouraging example for other perpetrators.




Oktay said: "Impunity in one case can become an encouraging example for other perpetrators and pave the way for further acts of violence. Consequently, we cannot assess the impact of decisions resulting in impunity solely in relation to the relevant case or perpetrator. These decisions have social consequences that affect the lives and safety of all women.




Just as we cannot regard violence as an isolated incident, we must not approach policies of impunity solely through individual cases. Every instance of impunity has consequences that can also determine the course of other women's lives."




'Law No. 6284 must be implemented'




Zilan Oktay said that women also encounter problems with the operation of legal mechanisms intended to protect them. She pointed to shortcomings in the implementation and monitoring of protective and preventive orders issued under Law No. 6284.




Oktay stressed that delays in intervention when protective orders are violated, inadequate coordination between institutions and the failure to take the risk of violence sufficiently seriously endanger women's lives. She said that issuing protection orders alone is not enough to guarantee women's safety and emphasised the vital importance of enforcing these orders and responding rapidly to violations.




'Women cannot speak out about violence because of pressure'




Zilan Oktay identified three main obstacles preventing women from reporting violence: social pressure, economic dependence and institutional problems. Oktay said: "Pressure from family members and the wider community, fear of stigmatisation and concerns about children can make it difficult for women to disclose the violence they experience. The lack of economic independence is also a major obstacle preventing women from leaving violent environments. From an institutional perspective, applications not being taken sufficiently seriously, bureaucratic obstacles and approaches that cause secondary victimisation make it more difficult for women to access justice. We must not forget that women's silence does not mean that violence is absent."




Zilan Oktay emphasised that combating violence against women must not be limited to judicial proceedings and that social support policies must be strengthened alongside legal protection mechanisms. She stressed the importance of regular training for judges, prosecutors and law enforcement personnel on gender equality and violence against women. She also called for effective investigations, monitoring of the implementation of protection orders and the completion of judicial proceedings within a reasonable time.




Zilan Oktay said that the capacity of women's shelters must be increased, free legal and psychological support must be provided, and conditions must be created to enable women to achieve economic independence. She also issued an appeal to judicial institutions and decision-makers ahead of 25 November.




Oktay stressed that combating violence against women must go beyond statements of intent and be supported by concrete policies. She said that protecting women's right to life is a fundamental obligation of the state.




'Effective policies against violence must be implemented'




Zilan Oktay delivered a message to judicial institutions and decision-makers on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Oktay said: "Our message to judicial institutions and decision-makers on 25 November is that the struggle against violence against women must not remain merely rhetorical but must be supported by concrete policies. Protecting women's right to life is a fundamental obligation of the state. To achieve this, effective investigations must be conducted, practices that lead to impunity must be prevented, and women's acquired rights must be protected. The experience of women's organisations and bar associations in this struggle must also be utilised, and their active participation in decision-making processes must be ensured. Women's right to live free and equal lives without violence is not a privilege but a fundamental human right."




Zilan Oktay reiterated that guaranteeing women's right to life is their foremost demand. She called for the effective implementation of Law No. 6284 and the elimination of the perception of impunity, outlining their demands as follows: "Our foremost demand is that women's right to life be guaranteed and that violence be combated through effective policies. We demand the effective implementation of Law No. 6284, penalties proportionate to the crimes committed by perpetrators of violence, and the elimination of the perception of impunity.




In addition, conditions must be created to enable women to achieve economic independence, the number of shelters must be increased, and access to free legal and psychological support must be guaranteed. Women's ability to live safely is not merely an aspiration but a legal and social responsibility that the state must fulfil."

title: Narges Mohammadi calls for the protection of women against cyber threats
content:
Women in Iran face legal and societal threats. While women's rights organisations continue to call for the strengthening and enforcement of existing laws and institutions that safeguard women's dignity and security, Nobel Peace Prize-winning activist Narges Mohammadi has released a video message.




In her message, shared on a digital platform, Narges Mohammadi called for solidarity with and support for women who are subjected to organised cyber threats and interference because of their activities in social, political, media and human rights fields.




Narges Mohammadi said that, in recent years, she herself has faced harassment, insults, death threats and widespread gender-based cyber violence, adding that these attacks continued even while she was imprisoned.




Addressing the methods of cyber harassment targeting women, Narges Mohammadi explained that these attacks include organised smear campaigns, the exposure of personal information, insults, misogyny, the spread of misinformation and the circulation of fabricated images generated using artificial intelligence (AI). She emphasised that the aim of these attacks is to isolate, intimidate and silence women.

title: Iranian regime detains Hazim Haşimî in Awdanan
content:
Following protests in the Awdanan district over a traffic accident involving a bus transporting workers from the Dehloran Refinery, in which 13 workers lost their lives, the number of people detained has risen to 13.




According to Kolber News, forces affiliated with the Iranian regime, along with masked groups, raided the home and workplace of Hemze Haşimî and Hisên Haşimî in the city of Awdanan, in Ilam Province. During the raid, Hazim Haşimî was beaten and tortured before being detained without a court warrant and taken to an unknown location.




It was reported that, during Hazim Haşimî’s arrest, armed individuals pointed their weapons at his mother and demanded that she hand over her other son, Husên Haşimî. The armed individuals also reportedly threatened and assaulted other members of the family.

title: DEM Party delegation travels to İmralı to meet with Öcalan
content:
The İmralı delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) has traveled to the Turkish prison island of Imrali on Sunday to meet with Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. The delegation consists of members of parliament Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, and lawyer Faik Özgür Erol from Asrın Law Office.




The DEM Party İmralı delegation last visited Öcalan on September 13.




DEM Party Co-Chair Tuncer Bakırhan stated during his party’s parliamentary group meeting on November 17 that Öcalan had been moved to a residential area specially built for him on Imrali. Accordingly, his working conditions have also changed following the relocation. In addition, his secretarial support has been increased to enable him to work more quickly and effectively, Bakırhan stated.




The changes are linked to the ongoing peace and democratization process. In his speech, Bakırhan emphasized that, following the cessation of armed hostilities and the initiation of dialogue, the focus must now be on establishing the legal and political foundations and opening up space for democratic politics.

title: Guerrillas on the PKK’s 48th founding anniversary: We will fulfill our responsibilities
content:
The Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) was founded on November 27, 1978, in the village of Fis in the Lice district of Amed (Diyarbakır). Speaking to ANF in Behdînan ahead of the 48th anniversary of the party’s founding, HPG and YJA-Star guerrillas said they regarded November 27 as a national festival.




Delal Çiya, Elî Dirêj, Amed Derik, and Ezîz Derwêş shared their assessments of the PKK’s influence in Kurdistan and the Middle East, the women’s movement, and the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




YJA-Star guerrilla Delal Çiya:

 We celebrate the anniversary of our party, the PKK, in the person of Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan], the martyrs of the revolution, and the entire people of Kurdistan. This is truly a very meaningful and important day. Thanks to the efforts of the comrades who took part in the founding of the party alongside the Leader and devoted themselves to it, the party has endured to this day, undergoing change and transformation and bringing about new developments within its own ranks. The struggle continues and grows stronger through the efforts of the comrades who have resisted and given their lives. With comrades Haki Karer, Mazlum Doğan, and Sakine Cansız resisting in prison and raising the slogan “Berxwedan Jiyane” [Resistance is Life], the resistance gained momentum. At the same time, our party also carried out a revolution within its own ranks, giving rise to the “Jin Jiyan Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom] revolution, which continues to this day. Women came to know themselves, grew stronger, and developed a will of their own. Once again, we celebrate our party’s anniversary in the person of the Leader, our fallen comrades, and all our peoples.

 We congratulate Leader Apo, all the martyrs of the revolution, and our patriotic people on the founding anniversary of our party. November 27 holds a very special meaning for us. The PKK was founded following the martyrdom of Comrade Haki Karer. The Kurdish people, who have endured great massacres throughout history, have remained standing through tremendous resistance. We must uphold this resistance. November 27 holds a special significance and spiritual value for us. Strengthening the struggle that has brought us to this day, in the spirit of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, is a fundamental duty for us. Our task is to further strengthen the struggle and demonstrate our commitment and dedication with this spirit and enthusiasm.

The efforts made over the years have made the struggle even more necessary today. We learned from our martyrs to persevere in the pursuit of a free life. With this awareness, we have sought to fulfill our duties and responsibilities. On this basis, it is the duty of all of us to uphold this process. title: Protests in Qamişlo: 25 Rojava University students injured
content:
A total of 25 students were injured on November 16 in Qamişlo during protests against the planned incorporation of Rojava University into Syria’s state higher education system. The university’s Student Council announced the figures at a press conference on Sunday. For the first time, the council also confirmed that shots had been fired on university grounds during the crackdown. The council condemned the use of tear gas and firearms against the protesters as a serious violation of the university’s autonomy and the safety of its students.




The statement was issued on the university campus in Qamişlo in the presence of students. Mehebad Adil Serhan read it in Kurdish, while Fadiya Ebdullah read it in English. The Student Council explained that the delay in issuing the statement was due to its efforts over the past few days to care for the injured students and investigate the consequences of the events.




Dispute over the future of Rojava University




The clashes were triggered by a visit from a delegation from Damascus on Monday. The delegation held talks with the university administration about the planned incorporation of Rojava University into al-Furat University in Hesekê. Following the meeting, students demanded information about the decisions reached and the future of their university. When the delegation refused to make a statement, the students blocked its departure.




The conflict stems from two measures introduced by Syria’s transitional government. In addition to the planned incorporation of Rojava University into al-Furat University, the dispute concerns the Ministry of Education’s decision to revoke the recognition of equivalency for degrees awarded by certain faculties. Students regard these measures as an attack on their university’s independent academic and institutional identity.




The protests were therefore directed not merely against an administrative restructuring, but also against interference in academic self-governance and the students’ future. When the students insisted on receiving information about the planned changes, security forces of the transitional government attacked the protesters.




“Unjustifiable under any circumstances”




The Student Council described the actions as a serious violation of university autonomy and a direct threat to the safety and health of students. The protests, it said, had been an expression of legitimate demands and a commitment to preserving the academic and administrative independence of their university. Rather than resorting to violence, it added, those responsible should have sought dialogue and listened to the students’ concerns.




“What we witnessed on university grounds was the use of tear gas and firearms, which left 25 students injured. These shocking scenes are unacceptable under any circumstances and cannot be justified in any way,” the council stated. It condemned the use of military force, weapons, tear gas, and smoke agents on campus as “an attack on the inviolability of the educational institution and the dignity of all students.”




The statement did not specify whether the students’ injuries were caused by tear gas, gunfire, or other forms of violence.




Protection against reprisals and preservation of university autonomy




The council also strongly opposed any potential reprisals related to the protests. “We firmly reject any decision or measure aimed at arresting or prosecuting students for their participation in the peaceful defense of their rights,” the statement read. Such actions would further exacerbate tensions within the university, the Student Council warned and therefore demanded binding guarantees for students’ safety and protection against intimidation, pressure, and all forms of discrimination.




Regarding the university’s future, the council reaffirmed its commitment to preserving its academic and administrative independence. “Students must be able to voice their concerns peacefully and participate in decisions affecting their education and the university’s institutional future. We reject the imposition of decisions with far-reaching consequences without dialogue and mutual understanding,” the council declared. It also stressed that students must not be made to bear the consequences of decisions that jeopardize their academic future.




Appeal to international academic and human rights organizations




The Student Council called on international academic institutions, human rights organizations, and student representative bodies to examine the events in Qamişlo, support those affected, and advocate for measures to prevent such attacks from recurring. In closing, the council emphasized the university’s responsibility to society: “The university is a place of science, dialogue, and the education of future generations—not a place for intimidation and violence against those making peaceful demands. The voices of students must be heard. Their dignity, their safety, and their right to education are red lines that must not be crossed.”

title: YRK reports ongoing attacks by the Iranian regime in East Kurdistan
content:
The Press and Liaison Center of the East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) issued a statement providing information about ongoing attacks by the Iranian regime in East Kurdistan (Rojhilat).




According to the statement on Sunday, the Iranian regime has once again bombarded the Serçûrî district of Merîwan using drones and 120 mm mortars. It said the attacks were launched from the military base in the village of Derê and surrounding positions.




According to the statement, the attacks caused damage to the local environment, landscape, natural resources, and wildlife.




The YRK confirmed that no fatalities occurred in their ranks as a result of the attacks.




The YRK also reported that the Iranian regime was preparing for a large-scale military operation in Serdeşt. It stated that the regime was preventing civilians from entering or leaving the area and attempting to create an atmosphere of fear and anxiety.




The YRK declared that it would respond to any attack carried out against its forces by the Iranian regime within the framework of “legitimate self-defense” and emphasized that it was prepared for any eventuality.

title: Protest against two years of state-appointed trustees in Dersim
content:
A rally was held in Seyîd Riza Square in Dersim (Turkish: Tunceli) to mark the second anniversary of the appointment of state-appointed trustees to the municipalities of Dersim and Ovacık district. The demonstration was organized by the Labor and Democracy Platform and attended by local residents and representatives of political parties and civil society organizations. Participants demanded the removal of the trustees and the reinstatement of the democratically elected municipal administrations.




“Social peace cannot be achieved through the appointment of trustees”




Demonstrators carried a banner reading: “The appointment of trustees is an attack on the will of the people and public resources. We do not accept it.” The platform’s joint statement was read out by Özcan Ateş, Co-Chair of the DEM Party’s provincial branch in Dersim. He criticized the fact that the democratically expressed will of the people of Dersim and Ovacık had been disregarded for two years.




Referring to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process, Ateş stated that ending the system of trustees was a necessary prerequisite for credible democratization. “Peace can only be achieved if democratic rights are genuinely guaranteed. Without recognizing the will of the people, a democratic society cannot be built. Social peace cannot be achieved through the policy of appointing trustees,” Ateş emphasized.




Birsen Orhan: State-appointed trustees must be removed




Birsen Orhan, the elected Co-Mayor of Dersim who was replaced by a state-appointed trustee, then took the floor. She criticized the consequences of two years of trustee administration, highlighting in particular the dismissal of municipal employees who have been unable to return to their jobs despite court rulings.




Orhan also recalled the case of Gülistan Doku, a university student who disappeared in 2020 and whose fate has remained a matter of concern for the people of Dersim for years. Tuncay Sonel, the governor and state-appointed trustee at the time, is currently in pretrial detention in connection with the suspected femicide of the then 21-year-old woman.




“For two years, the will of the people has been disregarded, and this disregard is even being portrayed as a success story,” Orhan said. She stressed that respecting democratic decisions was a fundamental prerequisite for the ongoing peace process. “The appointment of trustees contradicts the spirit of this process, and these administrations must be revoked.”




Trustee administration also targets identity




The ousted Co-Mayor Cevdet Konak also offered a critical assessment of the state-appointed administration in Dersim. He said the past two years had been marked by losses and institutional decline. He stressed that the interventions had targeted not only the elected municipal representatives but also the city’s social and cultural identity.




“The trustee administration was also imposed on the language, identity, faith, and memory of Dersim. Decisions are being made without transparency and with the public excluded from the process,” Konak stated. He demanded public accountability for the past two years: “Disclose what you have done over these two years. Can you do that? No, you cannot. You talk about the public interest and building trust. Why, then, have you closed the places where the people of Dersim could express themselves?”




Konak pointed to the contradiction between the peace process and continued state control over municipalities. “While we are engaged in a peace process, our will continues to be overridden by a state-appointed trustee. We say: Restore our democratic self-governance and remove the trustees.”




Criticism of environmental destruction and economic interests




Mustafa Sarıgül, the elected Mayor of Ovacık who was replaced by a state-appointed trustee, recalled that municipal officials had been elected to office by the people. “Only the people can remove us from office,” he declared.




Sarıgül noted that they had worked to protect the language, nature, and social identity of their region during their time in office. He particularly criticized the ongoing destruction of Dersim’s natural environment and the commercial exploitation of its landscape.




“Recently, the beauty of Dersim has been praised everywhere. If that is the case, why are roads being built through our forests, our natural environment being destroyed, and our natural resources being handed over to capital?” Sarıgül asked. He emphasized that regardless of how long the trustee administration remained in place, the people would continue their collective resistance against these policies.




Call for democratic steps in the peace process




DEM Party MP Ayten Kordu criticized the continued use of state-appointed trustees as a routine instrument for exercising political power. She argued that the practice was far from being abolished and persisted as a form of state control over democratically elected municipalities.




Representatives of other political parties also referred to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process. They called for concrete steps toward democratization, particularly an end to trustee administrations and the restoration of municipal authority to elected representatives.

title: Füsun Demirel calls on artists to march for women
content:
Actress and translator Füsun Demirel, who delivered a message against violence against women and femicides through ANF, stressed that artists must take responsibility for social issues.




Füsun Demirel drew attention to the fact that violence against women and femicides have become a deep social wound and a political issue. She said: "In this period, speaking out has become not merely a choice for artists, especially women artists, but a moral and humanitarian responsibility."




'We should not simply wait for money or awards'




Füsun Demirel said that actors do more than simply bring characters to life. She said: "Those who create art are not people who should simply produce their works, step aside and wait for awards or money. They should not be."




Füsun Demirel emphasised that artists are also witnesses to their times and the conscience of society. Demirel continued: "When a woman is killed, it is not only one life that ends. A future, a hope and a story also come to an end. We must become the voice of those unfinished stories. Our real responsibility is not to speak when and where everyone else is speaking, but to raise our voices when and where everyone else remains silent. Isn't it those silences that give birth to art?"




'Women artists were forced to behave like men'




Füsun Demirel also drew attention to male dominance in the arts, saying that it determines not only women's visibility but also how they are represented, which stories they can tell and whether they can become the subjects of their own stories.




Demirel said: "Women have been involved in art for centuries, but because they were not given the opportunity to express themselves as creators, they existed as the male artist's muse, the painter's model, the beautiful woman in a film or the self-sacrificing mother in a story. Women's stories were told, but because they were told from a male-dominated perspective, women were either wives, mistresses, mothers or victims. In other words, women were figures who merely complemented men's stories. Their rebellion, anger, objections and dreams were always treated as though they did not exist.




Even Bilge Olgaç, who established herself in the male-dominated world of Yeşilçam cinema and made films that brought women's stories to the forefront from a woman's perspective, was described as 'a director like a man'. In other words, we were forced to behave like men in order to survive in that world.




Of course, there are also things I have personally witnessed. For example, in one television series, the storyline had begun to focus more on the female lead, and the male lead immediately objected. The dispute escalated considerably, and the series eventually came to an end."




'

Sıdıka' memory: 'Whenever the father hit me, I hit back'




Füsun Demirel said that scripts which normalise violence deeply disturb her and that she tries to avoid such projects from the outset. However, she explained that problematic situations can sometimes emerge as a story develops and that she intervenes whenever possible.




Füsun Demirel described an incident from the television series Sıdıka. She said: "As much as possible, I avoid accepting such projects from the beginning. But sometimes situations develop later in the story. I intervene as much as I can. For example, in the series Sıdıka, there was constant violence by the father at home. It was a comedy series, filmed from a critical perspective. Nevertheless, to avoid legitimising violence against women, I eventually intervened one day. Whenever the father hit me, I hit back and defended myself. Our director was also a woman. She did not impose any limits on me. She said, 'Do whatever you want.' As a result, the male actor objected. He said, 'There is feminist solidarity on this set.' Filming stopped that day."




Füsun Demirel said that she takes inspiration from Iranian cinema. She said: "In the face of all forms of social and political oppression against women, directors in Iranian cinema have always found a way to speak out for women's freedom. Some were imprisoned, others were forced into exile. But they never refrained from speaking their minds."




'Those posing on red carpets should march for women for once'




Füsun Demirel also stressed that art should become a space of struggle and solidarity against violence against women. She made the following appeal: "Institutions representing the industry, such as the Actors' Union and the Writers' Union, as well as directors, should organise protests against femicides. Would it really be so bad if female actors, stars, those earning millions, those talented beauties who pose on red carpets every night at an opening, a premiere or a party, marched for murdered women for once?"

title: Alfred de Zayas: Why should Kurds be denied the right to self-determination? - Part Two
content:
Alfred de Zayas, an expert in international law and human rights who served as the United Nations (UN) Independent Expert on the Promotion of a Democratic and Equitable International Order from 2012 to 2018, spoke to ANF about the Kurdish people's right to self-determination and autonomy, the possibilities of obtaining status within the UN, the treatment of stateless peoples and double standards in international law.




The first part of this interview can be found 

here

. 




Under Article 4 of the United Nations Charter, UN membership is open only to states. However, there are peoples such as the Kurds who do not have their own state. How can these peoples obtain a status or the right to representation within the UN?




This is first and foremost a political issue. From a legal perspective, it is quite straightforward because the Palestinians have managed to obtain a certain degree of international recognition. We know about the genocides committed against Palestinians and the ethnic cleansing they have suffered. There is growing sympathy for the Palestinian people. By contrast, almost nothing is known about the Kurds. What do we see about the Kurds in the press? The first thing that comes to people's minds is "terrorism".




Turkey has demonised Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurds in Turkey to such an extent that a large proportion of people have accepted this propaganda. Therefore, this propaganda must be countered. The mechanisms known as the "Special Procedures" of the UN Human Rights Council must be activated. These mechanisms include special rapporteurs working in different fields. It is extremely important that what is happening in the Kurdish regions of Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria be made known through the UN and these rapporteurs. Therefore, the first step is to provide information.




Once awareness has been raised about the injustices suffered by the Kurdish people, a political coalition could emerge to support, first, extensive autonomy for the Kurdish people and then, if the people so wish, the right to secession. I believe that the United Nations has failed to fulfil its responsibility towards the Kurdish people. The UN has also failed in its duty to the world by not organising referendums where they were needed.




Referendums were held in East Timor, South Sudan and during the process of separation between Ethiopia and Eritrea. However, these initiatives came far too late. Action was taken only after tens of thousands of people had lost their lives. Preventive action should have been taken instead. You should also be very familiar with the Constitution of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), because UNESCO's responsibilities include protecting Kurdish culture, identity, language, cultural heritage and collective memory. UNESCO has organised numerous international conferences on these issues.




For example, I would like to recall the conference held in Barcelona in November and December 1998. Following that conference, a declaration was adopted on using the right to self-determination as a strategy for preventing conflicts. The right to self-determination does not cause war. On the contrary, the unjust denial of this right leads to violence. If we want to preserve local, regional and international peace, we must resolve these issues.




As we have seen in the case of Palestine, when a people is subjected to colonisation or an apartheid regime, the United Nations has a clear role and responsibility to fulfil.




But the UN has done nothing.




'

The UN has surrendered to political interests'




What concerns me deeply is the way the UN has surrendered to political interests. Let me give you an example. About a year ago, on 17 November 2025, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803. This resolution envisaged the creation of a so-called "Board of Peace" associated with Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu.




What does this mean? It is completely absurd, appalling and unacceptable. The UN Security Council cannot delegate its own obligations to a supposedly private body called the "Board of Peace". This is a fundamental contradiction and an entirely unacceptable situation.




I was genuinely surprised that Russia and China abstained from the vote. They should have exercised their veto powers. This was precisely a situation in which a veto would have been justified, even necessary. The issue was not merely about Gaza or Palestine. In my opinion, Donald Trump's objective with this "Board of Peace" was to replace the UN. In reality, it was an attempt to transfer the responsibilities of the UN Security Council into Donald Trump's hands.




'International law must protect the fundamental rights of Kurds'




Beyond the right to self-determination, the political, cultural and linguistic rights of the Kurdish people in the countries where they live are also important issues under international law. What legal mechanisms can be used to bring the human rights violations suffered by Kurds in these countries onto the international legal agenda?




International law is clear on this matter. It recognises not only the rights of peoples but also the rights of minorities. Minority rights are not limited to the right to freedom from discrimination. They are also positive rights. They include the right of a minority to preserve its culture, speak its own language and maintain its own institutions. This is what international law provides for in theory.




As you know, Turkey is not a member of the European Union (EU). However, it is a member of the Council of Europe and a party to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). Therefore, applications should also be made to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerning violations of Kurdish rights in Turkey.




The European Convention on Human Rights system also provides for interstate applications. In other words, a state party to the Convention can bring an application against another state, including Turkey, for violations of the rights guaranteed under the Convention.




This mechanism also exists under the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD). Where the necessary conditions are met, interstate complaints, as well as individual complaints, can be submitted to the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD).




There are already numerous cases concerning Israel. In particular, I would like to recall the proceedings initiated by Palestine against Israel before CERD. Numerous cases have also been examined by the Committee Against Torture (CAT).




It is also worth recalling that Article 41 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) provides for an interstate complaint mechanism under certain conditions. If I am not mistaken, approximately 172 states are parties to this Covenant. Therefore, although it is not entirely universal, it comes quite close.




Under this mechanism, states that have accepted the relevant competence of the committee can allege that another state which has accepted the same procedure has violated the Covenant.




In the case of Turkey, numerous articles of the Covenant can be invoked. Article 1 concerns the right of peoples to self-determination. Article 6 protects the right to life, Article 7 prohibits torture, and Article 14 guarantees the right to a fair trial and the independence of the courts. Article 25 concerns participation in political life, Article 26 guarantees equality and prohibits discrimination, and Article 27 protects minority rights.




'States do not dare to act'




I would like to see a state use the existing mechanisms to bring the situation of the Kurdish people before the UN Human Rights Committee. So far, no state has dared to do so. I do not understand why. This is precisely where you have a major responsibility. First, you must inform people about all the available legal avenues and international mechanisms, including interstate complaint procedures.




Perhaps a state could be found that is willing to undertake such an initiative against Turkey. This is an issue of universal importance. States parties to the Covenant have a legitimate interest in demanding compliance with its provisions.




I am very familiar with the procedures of the UN Human Rights Committee. I personally participated in drafting the committee's rules of procedure at the time. Therefore, I know very well how it operates. The legal avenues exist. However, the greatest obstacle is the lack of information and awareness. The world does not know enough about the situation of the Kurds.




Unfortunately, Turkey has succeeded in demonising the Kurds, just as Israel has done with the Palestinians. This perception, based on portraying Kurds as "terrorists", must be challenged. People need to understand that the Kurds have long possessed the right to self-determination.




You have spoken about the right of peoples to resist occupation and oppression under international law and emphasised that the Kurds are under occupation. In this context, could the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has now dissolved itself, have been considered a resistance movement? How should we interpret the EU's continued designation of the PKK as a "terrorist" organisation despite its dissolution and insistence on peace?




The problem is that the European Union is morally bankrupt. This may sound somewhat radical to you, but that is how I see the situation. For decades, the European Union has provided military, economic, political, diplomatic and media support to a state that I believe is responsible for genocide.




What values do Europeans actually defend? They no longer have any moral authority. They repeat the propaganda used by Israel against Palestinians. At the same time, they make use of Turkey's propaganda against the Kurds. This is easy to do because trade relations continue.




'The EU is morally bankrupt'




If you want to convince Erdoğan or the Turkish government that this situation can no longer continue, you can take action in the field of trade. You can stop selling certain products to Turkey or purchasing products from Turkey.




The same applies to the policies of the US and Donald Trump. Why do states continue to buy Boeing aircraft? Why do they buy military equipment manufactured by Lockheed Martin or Raytheon, or F-35 and F-16 fighter jets produced by the American defence industry? Why do they continue purchasing US Treasury bonds? These practices must end.




This is precisely the fundamental principle of the BDS movement, which stands for Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions. If this strategy were applied not only to Israel but also to the US, changes would occur. When economic interests begin to suffer, there can be significant political consequences. However, we need to be conscious of this. What concerns me is that we continue to act as though nothing has happened and carry on with business as usual.




Numerous statements are made in support of Palestinians, and strong language is used. But is anything concrete actually being done to save these people, who are suffering and facing severe oppression? No. We are merely talking. As I said earlier, I find it shameful that António Guterres has not used the term "genocide" when condemning crimes committed by Israel. I also find it shameful that, in my opinion, the United Nations continues to repeat Turkey's propaganda against the Kurds.




We live in a deeply flawed world. We need a forum where states can discuss peace, development, climate and the major challenges facing the world. We need to find global solutions to global problems. We need coordination, dialogue and a better understanding of one another.




I am deeply committed to the United Nations General Assembly and its universal character. I would also like the UN Human Rights Council to be based on universal participation rather than a system consisting of only 47 elected states. I know how these elections are conducted and all the political manoeuvring that accompanies them. I also know about the negotiations, reciprocal interests and agreements between states to secure a seat on the Human Rights Council.




If the Human Rights Council were transformed into a genuine human rights general assembly in which all states had equal voting rights, the world would be a much better place. The system would function much better and would be far less vulnerable to political manoeuvring. In any case, the Kurds know their rights. What matters to them is defending their culture, language and heritage. You are Kurdish, and you can be proud of being Kurdish.




Therefore, continue to struggle through peaceful means, as you have done until now. Continue to convince the world and inform international public opinion about your situation and your rights.




Who is Alfred de Zayas?




Alfred de Zayas is a lawyer, historian, academic and author known for his work on international law, human rights and the right of peoples to self-determination. He studied law at Harvard University and obtained a doctorate in history from the University of Göttingen in Germany. He is a professor of international law and history at the Geneva School of Diplomacy in Switzerland.




Between 1980 and 2003, de Zayas worked as a lawyer in the United Nations human rights offices in Geneva, serving as secretary of the UN Human Rights Committee and head of its petitions unit. From 2012 to 2018, he served as the first UN Independent Expert on the Promotion of a Democratic and Equitable International Order, appointed by the UN Human Rights Council. During this period, he submitted 14 reports to the UN General Assembly and the Human Rights Council.




De Zayas has written numerous books and academic articles on international law, minority rights, genocide, self-determination and UN reform. His works include Building a Just World Order and United Nations Human Rights Committee Case Law.







Alfred de Zayas: Why should Kurds be denied the right to self-determination? - Part One

The right of peoples to self-determination is one of the fundamental principles of international law. However, its implementation remains contested because of the political and economic interests o...

title: Batı: Maintenance and production overlapped at HABAŞ
content:
The working conditions, subcontracting system, lack of occupational health and safety measures, and trade union organisation at the HABAŞ iron and steel plant in Aliağa, Izmir, have come under scrutiny following the workplace massacre. Nineteen metalworkers lost their lives at the plant. Even before their colleagues trapped beneath the rubble could be recovered, production continued, and workers were called in for their shifts. Outrage grew further when workers were prohibited from bringing mobile phones into the factory, reportedly on the orders of HABAŞ owner Mehmet Rüştü Başaran, who had been released under house arrest and issued the instruction from his waterfront mansion in Istanbul. Workers protesting this brutal system of exploitation, built on their own blood, were then confronted by the state's gendarmerie. Lawyer Lütfi Sabri Batı, who represents workers in the industrial areas between Soma and Izmir, spoke to ANF about the conditions facing workers caught between the threat of death and the fear of unemployment, under a system involving employers, the state and company-friendly unions. Batı said that workers returned to their jobs on the morning of 16 November in all sections of the plant except the unit where the explosion occurred. He recalled Article 13 of Occupational Health and Safety Law No. 6331, saying, "Workers have the right to refuse to work in the face of serious and imminent danger. They need to submit a written application and exercise this right."




'

Only 500 to 600 of HABAŞ's approximately 6,000 workers are directly employed'




Lawyer Lütfi Sabri Batı said that the HABAŞ facility in Aliağa, where 19 workers lost their lives, covers an extensive industrial area of approximately 10 square kilometres and carries out various metal production activities, including steel, iron and steel, and aluminium production. Batı said that approximately 6,000 workers are employed at HABAŞ's metal smelting and refining facilities, which also have their own private port. Only 500 to 600 of these workers are directly employed by HABAŞ, while the rest work for subcontracting companies. Batı said that between 20 and 25 different subcontracting companies reportedly operate across the extensive production facilities. Batı said: "HABAŞ essentially operates through subcontracting companies. Job insecurity is extremely high. The company is classified as a heavy and hazardous workplace, with temperatures reaching 400 degrees. Many workers are not directly employed by HABAŞ. HABAŞ's directly employed workers are organised in Türk Metal, a union affiliated with the Confederation of Turkish Trade Unions (Türk-Iş). Türk Metal does not attempt to organise the subcontracted workers, nor does it allow another union to operate within these facilities. Because there is a gentlemen's agreement between the three trade union confederations in the metal sector, the United Metalworkers' Union (Birleşik Metal-Iş), affiliated with the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DISK), cannot organise here. It cannot even call Türk Metal a company-friendly union. This situation could change if workers collectively joined another union, but organising is difficult because most are employed through subcontractors. As a result, Türk Metal has effectively established a monopoly over these facilities."




'

Experienced workers are dismissed with severance pay and rehired on lower wages'




Batı visited the families of workers killed in the massacre to offer his condolences and met with five families. He said that most HABAŞ workers come from other provinces and work under extremely difficult conditions. Batı said that he met the families of Özcan Efe, Ferhat Maraşlı, Ersin Oğuz, Kadir Kaan Özçelik and Yasin Taşçı, five of the 19 workers who lost their lives. Batı said: "Özcan Efe was from Ağrı but lived with his family in Manisa. He was the father of one child and was directly employed by HABAŞ. Ferhat Maraşlı had also been a directly employed worker for 16 years. Ersin Oğuz belonged to the Çepni Alevi community and lived in Kınık. He was also the first cousin of the wife of Tahir Çetin, a founding member and honorary president of the Independent Mineworkers' Union (Bağımsız Maden-Iş), who died in a traffic accident. Ersin worked there as a subcontracted worker. Kadir Kaan Özçelik was a 25-year-old engineer. He also worked at HABAŞ through a subcontractor. Yasin Taşçı was directly employed. Workers employed by subcontracting companies in particular work their regular shifts plus four hours of overtime, bringing their daily working hours to 12. Subcontracted workers earn approximately 30,000 Turkish lira. They try to increase their wages to 40,000 lira by working overtime on their weekly days off. They are forced to sacrifice even their right to rest for approximately 10,000 lira in additional income. There is a system in these facilities under which directly employed workers receive pay increases according to their years of service. But particularly over the past two years, a different practice has been introduced for experienced workers. They tell experienced workers, 'Take your severance pay and leave.' They pay the workers their compensation and dismiss them. If the same worker wants to return to HABAŞ, they are forced to accept a 30 percent reduction in their salary. The company simply claims that their previous wages were too high. In other words, over the past two years, HABAŞ has been dismissing directly employed workers after paying their severance, then rehiring them at wages 30 percent lower, effectively resetting their seniority."




'The subcontracting system is a sham, and conditions are worse than in the mines'




Batı continued: "There is also a sham subcontracting system here. In reality, all the subcontractors are connected to the main company in one way or another. The same system probably exists at HABAŞ. Subcontracting companies recruit workers through a system similar to the labour recruiters known as dayıbaşı in the Soma mines. For example, workers hired for cleaning duties may also be assigned to production. The facility also has its own port, so there are separate subcontractors for port operations. In reality, an entire complex of companies operates within the facility because so many different activities take place simultaneously. Scrap metal arrives, is melted down and then processed into new products. The products must also be packaged, shipped and transported. Subcontractors have been assigned to every one of these auxiliary operations. The working conditions imposed at these facilities are so appalling that even miners would struggle to work there. Conditions are worse than in the mines."




'

Production was not stopped during crane maintenance on the day of the explosion'




Batı said that the explosion occurred on 9 November 2026, normally a weekly rest day, when workers had come to the factory to earn additional income through overtime. Batı also said: "When we spoke to the family of Ersin Oğuz, who died in the explosion, they told us that the workers had gone to the iron and steel plant that day to work overtime. Maintenance work was being carried out on the day of the explosion. In other words, maintenance was taking place in an area where production was also continuing. Özcan Efe, whose family we spoke to, was at the factory that day to carry out maintenance on the crane used to transport the molten metal ladles. We do not know whether the crane was faulty or whether this was routine maintenance. But the fundamental problem is that production should normally stop when maintenance is being carried out in a workplace. You should not operate machinery for production while simultaneously carrying out maintenance on it. Yet production was not stopped during maintenance at this facility. Consequently, there were many workers at the factory that day, and something probably triggered an incident during maintenance, causing the explosion. There was already a ladle containing molten metal at a temperature of around 1,000 degrees. Steel is also melted using natural gas. The crane struck the ladle, its chains failed to hold it, and the ladle overturned. It may have struck the natural gas pipes, or something spilling from it may have struck the pipes. Either possibility could have occurred. The molten metal inside the ladle had a minimum temperature of 1,000 degrees. Apart from the maintenance workers, 50 workers were on duty that day. So far, 19 workers are reported to have died, but searches are continuing for other workers trapped beneath the rubble. For example, we received information that the owner of the subcontracting company where Özcan Efe worked went there to search for his workers. The bodies of many workers have still not been recovered, and they are probably unrecognisable."




'Production continued while workers' bodies remained under the rubble'




Batı said that production continued at the factory even while the bodies of workers remained trapped beneath the rubble. He said that the explosion occurred during the morning shift, at approximately 11:30 am to noon, but production at the other facilities continued until 4 pm. Batı said that although production was subsequently suspended in the days following the massacre, workers continued to be transported to the factory by shuttle buses in three shifts. Batı said: "On the day of the explosion, Türk Metal told the workers, 'Occupational health and safety conditions at the workplace are satisfactory. Continue working.' Yet the workers' bodies had not even been recovered from the rubble. Workers were transported to the factory by shuttle buses, but production had stopped. They were kept inside without being assigned any work. Most recently, the employer also ordered that workers be prohibited from bringing their phones into the facility. They were probably trying to conceal evidence. They introduced the phone ban to prevent workers from entering and taking photographs, but they were unable to enforce it. Workers reacted against the ban. Workers who wanted to protest against Türk Metal during its public statement were beaten. Türk Metal brought its own members outside for the statement and attempted to have the factory workers who wanted to protest against the union attacked by the crowd. To allow Türk Metal to make its statement, the gendarmerie first removed the HABAŞ workers from the area and then detained them."




'Occupational safety exists only on paper, with no inspections in the explosion unit'




Batı said that HABAŞ has a long record of workplace deaths, claiming that more than 100 workers have been killed in workplace incidents at the facility since the 1990s. He said that 550 officially recorded workplace accidents occurred between 2021 and 2024, while the number reached 240 in 2025 alone, indicating a significant increase. Batı also recalled that Eyüp Eğinli, a 20-year-old subcontracted worker, was killed in a workplace incident on 5 November, just four days before the major explosion on 9 November. He said that the massacre had been foreseeable. Batı said that inspections at HABAŞ, as at other workplaces, were largely a formality. He said: "A worker I spoke to told me that occupational health and safety specialists had never entered the sections where the explosion occurred. There cannot be a section of a workplace that occupational health and safety personnel never inspect. Occupational health and safety exists on paper, but no inspections were actually carried out. These specialists work under Joint Health and Safety Units (ÖSGB). These units operate as joint-stock companies. Such companies sign contracts with other companies to provide occupational health and safety services. Consequently, the company responsible for inspections receives its payment from the very employers it is supposed to inspect. That is how the system works. Unfortunately, this is a reality in Turkey."




'

Workers now have to make a choice'




Batı said that workers were ordered to return to work on the morning of 16 November in all sections of the factory except the unit where the explosion occurred, despite the earlier suspension of production and the continuing search for workers trapped beneath the rubble. He recalled that Occupational Health and Safety Law No. 6331 gives workers the right to refuse to work in dangerous conditions. He explained that workers must submit a written application to their employer to exercise this right. Batı stressed that workers must overcome their fear of dismissal and struggle to protect their lives. Batı said: "The working class is strong when it becomes a class for itself, and it is workers' organisation that makes this possible. Therefore, workers must organise. They can establish workers' assemblies, form committees or join genuine trade unions. If genuine trade unions refuse to accept them because of a gentlemen's agreement or for some other reason, workers should establish their own independent unions, just like the Warehouse, Port, Shipyard and Maritime Workers' Union (DGD-Sen), the Independent Mineworkers' Union (Bağımsız Maden-Iş) and the United Textile, Weaving and Leather Workers' Union (BIRTEK-SEN). Six workers die every day in this country. Workers now have to make a choice. Either they overcome their fears and join genuine trade unions and organisations, or, if that is not possible, they establish their own unions and organisations. Otherwise, they might as well side with the employers and accept that workers can be killed. There is no middle ground anymore."

title: Kurdish Film Festival in Zurich: Let our stories not be forgotten
content:
The Kurdish Film Festival, which began on 19 November in Zurich, offered a packed programme. Organised by the Zurich Kurdish Film Festival Association, the event is being held with the support of the City of Zurich Department of Culture (Stadt Zürich Kultur), the Canton of Zurich’s Cultural Funding Office (Kanton Zürich Kulturförderung/Swisslos), Temperatio and the Migros Culture Percentage (Migros Kulturprozent).




Taking place for the first time, the festival brings together films by filmmakers from different parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora.




The programme on Saturday, 21 November, featured films exploring war, migration, women's struggles and the lives of Kurdish people across different geographical regions.




Xavier Koller’s 

Reise der Hoffnung

 (

Journey of Hope

) tells the story of a Kurdish family’s journey as they attempt to reach Switzerland. Meanwhile, Hasan Oswald’s documentary 

Mediha

 introduced audiences to the struggle for survival of a young Êzidî woman who survived attacks by ISIS.




The programme also included 

Arzela from Amed

 by Elif Yiğit and Johannes Paech; 

Dream’s Gate

 by Negin Ahmadi, which focuses on women fighters in Rojava; and 

All the Mountains Give

, a documentary by Arash Rakhsha about the lives of kolbers (cross-border porters).







 







Today, Sunday, the festival’s final day, screenings will include productions from Rojava’s cinema scene.




Zîlan Hemo’s documentary 

The Traveling Cinema (Sînema Gerok)

 tells the story of İsmail Mamo, who is working to bring cinema to villages in Kobanê. Meanwhile, Sevînaz Evidkê’s film 

Berbû

 focuses on the experiences of women displaced during attacks on Serêkaniyê.




The final day’s programme will also feature the documentary 

Kardeş Türküler ile 30 Yıl

 (

30 Years with Kardeş Türküler

) and 

Paradies!

 by Kurdwin Ayub. The festival will conclude at 6pm with a screening of 

The Last Word from Bavê Tayar

, directed by Ghamkin Saleh.







Alongside film screenings, the festival also features discussions with directors, workshops for children and cultural events. Activities are taking place at various cinema and cultural venues across Zurich.




There is great interest in Kurdish culture




Speaking to ANF, Deniz Ökmen, one of the festival’s organisers, explained that the idea for the festival emerged last year following a film screening they attended in Zurich.







Ökmen said their aim was to introduce Kurdish cinema not only to Kurds living in the diaspora but also to Swiss society.




“We asked ourselves: Why shouldn't we show Kurdish films and Kurdish art both to our people living in the diaspora and to the Swiss people with whom we share our lives? A few of us came together and established the Zurich Kurdish Film Festival Association,” he said.




Ökmen explained that, while putting together the festival programme, they had made a particular effort to include films from all four parts of Kurdistan. He added that despite this being the festival’s first edition, it had attracted a great deal of interest.




“We selected films from Rojhilat, Rojava, Bakur and Başûr. Despite this being our first festival, every screening was fully attended. In fact, we even had to accommodate many people by having them sit on the floor. We saw that people have a tremendous interest in Kurdish culture. Throughout this process, we also rediscovered just how rich Kurdish art and cinema really are,” he said.







We want to make the festival an annual event




Emphasising that the festival had attracted interest not only from Kurds but also from Swiss society, Ökmen said that approximately half of the audience was Kurdish, while the other half came from different communities.




“The most beautiful thing is that we are able to introduce Kurdish culture not only to our people in the diaspora but also to the communities we live alongside. Our Swiss friends are also involved in the festival. It makes us especially happy when Swiss people attending the screenings greet us in Kurdish,” he said.




Stating that they hoped to continue the festival in future years with even greater participation, Ökmen continued: “We started out as an amateur group, but we encountered an enormous amount of demand. Next year, we want to begin preparations earlier, expand the festival and make it more professional. This interest gives us the motivation to organise the festival again and establish it as an annual tradition.”




We must keep our culture and language alive




Hevi Öcal, one of the festival’s volunteer supporters, who was born and raised in exile in Switzerland, highlighted the importance of passing Kurdish culture and language on to future generations.







She said: “I am volunteering here because I think it is wonderful that our people are organising a Kurdish cultural festival in Switzerland for the first time. I feel incredibly proud of our people. I wanted to be part of this and contribute to ensuring that events like this continue in the future. In this way, we can continue watching wonderful films and telling our own stories. I want our voices to be heard, for us not to be forgotten, and for our language not to be forgotten either. This is very important to me.




It is especially meaningful to me that we are able to pass our culture on to future generations. After all, I was born here too. I grew up between two cultures. That is why, if we are not to forget our own culture and want to keep it alive forever, we need to practise it more and make sure it continues to live on.”

title: Certificates awarded to students completing Kurdish language courses in Mannheim
content:
A certificate ceremony was held at the Democratic Kurdish Community Centre in Mannheim, Germany, for students who had successfully completed Kurdish language courses. Attended by numerous Kurdish families living in Mannheim and the surrounding areas, the ceremony highlighted the importance of preserving, developing and passing the Kurdish language on to future generations.







Certificates were presented by the Mothers of Martyrs to numerous students who had successfully completed two terms of Kurdish language courses organised across Germany.




During the ceremony, Osman Kapan, a writer and member of the Kurdish Institute of Germany, as well as Erk, Selamet, Rojda Yıldız and Zeynep Kayaş, delivered speeches. Ruken Akça, Co-Chair of the Confederation of Kurdish Communities in Germany (KON-MED), also gave a brief address.







 







If a language goes, everything goes




In his speech, writer Osman Kapan described language as the cornerstone of a people's identity, culture and collective memory, stressing that keeping the mother tongue alive is a shared responsibility.







Emphasising the importance of children learning Kurdish from an early age and using it in their daily lives, Kapan said that Kurdish families living in Europe, in particular, must ensure that their children maintain their connection to their mother tongue in societies where other languages are do
