title: Kezban Doğan: Collective struggle against femicide is essential - Part One
content:
As activities continue in Germany to mark 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, the Kurdish Women's Movement has launched a new campaign to strengthen the collective struggle against femicide. The preparatory phase, running from 1 November to 8 March, aims to reach different sections of society through training sessions, seminars, panels, demonstrations and other activities.




Kezban Doğan, term spokesperson for the Kurdish Women's Union in Germany (YJK-E), said that treating femicides solely as individual crimes obscures the underlying causes of the problem. She spoke to ANF about a range of issues, from femicides in Germany and the difficulties faced by refugee women to state policies and the patriarchal mentality.







 







'The true scale of femicide is not disclosed'




Kezban Doğan said that the failure to publish comprehensive statistics on femicide was a major problem. She noted that governments compile daily figures during wars, disasters and economic crises but do not adopt the same approach to femicide. Doğan argued that this was a policy aimed at preventing a public response.




Kezban Doğan said: "The figures and statistics released in Germany are not simply statistics. In fact, this is one of the biggest problems. When a war breaks out anywhere in the world, daily figures are compiled for that country. When a disaster occurs, a record of the casualties is produced, even if official figures are unavailable. Similarly, when inflation or another economic problem arises, figures are compiled.




Unfortunately, however, we cannot access such comprehensive statistics or figures when it comes to femicide. We can regard this as a policy pursued by states, particularly nation-states. In fact, I would say that this is definitely the case. When figures are made public, they provoke a reaction, a response from society. I believe the reason the total figures are not disclosed is precisely to prevent that public response.




The United Nations says that a woman is killed every five minutes worldwide. If we calculate what that means, we can imagine the number of women killed over 24 hours. I believe the failure to present these statistics comprehensively is intended to prevent society from reacting to this reality."




Kezban Doğan also drew attention to figures on femicide in Germany, saying that some sources had recorded 105 cases and others 108 by October 2026. She added that two more women had been killed in November. She said: "One was a foreign woman staying in a women's shelter, while the other lost her life under different circumstances. This also reveals the state's policies. I think we need to examine this issue in greater depth." 




Doğan stressed that femicides committed in Germany over the past six years needed to be examined comprehensively, including deaths recorded as suicides and other dimensions of violence against women.




'Violence against women increased during the coronavirus pandemic'




Kezban Doğan recalled that violence against women increased dramatically during the coronavirus pandemic and that women's shelters had no places left. She also criticised government officials at the time for explaining domestic violence in terms of men's psychological difficulties.




Doğan said: "Violence against women increased enormously during that period. There were no places left in women's shelters in Germany. This was not simply because there were too few shelters, but also because they were experiencing overwhelming demand. Yet when we look at the statements made in parliament by government officials, particularly interior ministers and other ministers, they claimed that men were experiencing crises and depression and were therefore turning to domestic violence.




We should have examined this much more deeply at the time. Unfortunately, we failed to get to the heart of the issue or monitor it adequately. If we could obtain comprehensive official statistics on femicide and violence against women from 2020 to the present, just as we obtain figures on wars, we would see a much larger number and a far more serious picture. We need to examine both its psychological and social dimensions. We did not do enough at the time, but we must do so today."




'Women also face violence along migration routes'




Kezban Doğan also addressed the claim that Kurdish women account for 10 percent of women killed in Germany. She stressed that Kurdish women's experiences of migration to Europe differ from those of men, noting that women face multiple forms of oppression in their homelands from states, dominant powers, families, tribal structures and their immediate surroundings.




Doğan said that women had been forced to seek refuge in Europe because of oppression, torture, detention and threats to their lives, rather than seeing Europe simply as a place of liberation. She emphasised that women also experience rape, violence and forced prostitution along migration routes.




Kezban Doğan said: "Kurdish women already faced problems with dominant powers, colonial policies and the state in the countries where they lived, on their own lands. They also faced problems within their families, tribal structures and society. Thirdly, they experienced problems within their immediate families and closest surroundings, involving their children, husbands, siblings and fathers.




Women were forced to seek refuge in Europe because of the oppression, torture, detention and threats to their lives, not because they saw Europe as a place of liberation. But before reaching Europe, there is also the journey itself, the story of how they arrived. When you ask men about their migration journeys, their accounts tend to focus more on physical hardships and financial difficulties. But when we examine women's experiences, we see rape, violence, being forced into prostitution and many other serious problems. These journeys also have devastating consequences for women who manage to reach Germany. Unfortunately, many women fall into the hands of prostitution networks along the way or are killed. Their names and identities disappear, and their fate remains unknown."




Kezban Doğan said that women's problems did not end when they reached Germany. Instead, they encountered new forms of violence and oppression in refugee camps, where their psychological, financial, healthcare and educational needs were not adequately met.




Doğan continued: "After arriving in Germany, the same problems begin again, this time in refugee camps. The state already regards you as a burden. Yet under many of the international conventions Germany has signed, the psychological, financial, healthcare and educational needs of people arriving as refugees must be addressed. Instead, the opposite happens.




If we look at the past ten years, particularly the period beginning with developments in Rojava, even examining the years after 2014 provides one of the clearest examples. Women want to escape as quickly as possible and leave behind the conditions imposed on them as a burden. Yet there, too, they are pushed into the hands of prostitution networks and forced into drug use. To survive, they bury all their psychological suffering inside themselves and try to find a place in society."




Kezban Doğan said that refugee camps lacked therapy centres and that psychological and educational support was inadequate. She stressed that women's lack of knowledge about their rights and the support mechanisms available to them further aggravated their difficulties.




Doğan said: "There are no therapy centres, and psychologists and educational specialists are not brought in. In reality, you live a kind of open-prison existence. The only difference is that you are not living alongside your neighbours or being subjected to direct physical torture. But you are still exposed to psychological and economic abuse and violence. Many women do not know enough about their circumstances or their rights, so they do not know where to apply, who can support them or with whom they can build solidarity. Unfortunately, this can lead them in the wrong direction. The state, in particular, pushes women towards these situations."




'

Men establish their power over women'




Kezban Doğan said that the conditions associated with being a migrant or refugee further aggravated women's problems. She stressed that, alongside racism and discrimination, patriarchal relations within Kurdish society also needed to be questioned.




Doğan said: "We also need to look at the position of men within Kurdish society. You are now a migrant, a refugee, and different conditions are imposed on you. You are not regarded as a human being. Racism is already rampant. Within all these circumstances, women find themselves trapped and once again subjected to extremely difficult conditions. Unfortunately, there is a truth expressed by Abdullah Öcalan: The Kurdish man is the slave of the state, while the Kurdish woman is the slave of the slave. Unfortunately, Kurdish men establish their own power over women. They express all the crises and problems they experience by subjecting women to violence, killing women and taking their lives. In doing so, they are actually destroying their own future. But are they aware of this? I do not think so. If they were aware, if such awareness had been developed, we would not be discussing these issues today."

title: Jiyan Tosun: State rhetoric of violence fuels social violence
content:
Individual gun ownership and incidents of violence involving firearms are steadily increasing in Turkey. According to data from the Umut Foundation, approximately 70 percent of violent incidents and murders committed in the country over the course of a year involve firearms. The majority of these weapons are unlicensed.




It is reported that 80 to 90 percent of the weapons used in firearm attacks and murders are unlicensed. Data from the Ministry of Interior also reveal the widespread prevalence of unlicensed firearms in Turkey.




According to the ministry, operations carried out throughout 2025 resulted in the seizure of 110,104 unlicensed weapons, including 50,216 handguns, 35,724 shotguns, 22,669 blank-firing pistols and 1,492 long-barrelled firearms.




Figures released by the Ministry of Interior for the first three months of 2026 show that the proliferation of firearms has continued. According to the data, 25,580 unlicensed weapons were seized during the first quarter of the year.




Demand for unlicensed firearms has increased




The proliferation of unlicensed firearms is raising concerns about individual gun ownership and firearm-related violence. In Turkey, where the activities of criminal gangs have also become a prominent issue, public trust in security institutions and the extent to which individuals feel safe have come under scrutiny.




According to a survey conducted by ASAL Research in July 2025, one in four people in Turkey said they did not trust any institution. The police ranked third in the trust survey, with a rate of 10 percent.




Concerns about personal safety are among the factors driving individuals to seek their own means of protection. One significant factor behind the growing demand for unlicensed firearms is that these weapons remain outside registration and oversight mechanisms.




Social media platforms, messaging applications and sales networks established by criminal organisations are reportedly playing a role in the supply of firearms. Weapons are reportedly traded through closed online groups, while correspondence and screenshots included in court files concerning certain criminal organisations have also exposed these networks.




How are unlicensed firearms obtained?




Social media and messaging applications have increasingly become prominent channels in the illegal firearms trade. In sales conducted through closed groups, membership is reportedly obtained through referrals, while information about the characteristics and prices of weapons is shared among members.




Firearms are also reportedly traded through open groups. Some groups resembling the accounts of officially registered firearms dealers allegedly direct people who make contact with unlicensed weapons.




Beyond online trading, weapons held by criminal organisations are reportedly circulated through unregistered sales networks. These transactions involve direct, in-person delivery, while some businesses allegedly facilitate the networks under the guise of legitimate commercial activity.




How are unlicensed firearms classified?




In the unlicensed firearms trade, weapons are classified into different categories according to their characteristics and history. Whether a weapon has previously been used, whether it has been linked to a crime and how it was manufactured are determining factors in these classifications.




Terms used in the trade include "original", "clean", "dirty", "homemade" and "converted from blank-firing weapons". These descriptions are used to determine the commercial value of firearms.




The conversion of blank-firing weapons into live firearms is a particularly concerning aspect of the unlicensed firearms market. The technical characteristics and reliability of such weapons vary, while their circulation outside official registration systems creates serious security risks.




A report prepared by the Umut Foundation in 2025 stated that the number of unlicensed firearms in Turkey had exceeded 30 million. Easier access to weapons and the spread of individual gun ownership remain major concerns for public safety not only in Turkey but also in Kurdistan.







 







'Violence is being normalised through the media'




Jiyan Tosun, Co-Chair of the Istanbul Branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), said that one of the main reasons for the increase in individual gun ownership is the authorities' tolerance of firearms entering Turkey. She pointed out that a significant proportion of these weapons come from countries in the Middle East and Europe.




Jiyan Tosun said: "When we look at the data, we see that a large proportion of the weapons come from Middle Eastern countries or Europe. And we are not talking about a small number. As you mentioned, we are talking about approximately 50 million unlicensed firearms in 2025. The circulation of such a vast number of weapons within Turkey can be interpreted as a serious lack of oversight or deliberate tolerance. I do not think this is merely a security issue. People do not acquire weapons solely to feel safe. Violence is also being normalised by the state and through the media.




Secondly, I believe that children watching war games in digital environments, and the ease with which young people can obtain firearms, are also contributing factors. We can see that these weapons are not acquired solely out of a perceived need for security.




In Turkey, there is the issue of both licensed and unlicensed firearms. Of course, unlicensed weapons account for a much larger proportion. However, we also see that oversight of licensed firearms is inadequate. Requirements such as psychological assessments for people who are issued firearms licences, and the regular repetition of these assessments, are not being implemented with sufficient care.




On 6 November, the Ministry of Interior announced that new regulations concerning licensed firearms would be introduced. As you know, weapons belonging to parents were used in school attacks in Maraş and Istanbul."




'The state is failing to fulfil its obligations'




Jiyan Tosun said that the government's statements on preventing access to firearms were insufficient and that regulations concerning licensed weapons alone would not resolve the problem.




Tosun continued: "It has also been said that new regulations will be introduced, particularly to prevent children from accessing licensed firearms. But these measures are already inadequate. As we said at the beginning, licensed firearms actually account for a much smaller proportion than unlicensed weapons. What is needed is not simply new regulations on licensed firearms, but the elimination of the conditions that make unlicensed weapons so easily accessible. The state is failing to fulfil its obligations in this regard.




Poverty is also a contributing factor. People do not feel safe, and this has a significant impact. But we must not forget another important point: We are talking about a geography located in the middle of a major conflict zone, surrounded by wars. We know about the war in Syria, right next to us, which has lasted for more than ten years. There is also the war in Ukraine.




These wars and the environment they create cause people to resort to violence more frequently, while violence itself becomes increasingly normalised. The first step that should be taken is for the state to abandon its divisive rhetoric that legitimises violence. Because when the state constructs a language of violence, it also creates a sense of legitimacy for society itself to resort to violence.




Let us remember that, in the recent past, we witnessed the former Minister of Interior using language that directly praised or normalised torture, even though torture is absolutely prohibited by the state. Such language creates the perception in the mind of an ordinary citizen that violence is entirely legitimate. If we want to prevent so many incidents of violence in society, this language must first be eliminated."




'The state has constructed a language of violence'




Jiyan Tosun stressed that the state must abandon its rhetoric of violence, warning that violence is becoming increasingly normalised throughout society.




Tosun said: "To eliminate violence, the state must abandon language that encourages it. There is also a serious lack of oversight of games on digital platforms, including games that promote violence. Young people, particularly children, are exposed to content on these platforms that normalises violence and causes psychological harm.




On the other hand, the state itself has constructed a language of violence. If you adopt an approach that praises and legitimises torture, you also encourage citizens to normalise violence and resort to it."

title: First Kurdish Film Festival continues in Zurich
content:
The first 

Kurdish Film Festival

, organised in Zurich, kicked off on 19 November. Running until tomorrow, Sunday, the festival is presenting feature films, documentaries, short films, discussions with directors and various cultural events.




The festival is organised by the Kurdish Film Festival Zurich Association, established at the end of December 2025. The association, which aims to bring Kurdish cinema and Kurdish cultural and artistic producers together in Switzerland, describes the festival as a meeting space where diverse cinematic works about Kurdish life and stories can gain visibility.




Aiming to introduce the diversity of Kurdish cinema to international audiences, the festival also seeks to promote cultural exchange and dialogue through film.




A diversity of stories 




The festival opened on Thursday, 19 November, with a screening of 

Singing Wings

, a documentary by director Hemen Khaledi. Set in a Kurdish village in Rojhilat, the documentary tells the story of 78-year-old Khadijeh, who, while caring for her ill husband, tries to nurse an injured stork back to health and persuade her daughter, who wants to immigrate to England, to abandon her plans.







The programme on Friday, 20 November, featured four films exploring different aspects of the Kurdish people's historical memory, cultural identity, experiences of migration and social life.




The documentary 

Kî me Ez?

 (Who Am I?), directed by Esin Akgül, explores the life and literary work of Kurdish poet and intellectual Cegerxwîn, as well as his place in Kurdish cultural memory. Drawing on archival footage, historical documents and testimonies from family members, the documentary sheds light on an important period in Kurdish literature through Cegerxwîn's life.




The film 

Nachbarn

 (Neighbours), directed by Mano Khalil, tells the story of six-year-old Sero, who lives in a Kurdish village on the Syrian-Turkish border during the 1980s. Set under the rule of Hafez al-Assad, the film examines repression targeting Kurdish identity, relationships between people of different faiths and the social realities of the period through the eyes of a child.







My Uncle Jens

, directed by Brwa Vahabpour, tells the story of a young Kurdish literature teacher living in Oslo, Norway, and his experiences with his uncle, who arrives from Kurdistan. Using humour, the film explores family relationships, generational differences and the impact of European migration policies on Kurdish families.




The final screening of the day was 

One of Those Days When Hemme Died

, directed by Murat Fıratoğlu. The film follows Eyüp, who returns from Izmir to his hometown of Siverek and works in a tomato field. Through the conflict he experiences over unpaid wages, the film explores labour exploitation, poverty and the contradictions of everyday life.




Kurdish cinema from Rojava to Rojhilat




Today's programme (Saturday, 21 November) features films addressing war, migration, women's struggle and the lives of Kurdish people across different geographical regions.




The first screening of the day, at 14:00, will be Xavier Koller’s 1990 film 

Reise der Hoffnung

 (Journey of Hope). Based on a true story, the film depicts the arduous migration journey of a Kurdish family attempting to reach Switzerland in the hope of finding a better life.







Hasan Oswald's documentary 

Mediha

 will be screened at 16:30. It tells the story of a young Yazidi woman who was abducted during ISIS attacks against the Yazidis in 2014 and her struggle to rebuild her life and find her missing family after escaping captivity.




The documentary 

Arzela from Amed

, directed by Elif Yiğit and Johannes Paech, will be screened at 18:00, followed by 

Dream's Gate

, directed by Negin Ahmadi, at 18:30.




Dream's Gate

 follows a young woman filmmaker travelling from Rojhilat to Rojava, where she witnesses the lives of women fighters resisting ISIS and explores women's search for freedom.




At 20:00, Arash Rakhsha's documentary 

All the Mountains Give

 will focus on the story of two Kurdish friends who make their living as kolbers, carrying goods across the Iran-Iraq border.




The programme will continue with screenings of Mehmet Ali Konar's 

When the Walnut Leaves Turn Yellow

 and Rosida Koyuncu's 

Rêya Penaber

.




The festival also features a discussion about the Rojava Film Commune, meetings with directors, an acting workshop for children and various cultural events.




Closing day on Sunday 




On Sunday, 22 November, the festival's final day, further productions from Kurdish cinema will be screened.




At 11:30, the documentary 

The Traveling Cinema

 (Sînema Gerok), directed by the late Zîlan Hemo, will be shown. It tells the story of Ismail Mamo, who, after studying acting in the Netherlands, returned to Kobanê and launched a travelling cinema project to bring films to villages and people without access to cinemas.




Berbû

, directed by Sevînaz Evidkê, one of the founders of the Rojava Film Commune, will be screened at 14:00. The film explores the experiences of women displaced during the Turkish state's attacks on Serêkaniyê in 2019, the devastating consequences of war and solidarity among women.




At 16:00, the documentary 

30 Years with Kardeş Türküler

, directed by Çayan Demirel and Ayşe Çetinbaş, will be shown. Kurdwin Ayub's film 

Paradies! Paradies!

 will also be screened.




The festival will close at 18:00 with 

The Last Word from Bavê Tayar

, directed by Ghamkin Saleh. The film follows a father, portrayed by one of Kurdish cinema's well-known actors, Bavê Tayar, as he sets out to find his son, who has travelled to Europe. Through this journey, the film explores family relationships, social change and generational differences.




Workshops




In addition to film screenings, the festival programme includes various workshops, meetings with directors and discussions.




Events also include acting workshops for children and workshops on traditional Kurdish games, offering participants opportunities to engage with Kurdish cinema and culture through different activities.




Taking place at KINOKONI, Kino Xenix and Kunstraum Walcheturm in Zurich, the festival will conclude after four days of film screenings and cultural events.




Further information about the festival is available 

here

title: PUK and KDP hold talks in Hewlêr
content:
Representatives of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) met for talks in Hewlêr (Erbil). The meeting took place at the PUK Politburo headquarters, with senior political representatives from both parties in attendance. The talks come amid the ongoing political crisis in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI), which has intensified further since the KDP unilaterally filled the parliamentary presidency in early November.




The PUK was represented at the meeting by Rêwaz Fayîq and Yusif Goran, while the KDP delegation consisted of Piştîwan Sadiq and Mehmûd Mihemed. According to information obtained by the Roj News agency, the meeting has since concluded. Neither the PUK nor the KDP initially commented on the talks or any possible outcomes.




Dispute over parliamentary presidency escalates




The latest dispute began with a session of the KRI parliament on November 4. The KDP had unilaterally convened the first supplementary session and filled the positions in the parliamentary presidency. The PUK protested the move and questioned its legality.

title: HPG announces identities of eight fallen guerrilla fighters from Selmas
content:
The People’s Defense Forces (HPG) released the identity information of eight guerrillas from Selmas in Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat) who lost their lives between 2007 and 2018. In a statement, the HPG Press Center paid tribute to their efforts and reaffirmed its commitment to continuing their struggle.




The statement by HPG Press Center reads as follows:




“We commemorate our comrades Serhildan Selmas, Rodî Gabar, Rojhat Selmas, Cûdî Şikakî, Şêrîf Stêrk, Cegerxwîn Zagros, Şînya Cûdî, and Welat Özgür, the courageous sons and daughters of Eastern Kurdistan and self-sacrificing militants of the Apoist movement, with respect, love, and gratitude.




Our comrades were convinced that the PKK embodied the hope for freedom for the Kurdish people and joined our struggle with great determination. They embraced the Apoist philosophy and reshaped their personalities on the basis of freedom. Drawing on the extensive experience of our guerrilla forces, they developed into determined militants and insisted on being deployed to the most challenging areas of struggle. Through their spirit of Apoist self-sacrifice, their determination, and their unwavering will, they became outstanding representatives of Kurdistan’s revolutionary tradition.




Our comrades stood on the front lines of resistance in numerous regions of Kurdistan against attacks aimed at annihilating our people. They fought fearlessly to protect the existence of our people. Devoting all their strength, they played a leading role in the struggle for our existence and freedom.




Despite all the hardships and difficulties, our comrades never compromised their commitment to the Apoist spirit of self-sacrifice. Through their struggle, they became historic figures whose memory will endure. Their efforts gave hope to the oppressed and exploited Kurdish people. With their deaths, they left their comrades and our people another reason to continue the struggle and joined the ranks of the immortals.




We extend our condolences in particular to the esteemed families of our fallen comrades and to the entire patriotic people of Kurdistan. We pledge to carry forward the banner of struggle passed on to us by our martyrs, conscious of our responsibility toward all those who have fallen, to fulfill their goals without fail, and to keep their memory alive forever.”

title: Final declaration of the Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women meeting in Sulaymaniyah
content:
The Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women held a meeting in Sulaymaniyah on Friday to discuss political developments in the region, national unity, and the future of the Kurdish women’s movement. The meeting brought together political figures, activists, and representatives of women’s organizations from all four parts of Kurdistan. Participants exchanged views on women’s issues, recent developments, and the political situation in the region. Efforts to strengthen national unity among Kurdish women and preparations for the Third Kurdish Women’s National Congress were also key items on the agenda.




‘Unity is the only way to a solution’




The meeting’s final declaration outlined the following positions and proposals:




“We support the preservation of the constitutional status of the Federal Kurdistan Region and are working to promote unity among the Kurdish people, dialogue, and a return to the ballot box as the only way to resolve internal problems and crises.




We will under no circumstances be party to the division of the Kurdistan Region. On the contrary, we support the establishment of a broad-based, united, and democratic government founded on genuine partnership and the right to citizenship.




As a platform, we support the preservation and strengthening of the Democratic Autonomous Administration system in Rojava (Western Kurdistan) to guarantee the rights of all peoples and communities.




‘The peace and democratic society process must be supported’




We support initiatives for democratic solutions in all parts and regions of Kurdistan and efforts to address the demands of the Kurdish people. We call on democratic society and all political forces and parties to support the peace process in Bakur (Northern Kurdistan).




Our position on the situation in Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan) is clear and unwavering. More than 700 people have been arrested and executed across Iran this year. We therefore demand that the platform take a clear and urgent stance to halt these penalties and protect their lives.




We emphasize the importance of coordination and joint efforts with political parties, groups, and organizations to unite efforts and bring positions closer together.




We firmly oppose femicide, self-immolation, and all forms of violence. We will under no circumstances accept women’s rights being sacrificed to political crises. On the contrary, we are working to strengthen the position of women and ensure the continuity of their achievements in all parts and regions of Kurdistan under the slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ (Woman, Life, Freedom).




‘Act with historical responsibility and take practical steps’




As Kurdish women, we declare to the participants and platforms that we support the process of democratic integration in our struggle to protect our rights and achievements.




At this meeting, the importance of mutual support and solidarity among all parts of Kurdistan at every stage was highlighted.




Visiting all political parties and organizations to promote Kurdish unity and organizing a meeting with broad participation.




Making preparations to organize a culture and arts festival across Kurdistan.




Organizing a series of large-scale and comprehensive actions to protect the achievements of the women’s revolution.




Intensifying efforts and the struggle for Kurdish unity, particularly in Bashur (Southern Kurdistan).




Working toward the preparation and organization of a Kurdish Conference.




Supporting a common discourse in the media and publishing sector under the slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî.’




Protecting the legal rights of Yazidi women and ensuring justice by recognizing the crimes committed against them as genocide, punishing the perpetrators, and providing survivors with legal, medical, and psychological support and compensation. At the same time, combating sexual and physical violence, eliminating social stigma, and guaranteeing their security and active political participation in Shengal.




Finally, we reiterate that unity and joint efforts among Kurdish political forces and parties are the fundamental guarantee for safeguarding achievements and attaining peace, freedom, and democracy. We hope that all parties will embrace these proposals with a sense of historical responsibility and take practical steps to implement them.”

title: Hatimoğulları: Treatment of sick prisoners amounts to torture
content:
The vigil demanding the release of seriously ill prisoners outside the Turkish Ministry of Justice in Ankara continues. On the fifth day, Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), described the state’s treatment of sick prisoners as torture. She stated that prisoners were being denied timely medical treatment and prevented from being released despite suffering from life-threatening illnesses. The government must put an end to this practice, she said, referring to the ongoing peace and democratization process.




Relatives of prisoners Ömer Güneri, Yakup Akman, Mehmet Ali Taşkın, and Selim Çiftçi were among those taking part in the vigil organized by the Federation of Legal and Solidarity Associations of Prisoners’ Families (TUHAD-FED). The Co-Chairs of MED TUHAD-FED, Pınar Sakık Tekin and Kerem Canpolat, as well as representatives of various civil society organizations, also attended the vigil. Carrying banners and chanting slogans, the demonstrators demanded the release of sick prisoners, including Newroz Bozkurt and Evin Zapsu.




Criticism of forensic medical reports




Hatimoğulları accused the Turkish Forensic Medicine Institute of refusing to issue the medical reports needed by seriously ill prisoners, thereby preventing their release. “Everyone in Turkey now knows that the institute is incapable of issuing the necessary reports for sick prisoners. It remains an institution that fails to uphold the obligations of the Hippocratic Oath.”




The DEM Party politician addressed the medical professionals responsible directly: “You are doctors! Your duty is to keep people alive.” Even when prisoners obtained a medical report stating that they could no longer remain in detention, prison administrations often failed to act on it. This is another injustice that we cannot accept,” she said.




As an example of the consequences of delayed medical care, Hatimoğulları recalled political prisoner Tuncer Sağlam, who died recently after a long denial of treatment. “If families are holding a vigil outside the Ministry of Justice today, it is because they want to prevent another coffin from being carried out of prison. Correctional facilities have become places where prisoners are left to perish. From here, the families are calling out: Do not let prisons become morgues.”










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/fc17a848_20261121134205_2026-11-21-ankara-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-adalet-bakanligi-eylem-1.mp4










“Can you take responsibility for this?”




Hatimoğulları gave a particularly harrowing account of the situation of Evin Zapsu, who has been imprisoned for nine years. Zapsu, who is being held in Kayseri Women’s Prison, was diagnosed with stage-four cancer, yet the necessary treatment has not been initiated, she said. “Everyone has heard her daughter’s desperate cry. Evin Zapsu has been in prison for nearly ten years. Her daughters chose to study at Istanbul University so they could visit their mother. The burden falls not only on prisoners but also on their families. Transfers to prisons far from home make family visits even more difficult. Many families are already living in severe poverty.” Addressing the Turkish Minister of Justice, Hatimoğulları asked: “What conscience, what religion, what faith can justify knowingly leaving sick prisoners to die? Can you take responsibility for this?”




Delayed medical treatment of Newroz Bozkurt




Hatimoğulları also addressed the situation of seriously ill prisoner Newroz Bozkurt. During a visit to Sincan Women’s Prison, the women incarcerated there had given her detailed accounts of prison conditions and mistreatment. “We have repeatedly spoken with the Ministry of Justice to ensure that Newroz Bozkurt receives medical treatment. Our lawyers have worked day and night on this. Nevertheless, she has not received adequate treatment. It has been postponed again and again, repeatedly. The families’ desperation has now reached an unbearable level. When mothers say they will set themselves on fire if necessary unless their children are released, it shows just how hopeless they feel their situation has become. Our mothers are holding this vigil in tears. Enough is enough.”




“How do they intend to make peace under these conditions?”




Hatimoğulları directly linked the situation in prisons to the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She stated that the DEM Party was repeatedly confronted with the same question at public gatherings: “How do they intend to make peace with the Kurds while continuing to keep seriously ill prisoners behind bars?” This question is directed at the government, the president, the Minister of Justice, and all state institutions involved in the political process. Meet the families’ demands. The greatest contribution to this process will be to put an end to the torture endured by sick prisoners. This is a matter of humanity.”




The DEM Party Co-Chair also called on human rights and healthcare organizations to join the vigil outside the Ministry of Justice.




MED TUHAD-FED announces continuation of vigil




Kerem Canpolat, Co-Chair of MED TUHAD-FED, recalled that thousands of political prisoners who had advocated a democratic solution to the Kurdish question were being held in prisons across Turkey and Kurdistan. He stressed that their situation had not fundamentally changed although a political resolution process was now underway. “For two years, the process has had no impact on the prisons. Even prisoners whose medical reports from hospitals confirm that they cannot be left alone are not being released,” Canpolat said.




Canpolat pointed out that a genuine resolution of the Kurdish question also required a change in the state’s approach toward political prisoners. “As a federation, we will continue our actions until these prisoners are released,” he added.




The vigil outside the Ministry of Justice is ongoing.

title: Saturday Mothers demand answers about the fate of Hayrettin Eren, missing for 46 years
content:
At their 1,130th vigil in Galatasaray Square in Istanbul, the Saturday Mothers once again demanded that the fate of people who disappeared in state custody be clarified. This week’s protest focused on Hayrettin Eren, who was detained by police on November 21, 1980, and has been missing ever since. Exactly 46 years later, his relatives demanded that those responsible be brought to justice and that legislation be introduced to ensure such crimes are not subject to statutes of limitations.




The participants gathered in the square in Istanbul’s Beyoğlu district, carrying carnations and portraits of the disappeared. The joint statement was read by Ümit Tekay Dişli of the Istanbul branch of the Human Rights Association’s (IHD) Commission on the Disappeared.




Detained and erased from police records




Hayrettin Eren was 26 years old when he came under scrutiny by the security authorities following the military coup of September 12, 1980. He had been active in the youth movement during the 1970s. After the coup, an arrest warrant was issued for him. On November 21, 1980, Eren met a friend at the Haşim Işcan Passage in Istanbul’s Saraçhane district. Both were detained there and initially taken to the Karagümrük police station. Eren was subsequently transferred, along with eight other detainees, to the Political Department of the Gayrettepe Police Directorate.




When his mother, Elmas Eren, went looking for him, she initially found clear evidence of his detention. “Elmas Eren went to the Karagümrük police station and saw Hayrettin’s name in the custody register. She was told that her son had been taken to Gayrettepe,” Dişli said. On the premises of the police directorate, his mother spotted her husband’s car, bearing the license plate 34 F 6798, which Hayrettin had been using at the time of his arrest. However, the officers denied that he was being held there.




“When she asked about her son, the police officers replied: ‘No such person is in custody.’ Elmas Eren then returned to the Karagümrük police station. This time, she discovered that the page of the custody register containing Hayrettin’s name had been torn out.”




Witness testimonies have been available for decades




According to the IHD, eight people detained during the same police operation confirmed that they had seen Hayrettin Eren both at the Karagümrük police station and at the Gayrettepe Police Directorate. A criminal complaint was filed on the basis of these witness statements. Nevertheless, Eren’s fate remains unknown to this day, and no one has been held accountable for his disappearance.




“The state’s obligation to investigate the crime of enforced disappearance, uncover the truth, and punish those responsible remains in force,” Dişli stated. He noted that the Saturday Mothers are therefore demanding a renewed and effective investigation into the case, taking into account all available evidence and witness testimonies. “We want Hayrettin Eren’s fate and whereabouts to be established, and those responsible for his disappearance to be identified and brought to justice.”




“The state is making itself an accomplice”




Hayrettin Eren’s sister, Ikbal Eren, then took the floor. She recalled that 46 years ago, she had personally seen her brother’s car on the premises of the Gayrettepe Police Directorate. “Our loved ones were detained and murdered by state officials. By failing to bring these people to justice today, the state is making itself an accomplice to the crime,” Eren stated.




She particularly opposed the application of statutes of limitations in cases of enforced disappearance: “Crimes against humanity must not be subject to statutes of limitations. Abolish these limitations through legislation and bring those responsible to justice. For decades, the families have been denied their right to a judicial investigation. Many of the mothers who began their protest in Galatasaray Square 31 years ago have since died without ever learning the fate of their children. Nevertheless, our struggle would continue.”




“We will never leave unfinished the struggle of the mothers who sat down in this square 31 years ago to demand justice and died without learning the fate of their loved ones,” Ikbal Eren said. In closing, she reaffirmed that restrictions on their protests would not deter the families from continuing their struggle: “Whether you open this square to us or not, we will be here until the last of our disappeared loved ones is found, no matter which generation carries on this struggle. They thought the case files would disappear onto shelves and everything would be forgotten. But we have no intention of leaving. We will not forget our disappeared loved ones.”

title: Uğur and Ahmet Kaymaz commemorated on 22nd anniversary of their deaths
content:
“My son and my husband were people who would never have harmed anyone. Yet they were killed in front of our home without even being questioned.” With these words, Makbule Kaymaz commemorated her son Uğur and her husband Ahmet on Saturday. Both were shot dead by Turkish police officers on November 21, 2004, in Kızıltepe district, in the province of Mardin. Uğur was twelve years old at the time. He was struck by 13 bullets. Even 22 years later, no one has been held criminally accountable for the fatal shootings.




To mark the anniversary, family members and representatives of political parties and civil society organizations gathered at the graves of the two victims. The commemoration was organized by MEBYA-DER, an association that supports the families of people who have lost their lives as a result of the war in Kurdistan.




A twelve-year-old child branded a “terrorist”




The case of Uğur Kaymaz remains emblematic of the deadly violence perpetrated by uniformed state personnel against the Kurdish people and the subsequent impunity. DEM Party MP Beritan Güneş Altın recalled that the authorities had portrayed the twelve-year-old as a “terrorist” after his death.

title: Women artists: No peace or justice without women's freedom
content:
Actors Lale Mansur, Jülide Kural and Merve Asya Özgür spoke to ANF on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November.




The actors said that male dominance in the arts negatively affects women's creative work and visibility, while also drawing attention to television content that fuels violence. They said that men are emboldened by the failure of the justice system and stressed that there can be no justice, peace or democracy in a society where women are not free.




Lale Mansur: Male perpetrators are emboldened




Lale Mansur stressed that violence against women and femicide should be on the agenda not only on 25 November, but every day, even every moment. She said, "In Turkey, we need to talk about this five times a day. Turkey has become a slaughterhouse for women! We have reached this point because there is impunity. There is no rule of law, the law is not enforced, and there is no justice. Murderers walk among us. They search for the body of one woman and find the bodies of two more women in a well. How much worse can it get?"




Lale Mansur said that murders do not simply result in the loss of one life, but also devastate the lives of mothers, fathers and other relatives. She emphasised that the culture of impunity emboldens perpetrators, adding, "Male murderers are emboldened by impunity."




Lale Mansur also addressed the situation in the media and the shrinking space for opposition, saying that television programmes and series fuel violence: "The absence of any opposition, the disastrous state of television series... Truly disgraceful things are being produced on national television channels, including content that incites violence. They even made a television series about Abdullah Çatlı."




'Male dominance also prevails in television channels'




Lale Mansur said that male-dominated structures also prevail in the arts: "The owners and executives of television channels are mostly men. Male dominance exists there too. As for actors, many people have children to educate and support. With the high cost of living, they are forced to take part in such productions to earn money. Of course, there are very rare cases of people who refuse, saying, 'I'd rather sell lemons.' But when you have children or a family to support, you have little choice."




Lale Mansur said that impunity and the male-dominated mentality lie at the root of violence and femicide. She stressed that the problem cannot be resolved through criminal penalties alone, but requires a fundamental transformation of attitudes across society: "The biggest factor fuelling violence is impunity. They walk among us, and these people are murderers... This language, which targets and objectifies women, confronts us in every aspect of our lives. There is nothing we can tell women. You cannot say something like 'Don't let yourself be killed.' People say, 'Those men were raised by their mothers.' No, they were not raised by their mothers alone; they were raised by society. And society is now morally rotten."




Jülide Kural: There can be no democracy without women's freedom




Jülide Kural said, "25 November is a day of struggle and solidarity for women across the world against all forms of violence, discrimination and inequality. Violence is not directed only at the body. Discrediting a woman's character, disregarding her labour and will, and surrounding her with lies, insinuations and systematic attacks are also forms of violence."




Jülide Kural said that depriving women of their agency over their own lives, defining them through the existence of a man and attempting to confine them to a passive and dependent identity are among the most deeply rooted forms of violence produced by the male-dominated mentality. She emphasised that this violence is not perpetrated exclusively by men, adding, "Anyone who reproduces the male-dominated mentality and its discriminatory language can become part of this violence. Violence does not have a gender; it has a mentality that sustains it."




Jülide Kural stressed that no woman should have to prove her existence, worth or dignity through the judgements of others. She said, "25 November is not merely a day to condemn violence, but a day to confront the social and political order that produces it. In a society where women are not free, there can be no genuine democracy, justice or peace."




Jülide Kural declared that women would not remain silent, saying, "We will not be silent! We will strengthen solidarity and will not give up our right to have a say over our lives and our future. Because the struggle for women's freedom is the struggle for the freedom of humanity."




Merve Asya Özgür: From belittling our intelligence to harassment




Actor Merve Asya Özgür responded to our question about how courageously art challenges and transforms male-dominated language. Özgür said:  "What can the works we create and the encounters we experience, which freeze the ordinary flow of life and allow us to look at it from different perspectives, change in our lives? Perhaps that is one rather superficial way of describing art and its outcomes. Yet these encounters, or aestheticised confrontations, can certainly create awareness of gender and every identity crushed by gender roles, and open up a path towards confrontation and transformation. Indeed, that path is already open to such possibilities.




I am currently reading Cemil Meriç's Journal. At the very beginning of the book, he defines what he considers true art to be. He says that art means giving life to abstract and ghostlike imaginings, giving them blood, light and warmth. He describes how artists breathe life into these elusive dreams and abstract concepts by infusing them with a part of their own souls and lives. The experience of systematic violence and what it does to human beings inevitably finds its way into artists' work through their souls, including a spirit that resists and seeks change. The extent to which this happens is debatable, but even if nothing else remains, the traces of what a person has experienced can be seen in their eyes. However, I think the real key issue here is who presents artistic productions and how they are presented. I believe it would be more sensible to direct our attention towards that.




As for how courageous we are... In answering that question, I do not want to underestimate the achievements of the struggle. Nor do I want to paint an overly positive picture, as though everything were good enough and major transformations were taking place across society."




Merve Asya Özgür said that male dominance in the arts negatively affects women's creative work and visibility: "Exercising power, dominating, making women invisible or making them visible only according to your own aesthetic preferences... We could go on listing the destructive consequences, from belittling women's intelligence and failing to provide equal pay for equal work to dominating spaces of social and cultural production, harassment, violence and abuse.




Beyond all this, the achievements of the struggle are presented under the guise of patriarchal kindness and generosity, through expressions such as 'creating space for women', 'women artists' and 'supporting women artists'. It is a kind of celebrated tolerance, a supposed act of generosity intended to ensure that those considered 'lacking' are not left behind. You are repeatedly confronted, in every setting, with a superficial understanding that treats being a woman as though it were your only identity in life. It is truly infuriating."

title: Alfred de Zayas: Why should Kurds be denied the right to self-determination? - Part One
content:
The right of peoples to self-determination is one of the fundamental principles of international law. However, its implementation remains contested because of the political and economic interests of states. The international representation of the Kurdish people, who are divided among four countries and have no state of their own, and the protection of their political, cultural and linguistic rights remain among the unresolved issues of international law.




Alfred de Zayas, an expert in international law and human rights who served as the United Nations (UN) Independent Expert on the Promotion of a Democratic and Equitable International Order from 2012 to 2018, spoke to ANF about the Kurdish people's right to self-determination and autonomy, the possibilities of obtaining status within the UN, the treatment of stateless peoples and double standards in international law.




De Zayas said that the Kurdish people's right to self-determination has a strong foundation in international law, emphasising that the main obstacle to exercising this right is political rather than legal. He stressed that the UN has failed to fulfil its responsibilities towards the Kurdish people and said that Kurds should bring human rights violations before international mechanisms, explore interstate complaint procedures and build stronger networks of solidarity within the international community.




De Zayas also strongly criticised the European Union's approach to the Kurdish question, arguing that international law must be applied equally to all peoples. He asked, "If the right to self-determination has been granted to other peoples, why should it not be granted to the Kurdish people?"




ANF spoke to international law expert Alfred de Zayas.




Mr. de Zayas, you have worked for many years within the United Nations on international law, human rights and the right of peoples to self-determination. I would like to begin with a fundamental question. What does the right of a people to self-determination mean under international law? Does this right refer only to establishing an independent state, or can it also be exercised in other forms?




Of course, the right to self-determination can also be exercised internally. If there is a federal state and a people enjoys extensive autonomy, that system can work. But what happens when a state oppresses a people who have lived on their own land for thousands of years? The Kurds are not immigrants who recently arrived in the territories of Turkey, Syria, Iran or Iraq.




If we genuinely took the right to self-determination seriously, we would ask which people have the clearest claim to this right. I would say the Kurds. There are between 40 and 45 million Kurds, divided among four states. Yet they have no state of their own.




After the First World War, they could have had their own state if the Treaty of Sèvres had been implemented. However, Mustafa Kemal fought against the French and British forces at that time. Those forces were expelled from the territory of the new Turkey. The Treaty of Sèvres was subsequently replaced by the Treaty of Lausanne, which made no mention of the Kurdish or Armenian peoples.




What, then, are the legal foundations of the right to self-determination?




You can find them in Articles 1 and 55 of the United Nations Charter, as well as Chapters XI and XII. This right is also enshrined in the common Article 1 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. There is extensive literature on this subject, including my report A/69/272, which I submitted to the UN General Assembly in 2014. In that report, I examine the criteria determining which peoples may claim autonomy or independence.




Before continuing, I would like to mention a book that you may not know about because it has only recently been published. I supervised the doctoral thesis of a young Norwegian researcher, Blerim Mustafa, whose family originates from North Macedonia. He devoted his doctoral research to the right of secession, particularly the concept known in international law as "remedial secession".




His book is entitled Remedial Secession After the Cold War: Self-Determination and the Question of Secession. A substantial part of this work is devoted to the Kurds. The author examines three examples. The first is the people of East Timor, who were previously occupied, colonised and oppressed by Indonesia. The second is Kosovo, which is not recognised by all states and is not yet a UN member, but continues to exist as a state. The third is Iraqi Kurdistan, where a referendum produced an extremely clear result concerning self-determination.




'

International law must also apply to the Kurds'




What happens in these cases? The issue concerns perceptions and the application of different standards to different situations. As a professor of international law, there is one matter that has always particularly concerned me: the equal application of international law to everyone.




By definition, international law is international and universal. Therefore, you cannot say, "I will apply this law to Kosovo, but I will not apply it to Kurdistan." There is also a fundamental political dimension here, namely the recognition of a state by the international community, meaning other states.




Who, then, has the right to self-determination under international law? Without question, the Kurdish people do. The Kurds are a people, and they can rely on the UN Charter, the principles of international law developed through the process of decolonisation, and their right to preserve their identity, culture and language.




All these rights are protected by international human rights treaties and the jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice (ICJ). When we speak about territorial integrity, we must of course acknowledge that it is one of the fundamental principles of international law, just like state sovereignty. However, paragraph 80 of the ICJ's 2010 advisory opinion on Kosovo clearly states that the principle of territorial integrity applies to relations between states.




In other words, this principle protects a state's sovereignty against occupation, aggression or the seizure of its territory by another state. In my interpretation, it cannot be used to deny peoples their right to self-determination.




Therefore, in this context, the principle of territorial integrity does not apply to a state's internal relations. It concerns external relations between states. For example, State A cannot occupy or colonise the territory of State B or settle its own population there. However, when a conflict arises between a people's right to self-determination and a state's desire to preserve its existing borders, I believe that the right to self-determination should take precedence over the principle of territorial integrity.




You say that the right to self-determination is clearly recognised under international law. Nevertheless, serious obstacles prevent Kurds from exercising this right. Do you think the main reason is shortcomings in international law, or the political and economic interests of states?




What I have explained is the theoretical dimension of the issue. I address this subject in my book Building a Just World Order, which has also recently been published in Spanish. I devoted the fifth chapter to the theory and practice of the right to self-determination. However, there is a reality that we must understand, acknowledge and confront: this is an extremely political issue.




If international conditions are unfavourable and you cannot secure the support of sufficiently powerful states, exercising the right to self-determination becomes almost impossible, whether through autonomy or secession. In other words, it is a matter of power relations and the economic interests of states. For example, we must remember that Iraqi Kurdistan is a region rich in oil. There are significant resources, economic assets and interests there. Multinational corporations and other actors want to preserve the status quo and are concerned about Kurdistan's independence.




'

Kurdish rights are sacrificed to political and economic interests'




I believe that the people of Iraqi Kurdistan have a right to a remedy, particularly in view of the genocide committed in Halabja in 1988. In my opinion, that remedy should be independence, meaning secession.




What, then, can the Kurds do? International law is applied with double standards. Another people who have the right to self-determination and to establish their own state are the Palestinians. Every day, we see on television events that I consider to constitute genocide. We have extremely extensive information about Israel's oppression of the Palestinian people. What has the international community done to stop it? Nothing. There is the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement.




Has this movement achieved any progress? No. There is complicity on the part of European states, particularly the United States. The US, the United Kingdom and European Union countries have provided Israel with military, economic, political, diplomatic and media support. In my opinion, this makes them complicit in genocide.




'

Kurds have the right to resist occupation'




What is happening in the world? Nothing. Even UN Secretary-General António Guterres has not used the word "genocide". Not once. Similarly, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk can condemn crimes and human rights violations committed against Palestinians, but he has not dared to use the term "genocide".




You see, this is also a question of perception, and the media plays a role in it. In my opinion, the media has adopted a hostile attitude towards Palestinians. It has vilified them, portrayed them as terrorists and contributed to their demonisation. Yet the Palestinian people have the right to self-determination and the right to resist occupation, oppression and exploitation by a state such as Israel.




Of course, the right to resist also applies to the Kurds. According to my interpretation of international law, the Kurds also have the right to resist occupation and violations of their human rights. This principle is also addressed in Article 7 of UN General Assembly Resolution 33/14. However, I repeat that these are theoretical considerations.




You have said that the implementation of rights recognised under international law depends largely on political power relations. What path should the Kurds follow to bring their right to self-determination more prominently onto the international agenda and gain support? In particular, what should they do to mobilise international public opinion and different states?




In practice, economic interests determine the policies of the US, the United Kingdom and the European Union. At present, these powers have no interest in changing the situation in Turkey, Syria or Iraq. Of course, Israel and the US want regime change in Iran. We know this, and we can see it.




In my opinion, this is completely contrary to international law. However, we do not have sufficiently effective mechanisms to oppose it. So what can we do? What remains is public opinion, global public opinion.




'Kurds need to win the information war'




It is extremely important for the Kurds to find friends and allies among countries known as the "Global South" or the "Global Majority". However, to gain friends and allies, people must first know about your situation. If you mention the Treaty of Sèvres to someone here in Geneva or in New York today, they will probably look at you without understanding anything. Many people have no idea about this issue.




Similarly, when you mention the Kurdish people, some people may never have heard of them or may have learned almost nothing about their history. That is why the Kurds need to win the information war. You must ensure that people read about your situation, become informed and understand what you have experienced. As I told you, I deeply believe that the Kurds are among the peoples with the clearest and most fundamental right to self-determination. It is unbelievable that a people of 45 million should have no state of their own. It is absurd, absolutely absurd. But that is the reality. Nevertheless, very few people know about your situation.

title: Evren: Poor children pushed out of education into cheap labour
content:
The Ministry of National Education's (MEB) proposed 2027 budget, approved by the Turkish Parliament's Planning and Budget Committee on 12 November, continues to spark debate ahead of a vote in the General Assembly in December.




The ministry's initial budget for 2026 was set at 1 trillion 943 billion 965 million Turkish lira. The proposed budget for 2027 has been increased by 26.5 percent in nominal terms to 2 trillion 458 billion 762 million lira. Despite this increase, however, the ministry's share of the central government budget and national income continues to decline. Its share of the central government budget fell from 13.38 percent in 2016 to 10.24 percent in 2026 and 9.02 percent in the 2027 proposal. Its share of gross domestic product (GDP) also declined from 2.91 percent to 2.21 percent over the same period.




Of the proposed 2027 budget, 82.1 percent has been allocated to personnel expenses and payments to the Social Security Institution (SGK). Teachers' salaries remaining below the poverty threshold, alongside attempts to address shortages of permanent cleaning and security staff in schools through temporary employment programmes, have once again brought problems in public education to the forefront.




Problems in meeting basic needs at state schools persist, while private schools now account for 20.1 percent of all schools. This means that one in every five schools in the country is privately run. Meanwhile, the proposed budget of 229 billion 64 million lira for the Presidency of Religious Affairs has increased in real terms and exceeds the individual budgets of the ministries of Interior, Foreign Affairs, Trade, Culture and Tourism, and Energy and Natural Resources.




Including the budgets of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), the Measuring, Selection and Placement Centre (ÖSYM), and universities, the total proposed education budget for 2027 stands at 3 trillion 755 billion 688 million lira.




'The budget cannot be assessed through economic figures alone'




Sami Evren, co-spokesperson of the Education Policies Commission of the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), spoke to ANF about the budget proposal approved by the committee. Evren said that assessing the budget solely through economic figures would be insufficient. Evren said that problems concerning education, healthcare and justice in the country were directly linked to the question of democracy, adding that the government had closed its budget proposals to criticism from the opposition. Evren also said that the budget deficit of approximately 3.9 trillion lira, within an overall budget exceeding 27 trillion lira, would once again be covered by the public.




Evren said that the approximately 13 percent allocated to the Ministry of National Education was focused on mandatory personnel expenses rather than investment. Evren argued that the government's calculations, based on its own announced inflation figures, reflected a preference for capital interests rather than the public.




Evren said, "This actually means that, in real terms, the political government has prepared the budget according to the priorities of its own financial circles rather than in favour of public education and the people."




'T

he public character of education has been undermined'




Evren said that the future of approximately 17 million students, representing a quarter of Turkey's population, and 75,000 schools would be shaped by this budget. Evren argued that the existence of approximately 15,000 private schools had undermined the public character of education.




Evren said that state schools were increasingly becoming institutions attended primarily by children from poor families, creating a new class hierarchy in education. Evren also stressed that teachers working in private schools were being exploited as cheap labour. Evren argued that expanding private education meant pushing the public sector out of education. He said, "When public education is marginalised, you cannot see students with disabilities or students from poor families. You cannot address the debates about the content of education."




'Peace is impossible without education in the mother tongue'




Evren also addressed the Peace and Democratic Society Process, recalling that politicians had begun suggesting that less money would be allocated to war. Evren said that genuine peace required these resources to be redirected towards democratic integration and education. Evren stressed that the right to education in the mother tongue must be constitutionally guaranteed and that budgetary resources must be allocated to establishing the necessary infrastructure. Otherwise, discrimination would deepen.




Evren said that the government was attempting to manage the process solely through the rhetoric of a "terror-free Turkey" and administrative circulars, but that such an approach would not gain acceptance in society. Evren said, "Without resolving the question of education in the mother tongue, it is impossible to clarify the question of peace or the resolution process in Turkey. As long as this discrimination continues, you cannot force people in this country to live together."




Evren reaffirmed the party's determination on the issue, saying, "Education in the mother tongue is one of the most important priorities of our programme of struggle. It is a vital issue for us."




'The freer universities become, the sooner we will achieve peace'




Sami Evren recalled that the education system did not consist solely of the 17 million students in formal schooling, but also included approximately six million university students. Evren criticised the appointment of government trustees to universities and the repression of student movements.




Referring to the Interior Ministry's 17-point circular entitled "Security Measures at Universities", Evren said that higher education authorities were attempting to exclude young people from the process and were adopting an authoritarian approach that treated students as potential criminals. Evren described investigations against university students and their suspensions from education as unacceptable. Evren said, "The freer universities become, the sooner we will be able to achieve peace. If you destroy the youth movement, you also destroy democracy in Turkey."




'The government is strengthening religious orders for political purposes'




Sami Evren said that inequalities in income distribution were directly reflected in schools. Evren criticised the failure to allocate resources in the budget to provide students with one free meal a day, cover transportation costs and improve hygiene conditions in schools. Evren also criticised the outsourcing of cleaning and support services in schools to subcontracting companies, saying that children from poor families were being pushed out of the education system and turned into a source of cheap labour.




Evren said that the Presidency of Religious Affairs had been allocated a budget greater than the combined budgets of eight or nine ministries, while resources were being channelled to religious communities through foundations. Evren argued that these organisations, which were intervening even in preschool education, were undermining secular and scientific education. Evren also said that religious communities had effectively become corporate conglomerates and that the funds transferred to them could not be properly audited. Evren said, "While the budgets of schools providing quality scientific education are being cut, resources are being channelled to the Presidency of Religious Affairs and religious communities through various budget allocations."




Evren further stressed that the government was strengthening religious orders in pursuit of its political objectives, arguing that religious motivations were being used particularly in Kurdistan to suppress the democratic movement. Evren said that such policies were unacceptable.




'We will continue our struggle'




Sami Evren said that a school was more than just four walls. It was an institution encompassing parents, teachers, students and civil society organisations in the surrounding neighbourhood. Evren argued that the uniform, rote-learning curriculum imposed from Ankara had intensified social problems, particularly the recent incidents of violence in schools.




Evren said that the DEM Party was struggling for a scientific and public education system in which academics, trade unions and democratic civil society organisations had a say. Evren said, "Together with our poor people and those facing discrimination, we reject this budget. We will continue our struggle to ensure that this becomes a democratic budget and part of democratic politics."
