title: Şadiye Dalkıran: Women should never remain where they are subjected to violence
content:
Dilan Aslan was murdered by a firearm in March last year by Abdulvahap Aslan, the husband she was in the process of divorcing. Following the murder, it emerged that the man had attempted to stage the killing as a suicide and had driven around the city for approximately two hours in an attempt to destroy evidence.




During her marriage in Istanbul, Dilan (nicknamed Tuba) was subjected to systematic violence and repeatedly received death threats. After witnessing her children being subjected to violence as well, Dilan decided to divorce and moved from Istanbul to Amed (Diyarbakır), where her family lived.




After staying with her family for a while, Dilan tried to rebuild her life despite threats from the violent husband, Abdulvahap Aslan. However, following his request for reconciliation and pressure from both families, she agreed to reunite with him.




On the night of 31 March, Abdulvahap Aslan and Dilan arrived in the centre of the Xana Axpar (Çınar) district of Amed and went to the house where they were staying in the Bağlar district. There, Aslan first subjected Dilan to violence and then murdered her using a firearm.




After the murder, the perpetrator attempted to destroy evidence at the scene before leaving the house. Calling a relative, Abdulvahap Aslan claimed, “My wife shot herself in the head,” attempting to make the murder look like a suicide. He then drove around the city, remaining unaccounted for approximately two hours.




Approximately two hours later, Abdulvahap Aslan went to the police station and surrendered. Following police procedures that same day, he was arrested and sent to prison.




Killer sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment




Throughout the trial, the perpetrator, Abdulvahap Aslan, maintained that the incident had been a suicide. However, neither the report prepared by the Council of Forensic Medicine (ATK) nor the indictment supported his claim. Evidence and witness testimonies also disproved his defence of suicide, while statements given by Dilan Aslan’s children during the trial revealed the extent of the violence they had suffered and the circumstances surrounding the murder.




The lawyer representing the family in the case had previously made a statement about the incident, noting that Dilan Aslan still bore signs of physical violence when she arrived in Amed. The lawyer said: “Even when she arrived here, there were marks of physical assault on her face and body. Shortly after she arrived, the defendant followed Dilan to Diyarbakır. With family members intervening, attempts were made to reconcile the two. Following these meetings, Dilan did not return to Istanbul. During conversations that took place from time to time, the same threats continued. All family members witnessed the death threats in question. On the day of the incident, the defendant also sent his three children to different homes, leaving only his five-year-old child at home.”




The case, which was launched following the preparation of the indictment, concluded last month with the final hearing at Diyarbakır's 1st High Criminal Court. The court sentenced Abdulvahap Aslan to aggravated life imprisonment for the crime of “intentional killing of a spouse and a woman”, without granting him any sentence reductions.




She lived under violence and threats for years




Since her daughter's murder, Şadiye Dalkıran has regularly visited her grave. She refused to allow the perpetrator's surname to be inscribed on the gravestone. Instead, she had her daughter's family nickname, Tuba, and her own family surname written on it, and decorated the grave with mint and flowers.







 







Praying at her daughter's grave and commemorating other women who had been murdered alongside her, Şadiye Dalkıran spoke about the violence her daughter endured throughout her marriage, the death threats she received and her struggle to build a new life.




Şadiye Dalkıran said that her daughter had married of her own free will and had four children from the marriage. Despite this, she explained, her daughter had lived under violence and abuse for years.




Şadiye Dalkıran added that her daughter had hidden what she was going through because she did not want to upset her family. She continued: “After my daughter got married, I never once saw her smile. She suffered terribly, endured so much pain and was subjected to torture. She did not tell us what she was going through because she did not want us to worry; she constantly kept it hidden.




She suffered immense cruelty and insults at the hands of that man. She was constantly subjected to violence and received death threats. When we learned what was happening, we would tell her, ‘Come here,’ but she wanted to stay there for the sake of her children. I don't know how many times she came close to death. That man provided neither my daughter nor her children with what they needed. My daughter raised her children using her own resources. Whenever she asked for something or tried to speak up, she was subjected to violence.”













‘She resisted until the very end’




Şadiye Dalkıran said that the perpetrator concealed his true nature in front of the family, but that her daughter had eventually begun speaking about what she was experiencing when the threats escalated to death threats. She also explained that the violence was directed at the children as well.




Describing her daughter's struggle to build a new life with her children, Şadiye Dalkıran said: “He subjected not only my daughter but also his own children to violence. When the children could not bear seeing their mother being abused, he would beat them too. Eventually, when my daughter could no longer endure it, she sold her earrings and necklace and bought tickets for herself and her children. She fled here to escape that man's cruelty. Tuba wanted to build a new life, to live peacefully and happily with her children. She said she would resist every kind of difficulty. She came here, but she could not escape that man.”




‘My daughter wanted to build a new life’




Şadiye Dalkıran said that Abdulvahap Aslan had followed her daughter to her family's home and persuaded them with promises of reconciliation. She then described the day her daughter was murdered.













Speaking about the pain she continues to endure, Şadiye Dalkıran said: “Abdulvahap came here after my daughter. He said he regretted what he had done and wanted to reconcile, making promises. That was how he deceived us too. They left together, taking their five-year-old child with them. At five o'clock that morning, we received the news that my daughter had been murdered. He was telling everyone, ‘She killed herself.’




My daughter had endured so much torture, yet she resisted and stayed alive. Nobody believed that lie. Evidence emerged showing that my daughter had not killed herself. His lies were subsequently exposed in court and in the reports as well. If we had known this would happen, we would never have allowed it. I would never have sent my daughter with him. Despite everything, Tuba wanted to live and build a new life with her children. He did not even allow her that. My daughter was never able to smile throughout her life. May God ensure that he does not escape justice. I hope he never walks out of the prison gates again and remains behind bars until his final breath.”













‘Women should never stay where they experience violence’




Following her daughter's murder, Şadiye Dalkıran issued a call to prevent other mothers from experiencing the same pain. She urged women to leave environments where they are subjected to violence and not to remain silent. Emphasising that perpetrators of violence must receive deterrent sentences, she said: “As a mother whose heart has been broken, I say this: May no other mother ever suffer like this again, may no mother have to cry, and may no woman's child be murdered. Femicides must stop now. We have cried; my daughter was murdered. No more women should be murdered.




They should give everyone the same sentence they gave that man. If everyone received such sentences, women would not be murdered. Men get away with whatever they do. No more mothers should have to endure this heartbreak. No man who murders women or subjects them to violence should ever be released from prison.”




‘Families must not accept violence’




Emphasising that women should not accept violence or verbal abuse, Şadiye Dalkıran also called on families not to remain silent in the face of violence. Saying that she did not want her daughter's experiences to be forgotten, she continued: “I am calling on all women and mothers: Do not stay anywhere you are subjected to cruelty or violence. Do not accept it. Focus on your own lives and your own paths; do not stay in such places for anyone's sake.




We no longer want to hear news of femicides. Women must stand up against violence and raise their voices in every sphere. This violence and these murders must come to an end. We must resist and must not remain silent. They should accept neither insults nor violence. May nobody forget my daughter or what she went through. It is not only women who must refuse to accept this; their families, brothers, siblings and mothers must also refuse to accept such violence. Nobody should remain silent.”

title: Iraqi army takes control of Jurf al-Sakhar, stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah
content:
The Iraqi central government has taken control of security in the Jurf al-Sakhar region, which has been dominated by the pro-Iranian militia Kataib Hezbollah for more than a decade. On Friday, army units and other security forces entered the town, located approximately 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad. The deployment followed an agreement that temporarily averted an armed confrontation between government forces and the influential militia.




Jurf al-Sakhar, renamed Jurf al-Nasr by Shiite militias after its recapture from the Islamic State (ISIS) in 2014, is considered one of Kataib Hezbollah’s most important strongholds. The Iran-aligned militia has spent years establishing military structures there largely independently of the Iraqi central government. Baghdad’s attempt to regain control is therefore seen as a major test for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.




Joint security command assumes responsibilities




According to Iraqi security officials, a joint command comprising units of the army, federal police, Popular Mobilization Forces (Hashd al-Shaabi), and police responsible for energy infrastructure began operating on Friday morning. The new command structure is expected to gradually assume responsibility for security and coordinate the withdrawal of the militia units previously stationed in the area. According to Iraqi government spokesperson Saad Maan, security forces have already begun monitoring the oil pipelines running through the region.




A major road link toward Karbala is also scheduled to reopen on Saturday. Units of the Iraqi army and federal police are expected to secure the route. The agreement stipulates that Kataib Hezbollah groups will leave the area and make way for state security forces. However, it remains unclear whether the militia will actually lose its longstanding influence over the region. The handover is expected to take place over an extended period.




Press conference by Iraqi officials




Iraqi officials held a press conference on the security situation in the Jurf al-Sakhar region on Friday.




Speaking here, Ahmed Hatim Hamid, commander of the Main Control Base, announced that a base had been established for the Iraqi army and police forces. He also reported that the Chief of Staff of the Iraqi Army had visited the region to monitor the deployment of military forces and inspect the measures taken.




The spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces stated that all administrative and management responsibilities in the Jurf al-Sakhar region had been transferred to the control base.




Meanwhile, the head of the Security Media Cell announced that a commando battalion had been deployed to the region to protect its oil pipelines. Stating that handover procedures were underway between the forces in the area, the head of the Security Media Cell said that security in the Jurf al-Sakhar region would now be under the control of federal forces.







Oil smuggling triggered power struggle




The latest confrontation was sparked by investigations into an alleged network involved in the illegal trade of Iraqi oil. According to an investigation by the Reuters news agency, members of Kataib Hezbollah, together with individuals from state security agencies and oil authorities, are suspected of having diverted crude oil from pipelines and smuggled it for years. Investigators reportedly discovered tampered pipelines, concealed pumping facilities, and a small refinery. The financial losses could amount to several hundred million dollars. Kataib Hezbollah denies the allegations and views the government’s actions as an attempt to force the militia to surrender its weapons.




In connection with the investigations, Prime Minister al-Zaidi ordered the dismissal of nine senior officials from security agencies and the oil sector. At the same time, government troops were placed on alert and prepared for a possible operation against the militia. The escalating tensions eventually led to negotiations involving influential Shiite politicians. Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, also reportedly traveled to Baghdad to mediate between the parties. The handover now underway is seen as the outcome of these talks.




Closed off to the local population since 2014




The developments also affect the former residents of Jurf al-Sakhar. Before the town was captured by ISIS in 2014, it and the surrounding area were predominantly inhabited by Sunni families. Following its recapture by Shiite militias, residents were displaced or prevented from returning. Kataib Hezbollah subsequently transformed the area into a largely sealed-off military zone. Secret detention facilities are also believed to have been established there alongside military installations. The displaced population was barred from returning for years. With the deployment of state security forces, the question has once again arisen as to whether restrictions on access to the area will be lifted and displaced residents allowed to return. So far, no concrete commitments or timetable have been announced.

title: Solidarity reception for Rojava at New South Wales parliament
content:
The Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia (FDKS-A), the Sydney Democratic Kurdish Community Centre, and the Sydney Kurdish Youth Association organized a solidarity reception for Rojava at the Parliament of New South Wales (NSW), Australia.




Speaking at the event, members of parliament expressed their support for the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom, peace, and democracy. Representatives of political parties, civil society organizations, and members of the Kurdish community attended the reception.




Greens MP Abigail Boyd described the resistance in Kobanê as a symbol of international solidarity and the right of peoples to self-defense, affirming her party’s solidarity with the Kurdish people.




Labor Party MP Charishma Kaliyanda emphasized that Kobanê had become a symbol of courage, resistance, and, in particular, women’s struggle for freedom.




Liberal Party MP Justin Clancy also highlighted the significance of the Kurds’ struggle against ISIS for Australia and the wider world.




FDKS-A (Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia) Co-Chair Gülfer Olan stated that the resistance in Kobanê was a struggle that concerned not only the Kurdish people but all of humanity, stressing that protecting the achievements of Rojava was a shared responsibility.

title: COP31: Women’s organizations criticize inequitable distribution of climate finance
content:
Criticism of international climate finance is mounting at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya. Women’s rights and environmental organizations accuse industrialized countries of failing to adequately meet their financial commitments and disadvantaging the populations most affected by the climate crisis in the allocation of funds. They say the focus is not only on the amount of funding pledged, but also on who decides how it is used and which initiatives actually gain access to international climate funds.




On Thursday, the Women and Gender Constituency (WGC), a coalition of women’s rights and gender organizations involved in the UN climate negotiations, highlighted significant shortcomings in funding for climate adaptation measures, the participation of local communities, and a socially just energy transition. Together with other civil society organizations, it is calling for public climate finance to be directed specifically toward the people and communities most severely affected by the consequences of global warming.




Little funding reaches women-led initiatives




Figures from the Dutch environmental and development organization Both ENDS illustrate how unequally international climate finance is distributed. According to the organization, only around 0.1 percent of global climate finance goes to initiatives supporting women and the environment. Women’s organizations and local communities developing their own solutions to the impacts of the climate crisis thus receive only a tiny fraction of the available funding.




The Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action (GAGGA) points to another figure: Just 0.22 percent of climate-related official development finance reaches women’s rights organizations. Although the two figures are based on different definitions and scopes, the organizations argue that both highlight the structural barriers faced particularly by smaller initiatives.




International climate funds are largely administered through governments, development banks, and major institutions. For local women’s organizations, complicated application procedures, demanding administrative requirements, and short funding periods often pose significant obstacles. Daan Robben, who is responsible for locally led climate finance at Both ENDS, criticizes the notion that merely promising public participation is sufficient. Instead, women’s organizations and local communities need direct access to flexible, long-term funding.




Adaptation Fund falls far short of funding target




The funding gap is also evident in the international Adaptation Fund, which supports developing countries in addressing the impacts of climate change that have already occurred or are anticipated. Among other things, the fund supports projects aimed at protecting communities from droughts and floods, securing water supplies, and strengthening local livelihoods. At a high-level funding meeting on November 17, only Spain, Germany, and Ireland announced new contributions. Together with earlier pledges from Estonia, Portugal, and the Belgian region of Brussels, the announced contributions totaled US$50 million by the following day.




This means that only one-sixth of the annual minimum target of $300 million has been met. In a joint statement issued on November 18, the WGC and other civil society coalitions described the contributions as wholly inadequate. They called on industrialized countries to provide additional funding before the climate conference concludes.




The scale of the funding gap becomes clear when compared with actual needs. According to calculations by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), developing countries will require approximately $305 billion annually by 2035 to adapt to climate change. Taking inflation into account, this figure could rise to around $420 billion. The organizations emphasize that additional funding must not lead to further indebtedness among the affected countries. Instead of loans, they are calling for grants that do not have to be repaid and can be used as directly as possible for local adaptation measures.




Public responsibility instead of dependence on investors




Underlying the dispute over funding is a fundamental question of international climate policy. Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement obliges industrialized countries to provide financial support to developing countries for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. Women’s organizations warn against increasingly shifting this responsibility onto private investors. While private-sector investment can help finance the energy transition, many essential adaptation measures offer no immediate financial returns.




These include, for example, protecting small farms from droughts, improving water supplies in remote regions, and implementing local measures to prevent damage from flooding and extreme heat. Such projects are vital for the communities affected but are often of little interest to profit-driven investors. The WGC is therefore calling for a climate finance system guided by human rights and social needs. Public funding must be provided reliably rather than leaving its allocation largely to market mechanisms.




Energy transition must address social inequalities




Another key focus of the debates in Antalya is the social conditions under which the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy takes place. Ecofeminist Melania Chiponda of the international network Shine Collab warns against reducing the energy transition to technological modernization and the replacement of energy sources. She stressed that a just transition must also take into account people who currently lack adequate access to energy or live and work under precarious conditions.




Women’s organizations point out that new solar installations, electric vehicles, and investments in renewable energy do not, in themselves, guarantee socially equitable energy access. What matters, they argue, is whether previously disadvantaged communities gain access to affordable electricity, schools and hospitals receive a reliable energy supply, and new employment opportunities are created. Accordingly, the distribution of economic benefits must also be taken into account. Women and informal workers must not be excluded from new jobs and decision-making structures.




GAGGA also warns of the risk that the energy transition could perpetuate existing forms of exploitation, stating that the extraction of raw materials for new energy technologies could involve land dispossession and violations of the rights of Indigenous communities. The alliance therefore advocates community-led energy projects, the protection of natural resources, and greater recognition of unpaid care work.




Participation also means decision-making power




The demands of women’s organizations extend beyond increased financial support. They are also calling for a fundamental transformation of decision-making structures within international climate policy. Pabrya Lobos, who works on climate adaptation policy within the framework of the climate negotiations, emphasized that women and local communities must be involved in developing and implementing the programs that directly affect their living conditions.




According to the organizations, inviting women representatives to conferences or listening to their experiences during consultation processes is not enough. They must also have a say in deciding which projects receive funding, which priorities are set, and how the available resources are allocated. The experiences of women, girls, Indigenous communities, and other particularly affected population groups should therefore not merely be taken into account as an additional consideration but should form a foundation of climate policy.




More than 2,600 local initiatives supported




GAGGA points to its own funding practices as evidence that more locally focused financing is possible. According to the alliance, more than €50 million has so far been channeled to over 2,600 initiatives led by women and local communities across 60 countries. The funded projects address issues including forest protection, biodiversity conservation, the restoration of degraded soils, and strengthening the resilience of local communities to climate-related disasters.




GAGGA emphasizes that such initiatives need more than short-term project funding. According to the alliance, flexible, multi-year funding commitments are essential to enable them to operate effectively over the long term. The organizations and networks that connect local groups and facilitate their access to funding must also be strengthened.




As COP31 draws to a close, women’s and environmental organizations are calling on governments to move beyond general statements of intent. They are demanding additional public funding for climate change adaptation, binding financing mechanisms that do not create debt, and policies to ensure a socially just energy transition. The WGC emphasizes that the success of the climate negotiations must not be measured solely by the decisions adopted. What matters, it argues, is whether these decisions lead to tangible improvements for women, workers, Indigenous peoples, and communities particularly affected by the climate crisis.

title: “Tree of Remembrance” created for murdered women in Amed
content:
Since Friday, a “Tree of Remembrance” in Sümer Park in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) has commemorated women who were murdered in the city over the past two years. The Women’s Council of the Metropolitan Municipality attached the names of the murdered women to the branches of a tree to preserve their life stories in collective memory. The initiative was organized as part of events marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.




At the unveiling of the memorial tree, Rojda Çeçen from the Women’s Council Secretariat stated that violence against women was not limited to acts of violence themselves. “Looking the other way is also part of the violence. Confronting violence is therefore a shared responsibility of society as a whole," she emphasized.




Çeçen particularly commemorated two women who have been murdered in Sümer Park only recently. She said the pain of their deaths was still deeply felt. "The names attached to the tree represent not only individual victims of femicide but also lives cut short, voices silenced, and women whose memory must not be erased," she stated.

title: Kurdish women discuss shared political perspectives in Sulaymaniyah
content:
Representatives of women’s organizations from all four parts of Kurdistan gathered in Sulaymaniyah on Friday to discuss political developments in the region, national unity, and the future of the Kurdish women’s movement. Organized by the Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women, the meeting also serves as preparation for the third Conference on the National Unity of Kurdish Women. The central question is how women’s organizations can develop common positions amid political upheavals and strengthen their participation in decision-making processes.




In addition to representatives of women’s organizations, the gathering is attended by women politicians, activists, and other prominent figures from Kurdistan. In her opening speech, Şîrîn Tahir described the meeting as an important and decisive step in shaping the platform’s future work.




Tahir outlined three main priorities: assessing political developments in Kurdistan and the Middle East and their impact on women’s rights, critically reviewing the work carried out so far, and making organizational preparations for the third women’s conference. The aim, she said, was to bring Kurdish women’s collective strength and capacity for action into closer alignment across the borders of all four parts of Kurdistan.










https://rojnews.video/upload/videos/2026/11/w9XHyjDvqAHxEhNecCQM_20_5c6c0282c82d8f10f993c5ab1d3a7e1e_video_1080p_converted.mp4










Prioritizing national unity over party-political interests




During the first session, participants discussed the political challenges facing the Kurdish people and the impact of regional shifts in power on women’s rights and political status. It was emphasized that Kurdish women are internationally recognized as members of a single people, regardless of which part of Kurdistan they come from. “This shared identity must be matched by stronger political cooperation.”




The participants stressed that the national unity of Kurdish women must not be subordinated to party-political interests. Instead, they underlined, autonomous women’s organizing must take a leading role in developing shared political perspectives.




At the same time, participants warned against leaving the current transformations solely in the hands of existing, predominantly male-dominated power structures. They pointed put that, without women taking an active leadership role, there was a risk that political decisions would continue to be shaped by patriarchal attitudes. “The Kurds are not powerless in the face of the changes taking place in the Middle East. Through democratic struggle and collective political action, they can strengthen their rights and political status,” participants emphasized during the discussions.













Southern Kurdistan: Warning against political division




The political situation in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) featured prominently in the discussions. The participants strongly opposed any division of the region or weakening of its political status. In their assessment, such developments would primarily serve the interests of Turkey, Iran, and the Syrian transitional government, leaving the people of Southern Kurdistan more vulnerable to external interference.




The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) were therefore urged not to pursue their political differences at the expense of existing achievements. “Preserving the region’s political status must take precedence over party-political disputes,” the participants demanded.




The participants identified democracy, social unity, and political freedom as fundamental prerequisites for safeguarding these achievements. In this context, they also discussed a message from Abdullah Öcalan to the political forces of Southern Kurdistan, in which he had emphasized the formation of a democratic government and women’s participation in leadership as important steps toward overcoming the current situation.




The participants criticized the widespread exclusion of women from political decision-making processes. As a concrete initiative, they proposed forming a women’s delegation to hold talks with political parties and other political actors. The delegation, they said, would advocate for the protection of the political status of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and the effective participation of women.













Rojava: Recognition of Kurdish rights in the integration process




Another key focus was developments in Rojava and the political restructuring of Syria. The participants discussed the ongoing integration process, the future of the autonomous administration structures, and how the rights of the Kurdish population could be safeguarded within a new political order. The integration process was described as difficult and sensitive. According to participants, further efforts will be needed to ensure that the Kurds are recognized as a distinct social and political component of Syria.




The participants emphasized the importance of a social contract that would define Syria’s future political order and ensure meaningful Kurdish participation in political decision-making. “This must not be merely about the formal recognition of Kurdish existence. What matters is that Kurds are able to participate in shaping political and social structures.”




The efforts made so far to defend Kurdish rights and organize society were acknowledged, but were also considered insufficient. The participants called for continued support for democratic integration efforts, stronger grassroots organization, and greater political capacity for action among the Kurdish population.










https://rojnews.video/upload/videos/2026/11/gvTa4EsLd1tSAhdsmTRJ_20_9a769dfebbe9e7c32b7cdc113fa76622_video_1080p_converted.mp4










Eastern Kurdistan: Repression and death sentences against women




The situation in Eastern Kurdistan was also discussed in detail. The discussions focused on the economic and political crises in Iran, the ongoing repression of the Kurdish population, and the impact of regional conflicts. The participants pointed to the execution of at least 691 people of various national backgrounds since the beginning of the year, as well as death sentences imposed on several Kurdish women. They interpreted the state repression as a reflection of the Iranian regime’s fear of social resistance and independent political organizing.




At the same time, the participants warned of the consequences of regional power struggles, stating that the current external pressure would not necessarily lead to the end of the Iranian regime. Conversely, they said, a strengthening of the existing regime could further jeopardize the rights and security of the Kurdish population. Against this backdrop, the participants emphasized the need for an independent political strategy for Eastern Kurdistan. “The Kurds must have a clear strategy for protecting their population and securing recognition of their national identity.”




Particular importance was attached to raising the international visibility of women in Eastern Kurdistan. It was stressed that their experiences of repression, political demands, and resistance must receive greater attention worldwide.




Third women’s conference aims to deepen cooperation




Alongside current political developments, the organizational future of the platform is also on the agenda. Şîrîn Tahir explained in her opening remarks that previous activities and experiences are to be critically evaluated in order to draw lessons for future cooperation. The planned third Conference on the National Unity of Kurdish Women is intended to help renew organizational structures and bring the forces of the women’s movement closer together. To this end, the meeting in Sulaymaniyah is expected to develop concrete preparatory steps, working mechanisms, and shared political perspectives.

title: Bakırhan: The goal of the peace process is democracy and equal citizenship
content:
Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), criticized the Turkish government’s budget policies and outlined the objectives of the ongoing peace process at a meeting with civil society organizations in Mersin. The event was held as part of the DEM Party’s campaign, "Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice.” Bakırhan began by highlighting the social diversity of Mersin, where people of different backgrounds and faiths live together. He said the city, with its strong tradition of social and trade union struggles, could serve as an example for the whole of Turkey.




Budget not being used to meet the people’s needs




Referring to the budget deliberations, Bakırhan accused the government of spending tax revenues primarily on armaments, conflict-driven policies, interest payments, and companies with close ties to the government, rather than on the needs of the people. By contrast, he said, the DEM Party sought to prioritize the interests of workers, pensioners, women, young people, and low-income groups.




The DEM Party Co-Chair was particularly critical of rising child poverty, stating that many students could no longer afford their education expenses or were having to contribute to their families’ income. title: Resistance against solar power project in Arzoxlî on day 30
content:
The resistance against the construction of a solar power plant in Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır), has entered its second month. For 30 days, residents have been protesting against the energy project, which threatens their agricultural land and, consequently, their livelihoods. On Friday, numerous people once again gathered at the protest tent to continue the mobilization, which has been led primarily by women.




In addition to villagers, representatives of political parties, activists from the Peace Mothers Council, and members of civil society and environmental organizations took part in the protest. Chanting slogans including “We will prevail through resistance” and “Em axa xwe nadin” (“We will not give up our land”), the demonstrators marched from the village square to the protest tent.




“We will not bow to these companies”




Peace Mother Nezahat Teke, who also joined the protest, was particularly critical of the support the company was receiving from uniformed state personnel. “We will not bow to these companies. The women and men here must not be left alone in the rain,” Teke declared. She said the company could rely on military support in carrying out its activities. “This is not a matter for the soldiers, but for the company owner. Yet soldiers and police are supporting him. We mothers will resist until the end.”




Villager Güler Çiftçi also reaffirmed that the residents would not give up despite increasingly difficult weather conditions. “We wish the whole world had come out to support us today. We are fighting for our own land and our own water, through rain and drought, enduring hardship and difficult conditions. We will not surrender our land to anyone.”




Çiftçi accused the state security forces of siding with the company, saying: “The company has the state behind it. We do not want to see soldiers and the gendarmerie as our adversaries. We wish they would stand behind us. But unfortunately, today they are standing behind the company rather than us.” Çiftçi stressed that residents would continue to defend their living environment and the future of their children.




“Women are defending their livelihoods”




Halide Türkoğlu, spokesperson for the Women’s Council of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), praised the leading role of women in the resistance in Arzoxlî. Their struggle, she said, was directed not merely against a single construction project, but against the loss of the economic and ecological foundations of village life.




“The villagers’ resistance began under the leadership of women. Because when women defend their land, they are also defending their livelihoods and the future of their children,” Türkoğlu stated.




She stated that the government has deployed gendarmerie forces to surround the protest site rather than taking the concerns of the people seriously.




Türkoğlu criticized the fact that solar and geothermal energy projects, as well as mining operations, were threatening the livelihoods of rural communities in numerous regions of Kurdistan.




“While the alliance between capital and the government brings poverty into our lives, our natural environment is being destroyed day by day. Defending natural habitats is also a matter of fundamental rights: Our right to exist encompasses our identity, our language, and our natural environment. If anyone tries to take these away from us, we will never surrender them,” the DEM Party politician said.




Criticism of environmental policy amid the ongoing peace process




“The villagers’ resistance began under the leadership of women. Because when women defend their land, they are also defending their livelihoods and the future of their children,” Türkoğlu stated. Rather than taking the concerns of the population seriously, the government had deployed gendarmerie forces to surround the protest site, she said. Türkoğlu criticized the fact that solar and geothermal energy projects, as well as mining operations, were threatening the livelihoods of rural communities in numerous regions of Kurdistan.




Türkoğlu continued: “While the alliance between the capital and the government brings poverty into our lives, our natural environment is being destroyed day by day. Defending natural habitats is also a matter of fundamental rights. Our right to exist encompasses our identity, our language, and our natural environment. If anyone tries to take these away from us, we will never surrender them.”




Criticism of environmental policy amid the ongoing peace process




Türkoğlu also linked the conflict in Arzoxlî to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process. She stressed that policies that threaten the livelihoods of the Kurdish population are continuing while peace is being discussed at the political level.  “We describe the process we are currently going through as a peace process. But at the same time, another war seems to have been launched against the Kurds and other peoples. A war has been declared on nature,” she said.




Türkoğlu pointed out that the pursuit of profit by companies, in cooperation with state authorities, had developed into a policy that displaced people from their land and drove women in particular into poverty. “If our natural environment is taken away from us, what are we supposed to eat, how are we supposed to live, how are we supposed to exist at all?” Türkoğlu asked, expressing her solidarity with the protesting women.




For the residents of Arzoxlî, protecting their land remains the central motivation behind their resistance, even after a month of protests. Güler Çiftçi said: “We will continue to defend our land, the future of our children, and the places where we live.”

title: Yazidi women forced to relive trauma to access their rights
content:
Years have passed since the genocide that remains etched in the memory of the Kurdish people. Yet for Yazidi (Êzîdî) women, the darkness that began on 3 August 2014 has not ended. Many of the women abducted from Shengal are still missing, while their families continue to wait for news of their whereabouts and what happened to them. Some hope for a mass grave to be opened, others await DNA test results, while others still hope that a loved one who has not returned home for years will one day come back.




Massacres, abductions and captivity




ISIS carried out a systematic genocide against the Yazidi community when it attacked Shengal on 3 August 2014. Men and boys were separated from their families and massacred, while women and girls were abducted, sold in slave markets, forced into marriage and subjected to rape. Women's bodies became a target of ISIS's campaign to destroy Yazidi identity and the community's very existence.




2,474 women still missing




During the genocide, 6,417 Yazidi women were abducted. Of these, 3,647 regained their freedom, while the fate of 2,474 remains unknown. Among those registered as missing, 269 were confirmed dead, and their remains were returned to their families. The abducted women were first taken to Mosul, then to Tal Afar, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and Baghouz. Women and children were moved between different cities, separated from one another and cut off from their families.




For women, captivity was not limited to a single act of abduction. Some were transferred between captors, sold to different individuals and forcibly displaced within ISIS-controlled territories, leaving their whereabouts unknown for years. Some women managed to escape, while others reached different countries. The fate of thousands remains uncertain.




Those who sought refuge in Europe




For Yazidi women who escaped ISIS captivity, the struggle to rebuild their lives extended far beyond Shengal. Some survivors were forced to settle in different countries to access medical treatment, rehabilitation and safe living conditions.




Following the genocide, Germany launched a special humanitarian resettlement programme for Yazidi women and children. Under the programme implemented by the state of Baden-Württemberg in 2015 and 2016, approximately 1,100 women and children, the vast majority of them Yazidis, were brought to Germany. They were provided with accommodation, healthcare, psychological support and educational opportunities. Canada also implemented admission and family reunification programmes for ISIS survivors, including Yazidi women and children. In 2023, the Canadian government announced that it had enabled more than 1,400 survivors to build new lives in the country.




However, establishing a safe life in another country did not erase the absence of missing loved ones or the pain of families torn apart. Some women who settled in Europe are still trying to discover the fate of their relatives in Iraq, while survivors forced to live far from their homeland have encountered new obstacles in seeking their rights. The rupture caused by the genocide has therefore continued to shape women's lives not only in Shengal but also in the countries where they have been forced to settle.




The path to freedom in Rojava




Following the liberation of Shengal in November 2015, Rojava played an important role in reuniting women and children rescued from ISIS with their families. Those freed through the efforts of the Women's Protection Units (YPJ) and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) were reunited with their families through the work of the Yazidi Women's Freedom Movement (TAJÊ) and the Shengal Autonomous Administration.




Women rebuilt their lives




The struggle of Yazidi women did not end with their liberation from captivity. Following the genocide, women began organising to prevent similar attacks and gain control over their own lives. Women established self-defence forces within the Shengal Women's Units (Yekîneyên Jinên Şengalê, YJŞ), playing a major role in the defence and liberation of Shengal. The women's organising efforts that began in 2015 gained an institutional structure in September 2016 with the establishment of TAJÊ.




This process also brought significant changes to women's position in society. Previously largely confined to family and traditional social roles, women began taking responsibility not only for self-defence but also in education, politics, diplomacy and community organising. Through women's councils and organisations, Yazidi women sought solutions to their own problems and participated in decision-making processes within the committees and institutions of the Shengal Autonomous Administration. Women whose will ISIS had sought to break thus began struggling to shape the reconstruction of their society through their own collective will.




Thousands remain displaced




Despite women's struggle for liberation and organisation, the demographic and social devastation inflicted on the Yazidi community by the genocide continues. A significant proportion of those uprooted from Shengal have been unable to return to their homeland despite the years that have passed. Currently, 36,500 people have refugee status, while 200,750 live in Iraq and 150,000 in other countries.




ISIS attacks also targeted the Yazidi faith and cultural heritage, destroying 68 sacred sites. In addition, 2,753 children were left without one or both parents during the attacks, which separated thousands of children from their families. Displacement, family separation and the destruction of sacred sites remain among the main obstacles preventing the community from rebuilding life in its homeland.




Waiting beside the mass graves




One of the most serious obstacles to establishing the fate of missing women today is the existence of mass graves. Numerous sites in and around Shengal contain the remains of Yazidis massacred by ISIS. Exhuming these graves, identifying the remains and returning them to families is essential to determining what happened to the missing.




In Shengal, 77 mass graves have been opened, while 19 remain unopened. Of the remains of 857 people recovered from the excavated graves, 296 have been identified and returned to their families. The remains of another 561 people, whose identities have yet to be established, are being held at a forensic institution in Baghdad for DNA analysis.




A further 91 mass grave cases have been investigated, including 67 in Xanesor and the surrounding area and 24 in Shengal. However, the exhumation of graves and identification of remains are not progressing at the pace families of the missing have been waiting for. The need to collect DNA samples from relatives living in other countries, coordinate between institutions and conduct forensic examinations has prolonged the process. Unopened graves and unidentified remains mean that families seeking to learn the fate of their loved ones continue to wait.




The law exists, but implementation remains inadequate




The Iraqi Parliament adopted Law No. 8, known as the Yazidi Female Survivors Law, on 1 March 2021. The law recognises ISIS crimes against Yazidis, as well as Turkmen, Christian and Shabak communities, as genocide and crimes against humanity. It grants survivors rights including monthly pensions, rehabilitation, healthcare and educational support, land allocation and participation in social life. It also places responsibility on the relevant institutions to locate abducted women, men and children, exhume mass graves and return remains to their families.




However, the rights recognised under the law face new obstacles in practice. In particular, the requirement to file a criminal complaint to obtain compensation and other benefits makes it difficult for genocide survivors to access their rights. Women seeking justice after experiencing grave violations are expected to file criminal complaints and recount their experiences before official authorities as part of the application process. As a result, a significant gap remains between the legal recognition of these rights and survivors' ability to exercise them in practice.

title: Kurdish young man faces trial in Iran on charges carrying death penalty
content:
A young Kurdish man, Mehdî Roşanî, who was detained and arrested following protests held in the city of Melîkşah (Malekshah), in Iran’s Îlam province, between December 2025 and January 2026, appeared before a court in Îlam on 18 November. He is facing several charges, including “enmity against God” and “spreading corruption on earth.”




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) reported that Roşanî and his defence lawyers attended the hearing before the First Branch of the Revolutionary Court in Îlam. Roşanî denied all the charges against him.




Roşanî was first arrested on 16 January during protests in his hometown of Melîkşah. After spending approximately three months in prison, he was released on bail. The Revolutionary Court in Îlam subsequently sentenced him to three years in prison, a sentence that was later reduced to nine months.




Roşanî was arrested again by regime forces on 18 July and transferred to Îlam Central Prison.




Following his re-arrest, the Sixth Branch of the Investigation Department of the Public and Revolutionary Prosecutor's Office in Îlam opened a new case against him. The charges of “enmity against God” and “spreading corruption on earth” brought against Roşanî are offences under Iranian law that can carry the death penalty.

title: DFG pays tribute to newspaper distributors murdered in the 1990s
content:
In a written statement, the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) paid tribute to newspaper distributors who were murdered while taking part in the struggle for a free press during the 1990s. The statement recalled that Adil Başkan was murdered in Nusaybin on 9 November 1993; Yalçın Yaşa in Amed on 10 November 1993; Kadir Ipeksürer in Riha (Urfa) on 19 November 1993; Halil Adanır in Êlih (Batman) on 21 November 1992; Adnan Işık in Wan (Van) on 27 November 1993; and Nihat Yakut in Amed on 27 November 1998.




The statement noted that, despite the harsh conditions, threats and pressure of the time, the newspaper distributors struggled to deliver newspapers to the public. It said: “Risking their lives to bring the truth to the public under the most difficult conditions of the time, newspaper distributors stood on the front lines of the struggle for a free press.”




Emphasising that the distributors carried not only newspapers but also the public’s right to access information and the truth, the statement noted that they were known as Apê Musa’s “Little Generals”. It added that the struggle of the 17 newspaper distributors who were murdered, from Halil Adanır to Kadri Bağdu, remains an unforgettable part of the history of the free press.

title: Horuş: COP31's focus on implementation contradicts reality
content:
Mehmet Horuş, a lawyer specialising in environmental litigation, said that the emphasis on "implementation" at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), held in Antalya, was inconsistent with policies on the ground. He drew attention to continued reliance on coal, investments in nuclear energy and projects causing ecological destruction. Citing the urgent expropriation decision in Akbelen, the downgrading of Lake Eğirdir's protected status and nuclear cooperation agreements, Horuş said, "What we understand by 'implementation' is continued reliance on coal, nuclear opportunism and the pursuit of ecocidal projects."




Mehmet Horuş, a volunteer with the Climate Justice Coalition who has represented environmental cases concerning the Sinop Nuclear Power Plant and Kanal Istanbul projects, answered ANF's questions at the Peoples' Climate Summit in Antalya.




What has changed in environmental litigation since the struggle launched by Bergama villagers against cyanide-based gold mining in the 1990s? How are favourable court rulings implemented on the ground?




The Bergama struggle was one of the turning points for Turkey's ecological movement. It marked a stage at which the ecological struggle became a people's movement. Following the Bergama villagers, local resistance spread across the country through struggles against hydroelectric power plants (HPPs) in the Black Sea region. We can say that the Bergama villagers paved the way for the ecological struggle to become a mass movement.




The rulings issued in the Bergama case remain among the most important decisions in Turkish environmental law. The Council of State's legal precedent concerning cyanide-based gold mining remains a highly progressive ruling even today. However, the failure to implement court decisions and the efforts to circumvent them also turned the Bergama struggle into a symbol of a process in which the social state governed by the rule of law abandoned the villagers.




'The law has been placed at the service of corporations'




Since then, neoliberal policies have increasingly placed the law at the service of corporations and the market rather than the public interest. Legal obstacles facing companies, or the provisions on which our legal victories were based, have been amended in favour of corporations. Even attempts to change legislation concerning olive cultivation demonstrate how the law has been reshaped to benefit companies.




Changes made in favour of corporations, particularly in the mining sector, have deprived the ecological struggle of legal safeguards. This has pushed local movements and platforms towards a struggle that draws strength not only from legal proceedings inside courtrooms but also from society, the streets and collective resistance.




In ecological struggles, the law is no longer confined to courtrooms. It has become a practice of creating law. A dynamic has emerged in which people take action, seek to transform the law through their actions and create legal norms themselves. For this reason, we cannot describe what is happening as a conventional legal struggle.




The Italian thinker and legal scholar Giorgio Agamben uses the concept of the "state of exception", sometimes translated into Turkish as a "state of emergency", to describe situations in which states create exceptional circumstances that allow them to violate their own laws. Can we speak of a similar situation in the struggle for ecology and nature?




Yes. This situation also reminds me of Carl Schmitt's theory. We are living under a permanent state of exception in Turkey. Filing an environmental lawsuit is almost ceasing to be an effective legal remedy. Nevertheless, we have no intention of abandoning the legal struggle.




The reason is the erosion of law as a universal standard of justice. Today's summit also reveals the global dimension of the local problem we have been discussing through Bergama. Just as we question the law in Bergama, the United Nations' (UN) failure to implement its own regulations concerning biodiversity, climate change and desertification points to a similar problem on a global scale. The UN has moved away from its role as an institution capable of delivering genuine justice.




We are fighting for climate justice against global lawlessness. Peoples are trying to establish their own norms, struggles and moral, political and legal standards. Whether we call it capitalism, industrial society, capitalist modernity or capital, the international capitalist system is in crisis. This crisis is accompanied by a crisis of international law. The UN itself has become a symbol of that crisis.




'Can there be a legal summit attended by 100,000 people?'




COP31 is one of the UN's annual meetings to review international conventions. However, the UN has moved these meetings beyond their legal framework and turned them into public relations exercises. They have become a means of reproducing the legitimacy the UN has lost as a legal institution. Can there be a legal summit attended by 100,000 people? These summits are organised like automobile, construction and machinery trade fairs. They have become marketing events closely intertwined with corporations and capital groups. Nor do they succeed in gaining renewed legitimacy through this approach.




The demonstration organised as part of Peoples’ Climate Summit attracted far more participants than we had anticipated. One reason for this is that the ongoing summits have been emptied of substance. They no longer produce even a credible or remotely reassuring positive message about our future. That is why people turned towards Peoples’ Climate Summit  and the global march. The growing participation is a consequence of the failure and loss of credibility of the other summits. The crowds gathering here demonstrate this.




Turkey is emphasising "implementation" at COP31 and says it will put the summit's decisions into practice. What does this emphasis mean when the administration does not implement court rulings or comply with its own laws?




I think it is very clear. Last December, a presidential circular concerning COP31 was published. Two weeks later, an urgent expropriation decision was issued for Akbelen. This paved the way for the area to be seized for a thermal power plant through an expropriation procedure normally used in wartime. That was how they began COP. Far from discussing a phase-out of coal, they are turning towards coal. Akbelen is also a wetland area containing forests, agricultural land and water resources.




I gave Akbelen as an example of how this began. Now let us look at how it is ending. Amid all the commotion, nobody paid attention to this. At COP31, Murat Kurum said that they would restore and expand Lake Meke in Konya. Then, two days ago, another presidential circular was published in the Official Gazette, downgrading the protected status of Lake Eğirdir. Located right next to Antalya, Eğirdir is Turkey's second-largest freshwater lake and its fourth-largest lake overall. The decisions being taken point in precisely the opposite direction from the one being proclaimed.




'Continued reliance on coal and nuclear opportunism'




There had been some expectations, even if only symbolic, concerning a phase-out of coal. Instead, decisions were taken in the opposite direction. Moreover, these decisions were made as COP31 approached. A nuclear agreement was signed with South Korea a week ago, followed by a nuclear cooperation agreement with Canada a few days ago. Turkey is turning COP into an opportunity to advance its nuclear ambitions. Attempts to present nuclear energy as green are also part of the COP agenda. What we understand by "implementation" is continued reliance on coal, nuclear opportunism and the continuation of ecocidal projects.




How do you assess the Constitutional Court's ruling on the amendment exempting mineral exploration from the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process, which has been described as the "extractivism ruling"?




The term "extractivism" appeared in the opinion attached to the ruling. The Constitutional Court was examining an amendment intended to exempt mining activities from the EIA process. An attempt was being made to exempt Article 17 of the Mining Law, which regulates the collection of fragments, samples and core samples, from EIA requirements. On this occasion, civil society organisations were also invited to present their views through an exceptional procedure. I attended as legal counsel for the Chamber of Geological Engineers. As experts, we presented our opinions to the Constitutional Court.




We explained that the issue went beyond a conventional cost-benefit analysis or a debate over the public interest. Mining, particularly extractivism, is connected to universal problems such as climate change. We argued that the Constitutional Court needed to issue pioneering, forward-looking rulings that could serve as precedents for other courts. The issue is not simply whether samples can be collected in a particular area. We need a universal perspective on the continuous extraction of what lies beneath the ground and its removal to the surface.




What impact do omnibus laws have on environmental legislation? Were there significant provisions concerning this issue in the omnibus bills proposed in 2026?




When the latest omnibus bill came onto the agenda, we carried out the "We Will Not Give Up Our Land" campaign in parliament. The package contained provisions aimed at removing legal obstacles facing corporations, including those involved in renewable energy projects. Amendments concerning olive cultivation were among them and could have devastating consequences. The legislation is awaiting a ruling from the Constitutional Court. We expect and are working towards a decision being issued as soon as possible.




The Tortum case was dismissed because the statute of limitations had expired. Is the dismissal of environmental crime cases, whose consequences may last decades or even centuries, an exception or a systematic problem?




We are talking about a crime committed against nature. In Tortum, four to five times more excavation material than projected in the EIA data was dumped in a natural area. Thousands of tonnes of excavation waste reached the streams. Poplar trees in the valley were buried beneath the debris.




Our concern is not simply to see a few company employees or engineers punished. When villagers who exercise their most basic citizenship rights by organising demonstrations and press statements receive sentences, sanctions must also be imposed on those who commit crimes against humanity and the planet. We do not believe that the damage caused can be compensated through money, fines or imprisonment. It is impossible to understand how such crimes can be extinguished through a mechanism like the statute of limitations.




'Protecting the environment from the Ministry of Environment'




We encounter similar risks in cases concerning marine pollution in Muğla. A more specialised judicial procedure is needed. In the Tortum case, or in investigations into environmental pollution offences, we first file a criminal complaint. The Ministry of Environment then intervenes in some cases, seemingly just to avoid embarrassment, while staying out of others entirely. Ninety percent of environmental cases in Turkey are brought against the Ministry of Environment, in order to protect the environment from the Ministry of Environment.




At Peoples’ Climate Summit you are discussing ecology alongside peace and other social processes. What do you think about the policies concerning dams, mining and forests in Turkey, particularly in cities where Kurds live?




Last year, together with more than 100 ecological organisations, we published a report and declaration entitled "Peace with Nature Too". We submitted them to parliament. Parliament listened to many sections of society, but it did not listen to the ecological movement.




During the ongoing process, we are seeing a significant increase in mining, oil exploration, shale gas, solar power plant (SPP) and geothermal projects in the region. Capital is turning the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the period of non-conflict into an opportunity for profiteering. We are concerned that the geography will be made to pay the price of peace. Similar problems have occurred in Catalonia, Ireland and Colombia. We also addressed this issue during the session we organised at Peoples’ Climate Summit. We share these concerns.

title: Doğan: Individual armament is a problem for society as a whole
content:
Ikram Doğan, Istanbul Branch Chair of the Association of Social Workers (SHUDER), spoke to ANF about the impact of individual gun ownership and violence on public health. Doğan stressed that violence cannot be explained solely by individuals' anger management problems or aggressive tendencies, drawing attention to economic insecurity, inequality, the perception of impunity and easy access to firearms.




According to media reports, 110,470 unlicensed firearms were seized across Turkey in 2025. Between 1 January and 26 March 2026, another 25,580 unlicensed firearms were confiscated.




Doğan said that individual gun ownership cannot be addressed solely as a matter of security and public order, emphasising the need to strengthen public social services and develop social policies aimed at preventing violence.




'The structural causes of violence are being obscured'




Doğan said that explaining incidents of violence solely through individual characteristics conceals the social dimensions of the problem.




Doğan said: "In an environment where gun ownership is becoming increasingly widespread, inequalities are deepening and social problems are increasingly being resolved through power relations, explaining violence solely in terms of individuals' anger management, aggressive tendencies or personal pathologies makes the structural causes of the problem invisible.




Violence is a consequence. The social inequalities that produce it, economic insecurity, gender relations, exclusion, discrimination, polarisation, the perception of impunity and the resulting distrust of justice, easy access to firearms, the normalisation of violence in everyday life and problems with public security policies must all be considered together. It is impossible to explain violence without questioning the social, economic and political conditions that produce it."




'Access to firearms increases the risk of fatal consequences'




Doğan said that easier access to firearms contributes to the spread of individual gun ownership and encourages the use of force and the perception of violence as a means of resolving social problems.




Doğan continued: "Easier access to firearms, in particular, increases the likelihood that even ordinary disagreements arising in everyday life will have fatal consequences. While firearms are increasingly regarded by some individuals as instruments of power and security, they also increase the risk of conflict and violence in social relations. Therefore, individual gun ownership is not merely a problem of individual behaviour but also an issue that must be addressed in terms of public oversight and social security."




'The impact of violence extends beyond those killed or injured'




Doğan said that the most visible impact of individual gun ownership on public health is the threat it poses to the right to life, noting that armed attacks, murders, injuries and suicides place a serious burden on public health.




Doğan stressed that the problem is not limited to those who lose their lives or suffer physical injuries. Doğan said: "Those who witness armed violence, those who lose loved ones, those who live under the threat of violence and everyone who feels unsafe are also direct or indirect victims of this process."




Doğan outlined the effects of individual gun ownership: "The threat of armed violence and witnessing violence can cause fear, anxiety, trauma, depression and symptoms of post-traumatic stress. A constant sense of threat negatively affects individuals' daily lives and social relationships.




When violence and firearms become part of everyday life, they undermine children's sense of security, developmental processes and social relationships. They increase the risk of children learning to regard violence as a demonstration of power or a method of solving problems.




The presence of firearms in the home can increase the risk of domestic conflicts, particularly violence against women, resulting in fatal consequences. It can pose serious threats to the lives and safety of women and children.




When people do not feel safe in public spaces, this leads to greater social insecurity, withdrawal from social life and a weakening of mutual trust. Violence therefore damages not only individuals' health but also the quality of social relationships.




Gunshot injuries require emergency intervention, surgical treatment, rehabilitation and long-term care, placing an additional burden on healthcare services. Physical disability, withdrawal from working life and the need for long-term care can also have economic and social consequences."




'A security-oriented approach is not enough to create safety'




Doğan said that although the government defines security as one of its priority policy areas, people are increasingly being pushed into an environment characterised by insecurity and fear. Doğan drew attention to the distinction between security-oriented policies and genuinely safe living conditions.




Doğan said: "One of the main reasons for this lies in the difference between a security-oriented environment and a safe environment. A security-oriented approach is not enough to create a safe environment. It can even produce the opposite result."




Doğan stressed that security cannot be ensured solely through the presence of law enforcement agencies, harsher penalties and increased surveillance.




Doğan continued: "An approach that does not protect people's right to life, their economic and social security, their access to education, healthcare and social services, social equality and human dignity focuses only on a visible and limited dimension of security.




From a critical social work perspective, combating violence cannot be limited to punishing those who commit violent acts. The social relations that normalise violence, inequalities, discrimination, male-dominated power relations and social exclusion must also be questioned. The exclusion of children and young people from social support mechanisms, the inadequacy of public social services and the weakening of channels of social solidarity are also important parts of this discussion."




'The real measure is the ability to live without violence'




Doğan questioned the government's security policies, asking: "How does an administration that defines security as such a high priority explain why people do not feel safe and why violence has become so widespread in social life?"




Doğan said that the success of security policies cannot be measured by the number of detentions and operations or by the severity of penalties. Doğan also emphasised the importance of an approach that moves beyond speciesism and encompasses the safety of all living beings.




Doğan said: "The real measure is whether we can establish a society in which people can live without being subjected to violence, children and women feel safe, everyone has equal access to rights, and social problems can be resolved without resorting to violence.




Security is not merely about the state protecting people. It is about creating social conditions in which people can live without fear, without being subjected to violence and without anxiety about the future. From a social work perspective, genuine security is possible not through repression and surveillance, but through strengthening social justice, equality, solidarity and public responsibility."




'Individual gun ownership threatens social trust and solidarity'




Doğan said that the current situation cannot be regarded merely as a collection of isolated incidents, stressing that the emergence of violence in different areas of society, the escalation of interpersonal conflicts and the use of firearms in these conflicts pose serious risks.




Doğan emphasised that this situation points to the deterioration of social relations and the growing legitimisation of violence as a means of resolving problems.




Doğan said: "Individual gun ownership threatens not only society's physical health but also its psychological well-being, sense of social trust, relationships of solidarity and capacity to live together. Individual gun ownership and violence cannot be regarded as individual behaviours independent of social problems. Truly combating violence requires changing the conditions that produce it and considering security together with social rights."




'Social policies to prevent violence must be strengthened'




Doğan stressed that the responsibility of social work is not limited to assessing the harm already caused and providing psychosocial support to those subjected to violence.




Doğan concluded: "It also includes advocating for the development of social policies to prevent violence, effective regulation of access to firearms, stronger access to public social support mechanisms for children and young people, the protection of women's safety and the development of social solidarity."

title: Families of ill prisoners call for action outside Ministry of Justice
content:
The protest, initiated under the leadership of the Federation of Associations for Legal Solidarity with the Families of Prisoners and Convicts (TUHAD-FED), following a call by DEM Party MPs and the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), continued into its third day.




The protest was supported by the families of ill prisoners Newroz Bozkurt, Ömer Güneri, Yakup Akman, Mehmet Ali Taşkın and Selim Çiftçi, members of the Istanbul Peace Mothers’ Assembly, and the Human Rights Association (IHD).




A banner bearing the names of seriously ill prisoners was unfurled, reading: “We are at the gates of justice; we will open the prison gates through resistance. Freedom for sick prisoners.” Protesters chanted slogans including “Release sick prisoners!” and “Revolutionary prisoners are our honour!”




Families said they didn't want their children to die 




Fince Akman, the mother of ill prisoner Yakup Akman, said that their children were not receiving treatment in prison despite suffering from serious illnesses.




“We no longer want our children's coffins to be brought out of prisons. My child and thousands of other ill prisoners are not receiving treatment in prison. We say, ‘Peace’. The PKK has laid down its arms, but the state has taken no steps. The first thing that needs to happen is the release of sick prisoners,” she said.
