title: The AKP is expected to take steps
content:
In recent days, several statements have been made by both the state and the Kurdish side concerning the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Although the AKP government has taken no concrete steps, optimistic interpretations and expectations have nevertheless been expressed.




At a time when people are speaking of a deadlock and stagnation in the process, and the AKP government is being seriously criticised for this, it is unclear where these optimistic interpretations are coming from. We hope that the Free Movement of the Kurdish People's Leader, as demanded by the Kurdish people and public opinion, will be ensured. This leadership should be able to hold regular meetings with journalists, intellectuals, politicians and civil society organisations. After all, all the peoples of Turkey, as well as domestic and international political circles, are curious about the views of Imrali.




A few days ago, the Movement's Leadership issued a statement. Although it was not explicitly stated, the statement was criticising remarks made by Ibrahim Kalın, the head of the National Intelligence Organisation (MİT), during a meeting. Ibrahim Kalın had identified the leadership of the Kurdish Freedom Movement as the reason why the process was not progressing. He had claimed that no progress was being made because the organisation's leaders were concerned about their own positions. However, just a few sentences later, he contradicted himself by acknowledging that the Movement's Leadership remained committed to the process. Ibrahim Kalın's remarks had created confusion. In its statement, the Movement Leadership emphasised that, despite the AKP government taking no steps, Ibrahim Kalın was attempting to conceal this reality.




Both international and Turkish public opinion believe that the PKK has taken radical steps that nobody expected, while the AKP government has failed to take any significant steps of its own. The Kurdish people and all democratic institutions are already expressing their frustration with the AKP's inaction. The Kurdish People's Leader is still unable to work freely, nor are those imprisoned being released. Even prisoners who have completed their sentences are not being freed.




The Movement's Leadership announced that it had withdrawn all military units from within Turkey and abandoned military positions near the border, including fighting positions in caves (known as 

şikeft

). It also emphasised that no factors remained that could pose a risk of confrontation for the Turkish state or military. For this reason, it stated that the AKP government must now take action. In short, the Movement's Leadership demonstrated that Ibrahim Kalın's accusations against it did not reflect reality; on the contrary, it had acted with considerable responsibility.




Indeed, the steps taken by the Kurdish side have been surprising, and it was expected that the AKP would respond accordingly. It appears that the Kurdish side has done everything required of it. The statement also indicated that the guerrillas could return to Turkey if the Turkish state enacted laws guaranteeing the freedom to engage in democratic politics. It is difficult to understand why the AKP government is not taking the steps necessary to facilitate and accelerate their return to Turkey.




The Turkish state is demanding that the fighters return without first enacting laws protecting democratic political activity. It is even excluding all leaders, commanders and organisational cadres from this process of return. Everyone knows that the fighters will not return if no legislation is introduced covering the leaders and commanders as well. It is also well known that the entire leadership and organisational structure of the PKK is committed to the Kurdish People's Leader. Unless the Kurdish People's Leader is able to work freely and the path towards his freedom is opened, no organisational cadre or fighter will return to Turkey. Yet the Kurdish People's Leader has still not been granted a status that would allow him to freely direct and manage the process.




At a time when the AKP has failed to take the necessary steps and public opinion is expecting action from the government, Ibrahim Kalın's claim that the leaders are worried about their own positions is a distortion of reality. The Movement's Leadership has not expressed any concerns about its own interests so far. It has called for steps to establish a democratic political environment. Indeed, in its statements, it has made clear that its only concern is democratisation and the resolution of the Kurdish question.




Ibrahim Kalın acknowledges that the factors which gave rise to the Kurdish question still exist. For this reason, he says that disarmament alone will not resolve the problem. If so, the necessary steps should be taken in accordance with these statements, and measures towards democratisation should be implemented. Yet, rather than taking democratic steps, the AKP government continues to insist on anti-democratic practices. Ibrahim Kalın should be calling on the AKP government to take steps towards democratisation. Otherwise, statements claiming that the process is progressing well are meaningless. When AKP officials say that the process is going well, their words amount to nothing more than an attempt to buy time.




Most recently, Devlet Bahçeli has also spoken of taking certain democratic steps without explicitly mentioning the fundamental democratic rights of the Kurds. Devlet Bahçeli, who played a role in initiating the process, now needs to speak more openly and clearly.




The Kurdish side has fulfilled its responsibilities to an unexpected extent. Therefore, the AKP government no longer has any justification for failing to take action.




Source: Yeni Yaşam Newspaper

title: Clara Mattei: Capitalism deliberately produces poverty
content:
Historically, how have governments used austerity policies as an economic instrument to protect capitalism, suppress wages, dismantle social protections and prevent democratic oversight? Economist Clara Mattei, who examines these issues in her book 

The Capital Order: How Economists Invented Austerity and Paved the Way to Fascism

, answered our questions.




With Mattei, one of the most prominent researchers working on the history and critique of austerity policies, we discussed the rise of right-wing governments around the world, wars in the Middle East and the rapidly accelerating militarisation of Europe from a political economy perspective. We also explored how an effective strategy of resistance against these developments could be built.




According to Oxfam, the twelve richest people in the world — all men — now own more money than the poorest half of the world's population, which is more than four billion people. How is this exploitative “capital order” created? 




Inequality is not an accidental or corruptive element of our economy. Inequality is deeply rooted in the very formation of economic growth and what can be called “accumulation of wealth”.  




There wouldn't be any wealth without the creation of market dependence and the precarity to compel workers to work for a wage — for someone else. This is a crucial point about the capital order — capital money is really based on this political relation of exploitation that is never mentioned by economists but is fundamental to understanding any dynamic of capitalism, including impoverishment, inequality, and structural violence. 




Many people find economics incomprehensible — yet politicians make far-reaching decisions. Is "complexity" a real problem or also a political tool to depoliticize decisions? Who wins when the public merely watches instead of participating in decision-making? 




This is crucial, and it is the reason why we founded the Forum for Real Economic  Emancipation (freefreeforum.org): to create a space where economic ideas can actually  become empowering to people, a space to explain the problems people feel in their own skin. 




The fact is, economics is a discipline meant to be kept in the hands of very few, who protect that knowledge as something absolutely inaccessible to the undereducated majority. Yes, complexification, mathematization, and technical language are wonderful ways to maintain explanatory power, and thus retain political power. 




And so, the reason people have not fully rebelled against the system is that they are told they don’t understand how it works, and have to listen to the experts. But these experts are merely hiding all of their extremely classist assumptions beneath formulas, mathematics. These assumptions oblige people to accept a system based on structural exploitation and violence. One important example of this that I give in my book is the harsh rejection of the labor theory of value – that explains profit as the product of unpaid labor – in favor of a theory of abstinence by which value is not coming from exploitation of one class over the other, but rather it is the outcome of the virtuous capacity to save of the rational savers-investors. 




You criticize the Western-dominated academic world: to what extent is modern economics/economic science historically and politically influenced by the West? What does this obscure, and what models of thinking and politics are exported globally as a result? 




I show in my first book how mainstream economics — the economics that is still taught in schools and still informs public debate — was championed at a moment of extreme and widespread criticism and challenges to capitalism as a way of organizing our society. This is because economics was meant to protect society from any upheaval and from any challenge.




And so, what you find is that a lot of its theories, for example, the idea that exploitation does not exist, that everything is just and fair because people get exactly what they deserve from their market transactions, and the idea that the entrepreneur counts much more than the worker, or that harmony is the consequence of self-interested behavior — are ideas that really help propel a sense of the impossibility of escaping capitalism. They deeply naturalize capitalism and the hierarchy that it produces. 




So economic ideas emerged especially to tell workers that they could not participate in  changing the world. And this is still the case today. Clearly, these ideas are exported to the Global South, where people suffer even more from plunder and exploitation. They also help create a sense of impotence among the experts who lead economic organizations in the Global South, because they feel that they are epistemically inferior to Western scholars and thus cannot emancipate themselves intellectually. And this means no emancipation in policy. 




Part of the world structurally thrives on the exploitation of other regions — through resources, trade conditions, supply chains, wages, debt and unequal power. How would you explain this structure without resorting to pure moralizing: what rules and institutions make it possible? 




This is a crucial point. My new book, 

Escape from Capitalism

, really tries to explain the functioning of the system, its tendencies, and the deeply rooted historical features of capitalism, without resorting to the typical left-wing moralizing that says it is all because we have bad people in power or greedy heads of corporations. 




What we see is that, of course, so-called development in the rich parts of the world presupposes a lot of inequality within rich nations, too. In the United States, over 70% of workers can't afford an emergency expense of around $400, and so they are structurally indebted and are working poor. 




But apart from this, the point is that the wealth hoarded largely in the Global North  depends on the underdevelopment of the Global South. So I revive a very longstanding  tradition of dependency theory, which shows, again, that it's not as if so-called developing countries can just catch up, improve their market efficiency, and thus become just as developed and modernized as Western countries. Rather, they have been made poor and kept underdeveloped in order to provide cheaper raw materials, cheap labor, and especially markets — open markets — for capitalists in the West. 




Oxfam reports that in 2024, the super rich in the Global North extracted $30 million per hour from the Global South — an amount far exceeding any money coming in through official development aid. It’s actually through interest rates, debt payments, and capital outflows where you really see how developed countries are completely subsidized by the Global South.




The Middle East is being transformed by wars, interventions and restructuring, often with reference to stability, security or development. Who benefits economically from this restructuring (raw materials, reconstruction, armaments, infrastructure, control of trade routes)? Why do democracy and freedom regularly fall by the wayside in the process? 




Yes, I just did a really great interview with Francesca Albanese on our FREE podcast (@freefreeforum). She looked at one specific but very, very telling example of how all sectors of the economy are complicit in the Palestinian genocide. 




The Palestinian genocide is a very profitable deal for the capitalist economy, in terms of the markets and means for destruction. Investing in bombs, surveillance, and very advanced military technologies, for example, are among the most profitable sectors of the economy right now. But also, all the reconstruction efforts and huge investments in real estate and related apparatus — including asset managers, Airbnb, universities, and so many different sectors of our economy, benefit from this.  




So we also know that, of course, Israel is the outpost through which the West controls the Middle East and, in general, the Global South. So it is a very strategic point, also in terms of raw materials and oil. 




It is impossible to understand the genocide and the constant destruction in the Middle East without understanding them from an economic perspective, which is, of course, the perspective that is least discussed in the public media. 




Actors such as Trump, Modi, Milei and Meloni exploit crises to push the boundaries of what is permissible, for example, through emergency rhetoric, deregulation or shifts to the right. What exactly is happening economically: which interests are being protected and which rights are being weakened? 




Yeah, I think what's interesting about the extreme austerity hawks of today is that they have completely eliminated the farce — proper to liberal capitalism — of the idea that the state represents the so-called general interest. The idea that the state is neutral and genuinely wants to foster economic growth for its own sake, as if that were something that benefits everyone. 




I think what we see here is that they are overtly and explicitly benefiting certain sectors of the economy, especially those that are currently the most profitable, such as extractive industries, technology, surveillance, and war. 




In this way, they are really showing how you couldn't have capitalist relations without  constant government intervention. And I explain how austerity is not about less state and more market. It's actually about the state shifting resources from the many to the few, and how this is done even more aggressively by these right-wing governments. So what we see here is nothing new. It's just much more explicit and more violent. But this is the real face of capitalism. 




Europe is doing relatively well in global comparison, yet military spending is rising sharply, militarization is increasing, and debates about conscription are returning. How does this relate to economic policy, and what are people afraid of, who are they arming themselves against? What role do industrial interests, energy and raw material issues, and geopolitical competition play? 




Yeah, I think militarization really shows the real point about austerity: the state is spending a lot of money. It is very expensive not to tax the rich and instead to use this money to permanently subsidize the war machine. 




And this is important because crises of overproduction are endemic to capitalism. One of the roles of the state is to protect against overproduction by making sure that taxpayer money, especially money from workers, goes to subsidize the sphere of destruction. 




I think this helps us understand how irrational capitalism is as a way of organizing society, even though it is not irrational according to its own logic. The logic of capitalism, the logic of profit, is very much fulfilled by austerity. But austerity is irrational, and capitalism is irrational according to the logic of need. 




So, of course, people are made to be afraid, or made to think that somehow government officials are investing to protect them. The reality is that the interest is in constantly  creating a need to purchase more weapons. And, as we know, this means permanent destruction and reconstruction. 




Why does extreme inequality not automatically lead to uprisings, and why does austerity often strengthen right-wing/authoritarian forces? What would an effective counter-strategy (left-wing, civil society, collective) need to achieve? 




This is the interesting point: a lot of Marxist analysis is based on an accelerationist theory, according to which the more people are starving, the more they will rise up. I think what you see is that it is far more complex, and it also speaks to the fact that there is no deterministic answer to how we change our economic system. It really requires a good dose of organizing and effort to bring people together. 




Because what we see is that the more precarious you have been made by austerity policies, the more divided and suspicious you become, and the more you come to hate  those who are weaker than you. And this is, in fact, the success of austerity that I speak  about in my book: austerity works very well to disempower workers by increasing their precarity.




This is what industrial austerity does by killing labor laws that protect workers and making work more flexible. This is what cutting social expenditures does. This is what increasing taxes on workers and taking taxes away from capitalists does. This is what increasing unemployment through monetary austerity does. It just creates a very vulnerable working class that then, of course, ends up buying into the scapegoating narratives of the extreme right. 




So what we know is that it is not going to be enough for people to be in a very uncomfortable economic situation to rise up. What we need is active organizing efforts. This is what the Forum for Real Economic Emancipation is attempting to do, like many other groups around the world. And we want to be in solidarity with these groups, to open up the experiments that already exist. 




I think it is also very interesting to think more realistically about what China is doing right now and how China differs from our economic system, even if it maintains certain aspects of capitalism. It certainly provides some aspects that are really visionary for the future. There are a lot of democratic assemblies. Of course, Rojava is a very good example of how, when people get together, they can challenge the structure of exploitation that is the foundation of economic growth under capitalism. 




So I believe that this is what we need to do: not just wait for people to fare worse, because when people fare worse, they turn towards the right. We need to be able to provide our own resources, push government officials, and learn from existing alternatives around the world. We need to learn from them and grow stronger through collaboration.




Clara Mattei




Born in the United States in 1988, while her parents were studying law, Clara Mattei grew up in Italy. The granddaughter of partisans who took part in the resistance movement against fascism during the Second World War, Mattei completed her undergraduate degree in philosophy at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom. She subsequently earned a master's degree in Pavia, Italy.




She completed her PhD on the history of austerity policies, and the book that emerged from this research has since been translated into ten languages.




Mattei is a Professor of Economics at the University of Tulsa in the United States, where she also serves as the director of the Center for Heterodox Economics, established in February 2025. In addition, she is the founder of the Forum for Real Economic Emancipation (FREE), an initiative established to challenge economic myths.




She is the author of 

The Capital Order

.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

title: Prisoner Newroz Bozkurt brought to hospital
content:
Newroz Bozkurt, who suffers from Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL), was transferred to Etlik City Hospital on Saturday, 14 November, after becoming unwell.




Newroz Bozkurt has been in detention since January 1999 and was diagnosed with leukaemia in June.




It was reported that Newroz Bozkurt had previously been taken to Etlik City Hospital in December 2025. Despite medical examinations revealing that her blood levels were low, no medical intervention was carried out. It was subsequently reported that her lawyers filed a criminal complaint against the doctor concerned.

title: Peoples’ Climate Summit addresses energy trade and war in Gaza
content:
At the Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya, international environmental and solidarity organizations focused their discussions on the economic links between the fossil fuel industry and military violence. On the third day of the gathering, organized as an alternative to the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), discussions centered on the destruction of livelihoods in Gaza, the role of international energy supplies and demands for a comprehensive embargo against Israel. Participants examined the extent to which climate justice also required overcoming war, occupation and military expansion.




Representatives of Energy Embargo for Palestine, the Global Sumud Flotilla, the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and various international solidarity networks were among those taking part in the event.




Destruction in Gaza as an ecological crisis




Asad Rehman of Friends of the Earth highlighted the long-term environmental consequences of the war in Gaza. He stated that the destruction of water supply and sewage systems, damage to essential infrastructure and soil contamination caused by munitions, debris and untreated wastewater had devastated livelihoods that could take decades to restore.




Rehman argued that this destruction should also be examined from the perspective of ecocide. He also raised the question of political and economic control over natural resources: “Who extracts which resources, from whom, for whose benefit and under whose authority? That is the fundamental question.”




Ana Sanchez drew a connection between Israeli military policy, international arms trade relationships and the rise of far-right movements. In her assessment, Israel benefited from diplomatic support while supplying military and security technologies to right-wing governments. She argued that an effective arms embargo must go beyond halting individual arms deals and encompass entire supply chains, including the disruption of fuel shipments.




“Solidarity means disrupting supply chains. That means a two-way embargo: neither buying nor selling. It means stopping fuel deliveries,” Sanchez explained.




She emphasized that the liberation of Palestine was not an issue separate from the climate movement. Rather, she said, the fossil fuel-based economic system, patriarchal power structures and military violence were closely interconnected. “There can be no climate justice without freedom for Palestine,” she stressed.




Criticism of oil shipments through Turkey




Celine Isimbi of Energy Embargo for Palestine addressed specific economic ties, highlighting the importance of international oil trade to Israel’s energy supply, particularly shipments from Azerbaijan. According to Isimbi, Israel obtains more than 40 percent of its crude oil requirements from Azerbaijan. The oil is transported through the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, from where it is shipped to Israel by tanker.




Isimbi stated that her organization had documented a total of 77 oil shipments along this route to Israeli ports between May 2024 and June 2026. She alleged that vessels had temporarily switched off their automatic tracking signals to conceal their actual destination ports.




Isimbi also said that Turkey’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure had confirmed that ships had provided false information to port authorities and that legal proceedings had been initiated in connection with these incidents.




The activist called for fossil fuel supplies to no longer be considered separately from their military and political uses. She argued that an energy embargo must also cover transportation routes and the companies involved.




Calls for reparations rather than development aid




Abeer Al Butmeh of the Palestinian environmental network PENGON called for reparations and the restoration of destroyed livelihoods. She argued that international development aid alone could not adequately address the political and material consequences of the destruction. She pointed out that the Palestinian population must be able to make its own decisions regarding energy supplies, water resources, land and reconstruction. “Palestinians must determine their own future and have the right to remain on their land, return to it and rebuild it,” Al Butmeh stated.




Şenol Karakaş of the Freedom for Palestine Platform also placed the war in Gaza within the context of global economic and political power structures. He criticized the support Israel receives from international capitalist and imperialist structures and emphasized that solidarity with Palestine must not be limited to individual protest campaigns. Rather, he said, the struggle for Palestinian freedom must become an integral part of movements for social emancipation worldwide. “The struggle for Palestine must not be interrupted,” Karakaş said.




Şeyma Altundal of the Thousand Youth for Palestine initiative called on the Turkish government to sever all trade relations as well as diplomatic and military ties with Israel. She criticized the continuation of economic relations despite public declarations of solidarity with Palestine. “For us, the freedom of Palestine is not a secondary issue in the climate struggle, but its political compass,” Altundal stated.




Militarism and authoritarian politics on the agenda




Later in the day, the Peoples’ Climate Summit continued its discussions under the slogan “No to Fascism – Siamo Tutti Antifascisti.” The program includes presentations on political repression in Turkey, the situation of dismissed public sector employees, the peace movement and the struggles of LGBTIQ+ organizations.




Other topics include the appointment of government trustees to opposition-run municipalities in Turkey and North Kurdistan, as well as the rise of far-right and authoritarian movements in Europe and Latin America. A commemorative event honoring women’s rights activist Margaret Papandreou is also planned.

title: Six lawyers detained in raids in Izmir
content:
Six lawyers were detained during a police operation in the western Turkish city of Izmir on Tuesday morning. Five of them are members of the Contemporary Lawyers’ Association (ÇHD). According to the organization, the lawyers were taken into custody during searches of their homes in the early morning hours.




Those detained include Veysi Çetin, secretary of the ÇHD’s Izmir branch, as well as association members Yemen Cankan, Emrah Kanbay, Göksel Akbaba and Erdoğan Akdoğdu. Lawyer Bahattin Özdemir was also detained.




According to the ÇHD, police seized electronic devices and data storage media during the house searches. Access to the investigation file has also been restricted. The detained lawyers have reportedly been unable to exercise their right to consult with legal counsel.




The ÇHD views the detentions as part of a systematic policy of repression against social opposition movements. The authorities are attempting to criminalize the practice of law and intimidate independent defense lawyers, the association’s Izmir branch stated. “This attack on the right to legal defense is nothing more than an attempt by the government to cover up the violations of the law, arbitrary practices and human rights abuses it perpetrates through the judiciary,” the statement said.

title: Sebahat Tuncel: Silencing the guns is not enough; rights must be guaranteed
content:
The relationship between militarism, the climate crisis and ecological destruction was discussed during a session titled “Combating Militarism from a Climate Justice Perspective” at the Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya. The session addressed the environmental impact of military spending and armed conflicts, as well as opportunities for cooperation between the climate justice movement and antimilitarist movements.




Speaking at the session, Free Women’s Movement (TJA) activist Sebahat Tuncel highlighted the links between the climate crisis and the capitalist system, policies of exploitation, wars and repressive practices.




Tuncel stated that while government representatives at COP31 were discussing ways to maintain capitalism and the system of exploitation, the Peoples’ Climate Summit was exploring how to build an alternative way of life in opposition to these policies.




Sebahat Tuncel stated that the situation in Palestine could not be considered separately from the policies of repression and violence faced by peoples in other parts of the world. “The injustice, climate crisis, policies of war and policies of genocide we are witnessing in Palestine actually affect all peoples. Replace Palestine with Kurdistan. Similar policies are being pursued in Kurdistan as well. Think of the Alawites in Syria, or all the peoples in the Middle East who face repression because of their identity, faith or culture. Therefore, the struggle for climate justice is a struggle that concerns us all,” she said.




Emphasizing that wars cause not only loss of life but also ecological destruction, Tuncel stated that the situation in Palestine, Kurdistan and Lebanon concerned all of humanity. She said that policies of war and conflict devastated living environments and that the effects of the ecological crisis were not limited to those living in conflict zones.




‘Solidarity alone is not enough’




Sebahat Tuncel stated that policies of war erected barriers between societies and alienated peoples from one another, calling for a united struggle against these policies.




“The policy imposed on us by states is one of divide and rule. What we must do in response is unite and struggle together. Solidarity alone is not enough. We need to go beyond solidarity and build a common internationalist struggle to change and transform the male-dominated capitalist system. Only an organized society can achieve this,” Tuncel said.




Referring to the LGBTI+ movement’s slogan, “We exist, and we will continue to exist,” Tuncel stated that Kurds, women and people of different identities would also continue their struggle for existence. Describing the denial of peoples, identities and beliefs as fascism, she said that it brought with it repression, oppression, exploitation and marginalization.




‘Turkey has been turned into a giant prison’




Addressing prison policies in Turkey, Sebahat Tuncel stated that there were 16 prisons of various types in Antalya. She criticized the government for presenting the construction of new prisons as good news, describing it as a continuation of policies of repression and punishment.




Recalling the arrest of Kurdish politicians in 2009 as part of the KCK investigations, Tuncel said that those demanding rights, freedom, democracy and peace faced the threat of prosecution. Arguing that the law had been turned into a political instrument, Tuncel said, “They have turned Turkey into a giant prison.”




Tuncel argued that the isolation imposed on Abdullah Öcalan in İmralı had spread throughout Turkey and its prisons. “In fact, it has spread across the whole of Turkey and into every prison. There are not only prisons being built physically, but also prisons being constructed in our minds. We cannot achieve freedom without dismantling all these policies of isolation,” she said.




Tuncel emphasized that freedom could not be achieved without overcoming the policies of isolation, stating that freedom required a social order in which people could express their thoughts, organize and live with dignity.




Time to build positive peace




Addressing the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Sebahat Tuncel said that a struggle had been waged for many years to resolve the Kurdish question through democratic means rather than war and conflict.




Emphasizing that silencing the guns alone did not constitute peace, Tuncel stated the following:




“The state wants negative peace. It wants the guns to fall silent without granting rights to Kurds, without granting rights to women, without granting any rights to socialists, and with everyone submitting to its authority. We, on the other hand, say that we will build peace based on our rights and freedoms. Can there be peace without addressing the Kurdish question? Even if the guns fall silent today, much deeper conflicts could erupt in the future if the issue remains unresolved.




What do we want? We want equality, freedom, democracy, justice and a free future. We want to be equal and free citizens who do not have to worry about whether something will happen to us when we go out into the streets or whether we will be imprisoned for speaking our minds.




Society must have confidence in its own strength. The power lies within us; it lies within women. We must not underestimate our own strength. Whatever needs to be achieved, we can achieve it ourselves. This struggle cannot succeed through solidarity alone, but only through a common struggle.




From Palestine to Kurdistan, from Latin America to Lebanon, we will succeed if we stand together and unite our struggles in an internationalist movement for equality, freedom, justice and democracy. We will succeed. We have no other choice.”




The session also featured presentations by Karen Hallows on behalf of Peace Boat, Hala Kilani on behalf of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom, Ellie Kinney on behalf of the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS), Deborah Burton on behalf of Tipping Point, Andrew Metheven on behalf of War Resisters’ International, Stephan Brües on behalf of the Federation for Social Defence, and Merve Arkun on behalf of Conscientious Objection Watch.




The presentations addressed the environmental impact of wars and militarist policies, ecological destruction, anti-war activism and conscientious objection, while participants from different countries shared their experiences of struggle.

title: Oil exports begin through Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline
content:
Iraq’s Ministry of Oil issued a statement announcing the resumption of oil exports through the Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline.




The statement confirmed that crude oil would be exported through the old pipeline between Iraq and Turkey, with an initial export volume of 120,000 barrels per day.




Export capacity is expected to increase gradually in the coming period, with plans to reach 500,000 barrels per day.




The ministry described the reactivation of the pipeline and the resumption of exports as a “strategic step,” stating that it would strengthen Iraq’s oil export capacity and help diversify the country’s oil export routes.




The statement emphasized that reopening this export route would provide an important source of additional revenue and support the Iraqi economy.

title: Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil in Amed: Stories of seven women shared
content:
At the “Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil” organized by the Network Against Violence outside the courthouse in Amed (tr: Diyarbakır), participants carried photographs of women who had been killed. Representatives of numerous political parties and civil society organizations attended the demonstration, chanting slogans including “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), “Femicide is political” and “Stop protecting and exonerating perpetrators, prosecute them.”




Reading the statement on behalf of the organizers, Nermin Unat, a member of the Rosa Women’s Association, said that the stories of seven women who lost their lives in different cities between November 9 and 15 had been added to the collective memory. Unat emphasized that women who had been killed despite filing complaints and requesting protection, as well as those whose families were still seeking justice, would not be forgotten.




The women whose stories were shared this week included Pelin Pınar and Nuran Tay, who died after falling from balconies in Istanbul, Rukiye Demirel, who lost her life in Niğde, and Sema Gündüz, who died in Uşak. title: IRGC bans civilian access to Shaho Mountains
content:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has banned civilian access to the Shaho Mountains in Ravansar County until 21 November, citing military exercises.




Residents of several nearby villages told the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) that the IRGC announced the ban through village councils and village heads on 15 November.




Residents were told that the IRGC’s Ansar Rasoul Commando Unit in Javanrud would conduct military exercises in the mountains until 21 November and that all civilian access to the area was prohibited.




The sources said a military convoy carrying heavy and medium-heavy equipment had been dispatched from the unit’s barracks and deployed around the mountains as the exercises were announced.




The IRGC previously banned civilian access to the area from 2 to 7 October during military exercises and artillery shelling of the Shaho Mountains.




The exercises and shelling take place in an area designated for environmental protection. The Shaho and Kusalan Mountains were granted protected status in 2009 under Resolution No. 303 of the Supreme Council for Environmental Protection and are managed by the Department of Environment.




Environmental activists say the IRGC has built several military bases in the area since 2007, under the pretext of countering the presence of forces affiliated with Kurdish opposition parties.

title: Hatice Yakışır: Let these lands finally see peace
content:
The Peace Mothers recently travelled to Ankara to demand peace and held a two-day Peace Vigil. The mothers, who left the city after meeting with Speaker of Parliament Numan Kurtulmuş, reiterated their demands for peace and called for the release of political prisoners.




Hatice Yakışır (76), whose two sons are imprisoned, was among the mothers who travelled to Ankara to demand peace despite her advanced age and health problems. Having endured numerous losses throughout her 76 years while continuing her struggle and determination to live, Hatice Yakışır now spends her days looking at framed photographs of her lost loved ones.




Despite everything, Hatice Yakışır continues to demand peace. She said, "I want to see my children walk through this door," expressing her hope that the peace process will succeed and that she will be reunited with her imprisoned sons.







 







Forced into exile after their village was burned




In 1994, Hatice Yakışır was forced to leave her home after soldiers burned down the hamlet of Xizginos, in the Genç (Darahênî) district of Bingöl (Çewlîg). She first moved to Genç and later to central Amed (Diyarbakır). Hatice Yakışır, a mother of nine, lost her husband, Mehmet Ali Yakışır, after he was detained while attempting to visit his father, who had remained in their burned village. Nothing was heard from him again following his detention.




Following her husband's enforced disappearance, Hatice Yakışır was forced to raise her nine children alone. Despite all the hardships and deprivation she experienced, she continued her struggle to survive.




Lost several relatives in the conflict




Hatice Yakışır's son Cûdî (Mehmet Yakışır) joined the guerrillas in 1998 and was martyred in the Black Sea region in 2018. Another son, Şervan (Yakup Yakışır), was martyred the same year during the resistance against the occupation of Afrin (Efrîn). Her grandson Mahsum Gürkan was martyred in 2016 during the self-government resistance in the Sur district of Amed.




Her son's release was postponed




Hatice Yakışır said that her sons Orhan Yakışır and Talip Yakışır are also imprisoned. She explained that the release of Orhan Yakışır, who was sentenced to 12 years in prison and is held in Sincan Closed Prison, has been postponed three times. His release was postponed twice for three months and once for nine months, preventing him from leaving prison. Hatice Yakışır said that the sentence of her other son, Talip Yakışır, who is imprisoned in Aliağa, Izmir, is due to end in February. She called for an end to human rights violations in prisons.




'I want my children to walk through this door'




Hatice Yakışır described her experiences in the following words: "I have nine children. In 1994, my husband was killed in an unsolved murder. Our village was burned down, and afterwards we were forced to move to Amed. There was nowhere we did not go and nothing we did not endure. We suffered enormously. Despite all these hardships, I raised my children. I raised them with the zakat donations of other people. Today, none of my children are with me. Some are in photographs, others are in prison. I want my children beside me, in this house. I want them to walk through this door."




'Everything is for peace'




Hatice Yakışır said that they had been struggling for peace for years and had travelled to Ankara to express their demands by holding a Peace Vigil.




Hatice Yakışır said: "As mothers, we left our homes and travelled to Ankara to demand peace. I went there so that the prisons would be emptied and no one would have to shed tears anymore. The Leader must be free, and no one should lose their life anymore. This war must end as soon as possible. Neither guerrillas nor soldiers, no one should die anymore. There must be peace so that people can live freely and peacefully in their homes. We travelled a thousand kilometres from here and back. People who saw us there and understood that we had come for peace supported us. There are millions of people throughout this country who want peace and do not want any more tears to be shed."




'These lands must finally see peace'




Hatice Yakışır drew attention to the suffering she had endured and reiterated her demand for peace.




Hatice Yakışır said: "My village was burned down, my husband was killed in an unsolved murder, I lost two of my children, and two are still in prison. As a mother who has experienced all this, I say enough is enough. I am not the only one. Thousands of mothers who have experienced the same suffering want the same thing. We did not get to see peace, but I want our grandchildren and children to experience it. I am 76 years old, and even in this condition, I got up and travelled to Ankara. These lands must finally see peace."

title: Nesrin Akgül: Women are not spectators but architects of peace
content:
Women's direct participation in decision-making mechanisms and their role as founding actors are crucial to achieving a lasting and democratic solution through the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Women emphasise that peace must not be limited to the silencing of weapons or negotiations between political actors. They argue that women must participate in decision-making mechanisms through their own political will if the process is to become rooted in society and achieve lasting results. Questions remain over the extent to which women's demands are reflected in negotiations and political processes, how much representation they have in decision-making mechanisms and whether they are being excluded from the process. Women stress that they must not merely serve as a supporting force but must be actors who make decisions and determine the direction of the process. Equal representation, the establishment of independent women's mechanisms and guarantees for women's participation in concrete decision-making bodies are among the key demands. Women's involvement in the process on the basis of their own demands is considered essential to strengthening the social struggle and establishing peace throughout society.




Free Women's Movement (TJA) activist Nesrin Akgül spoke to ANF about the issue.




'Peace is not merely the silencing of weapons'




Nesrin Akgül said that peace cannot be defined solely as the silencing of weapons and that the conditions which gave rise to the war must be eliminated to build lasting peace. Akgül said: "How do we define the process we call peace? If the forces involved in the war cannot establish common ground, even at a minimal level, the question of how peace can be built becomes a matter of debate. Peace is not an achievement that can be secured simply by silencing weapons. Of course, the greatest devastation caused by war is the loss of human life, and ending that loss is the most valuable achievement. However, this war did not take place between two hegemonic powers. It began when a sovereign state denied the existence of a people and an oppressed people rose up against that denial. A people began a war of self-defence in pursuit of their right to self-determination. This was a war entered into out of necessity, but also by choice. It became a struggle to regain dignity. What gained acceptance was that a people reclaimed their dignity through this struggle. For 52 years, this war continued on the basis of that reality.




It is impossible to envisage how peace can be established without identifying the causes of this war. Abdullah Öcalan has repeatedly stressed this point to the state throughout the process. The issue is not disarmament. The Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) may cease to exist today, but another organisation could emerge tomorrow. The real issue is eliminating the conditions that gave rise to the war. This is the framework within which the peace process must be defined. In other words, we must move from a negative peace process that begins with the silencing of weapons to a positive process of construction that consolidates the elimination of armed conflict. This process can sustain itself through the socialisation of peace and the social reconstruction conceptualised within the Peace and Democratic Society Process. It will acquire a comprehensive character when the state, as a party to peace, becomes responsive to democracy, consolidates peace legislation and moves towards democratic integration."




'Women cannot be defined by their victimhood'




Nesrin Akgül emphasised that women's responsibilities and role in the Peace and Democratic Society Process are decisive. She continued: "It cannot be a coincidence that women are regarded as the most effective force responsible for both silencing weapons and achieving social reconstruction in discussions surrounding the Peace and Democratic Society Process. In every conflict-resolution process, how women will participate has been one of the central questions and challenges. We must ask: Why are women the first to come to mind when peace is mentioned? Let me take that question further: Why are women primarily defined as those who have suffered the most and whose rights have been violated most severely? For women like us, who have waged a struggle for liberation, the identity and historical position from which women's presence in the peace process is defined are even more important.




During this transitional period, many people ask where we, as Kurdish women, stand or will stand in the peace process. We ask ourselves the same question. However, defining Kurdish women primarily through the suffering we have experienced is an incomplete and potentially problematic approach. Why? Because we are a women's movement that has not only paid the price of this war through resistance but has also decided how we want to live and succeeded in building that life.




As women who have waged a liberation struggle, we have a history of becoming guerrillas in the mountains, being captured and imprisoned, and establishing ourselves within political mechanisms in society. As women who resisted throughout this war, we built and institutionalised many things. Through our organisation, we became a distinct and autonomous structure. We achieved these gains through extraordinary acts of courage. We cannot become a party to peace solely on the basis of our victimhood. We want to consolidate our achievements and extend them throughout society. We want to realise the peace process through the political development of women's liberation.




We do not envision peace merely as a means of ending the suffering we have experienced. That would make us passive. We participate in the peace process as subjects of social transformation, and we will continue to do so. Of course, I do not regard these definitions as opposites. Both suffering and resistance are outcomes that emerge through a process. The question is knowing how to transform those outcomes into achievements. We position ourselves as the bearers of the political vision and social will that will build peace. We are women who intervene in the construction of a new social life through our experience of resistance. As women, we are the force that will shape the social and political relations of that new life."




'Women's achievements must lead to social transformation'




Nesrin Akgül said that Kurdish women had achieved significant gains through their struggle, ranging from free and equal relationships and equal representation to establishing their own decision-making mechanisms and challenging male-dominated thinking. She said: "We have extraordinary experiences, but these experiences and achievements have not yet become a force for social transformation. As Kurdish women, we have made gains that were far from easy, from free and equal relationships and the culture of comradeship to equal representation and the establishment of our own decision-making mechanisms. We have developed the capacity to transform men and created practical spaces in which to achieve this. We have numerous areas of success. These have naturally been recognised as achievements of Kurdish women's struggle and resistance. However, we have still not generated sufficient transformative power in society on issues ranging from family relationships and relations between women and men to policies concerning children. One of the conditions necessary for this is the establishment of peace so that the women's movement is no longer criminalised, obstructed or subjected to legal repression. These are all areas of reconstruction that can only be secured through democratic integration. For the state to adopt a democratic approach to integration, it is not enough merely to recognise the legal existence of the Kurdish people, other peoples and identities. Its deeply entrenched patriarchal laws and practices must also change.




Preventing violence against women is important, but so is legally recognising women as equal citizens, guaranteeing their right to make decisions about their own bodies and introducing comprehensive legal arrangements to ensure their equal participation in political and economic decision-making. There must be a legal process that transforms the social and institutional relations that make violence against women possible. Women's access to healthcare, education and public services in their mother tongues must be guaranteed, and the multiple forms of discrimination against women must be legally eliminated. We believe genuine peace can be established through a series of legal arrangements for peace, extending to the creation of autonomous but public courts for women in cases of femicide."




'Women are developing their own peace policy'




Nesrin Akgül said that women were establishing their own organisations and mechanisms to facilitate the transition from negative to positive peace. She also emphasised the importance of bringing women from different backgrounds together and creating opportunities for dialogue.




Nesrin Akgül described the conference "Women Side by Side, Talking About the Future", organised by the Peace and Reconstruction Foundation (BİV), as an important gathering. She said: "To move from the negative peace process we are currently experiencing towards positive peace, we are working to develop our own autonomous forms of organisation and establish the necessary mechanisms. What matters to us is ensuring that this becomes a process encompassing all women through an understanding of the democratic nation. The recent conference organised by BİV, 'Women Side by Side, Talking About the Future', was an important gathering in this regard. Women from all sections of society participated.




It was also important that we wanted to hold this gathering with women representatives from the Justice and Development Party (AKP), which belongs to the political side with which we are negotiating. Although the relevant representatives did not attend the conference, and despite some criticism of their proposed participation, I believe the invitation itself was important. It was a significant call to overcome the divisions created by those in power and the dominant patriarchal political system. Of course, everyone has political grievances and matters that need to be confronted. Everyone would surely acknowledge that Kurdish women, as one of the groups that have paid the highest price, have demands for accountability and confrontation with the state.




However, meaningful confrontation in such processes first requires spaces where people can develop empathy, understand one another and listen to each other face to face. This is what we call dialogue and negotiation. By creating these spaces, we can listen to one another, criticise one another, make ourselves understood and learn tolerance. We can call this the establishment of internal peace. Politics is achieved, above all, through the ability to live together, talk and communicate. Such gatherings therefore acquire meaning not only as expressions of our shared desire for peace but also as spaces where we can discuss how to achieve it. Organising peace as women and succeeding together can make us a leading force."




'We are establishing women's monitoring committees'




Nesrin Akgül stressed that women must not merely observe the process but must actively monitor and implement it. She concluded: "Together with BİV, we are establishing women's monitoring committees, both for women guerrillas who will return from the mountains and to observe, monitor and implement possible steps towards peace. By correctly identifying the needs and priorities of this period, we are coming together as women to develop our own peace policy and the path through which it will be pursued.




The most important need of this period is to believe that we will bring about peace. Notice that I am not saying we should believe peace will come. I am saying we must believe that we will bring peace and build it ourselves. Unfortunately, the negative experiences of the past and the failure to take necessary steps can create a sense of disbelief. This leaves us passive and reduces us to spectators. As women, we will discuss how to build peace and act with confidence in our own collective strength to achieve it."

title: Karayılan: The first step that must be taken is to open the doors of Imrali
content:
Murat Karayılan, Commander of the People's Defence Centre (HSM), talked to Egîd Sîrwan on Stêrk TV about the ongoing political process.




Karayılan said that journalists, politicians and intellectuals must be allowed to visit Imrali.




We publish excerpts of the interview. 




There has been a political process underway in Bakurê Kurdistan (North Kurdistan) for the past two years. During these two years, you have taken numerous steps. Most recently, you withdrew your forces from Bakur and Metîna. The Movement Leadership also issued a statement, declaring that there is no longer any situation that could lead to a risk of confrontation between you and the Turkish state. However, there have been no visible steps taken by the state, and the Peace and Politicisation Commission has still not been put into operation. What is the current situation, and how do you assess the process?




Two days ago, an official statement was issued on behalf of our Movement Leadership. The steps taken, and the results achieved were outlined in that statement. Therefore, there is no need to repeat them here.




In brief, the situation is as follows: From the day the process began until today, we have taken numerous steps. We have done everything necessary to demonstrate that we are determined to advance this strategy, that we have no hesitation in it, and that we genuinely want this Peace and Democratisation Process to move forward.




In contrast, however, very few steps have been taken by the Turkish state or government. The measures necessary to build trust have yet to be implemented. MIT President Ibrahim Kalın spoke at a conference in recent days and said: "This issue has two dimensions. One is the laying down of arms, and the other is democratisation and democratic reforms."




I would therefore ask Mr Ibrahim Kalın: "That is correct, but where is democratisation? Where are the reforms?" Developments in Turkey are moving not towards democratisation, but in the opposite direction. There is repression and a continuing situation of arrests and detentions. So far, nothing has happened that would give us reason to hope that democratisation will take place.




They may say: "First, lay down your arms, and then we will implement reforms." But if they genuinely intend to introduce reforms, there are many things they can do right now, and they should do them. This cannot work through an approach of "You do this first, and then I will do that." The way forward must be opened.




Steps that build trust are necessary 




The issue of trust is extremely important. It cannot be treated as something ordinary or superficial. Concrete steps that inspire confidence are necessary. Turkish state officials sometimes make various statements. They interpret many things according to their own perspective. They present the steps taken by Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] by us as their own achievements and try to portray them to society in that way. However, no steps that would genuinely build trust have been taken so far. These are the circumstances that cause us concern. There is nothing else behind our concerns.




The Turkish state is still pursuing anti-Kurdish policies




We said: "We have made strategic decisions. We are now removing armed struggle from our agenda. We will no longer wage war against Turkey. We will integrate into the Democratic Republic."




Isn't that precisely the purpose of democratic integration? Yet those on the other side are not putting an end to their hostility. They continue to use the language of opposition and enmity. Politics is still being conducted on this basis. Even diplomacy is being pursued on an anti-Kurdish basis.




We say that the Turkish state must abandon its anti-Kurdish stance. On this matter, we have not developed an optimistic assessment. The Turkish state's conduct up to now has given us no reason to form such an assessment. These are the things that create doubt and concern for us.




We are neither inexperienced nor children; we have experience. Our people and our Movement have accumulated historical experience. Leader Apo says: "I neither deceive nor am I deceived." Therefore, it is entirely wrong to portray our concerns as though they stem from some kind of personal reservations. That is not the case, nor is such a thing possible. We are people who have sacrificed ourselves for our people. That is the truth.




Our concern is the future of Leader Apo, our people and Turkey




What concerns us is the future of Leader Apo, our people and Turkey. Leader Apo is the leader of this people, and he is still in prison. How could we not be concerned about that? We do have certain reservations, and that is true. This is because the state has still not taken the steps necessary to build trust. However, everything we have done has been aimed at building trust.




At the theoretical level, we developed a Manifesto. This was not simply the development of a tactical approach! We made a Congress decision. Leader Apo developed the Manifesto for Peace and a Democratic Society. Now all our cadres are receiving training on the basis of this Manifesto.




What did we say at our Congress? "We are dissolving the PKK, abandoning armed struggle and making democratic politics our fundamental approach. However, Leader Apo must lead this process."




So, go ahead and open the way for Leader Apo so that the process can move forward more rapidly. Without this, naturally, it will not progress quickly.




We have always emphasised that Leader Apo must lead the process. If the way is not opened for him to do so, the process cannot move forward in this manner. Some people interpret the slow pace of the process in different ways. But this is the reason: the state is not taking the necessary confidence-building steps. The most important factor in building trust is the state's attitude towards Leader Apo, its attitude towards our people and towards our comrades in prison. There is still hostility in the prisons.




Our steps demonstrate our sincerity




For example, a few days ago, Tuncer Sağlam lost his life in prison. He had cancer, but he was not released, and he died as a martyr. What crime had he committed? He had allegedly engaged in propaganda for the organisation. Yet we have already dissolved the organisation. In other words, the organisation has dissolved itself, and there is a ceasefire process underway. At a time when efforts should be made to develop friendships, a Kurdish politician is arrested on the grounds that he "engaged in propaganda for an illegal organisation". He is not released despite his condition, and he dies as a result. Even though the Forensic Medicine Institute had issued a medical report stating that he should not remain in prison, he was still not released.




It is clear that a fascistic mentality remains in operation. So how can we not be concerned? There is no visible progress here, only rhetoric. What is needed is action, and we have taken action.




Look, let me be clear: we are continuing to take practical steps even now. The steps we have taken previously, as well as those we have taken in recent days, demonstrate just how determined and sincere we are about this process.




Now let the state demonstrate its sincerity as well.




Leader Apo's role must be clearly defined




There is an agenda for the Peace and Politicisation Commission to begin its work in the coming days. Of course, this commission must be officially recognised by the state. In other words, the state needs to make an official announcement. It must also clearly state what Leader Apo's role in this commission will be, and the commission must officially begin its work.




The first step to take is to open the doors of Imrali 




Another issue is what the state or the AKP government is saying. They claim: "Society is not ready for Öcalan's release or freedom." But you are not doing anything to prepare society! Does Turkish society know how beneficial Leader Apo has been to the Turkish state over these past two years? No, it does not.




Why? Because the authorities claim credit for the developments that have taken place, saying, "We did this."




There have been so many developments during this period, and the region is in turmoil. Everyone is preparing for war. Yet Turkey is in a relatively comfortable position under these circumstances, isn't it? Why is it comfortable? Because of this process.




If the work being carried out were accurately communicated to the public, public opinion would change.




The authorities are not doing this themselves, and they are not allowing Leader Apo to do it either. Therefore, as they previously promised, both the commission must be officially established and the doors of Imrali must be opened.




That is the first step that needs to be taken.




Leader Apo must be free. However, the first step that must be taken is to open the doors of Imrali. At the very least, he should be able to speak to the Turkish press and explain his position himself. You are not doing it, so let Leader Apo do it himself.




Some sections of society now ask: "Why do they attach so much importance to the press? Why do they want journalists and intellectuals to come?"




This is the reason.




We want to advance the process. Therefore, Turkish public opinion must also be able to see the truth and be prepared. Making the truth known is an important matter in this regard.




The ball is now in Turkey's court




In short, the Turkish state must take action. I said this once before, but subsequently we took further steps. Therefore, the ball is now entirely in Turkey's court.




We need to see what they are going to do.




We have fulfilled everything that was within our power during this period. As stated in the declaration issued by the Movement Leadership, the situation is now such that the Turkish state or the Turkish military can no longer claim that there is a threat against them from the PKK or the Apoist Movement. For this reason, it is now up to them to take the necessary steps.




Naturally, the fundamental issue is Leader Apo's freedom. However, before that, Leader Apo's working conditions must be improved, the commission must be officially established and journalists, politicians and intellectuals must be allowed to visit Imrali.




In other words, conditions must be created that will enable Leader Apo to lead the process. Creating these conditions is essential.

title: Two Revolutionary Guards killed, two others wounded in YRK actions
content:
The Press Center of the East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) issued a statement announcing the details of two actions they carried out in the cities of Bane and Serdeşt in Rojhilat (East Kurdistan).




The YRK stated that two actions had been conducted in central Serdeşt and the Bane region on November 15 and 16. Both actions were carried out in memory of Dersim Behar.




Dersim Behar, a member of the YRK, fell a martyr during clashes that followed an ambush by Iranian forces in Serdeşt region on the night of November 11.




According to the statement, specialized and professional YRK teams targeted a base of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in central Serdeşt on November 15. The base commander and one Revolutionary Guard were killed, while two other Revolutionary Guards were wounded.




On the other hand, another YRK unit killed an officer affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in Bane at 3:10 p.m. on November 16.




The YRK stated that both actions had been carried out to honor Dersim Behar’s memory and avenge her death.




The statement stressed that the YRK would respond to any attacks against its forces, defend itself within the framework of legitimate self-defense and deliver the necessary response at the appropriate time and place.







YRK announces the death of one of its members in Iranian attacks

title: Mass grave discovered in Harasta
content:
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) has reported that the remains of six people have been recovered from a mass grave in Harasta. According to SOHR, 28 mass graves containing the remains of 231 people have been discovered across Syria since the beginning of 2026.




The mass grave was discovered in the Al-Ajami neighbourhood of Harasta, in the Damascus countryside, an area that was heavily damaged during the war, according to SOHR.




The remains of six people were found during clearance work to remove rubble from destroyed buildings. SOHR said forensic experts were examining the remains in an effort to identify the victims and notify their families.




According to SOHR, a total of 28 mass graves have been uncovered across Syria since the beginning of 2026, containing the remains of 231 people.
