title: The Republic’s second century: Whose future?
content:
As the Republic of Turkey enters its second century, it is seeking to redefine not only its past but also its future. Amid shifting balances in the Middle East, new alliances and regional power struggles, Turkey is searching for ways to adapt the continuity of the state to new circumstances. The Kurdish question is once again being placed at the centre of this search.




However, there is a historical distinction that must not be overlooked: the Republic's attempt to reshape its own future is not the same as the Kurds determining their own future.




Today, a new political language is being constructed around concepts such as “brotherhood”, “the domestic front”, “common destiny”, “democratic integration”, “a terror-free Turkey” and “a terror-free region”. Each of these concepts can carry different meanings. Yet political language does not merely describe reality; it also determines which demands are considered legitimate and which futures are regarded as possible. As this new semantic space is constructed, the aim is not only to reshape political language but also to redefine which demands are considered legitimate and which futures are deemed possible.




The founding period of the Republic and its historical context cannot be excluded from today's debate. Stefan Ihrig, a professor of history at the University of Haifa who has researched the influence of the founding of modern Turkey on German political thought, demonstrates in his book Atatürk in the Nazi Imagination how the nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal was followed, discussed and taken as a model by the German far right and emerging Nazi circles, drawing on publications from the period.




One striking example of this influence was the demand for an “Ankara government” in Germany, expressed in publications associated with the Nazi movement in 1923. These findings do not equate the two regimes. However, they show how the founding of the Republic was interpreted in European fascist circles as a model for overcoming defeat, national reconstruction and strong centralised power. This represents a historical dimension outside the official founding narrative that cannot be ignored.




The significance of Ihrig's research for today's debate lies not in establishing a direct parallel between the past and the present, but in demonstrating that processes of state formation cannot be understood solely through their own narratives of legitimacy. The founding of the Republic held different meanings for different political circles. Similarly, the “Turkey model” being brought back onto the agenda today cannot be assessed solely through the concepts used by its advocates. What matters is whether this model recognises the Kurds as equal political subjects capable of determining their own future, or whether it places their future within boundaries redefined by the state.




This question had a concrete significance for the Kurds during the founding period of the Republic. The research of Ismail Beşikçi and historical studies of the Koçgiri Rebellion reveal the conflict between Kurdish demands for political status and autonomy and Ankara's conception of centralised sovereignty even before the Republic was proclaimed. The events in Koçgiri in 1920 and 1921 brought into focus the question of who would be recognised as a founding political subject of the new state. Would the Kurds become political partners in this order, or would their existence be defined within boundaries determined by the state?




Behind this question lay continuities carried over from the final period of the Ottoman Empire into the Republic. The demographic and property arrangements that emerged following the Armenian Genocide of 1915, together with the continuity of certain administrative and political cadres, demonstrate that 1923 did not represent a complete break with the past. The Republic did not merely establish new institutions; it also made national homogenisation one of the fundamental instruments of state formation. The tension between this approach and democracy was not directed solely against the Kurds. The single-party system, the authoritarian turn of the Democrat Party and the military coup of 27 May also demonstrate the Republic's troubled relationship with political pluralism. For the Kurds, however, the issue was more fundamental: restrictions on democratic rights were accompanied by the denial of a people's collective existence and political future. Denial would become institutionalised as a form of governance.




Koçgiri (the 1920–1921 Kurdish uprising), the Sheikh Said Rebellion of 1925, Dersim (the site of the 1937–1938 massacres), Diyarbakır Prison (a symbol of the torture and repression of Kurdish political prisoners, particularly after the 1980 military coup) and the periods of emergency rule are not identical historical events. However, under different circumstances, they demonstrate how the conflict between Kurdish demands for political agency and state sovereignty has repeatedly been reproduced.




The state does not change; it transforms. Yet the mentality of a state that transforms in order to preserve itself does not automatically change along with that transformation.




Today, the Kurds cannot be presented with a new narrative of the Republic as though they had never experienced this history, as though they had never known denial, assimilation, prisons or military interventions. The Kurds know the Republic not only through what the state says about itself, but also through their own collective memory.




This is precisely why the way in which the new political language is constructed matters. Devlet Bahçeli's emphasis on internal unity and security, Mehmet Uçum's search for a legal framework, Numan Kurtulmuş's approach to regional integration and Ibrahim Kalın's references to identity, discrimination and democratisation are not identical. Ignoring these differences would also mean ignoring the debates taking place within the state. However, the growing convergence of these different approaches around a “common future” and “integration” does not eliminate the question of whose concepts are being used to define that future.




Kurtulmuş's presentation of the process as the major project of the Republic's second century at the conference titled The Search for a New Regional Social Contract in the Middle East, organised in cooperation between the Center for Middle Eastern Studies (ORSAM) and the University of Oxford, is noteworthy in this respect. So is his association of the “Turkey model” with regional reintegration. This does not justify concluding that there is a secret plan drawn up by a single centre. Nevertheless, as the Republic's regional future is being redesigned, it is necessary to ask within what framework the political future of the Kurds is being considered.




This question is also connected to how the process is being conducted. Kalın says that democratisation measures are needed alongside disarmament. Kurtulmuş, meanwhile, states that there is no need for an external observer in the process. Which rights will be recognised, what guarantees will be established and who will monitor their implementation remain unclear. The state determining the framework, timetable and oversight of the process is not the same as the Kurds participating in that process as equal political subjects.




The Kurds do not enter today's discussions on a solution without their own history. Since 1993, there have been eleven ceasefires, withdrawals and negotiation processes at various levels, yet none has resulted in a comprehensive and lasting political agreement. Throughout these processes, the Kurdistan Freedom Movement repeatedly took concrete steps, but no basis for a mutual solution was established that could guarantee the collective rights and political future of the Kurds.




Ignoring this history, the current process cannot be presented as a new beginning in which the Kurds have demonstrated their willingness to seek a solution for the first time. The decisions taken in 2025 to end the armed struggle and dissolve the organisational structure represent an important turning point. However, while disarmament is progressing through concrete steps, it remains unclear how political rights and democratic guarantees will be secured. The measure of a solution is not merely the steps taken, but the extent to which the Kurdish question is resolved politically.




The struggle here is not only over political decisions, but also over meaning.




Does “integration” mean a partnership between equal political subjects, or the adaptation of Kurdish demands concerning their own future to the existing state structure? Will “common destiny” describe a freely established union, or will it become the name given to predetermined boundaries?




A people's right to determine its own future cannot be realised by allowing others to decide which future is appropriate for that people.




This is precisely where the historical connection between Kurdistan's freedom and Turkey's democratisation becomes important. Turkey's democratisation cannot be considered independently of Kurdish freedom. Yet Kurdistan's freedom cannot be reduced to a secondary issue within Turkey's democratisation that can be postponed. Being interconnected does not mean being absorbed into one another.




This does not remove the responsibilities of Kurdish politics itself. Those who support the process, those who maintain their distance, and those who advocate democratic autonomy, federalism or independence do not share the same political vision. This plurality must be openly discussed. Peace processes can lead political movements towards new relationships, compromises and flexible positions. This is inherent in politics.




However, flexibility does not mean erasing historical memory. It must be possible to explain to society why certain objectives have changed, which achievements have been preserved and which intellectual legacies are being carried into the future. Questioning the state's discourse must not exempt the transformation of Kurdish politics itself from criticism. The ability of Kurds to freely discuss different visions of their political future is an inseparable part of this responsibility.




As 27 November approaches, it is impossible not to reflect once again on the stance and defences of Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) Central Committee members and other resistance fighters in Diyarbakır Prison against the imposition of surrender. This determination, expressed particularly in the 14 July Resistance, did more than defend the Movement's organisational and political existence. It transcended prison walls and national borders, influencing its cadres, new generations and society's relationship with the struggle. The defences of Hayri Durmuş and his comrades carry particular significance in this respect. They had already said everything that needed to be said. Yet what gave their words their true weight was their refusal to abandon what they defended under the harshest conditions and their willingness to pay for it with their lives.




Returning to this legacy today does not mean treating every method and programme of the past as an unchanging truth. Political circumstances may change, and forms of struggle and ways of achieving objectives may be reconsidered. However, change itself cannot serve as an explanation of the relationship established with the past. The essential question is on what historical grounds ideas for which heavy sacrifices were made are being reinterpreted today, and how that interpretation relates to the Kurdish people's determination to decide their own future.




The historical connection between Kurdistan's freedom and Turkey's democratisation must not become invisible amid the Republic's need to shape its own future. Every concept used and every choice made today must be evaluated not only in terms of its immediate political consequences, but also according to the legacy it will leave to future generations.




Today, by reading the defences, writings and historical positions of Hayri Durmuş and his comrades, we are not merely learning what happened in the past. We are also trying to understand the circumstances in which a political will was preserved, the ideas for which it was defended and the sacrifices that were accepted. Tomorrow, other generations will read today's speeches, decisions and texts with the same attention. They will ask why certain concepts were changed and on what grounds certain objectives were redefined. The historical standards we use to question the past will one day also apply to the choices made today.




For this reason, creating an independent and modern Kurdish semantic space is not merely about producing new concepts. It means establishing a free space in which Kurds can understand and interpret their own history, political existence and future through their own intellectual references. Kurdish-language education, independent research, independent publishing, historical and archival studies, and institutions where different political ideas can be freely debated are indispensable foundations of this space.




A people's right to interpret its own history cannot be separated from its right to determine its own future. The Kurds' ability to think about and define their own future cannot be subordinated to the Republic's need to shape its own future or to the political boundaries drawn by the state.




The Republic is attempting to shape its second century. The question facing the Kurds is not simply what place will be allocated to them within that century.




The fundamental question is what ideas the Kurds will use to shape their own future centuries, and what kind of political memory, freedom and vision of struggle they will leave to future generations.

title: Peoples’ Climate Summit calls for a democratic energy transition
content:
The Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya continued its discussions on the second day with a fundamental critique of global energy policy. During a three-part event titled “Phasing Out Fossil Fuels and Energy Democracy,” representatives of international climate movements, trade unions and environmental initiatives discussed alternatives to an energy system dominated by fossil fuels and the interests of major corporations.




The summit is being held as an alternative event to the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). While the official negotiations focus on international climate policy, participants at the alternative summit emphasized the social consequences of the climate crisis, the historical responsibility of industrialized countries and the right of affected communities to participate in decision-making.




“It is not about charity, but justice”




Opening the session, Leon Sealey-Huggins of the British organization War on Want criticized the growing concentration of economic and political power. He argued that the current environmental and social crises were not accidental developments, but consequences of an economic system that prioritized the interests of a privileged few over the needs of the majority. Those particularly affected, he said, included low-income communities, small-scale farmers and people whose livelihoods were threatened by environmental destruction and rising energy prices.




Sealey-Huggins warned against reducing the energy transition to the electrification of consumption in the Global North. “While increasing amounts of energy are being supplied to electric cars, air conditioning systems and data centers, around 700 million people worldwide still lack access to basic electricity. A just transition must therefore prioritize the needs of the people.”




Sealey-Huggins also highlighted the colonial history of economic inequality. He noted that the Global North had benefited for centuries from the extraction of raw materials and labor from colonized societies, arguing that these historical relationships must also be taken into account when financing the energy transition.




“It is not about charity, but justice. It is about redistributing wealth and power,” Sealey-Huggins stated. He called for a global Green New Deal that would have to be achieved through the collective struggle of trade unions, feminist movements, Indigenous communities and environmental initiatives.




Climate justice and the rights of Indigenous communities




Rukia Khamis of the international climate organization 350.org emphasized that economic development models from the Global North could not simply be transferred to other societies without taking local conditions into account. She argued that economic growth did not automatically translate into environmentally sustainable development. The historical responsibility of industrialized countries toward the Global South must therefore be a central component of international climate policy, she underlined.




Her colleague João Cerqueira addressed disputes over Indigenous territories in Brazil. Citing the example of the Guarani-Kaiowá people, he described a ruling by a Brazilian federal court prohibiting the issuance of new project permits in the area concerned without prior consultation with Indigenous communities. “A territory does not have to be officially recognized by the state in order to be protected,” Cerqueira explained.




He stressed that Indigenous communities should not merely be consulted on energy projects that had already been approved. Instead, he added, they must have the right to decide for themselves what kinds of economic and environmental development take place on their land. This includes the right to reject new fossil fuel extraction projects.




“In Brazil, in Turkey and everywhere around the world, communities are at the forefront of resistance. Along rivers, in courtrooms and on the streets, they are deciding their own future,” Cerqueira said.




Women bear the social consequences of energy policies




Süheyla Doğan, chair of the Association for the Protection of the Natural and Cultural Heritage of Mount Ida, addressed the gender-specific impacts of the energy crisis. She noted that the coal and energy industries remained heavily male-dominated. Women, she said, were underrepresented both in the workforce and in leadership positions, yet bore a significant share of the social consequences of job losses and workplace accidents.




“When employees in the energy sector lose their jobs or die in workplace accidents, women often face increased financial burdens and unpaid care responsibilities within their families,” Doğan said. She also pointed to the experiences of environmental protest movements in the Çanakkale region, where several coal-fired power plants operate. She remarked that women had played a crucial role in organizing resistance against new energy projects and defending their communities’ livelihoods.




“A socially just phaseout of coal must therefore go beyond job protection and retraining programs. What happens to the women who perform unpaid care work at home? That is why we need a socially just transition that also takes gender relations into account,” Doğan explained.




Coal-fired power plants and their impact on health




The second part of the event, held under the slogan “No to Fossil Fuels,” focused on the health and environmental consequences of the coal and oil industries. Deniz Gümüşel of Turkey’s Right to Clean Air Platform criticized the continued government support for fossil fuels. She argued that although the health impacts of coal-fired electricity generation were well documented, their true cost to society was not taken into account in energy policy decisions.




According to Gümüşel, air pollutants from coal-fired power plants in Turkey have caused approximately 196,000 premature deaths over the past 40 years. She also warned that exposure to these pollutants posed serious risks to children’s health. Gümüşel pointed to the national energy plan through 2040, which continued to provide for government support for fossil fuels, as well as plans to expand nuclear power capacity to 20 gigawatts.




“Fossil fuels are a declaration of war on life, on this planet and on us as societies,” Gümüşel said. As examples of resistance to these policies, she cited struggles against coal-fired power plants in Aliağa, Yatağan and Afşin-Elbistan, as well as successful local mobilizations against power plant projects in Çırpılar and Gerze.




Mehmet Dalkanat of the Elbistan Platform for the Protection of Life and Nature described the consequences of the region’s two coal-fired power plants. He stated that the Elbistan Plain, once predominantly agricultural, had been subjected to severe environmental pollution as a result of industrial energy production.




“We are not drowning, we are fighting”




International climate movements also emphasized that phasing out fossil fuels must go hand in hand with transforming economic power structures. Kumi Naidoo of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative described the climate crisis as a systemic crisis that could not be viewed separately from social inequality, exploitation and wars. He called for a broad-based social movement to bring about fundamental change.




Fenton Lutunatabua of the Pacific Climate Warriors highlighted the resistance of Pacific Island communities against fossil fuel projects and their initiatives to establish community-managed renewable energy systems. He stressed that affected communities should not be viewed solely as victims of climate change, but must be recognized as political actors. He recalled his movement’s slogan: “We are not drowning, we are fighting.”




Meanwhile, Özdeş Özbay of the platform “Change the System, Not the Climate” criticized the influence of fossil fuel corporations on international climate negotiations. According to Özbay, more than 100 representatives of the fossil fuel industry attended COP31.




Özbay called for a fundamental restructuring of energy policy, with trade unions and workers directly involved in the process. He emphasized that climate justice required a concrete transition program that would transform economic power structures and provide social protections during the phaseout of fossil fuels.




Bringing energy supply under democratic control




In the third part of the event, titled “Another Energy System Is Possible,” Kıvanç Eliaçık of the Sosyal-İş trade union, Lala Peñaranda of Trade Unions for Energy Democracy, Ecehan Balta of the Coalition for Climate Justice and Nuran Yüce of the platform “Change the System, Not the Climate” discussed democratic alternatives to existing energy policies.




The discussions centered on the demand that energy production and supply should no longer be driven solely by private-sector profit interests. Speakers stressed that workers, trade unions and local communities must be involved in decisions concerning investments, methods of production and energy distribution.




According to the participants, a just energy transition could not be limited to replacing coal, oil and natural gas with renewable energy sources. They said it must also transform ownership structures and decision-making processes in the energy sector, enabling an energy system that prioritizes the needs of the population.




In addition to the panel discussions, the second day of the summit featured events addressing labor rights, climate justice, environmental struggles and feminist perspectives on the energy transition, as well as workshops and film screenings.

title: Iranian border guards kill a Kurdish kolbar
content:
Iranian border guards shot and killed a Kurdish border kolbar on 14 November in the border area of Baneh, Kurdistan Province.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that in the early hours of Saturday, Iranian border guards opened fire on a group of kolbars from close range and without prior warning in the Surkew border area, killing 34-year-old Tayeb Rostami.




The authorities transferred Rostami’s body to the forensic medicine department in Baneh before handing it over to his family, who buried him later that evening.




Rostami was the father of one child, and his wife is reportedly pregnant.




Since the beginning of this year, Iranian border guards have shot and killed at least eight kolbars in various border areas of Kurdistan. Another kolbar died this year from injuries he sustained when border guards shot him last year.

title: The silent friendship between guerrillas and mountain goats
content:
When human beings become one with nature, they can understand its language. To achieve this, people must live in nature, care for it and protect it. Those who have come to understand this truth are the freedom guerrillas. That is why they establish their bases on mountaintops where the earth meets the sky. All kinds of plants and animals gather around them.




The mountain goat is one of the animals that inhabit the mountain peaks. It is an extremely alert and sensitive animal that is difficult to capture or tame. Mountain goats do not approach humans unless they are convinced that no harm will come to them.




Guerrillas are known for their commitment to protecting nature. Indeed, one of the fundamental pillars of Abdullah Öcalan’s paradigm is environmental protection. For this reason, guerrillas carry out their struggle and live their lives with this awareness.




Guerrillas take mountain goats into their care for a while, helping them survive. They later release them back into the wild.

title: Yılmaz: Failure to implement ECtHR rulings is a constitutional crime
content:
Turkey's continued refusal to implement rulings issued by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerning human rights violations is deepening debates over the rule of law and human rights.




Legal experts point out that the failure to implement ECtHR rulings not only perpetuates individual rights violations but also undermines the principle of the rule of law and public confidence in justice.




Ercan Yılmaz, co-chair of the Amed (Diyarbakır) branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), spoke to ANF regarding Turkey's non-compliance with ECtHR judgments and the consequences.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/22868199_20261111145819_2026-11-12-amed-ercan-yilmaz-ihd-sube-baskani-uygulanmayan-aihm-kararlari-1.mp4










'Failure to implement ECtHR rulings is nothing new'




Ercan Yılmaz recalled that Turkey's failure to implement ECtHR rulings was not a new issue as the problem had long become much more visible, particularly after 2016 and the transition from the parliamentary system to the Presidential Government System in 2017.




Yılmaz stated: "Following the attempted coup in 2016, Turkey introduced a change to its system of government in 2017. The parliamentary system was abandoned and replaced by a presidential system.




Since then, the failure to implement ECtHR rulings has become a much more prominent issue in our lives. In particular, non-compliance with judgments finding violations of the rights of people imprisoned for political reasons, and the continued refusal to carry out release orders, have called into question the position of the ECtHR and the judicial authority that Turkey has recognised.




Particularly in the 1990s, no results were achieved through Turkey's domestic legal system regarding crimes committed against citizens by state forces or paramilitary groups. Once domestic legal remedies had been exhausted, numerous cases and applications were brought before the European Court of Human Rights. The Court issued very serious judgments against Turkey. There are thousands of judgments concerning violations of the right to life, enforced disappearances, the prohibition of torture, and freedom of thought and expression. Even at that time, these judgments were not properly implemented within Turkey's domestic legal system."




'The Demirtaş and Kavala rulings undermined confidence in the law'




Ercan Yılmaz said that the failure to implement ECtHR rulings had become particularly visible through judgments concerning well-known public figures.




He continued: "The non-obedience with the judgments concerning Selahattin Demirtaş and Osman Kavala within domestic law has had serious consequences both for individual citizens and society as a whole. Confidence in the principle of legal certainty, the belief that there are courts people can turn to and seek protection of their rights, has been severely undermined.




The fact that courts act on political motives has existed for a long time. However, this has now become much more visible throughout society because the individuals concerned are well known. Among them are Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, the former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP), and businessman Osman Kavala, who is also well known among civil society organisations in Turkey. The failure of domestic courts to implement the judgments concerning these cases has also caused serious concerns among ordinary people.




We are facing an approach that has completely destroyed confidence in the law. People are losing faith that courts will protect their rights and remedy unlawful practices. A court finds a violation, yet the judicial institutions of the country responsible for implementing that judgment refuse to do so. This also places serious obstacles in the way of people's pursuit of justice."




'The right to hope ruling has not been implemented for 12 years'




Yılmaz said that the ECtHR's 2014 ruling concerning the "right to hope" for Abdullah Öcalan had not resulted in the necessary legal or practical changes in Turkey.




Yılmaz further stated: "There was a ruling concerning the right to hope in 2014. There are also judgments concerning other prisoners. The judgments concerning Mr. Öcalan and Civan Boltan are among them. However, no changes have been made to Turkey's domestic legal system in the past 12 years.




When we speak about law and human rights, the failure to implement such judgments causes a serious breakdown of trust. It also strengthens the perception that decisions in Turkey are made not by the courts but by the political authority. Courts should make decisions independently, yet the impression that they act in accordance with the government's position is becoming increasingly widespread."




'Demirtaş remains imprisoned despite judgments finding violations'




Ercan Yılmaz described the failure to implement the ECtHR's judgments concerning Selahattin Demirtaş as one of the clearest examples of this approach.




He said: "You will remember that the first ECtHR judgment concerning Demirtaş was announced in November 2018. Immediately afterwards, because it was known that he would have to be released in that case, a detention order was issued as part of another investigation. This allowed his imprisonment to continue through a legal manoeuvre.




Despite five separate judgments finding violations in the case against him over the years, Demirtaş, Figen Yüksekdağ, those imprisoned as part of the Kobanê case and other prisoners detained for political reasons continue to be held behind bars.




Therefore, there is no legal basis on which the Republic of Turkey can exercise discretion not to implement ECtHR judgments. Article 90 of the Constitution clearly states that judgments issued by international courts are binding within Turkey's domestic legal system."




'The judiciary acts according to the political government's messages'




Yılmaz drew attention to the increasing restrictions on constitutional rights in Turkey, particularly freedom of expression and the right to assembly and demonstration.




He continued: "When we look at society as a whole, we witness almost every day how freedom of expression, the right to assembly and demonstration, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution are being suppressed. This is a reflection of the system under which Turkey is governed following the introduction of the current presidential system.




Since the change of regime in 2017, we have repeatedly witnessed that courts cannot be considered separate from or independent of the government. We have seen courts issue decisions according to the messages conveyed by those in power. The failure to implement ECtHR judgments directly reflects this situation.




The Mustafa Balbay ruling is one example. After Balbay was elected as an MP, the Constitutional Court found a violation of his rights, and that ruling was implemented. He was released from prison. However, following the change in the system of government in 2017, we have increasingly seen how courts are unable to act independently of the government on such matters. The failure to implement ECtHR judgments is also a consequence of this political approach."




'Political will is needed, not legal reform'




Ercan Yılmaz emphasised that implementing ECtHR judgments did not require new legislation or legal reform, as the existing provisions of the Constitution and the international conventions to which Turkey is a party already contained sufficient and explicit regulations. He said that the real problem was the government's failure to adopt an approach that would expand rights and freedoms.




Yılmaz said: "No legal changes are necessary in this regard. There is no need for any legislative amendment. The relevant provisions of the Constitution and the international conventions to which Turkey is a party clearly state that ECtHR judgments must be implemented. What is needed is a political approach that opens the way for rights and freedoms. There must be a political will to advance democracy.




We are talking about a very fundamental issue. There is a court ruling. Another court, whose jurisdiction you have recognised, determines that the original ruling was not in accordance with the law. If you say that you are a state governed by the rule of law, if you claim that the country is governed according to law, then you must implement that court's judgment. This is what the rule of law requires.




We constantly discuss this issue in relation to imprisonment, but ECtHR judgments on many other matters are also not implemented within Turkey's domestic legal system. If your Constitution declares that the country is governed by the rule of law, you are obliged to fulfil the requirements of the Constitution. It is widely acknowledged that doing so would bring relief to society and constitute a step towards greater democracy. Yet no meaningful steps have been taken in this regard, despite repeated calls."




'Failure to implement ECtHR judgments is a constitutional crime'




Yılmaz stressed that the failure to implement ECtHR judgments could not be regarded merely as a legal shortcoming but constituted a violation of constitutional obligations.




Yılmaz concluded: "Domestic courts are obliged to comply with the judgments of the European Court of Human Rights finding violations. If they issue any other decision, they are acting unlawfully. Perhaps this offence is not being discussed today, and the question of a constitutional crime is not being raised. However, in a normal legal system, it must be recognised that failure to implement ECtHR judgments also constitutes a constitutional crime.




If you claim to be a state governed by the rule of law, you are obliged to implement the Constitution and the international conventions to which you are a party. The question that should be discussed is not whether ECtHR judgments should be implemented, but why they have still not been implemented. Because implementing these judgments is not a matter of choice, but a legal and constitutional obligation."

title: Kılıç: Villagers are leading the ecological struggle
content:
The growing number of mining, solar power plant (SPP) and hydroelectric power plant (HPP) projects in Kurdistan and Turkey are being pushed forward through favourable Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) decisions. The planned projects threaten pastures and groundwater resources, which are among the main sources of livelihood for villagers in the region. Local people seeking to protect their living spaces and livelihoods continue to organise against these projects across villages and districts.




In the past year alone, eight local platforms have been established in Kurdistan to oppose planned projects, while protest camps have been set up in numerous villages. Varto (Gimgim), Sur, Karlıova (Kanîreş), Kulp (Pasur) and Şırnak (Şirnex) have emerged as prominent centres of ecological resistance. Hundreds of villagers have come together through these platforms to pursue legal action and organise resistance on the ground.







 







Sabri Kılıç, spokesperson for the Amed (Diyarbakır) Ecology Council, who has closely followed and participated in recent protests, said that the social base of the ecological struggle is expanding and that the resistance is generating ecological and social awareness. He said: "It is particularly valuable to see people of all ages, from children to the elderly, coming together to defend their living spaces in villages directly affected by ecological destruction."




166 EIA announcements published




A total of 166 EIA announcements were published in Amed between 1 January and 17 October 2026. Of these, 73 resulted in favourable decisions, while six applications were cancelled or returned. Solar power plant projects also accounted for a significant share of the city's EIA procedures. During this period, announcements were published for 29 SPP projects, eight of which received favourable decisions.




'Companies are exploiting the process'




Kılıç said that ecological destruction in Kurdistan cannot be understood merely as the result of projects undertaken by a handful of companies, describing it instead as a systematic policy of exploitation. He stressed that the issue extends beyond environmental destruction and must be considered in its economic, social, cultural and political dimensions. Kılıç also said that this policy had intensified again following the beginning of the peace process.




Kılıç continued: "Since the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society, we have seen capital, through certain monopolies, develop an increasingly voracious appetite for Kurdistan, attempting to turn every area into a site of capital accumulation. Operating entirely according to a logic of exploitation, they are causing ecological destruction across Kurdistan through mining sites, quarries, oil exploration wells, energy projects and similar activities.




The important point is that these projects are being imposed on village pastures, agricultural land, water resources and forest areas. People who were forced to migrate through the burning and evacuation of villages in the 1990s are now being driven from their homes by capital through a different approach. This also threatens villages' relations of production, livelihoods, collective memory and the cultural and historical ties that people have established with the land they inhabit."




'Villagers have become active agents of resistance'




Kılıç emphasised the importance of the struggle waged by villagers against ecological destruction, saying that they should not be regarded merely as victims. Instead, he stressed that villagers have become social actors who speak for themselves, defend their right to make decisions about their living spaces and develop organised resistance.




Kılıç said: "This growing struggle should be recognised not only as resistance against ecological destruction and an effort to protect living spaces, but also as a valuable contribution to the development of local democracy and social organisation."




'Social awareness against plunder has emerged'




Kılıç also highlighted the continuity of the villagers' struggle. He said: "Based on our observations over the past year, we can say that the social base of the ecological struggle has expanded and that the resistance has generated ecological and social awareness. Furthermore, in villages directly affected by ecological destruction, it is particularly valuable to see people of all ages, from children to the elderly, standing together to defend their living spaces.




The role of women in this process deserves particular emphasis. In many areas, women are not merely participating in protests but are emerging as the organisers of the struggle and the driving force sustaining social resistance. From Arzoxlî to Koçmarin, from Husika to Cixse, we have witnessed women in numerous areas of resistance across Amed sometimes closing drilling wells with their own hands and at other times risking their lives by standing in front of the machinery used to carry out this plunder."




'The ecological struggle has created a solidarity network'




Sabri Kılıç also described the damage caused by companies to villagers' living spaces and stressed that struggles against ecological destruction in different regions cannot be considered independently of one another.




Kılıç continued: "Such an approach contradicts the very nature of the ecological struggle because ecological life represents an interconnected whole and a fundamental understanding of life. For example, cyanide ponds planned for water basins in Ergani would poison our underground and surface resources. How can we consider this independently of all the living spaces through which the water flows, from Amed to Cizre and from Mosul to Baghdad? Just as we do not regard these as separate issues, we cannot treat ecological struggles as isolated practices. This is why the ecological struggle also creates a network of solidarity among people resisting in other regions and areas."




Kılıç said that the gains achieved recently should also be understood within the framework of this solidarity network. He emphasised the importance of strengthening solidarity and continuing a united, organised struggle against ecological destruction.

title: Narges Mohammadi calls for solidarity with imprisoned writers
content:
Human rights activist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi issued a statement from prison to mark International Day of the Imprisoned Writer.




Drawing attention to authoritarian governments’ attitudes towards freedom of expression and thought, Narges Mohammadi stated that Iran’s history was also filled with methods of repression ranging from executions and imprisonment to fabricated cases and threats.




Narges Mohammadi said that journalists, writers and poets Arash Galeh-Golab, Mandana Sadeghi, Reza Mohammadi, Kourosh Keram-Pour and Farzaneh Yahya-Abadi were being retried in connection with the same case. She noted that all five had been charged on 9 November by Branch 103 of the Abadan Criminal Court No. 2 with “spreading false news with the aim of misleading public opinion” and “participating in illegal gatherings”.




Narges Mohammadi added that the death sentence handed down to poet and songwriter Peyman Farah-Avar had been referred to the Execution Office. The statement also highlighted the five-year-and-one-month prison sentence imposed on Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, along with the confiscation of his assets; the detention of Mahshahr-based poet and writer Ilyas Kenavati-Lari; and the four-year-and-eight-month prison sentences handed down to two writers and poets from Gorgan, Ruzbeh Gilasian and Nima Saffar.

title: Kongra Star mobilizes against violence against women in Rojava
content:
The women’s movement Kongra Star has mobilized against gender-based violence and discrimination in several cities across Rojava. As part of activities marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25, a demonstration was held in Dêrik, while political gatherings took place in Til Temir and Dirbêsiyê. Alongside the struggle against patriarchal violence, the events focused on women’s social self-determination, the right to education in their mother tongue and demands for constitutional guarantees of women’s rights in Syria.




The events are part of a joint campaign organized by women’s movements and organizations in Rojava. Under the slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), they are linking the struggle against violence against women with demands to safeguard the social and political rights won during the Rojava Revolution within Syria’s future constitutional framework.




Demonstration in Dêrik: Enshrining women’s rights in the constitution




In Dêrik, Kongra Star organized a march from Freedom Square to the city center. Participants chanted slogans highlighting the role of women in society and opposing violence and gender-based discrimination. Following a moment of silence in memory of those who had lost their lives, Wefa Elî spoke on behalf of Kongra Star. She reaffirmed that the women’s movement would continue its struggle against all forms of violence and support women in their pursuit of self-determination.




Elî described women’s social and political participation as a fundamental prerequisite for a democratic society. She emphasized that the achievements of the women’s movement must be defended and protected through binding legal guarantees. In particular, she called for women’s rights to be explicitly enshrined in the Syrian constitution.




She also recalled the leading role of women in the Rojava Revolution. Elî stated that the women’s movement had developed its organization and resistance on the basis of Abdullah Öcalan’s ideas and philosophy and would continue along this path.




Violence against women goes beyond physical assault




Student Aya Hesen brought a broader perspective on the different forms of gender-based violence to the demonstration. She read out a statement emphasizing that violence against women was not limited to sexual harassment, physical assault or domestic violence.




“The systematic silencing of women, the denial of their identity and the deprivation of their right to speak and receive education in their mother tongue are also forms of social violence and oppression,” she said. Hesen stressed that the Kurdish language was an essential part of Kurdish women’s identity and social existence.




The female students also spoke out against the segregation of girls and boys in education. They argued that such practices were rooted in patriarchal attitudes and reinforced existing gender inequalities. They called for an education system that guaranteed equal rights for girls and boys and enabled their shared development within society.




Til Temir: Self-determination as the result of organized struggle




In Til Temir, Kongra Star organized a gathering ahead of November 25. The meeting, held in the hall of the Council of Families of the Martyr, was attended by representatives of political parties, staff members of civil society organizations, women’s organizations and numerous other interested participants.




Hedla Yûnis, head of the Til Temir Women’s House, addressed the social changes women had achieved through their organizing efforts and political struggle. She highlighted the connection between patriarchal notions of ownership and domination and the historical denial of women’s rights.




“Women have freed themselves from the notion that they are the property of men. Today, they can determine their own destiny and make decisions about their future,” Yûnis explained. She attributed this development in large part to engagement with Abdullah Öcalan’s ideas.




For a long time, families and society have denied women the right to make independent decisions about their own lives, Yûnis said. “Men thought and acted on their behalf. Overcoming these conditions was the result of years of struggle and considerable sacrifice. Women have gone through many stages, fought and paid a heavy price. They have developed a will of their own, become decision-makers and taken their place in political and social life,” Yûnis said.




Despite these advances, she said, women in many societies continued to face oppression and violence. The struggle for equality must therefore continue at the social, political and legal levels.




Calls for constitutional guarantees also raised in Dirbêsiyê




In Dirbêsiyê, another gathering organized by Kongra Star also focused on the connection between the struggle against violence against women and Syria’s future political order. Under the themes “No to Violence against Women” and “Guaranteeing Women’s Rights in the Syrian Constitution,” participants discussed the legal and social changes needed.




The women emphasized that protection against gender-based violence could not be guaranteed through public declarations alone: “Binding legal rights and their effective enforcement are essential. Women in other parts of Syria also have a crucial role to play. They need to organize and demand their rights for themselves within the political process.”

title: Former long-term political prisoner Abdulvahap Adsoy dies
content:
Former political prisoner Abdulvahap Adsoy has died of cancer in Kızıltepe, in Mardin province. Adsoy had spent more than 30 years in Turkish prisons and was released from Bandırma Prison in the western Turkish province of Balıkesir on April 28, 2024. He had developed cancer during his imprisonment.




Adsoy was arrested in Kızıltepe in 1993 and subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment in an arbitrary trial by one of the notorious State Security Courts (DGM). Following his release, he underwent medical treatment for his illness. He died at a private hospital in Kızıltepe.




Upon his release, Adsoy had stated: “I made a promise, and I will live to fulfill that promise. I spent 30 years behind bars, but my heart was always with you. I will fight until the last drop of my blood. We draw our strength from our people. As long as our people stand behind us, no one can harm us. I thank you all.”




Following the completion of the necessary formalities, Abdulvahap Adsoy was laid to rest at Heci Hasan Aksoy Cemetery in Kızıltepe.

title: 16 trees planted in Amed in memory of murdered women
content:
Since Monday, 16 newly planted trees in Peace Park in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) have stood in memory of women murdered by men in the city in 2026. Through this symbolic initiative, the city administration is taking a stand against femicide and promoting social solidarity ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.




The tree-planting event in the Seyrantepe neighborhood was organized by the Women’s Council and the Department of Women’s Policies of the DEM Party-run metropolitan municipality. It is part of a series of events held under the slogan “Now Is the Time for Women – Fighting Violence Through Organized Struggle.”




Co-Mayor Serra Bucak recalled that the municipality had commemorated victims of gender-based violence with a similar initiative last year. The trees planted at the time were intended to grow and symbolize hope for a society free from violence, exploitation and discrimination.




Bucak emphasized that this year’s initiative reflected the same vision. “Our struggle against violence against women will continue until we achieve a world where femicides and massacres no longer occur,” she stated.

title: Two Kurds arrested in Bokan
content:
According to information reported by Kolbernews, Iranian regime forces arrested two Kurdish citizens in the city of Bokan.




The individuals arrested were identified as Nasir Qorxçî and Şehab Qorxçî, both from the village of Reşan, in the Bokan area. No information has been obtained regarding the reasons for their arrests or their current whereabouts.

title: Biçer: Kurdish cinema must build historical awareness in peace process
content:
Kurdish cinema in Turkey has faced censorship and repression throughout its history. Not only Kurdish cinema but also film and television projects dealing with Kurdistan have been forced to contend with censorship and pressure from successive governments.




Documentaries and films struggle to find venues for screenings, while cinemas refuse to show these productions. Most recently, the film Rojbash, which focuses on Teatra Jiyana Nû, has still not been released. Legal proceedings concerning the film are also ongoing. Another production unable to secure screening venues is a documentary about the Vartinis massacre.




Director Ömer Biçer, who documented the Vartinis massacre, spoke to ANF about the problems facing Kurdish cinema and the role of cinema in the struggle for peace.




‘I saw cinema as a responsibility’




Director Ömer Biçer, who began working in cinema in 2021, described how he became involved in filmmaking and his journey towards directing. Biçer said that he entered the world of cinema after meeting friends at Istasyon Akademi Mezopotamya Sinema.




Biçer said: “I was looking for an answer to the question, ‘Could I become a filmmaker?’ I believed that cinema was a collective art form and that we could become filmmakers by taking part in any aspect of it. However, looking at my earliest works, I found myself directing, which is one of the areas of cinema that carries the greatest responsibility in terms of production.




The reason was that, in 2021, Kurdistan and Turkey were experiencing difficult conditions of war, which affected every field of art. Making art was becoming increasingly difficult, particularly filmmaking. I saw this as a responsibility. It reminded me of something Ahmedê Xanî said when writing Mem û Zîn: ‘Hanî ji kemala bêkemalî / Meydana kemalê dît valî.’ In other words, Xanî saw a void in the field of artistic excellence. He wrote Mem û Zîn not because he considered himself exceptionally talented, but out of love for his people and a sense of national responsibility. I can say that I found myself in a similar situation and felt something similar.”




‘Kurdish society also guides its artists’




Biçer said that before making the Vartinis documentary, he had produced a short film addressing a public health problem that emerged during the resistance in Sur. 




Biçer continued: “Before Vartinis, I actually made a film called Sêhiya Gel in 2024. It dealt with a public health problem during the Sur resistance in 2015. During the post-production stage, after filming had been completed, this story and project came to me. It was actually a request from the people of Vartinis.




I think I felt ready for it, as though I had been preparing for years. A group of people came and said, ‘This is what happened to us, and this is how it ended. There was a massacre, followed by a second massacre through the legal system. We do not want this to be forgotten.’




At that point, regardless of whether someone is a filmmaker, whether new or experienced, any human being would try to become part of that story.




Anyone with a sense of moral responsibility would say, ‘Something like this has happened, I have been asked to take part, and I will accept that responsibility.’ That was the concern that motivated us to begin.




But both while making Vartinis and through the reactions we received afterwards, we were reminded of something: Kurdish society is genuinely dynamic and political. What I saw was that Kurdish society can also guide its artists. What was Kurdish cinema dealing with? What kind of narrative was it pursuing? When the issue of Vartinis emerged, we could see that everything else it had been dealing with suddenly lost much of its significance. That is how the process of telling the story of Vartinis began.”




‘There was also a public health crisis during the Sur resistance’




Biçer also discussed his short film Sêhiya Gel, which addresses events during the Sur resistance: “I was in Amed (Diyarbakır), about 100 metres from Diyarbakır Square, close to Sur. I was dealing with some paperwork at a notary's office when we learned that a woman had been killed by the police. The woman, Mızgın Kılıç, whose code name was Ruken Amed, was killed by police officers while trying to enter Sur to support the resistance fighters there.




That was when I felt that the war was continuing and that its psychological effects were affecting public health. How healthy were those who remained healthy? What was the ethical cost of remaining healthy?




This is being discussed now and will certainly continue to be discussed in the future. I questioned myself: ‘Have we become too accustomed to this war taking place right beside us? Has it become too much a part of our everyday lives?’ It was happening right beside me, very close to where I was. Once again, driven by a sense of responsibility, I began asking, ‘Such an event has taken place in history. What can we do as individuals and as artists?’ That was how the idea of developing this story emerged.




If we were going to make a film about the war in Sur, there were two conventional approaches. The first was to make a film directly depicting the front line and the war itself, as Ersin Çelik did in Ji Bo Azadiyê. The second was to tell the story more indirectly, through its consequences. I chose the second approach, both because of the technical conditions and because I preferred that narrative style.




When we ask, ‘What happened in Sur beyond what we witnessed?’, we find that there was a very serious public health crisis. The first observed problem was that women in Amed experienced irregular menstrual cycles due to stress during that period. The second was that psychiatric patients receiving treatment at home deteriorated to the point of requiring clinical care, again because of stress. This increased pressure on the healthcare system and eventually led to its collapse in some areas.




I chose the second issue. I did not want to risk making technical mistakes as a man when telling a woman's story, so I did not take that path. I hope a female colleague will tell that story in the near future.




Regarding the second issue, the deterioration of patients receiving treatment at home and the collapse of the healthcare system, I tried to portray something specific in the film. Everyone except the patient character was carrying on with their lives as before. The boy was the only person whose behaviour negatively affected everyday life. Yet, at the same time, he was the only one who did not pay the ethical price of remaining healthy in a place where war was taking place. If the psychiatric difficulties he experienced amounted to a state of madness, I think we need to question our own state of being healthy.




Another issue is how people gradually adapt to such situations within the system. In the film, everyone, from the patriotic doctor to the nurse and the family, works together to suppress the boy's reaction. People living in an area where the war was extremely intense wanted the clashes to end. The effort to silence the boy's screams was actually a form of self-criticism.”




‘We must create more opportunities for Kurdish films to reach Kurdish audiences’




Biçer said that Kurdish cinema had fallen short in portraying what people had experienced. He argued that Kurdish filmmakers must first answer whether they make films to reach audiences or to have their work screened at festivals.




Biçer also said: “If I were to answer whether Kurdish cinema reflects these experiences from the perspective of a viewer, I would say that it falls considerably short. In fact, there is another issue. I think the question ‘Why do we make cinema?’ is one that everyone involved in Kurdish cinema, from producers to screenwriters, must ask themselves from the outset.




One of the most fundamental problems facing Kurdish cinema is its inability to reach its audience. As a result, filmmakers move away from general audiences towards film festivals where they can screen their work. This leaves them facing a choice: Kurdish audiences or festival audiences? Many of these festivals take place abroad or in Turkey.




Public screenings of films in Kurdistan have been extremely limited. Eventually, filmmakers began producing films suited to the platforms where they can secure screenings. This takes the question ‘Who are we making cinema for?’ in another direction. Unfortunately, we cannot see a cinema being created for Kurdish people.




Returning to the question of how adequately Kurdish cinema reflects these problems, we can say that it falls short. Filmmakers cannot convey their work directly to the people whose concerns they are addressing. To close this gap, we must first increase opportunities for Kurdish films to reach Kurdish audiences. If filmmakers were as committed to their own audiences as they are to festivals, they could establish a closer connection with their own stories.”




‘I think some filmmakers have abandoned resistance cinema too early’




Ömer Biçer said that cinema also has an important role to play in the Peace and Democratic Society Process. He said: “We can regard Kurdish cinema as a reflection of the Kurdish people's own circumstances. As the problems underlying the Kurdish question are resolved, some of the obstacles facing Kurdish cinema will also disappear. I see a very strong parallel here. However, I have also noticed something. There have been certain developments and gains in the political sphere. The peace process itself is a major achievement, but these gains have not yet been translated into cultural achievements.




Therefore, I think certain groups within Kurdish cinema have prematurely abandoned the legacy of anti-colonial Kurdish cinema and resistance cinema. Despite the difficulties surrounding production, Kurdish filmmakers maintained a very strong stance. Yet I can see that these values are being abandoned earlier than they should be.




The cessation of hostilities is a major achievement, but it is not a cultural achievement. Cultural workers should be continuing their struggle from where they left off, and even more intensively. Instead, I think we have somewhat loosened our commitment to the legacy of anti-colonial and resistance cinema, as though these political developments had already become cultural achievements. Actions that would have been met with opposition just a year ago are now reaching a point where they are being encouraged. I think it is too early for that.




Therefore, the greatest contribution Kurdish artists can make to peace is to continue telling the stories of resistance and anti-colonial cinema, convey these experiences to their own people and build historical awareness. I believe we must act within the framework of our existing cinematic and political traditions to prevent this legacy from being abandoned prematurely.”

title: Social siege in Yüksekova: Children, women and youth targeted - Part One
content:
Allegations of child sexual abuse, harassment and sexual assault against women in Hakkari (Colemêrg), particularly in Yüksekova (Gever), have brought long-standing social problems in the district back into focus. A case involving allegations of sexual abuse of a 13-year-old child, in which school bus driver Eren Oğuz and local musician and security guard Necat Koparan are named, has been brought before the judiciary. Separately, several women have filed complaints alleging harassment and sexual assault by Nevzat Çiftçi, a local musician who performs at weddings. The fact that both men are well known in the district, perform at weddings and maintain connections with different sections of society raises the need to examine these incidents in a broader context. Are these merely isolated cases, or are they part of a wider social siege targeting young people, women and children through special warfare policies?




Yüksekova is a Kurdish town known for its strong neighborhood culture, close relations among neighbors and tradition of social solidarity. Over the years, this social structure has become a target of the state's repression and security policies. The curfews and clashes that began with the declaration of self-rule in Yüksekova on 13 August 2015 resulted in widespread destruction. Neighborhoods were demolished and thousands of families were displaced. The destruction targeted not only physical spaces but also relations of neighborliness and solidarity. The subsequent reconstruction of the town accelerated the replacement of neighborhood culture with a consumption-oriented way of life.




Today, discussions about Yüksekova point to a multidimensional social siege, ranging from abuse targeting children and women to drugs, loan sharking and money laundering networks, and from the criminalization of young people to divisions deepened through tribalism. The erosion of social values, from wedding culture and everyday life to economic relations and local power networks, is also part of this picture. The latest case involving the alleged sexual assault of a 13-year-old child has once again highlighted the extent of the problems surrounding children's safety and protection. This report examines how social life in Yüksekova has been targeted through special warfare policies and the transformations these policies have brought about.




Child sexual abuse and threats involving images




The sexual abuse case involving a 13-year-old child in Yüksekova has once again raised concerns about children's safety and protection in the district. The case, which has been referred to the judiciary, names school bus driver Eren Oğuz and Necat Koparan, a local musician, wedding performer and security guard. The child reportedly described the abuse in a statement given at the Child Monitoring Center, saying that images of the child had been used to make threats and that attempts had been made to obstruct the child's education. The threats and pressure the child reportedly faced after the abuse indicate that the incident was not limited to the alleged sexual abuse itself. Threats involving images and interference with the child's right to education are also significant aspects of the case. The suspects' release after giving their statements has raised questions about how the investigation is being conducted, how the child is being protected and what support mechanisms will be put in place.




Eren Oğuz's position as a school bus driver is particularly significant because families entrust their children to drivers during their journeys to and from school. Children's safety and the protection of this relationship of trust are therefore central concerns. Necat Koparan's status as a security guard and his position in society as a local musician are other notable aspects of the case. Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP for Hakkari, Öznur Bartın, also brought the issue before parliament, submitting a parliamentary question to the Ministry of Family and Social Services.




Years of abuse and harassment cases in Yüksekova and Hakkari




The latest case involving the alleged sexual assault of a 13-year-old child is not the first such incident reported in Yüksekova or other districts of Hakkari. Over the years, allegations of child sexual abuse, harassment and sexual assault against women, as well as cases involving threats and blackmail, have emerged at different times. Some of these cases have resulted in convictions, others remain before the courts, and some have ended in acquittals.




2024: Allegations of harassment involving specialist sergeants in Çukurca (Çelê):

 Two girls aged 16 and 17 were reportedly harassed by specialist sergeants during a festival concert in Çukurca. Two specialist sergeants were detained and subsequently released. In a statement, the district governor's office described the incident as an intoxicated person holding the hand of a 16-year-old girl.




2024: Harassment allegations against a specialist sergeant in Hakkari:

 A specialist sergeant was accused of harassing a young woman for approximately one month and continuing to send her messages on social media even after her family filed a complaint. Members of the family were reportedly detained following an argument with the suspect.




2023: Alleged child sexual abuse in Derecik (Rûbarok): 

A child aged nine or ten was allegedly taken to a barn by a neighbor and sexually abused. The child was heard in court in the presence of a child development specialist. The trial was postponed until 2026.




2023: Security guard sentenced to 17 years and six months in prison: 

In the case of D.E., who was reportedly subjected to systematic sexual abuse by two cousins from the age of 13, one of the defendants was identified as a security guard. One defendant died in 2017. In December 2023, the other defendant, Sedat E., was sentenced to 17 years and six months in prison following a retrial.




2023: Acquittals in the Esra Yücel case:

 Eleven-year-old Esra Yücel, who lived in Oğlaklı village in Şemdinli (Şemzinan), was allegedly sexually abused and then thrown from a cliff. In November 2023, three defendants were acquitted due to insufficient evidence.




2022: Photographs of 26 women stolen: 

Photographs of 26 women in Yüksekova were reportedly obtained and used on fake social media accounts, exposing the women to threats and harassment. The women sought assistance from the Human Rights Association (IHD).




2021: Alleged blackmail network involving security guards and specialist sergeants:

 Allegations emerged concerning a blackmail and prostitution network in Hakkari and Şırnak (Şirnex), reportedly involving security guards, specialist sergeants and civilians. Women were allegedly drugged and subjected to abuse, while images of them were recorded and used for blackmail. An investigation into the allegations was reportedly launched.




2021: Alleged sexual abuse of a five-year-old child in Derecik:

 A suspect was arrested in connection with allegations of sexual abuse involving a five-year-old child. The Hakkari Bar Association stated that the family had been pressured not to file a complaint.




2021: Sexual assault complaint against a police officer: 

A complaint was filed against police officer E.T. over allegations that he sexually assaulted G.A.Ü., who worked at the same institution, in Hakkari. In a statement, the governor's office said that the complaint had been withdrawn and subsequently filed again after an attempted marriage arrangement failed. The suspect was suspended from duty and an administrative investigation was launched.




2019: Assault and threats allegedly involving a village guard commander in Akocak:

 Village guard commander Ümit Yalçıntuna was accused of sexually assaulting a young woman and threatening her family. The family was allegedly pressured to withdraw its complaint, while police reportedly proposed marriage as a means of reaching a settlement.




2019: Alleged abuse of two siblings in Büyükçiftlik: 

Security guard Sedat E. was prosecuted over allegations of sexually abusing two siblings aged six and twelve. The court ruled that the defendant could stand trial without being held in custody.




2019–2020: Sexual abuse of a nine-year-old child in Yüksekova: 

In a case involving the sexual abuse of a nine-year-old child, defendant M.A. was sentenced to a total of 62 years and six months in prison.




These cases reveal common patterns among allegations involving different individuals over several years: children and women being subjected to sexual violence, attempts to silence them through threats and blackmail, incidents involving allegations against public officials, and serious questions surrounding investigative procedures.




The incidents in Yüksekova, together with the lack of social response, also highlight the need to examine special warfare policies beyond the sphere of security and armed conflict. They raise questions about the impact of these policies on social relations, the lives of women and children, and the future of young people.




What do these cases tell us?




What do these sexual assault cases spanning several years tell us? On one side are allegations of abuse, harassment and assault targeting children and women. On the other are threats, blackmail, coercion involving images and pressure to withdraw complaints. Security guards, specialist sergeants and public officials are named in these criminal cases. Some trials have resulted in convictions, others in acquittals, while some cases have remained unresolved for years.




Two individuals whose names have recently returned to public attention, Necat Koparan and Nevzat Çiftçi, are well-known local wedding musicians. The fact that Koparan is also a security guard makes the child sexual abuse allegations brought before the judiciary against him particularly significant. Eren Oğuz, meanwhile, is a school bus driver. The involvement of someone entrusted by families with the safety of their children in such a case raises serious concerns. Moreover, the victim in the latest case is a 13-year-old child.




But how much of what has happened do these publicly reported cases actually reveal? How many women and children have been unable to file complaints, remained silent because of threats, been forced to withdraw under family pressure or lacked the strength to speak about their experiences? How many cases were never opened, and how many victims were never heard? The answers to these questions remain unknown. But one thing is clear: The safety of children and women, the future of young people and solidarity within society in Yüksekova are under severe siege. Treating these incidents as isolated criminal cases means ignoring the broader picture.




State repression, social disintegration, drug trafficking and criminal networks, and the targeting of women and children are all interconnected. This is what is known as special warfare.
