title: The memory of a cartoon: From Qırıx to Bajar
content:
Doğan Güzel's cartoons carry a collective memory stretching from the streets of Diyarbakır (Amed) in the 1990s to the present day. Born out of everyday life, political conflicts and social contradictions, Qırıx gradually became more than a cartoon character, emerging as a figure representing the youth of the period and the transformation experienced by Kurdish society. Güzel's work, which continued through humor publications such as Gırgır, TEW-LO, Pîne and Zrîng, has now taken a new form with Bajar magazine. This long-running journey seeks not only to preserve the collective memory of the past but also to create space for the written use of Kurdish through cartoons and comics.




Güzel's journey as a cartoonist began with a character he created by observing the people around him and the political atmosphere of the time. Doğan Güzel, who spoke to ANF, said that he began drawing cartoons for Gırgır magazine and described his need to create a character he could draw every day.




Güzel said: "Since I was among patriotic young people, I wanted to create a character I could draw every day without too much difficulty whenever I needed to produce something in response to newspaper headlines. I looked around and observed my fellow students. I tried to create a character by combining Kurdish culture with something familiar to me. I think the character resonated with people because I drew him sincerely, without forcing myself too much.




Although my drawings were amateurish, I was naturally reflecting the period as I tried to portray the people around me. I was depicting the world of young people who were just becoming involved in politics, taking part in protests and experiencing uncertainty. I combined the experiences of students in Istanbul with the social reality of Kurdish people. Perhaps that is why the character became popular. When you draw by observing your surroundings, you also reflect the pulse of the country you live in."




Qırıx first appears in Özgür Gündem




Qırıx appeared in the pages of Özgür Gündem between 1992 and 1995. Politics in the character's world was not limited to developments reported in newspaper headlines. Young people's friendships, everyday decisions, uncertainties about joining the struggle and questions about how to lead their lives were also part of that world.




Güzel described the political atmosphere in which the character emerged and the uncertainties experienced by young people. 




Güzel said: "There was intense political activity in Istanbul in 1991, 1992 and 1993. It was a period when Kurdish young people were discovering their identities and becoming involved in politics, with demonstrations taking place every day. Young people felt they had to make major decisions. They were asking themselves, 'What should I do? How should I act? Where do I stand in this struggle?' This atmosphere was reflected in my cartoons. Keko's incomplete understanding of politics, his uncertainty about whether to join the struggle, his constant changes of mind and the ambiguity over whether these feelings were sincere or driven by other reasons reflected the experiences of young people at the time. There were strong similarities between what was happening in Kurdistan and the experiences of young people in Istanbul. The problems were shared, and young people were confronting similar questions."




Qırıx's significance lay not in being a character who observed the political struggle from the outside, but in embodying the contradictions experienced by young people in his own everyday life. The character reflected a generation struggling to make decisions, changing alongside social conditions and sometimes confronting its own contradictions.




T

he politics of everyday life







The years in which Qırıx emerged were marked by armed clashes, detentions, village evacuations and state violence that shaped everyday life in Kurdish cities. Güzel's cartoons, however, portrayed this harsh reality not simply through political messages but also through the seemingly ordinary lives of people.




Güzel said that he had not initially expected his drawings to attract so much attention. He described his style as different from conventional newspaper humor and reflected on both the character's popularity and the discomfort it caused.




Güzel also said: "I started drawing cartoons at a very young age. Initially, I did not think my work would attract so much attention. My style was different from conventional newspaper humor. I had a more absurdist approach to humor, and I did not expect my drawings to receive much attention. Over time, however, I realized that portraying Kurdish experiences so naturally and as something legitimate through a character loved in patriotic circles was itself enough to cause discomfort.




I was portraying someone who could be seen as a terrorist by Turks and as an adventurer by Kurds, but I was showing his human side. I drew him as one of us, someone who lived and thought like us. I think that was what attracted the most attention."




The human qualities, fears, weaknesses and contradictions of Güzel's characters also found expression in his drawings. A way of life portrayed from the outside as dangerous or extraordinary was thus depicted through the everyday reality of the people who experienced it.







Güzel particularly valued the character's ability to express Kurdish politics and social life in his own language. He also believes that this aspect of his cartoons contributed to his prosecution and imprisonment: "Keko was a character who could speak about Kurdish politics and social reality in his own language without being ashamed of himself. At the time, it was unusual to portray Kurdish political experiences, the struggle and everyday life so naturally. Newspapers featured harsher, more rigid drawings with explicit political messages. But portraying our experiences from within, sincerely and as an ordinary part of everyday life, had a different impact. For us, these experiences were already a natural part of life.




What Keko did was make a reality portrayed from the outside as frightening or dangerous visible in its natural form. I believe this approach was also a factor behind my prosecution and imprisonment over these works."




Cartoons on trial




Doğan Güzel was prosecuted in 1993 over the Qırıx cartoon strips he drew for Özgür Gündem. He was charged under Article 159 of the Turkish Penal Code in force at the time and sentenced to a total of 40 months in prison in 1998. Güzel was imprisoned on 31 July 1998 and released on 16 September 1999. That same year, he received the Courage in Editorial Cartooning Award from Cartoonists Rights Network International.




Güzel's experiences became one example of the repression of the Kurdish press and freedom of expression in the field of cartooning. In his account, the underlying issue was his approach to portraying Kurdish experiences naturally, within the context of everyday life.







From Pîne to Zrîng




Güzel continued producing work for different publications after Qırıx. Pîne magazine, which began publication in 1999, marked a new period in Kurdish-language humor and continued until 2002. Years later, in 2019, Zrîng, edited by Doğan Güzel and İmam Cici, began publication. The magazine was planned to appear in two separate editions, in Kurmanji and Kirmanjki.




These publications were part of an effort not only to sustain Kurdish-language humor but also to create opportunities for new cartoonists and stories. However, the future of written humor depended not only on publishing conditions but also on the development of reading habits and the wider use of Kurdish as a written language.




Güzel said that he does not follow contemporary Kurdish-language humor very closely, although he has seen work produced on platforms such as YouTube: "Sometimes amateur productions can be of higher quality than work created with professional equipment and resources. This development was natural, and I believe even better work will emerge. In this sense, we continue to learn and develop."




Güzel believes that the relationship between cartoons and written language is both one of the art form's defining characteristics and a challenge for written culture. He said that the decline of humor magazines has also affected Kurdish-language publications, emphasizing the need to develop the written use of Kurdish and reading habits: "An important characteristic of cartoons is that they exist alongside writing. The combination of drawings and words in humor distinguishes it from other forms of expression. However, its dependence on written culture also creates difficulties. Today, humor magazines are declining not only in Kurdistan but throughout the world.




In Turkey, magazines have closed one after another. It is impossible for this not to affect Kurdish-language humor. But there is another issue concerning Kurdish: the need to develop its written use and a culture of reading. Kurdish needs to be taught in schools, used as a written language and made more widespread. For people to engage with written humor, they need to have developed reading habits to some extent. Although this presents a challenge, it also offers an important opportunity. Cartoons and comics can help encourage people to start reading in Kurdish."




Continuing to draw in exile




The legal cases and pressure Güzel faced also changed the course of his life. He applied for political asylum in Spain in 2012 and subsequently obtained Spanish citizenship. He continued producing work for the Kurdish press while living in Europe.




Exile, however, did not erase Diyarbakır from Güzel's drawings. The city remained present in his work as a world where language, characters and collective memory came together.




Detained again




Doğan Güzel was among the journalists detained during a police operation against the Özgür Gündem newspaper on 17 August 2016. A photograph showing his torn shirt as police took him away during the raid on the newspaper's offices became one of the symbols of repression against the press. Güzel and the other journalists were released two days later.




Güzel, who had been imprisoned years earlier over his cartoons, was now detained outside the newspaper where he worked. The incident showed how questions of press freedom and freedom of expression had resurfaced at different stages of his life.




Bajar: Comics to encourage reading in Kurdish




One of the latest chapters in Güzel's artistic journey is Bajar magazine, which began publication in 2026. The Kurdish-language cartoon and comic magazine, produced under the auspices of Diyarbakır Metropolitan Municipality, is edited by Doğan Güzel and İmam Cici. The first issue of the magazine, published in Kurmanji, was introduced in June 2026. It aims to support the practical use of Kurdish and encourage children to begin reading in the language.




Güzel emphasized that the idea behind Bajar was to establish a mutually supportive relationship between Kurdish and publishing: "We thought that publishing the magazine only in Turkish would limit our ability to reach readers. Instead, we wanted to establish a reciprocal relationship with Kurdish and the language itself. Our aim was to create a publication that could contribute to the written use of Kurdish and help people learn the language through reading. That was why we launched Bajar. The magazine is currently published every two months and consists of 24 pages.




I believe this is a project that can be developed further in the coming period. If Kurdish-language education becomes more widespread in schools and courses, publications of this kind could once again play an important role. The magazine contributes to the development of Kurdish while also drawing strength from the language's continued existence and development. I consider this mutually beneficial relationship important."




Bajar takes the aspirations behind Güzel's earlier publishing experiences into a new field. The cartoons that spoke from within everyday life and political transformation in the world of Qırıx took on new forms in Kurdish-language humor magazines through Pîne and Zrîng. Bajar, meanwhile, approaches comics as a means of helping children develop reading habits in their mother tongue.




Why is Qırıx still remembered?




Qırıx is remembered decades later not simply because he was a humorous character. He portrayed the youth of the 1990s, Diyarbakır's neighborhood culture and the political atmosphere of the period through everyday life. Young people's uncertainties, social transformation and their changing relationship with politics were central elements of the cartoons.




The character reached new generations when Diyarbakır City Theatre brought Qırıx to the stage in 2017. Moving from newspaper pages to the theater, the character found a new form of storytelling.




Güzel's work was not limited to a single character. The artist, who portrayed the youth, everyday life and social contradictions of the 1990s through Qırıx, continued his work in Kurdish-language humor in subsequent years through publications such as Pîne and Zrîng.




Bajar carries this legacy forward through a new publishing approach aimed at helping children develop the habit of reading in Kurdish.




The memory carried by cartoons




Qırıx portrayed the young people of his time, Diyarbakır's neighborhood culture and its political atmosphere through everyday life. The character's adaptation for the theater years later also demonstrated that his story had not remained confined to newspaper pages but could reach new generations in different forms.




Pîne and Zrîng represent different periods of Güzel's work in Kurdish-language humor, while Bajar approaches cartoons and comics as tools that can encourage children to read and write in their mother tongue. Güzel's artistic journey therefore encompasses not only a cartoonist's decades of work but also an effort to give Kurdish a greater place in everyday life through humor and publishing.




The journey from Qırıx, which portrayed the youth and contradictions of an era in newspaper pages, to Bajar, which aims to encourage children to enjoy reading in Kurdish, reflects a change in both the audience and the purpose of the cartoons. Yet the effort to tell stories through drawings, document lived experiences and create space for the written use of Kurdish continues to connect the different periods of Güzel's work.

title: Uysal: Art's unifying and healing power can contribute to peace
content:
Theatre in Turkey is increasingly drifting away from its essence, influenced not only by longstanding structural problems but also by the political climate. Even plays that claim to be political remain under the influence of Turkish nationalist ideology.




The launch of the Peace and Democratic Society Process has sparked public debate about the role of art in the struggle for peace and the experiences of the past. For years, plays featuring racist rhetoric targeting the Kurdish people and other communities under the influence of war have been staged. The new process has also brought discussions about the need to transform the language of art.




Theatre director and dramaturg Abdullah Uysal spoke to ANF about the current state of theatre in Turkey and the role of art in the struggle for peace.




'Theatre is a technically and economically demanding profession'




Abdullah Uysal said that theatre has been affected by the cultural erosion experienced particularly under the rule of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), emphasizing that the problems facing theatre have economic, social and political dimensions.




Uysal said: "What is the state of theatre in Turkey? The situation is actually good, but at the same time, it isn't. It is difficult to fully grasp the cultural erosion that has taken place over the past 25 years, particularly under AKP rule, and its consequences. Theatre is already a technically and economically demanding profession. You create a work, an artistic aesthetic, and you need spaces in which to present it. You sell tickets to audiences who come to those spaces. This is directly connected to society's entire network of relationships and its economic and sociological structure. Theatre naturally finds its audience in places where people are comfortable, economic difficulties are not overwhelming and democracy is not under threat. People can create opportunities to relax and devote time to themselves. This directly affects theatre. Tickets are sold, and you can bring your work to audiences.




However, Turkey has struggled with economic problems since its establishment. Over the past 25 years, particularly under AKP rule, the economy has deteriorated dramatically and is now in a very poor state. As a result, theatre practitioners have either been forced to scale down their productions, performing in smaller venues with capacities of 30, 20 or even 15 people, or to reduce their expenses significantly.




For example, productions with large casts are no longer being staged. Look at what is being produced today: one-person plays, musical cabaret-style performances and stories that do not challenge audiences intellectually but instead distract them from everyday life. These are often what might be called 'cheesy' productions, built around cheap, stale narratives.




The popularity and celebrity culture that have emerged with the use of social media, along with people's reactions to momentary events, have changed the reasons audiences choose certain performances. There is a group in Turkey that claims to be producing theatre, and their tickets sell out. Let me give you an example. A simple story that has been adapted into films since the 1970s, staged perhaps 20 times and turned into television series is currently being performed in Turkey. They stage it in venues seating between 3,000 and 5,000 people, with tickets costing 5,000 Turkish lira, and every performance is sold out. Some viewers may even remember a theatre performance in Turkey where arguments broke out because people complained, 'I can't see my seat.' If you showed footage of that performance to someone abroad, they would conclude that Turkey has no audience problem and that theatre is thriving."




Uysal also said: "Yet at the same time, we hear that many theatre venues in cities across Kurdistan and in Turkey's major metropolitan areas are closing because of economic difficulties. As economic, political and class contradictions deepen in Turkey, and the cultural divide widens alongside them, it becomes increasingly difficult to speak of theatre's continued existence.




This raises a fundamental question: What is theatre, and what is not? Theatre, as we understand it, means producing works of art that touch society and have the power to transform it. It should enable people to look at communities, individuals, women, ecology, animals and the world with renewed hope, or give them the strength to change the world. Unfortunately, this kind of artistic production is lacking. This is partly due to political restrictions on art and censorship. There is also self-censorship, which has become another reality. Even if you are not directly censored, there is no guarantee in Turkey that you will not be detained, prosecuted over a tweet or imprisoned for something you said in a particular place. Inevitably, you begin to censor yourself. For all these reasons, the situation of theatre in Turkey is not good."




'Everything that challenges the enemy's laws becomes political in Turkey'




Uysal said that political theatre in Turkey must be examined alongside the broader question of how politics is practiced, arguing that even Kemalists now claim to produce political theatre.




Uysal continued: "Is political theatre being produced in Turkey? This is actually connected to my answer to the previous question. From a sociological perspective, is politics really being practiced in Turkey? Or how has politics been practiced here for a long time? Does being political mean that the content of your work is political, or that the position you occupy as an individual becomes politicized?




We had a colleague who headed Izmir City Theatres and has now resigned. He previously worked at Istanbul City Theatres but was removed from his position under AKP rule. His discourse largely follows a narrow Kemalist line that does not embrace other peoples or beliefs, yet today he claims to produce political theatre. However, there is no place for Kurds, women, other peoples or other faiths in his political theatre. In Turkey, anything that responds to the enemy's laws with hostility can become politicized.




Political theatre, however, is not simply about opposing someone. It is about drawing on the strength that comes from life itself and using that strength to bring about change. Brecht speaks of this. Augusto Boal, meanwhile, describes political theatre as 'a rehearsal for revolution.'




Do you have a vision of revolution or not? Where does your theatre stand within that vision, and how do you imagine revolution? Once you can answer these questions, stages, streets and every other space can become a stage, a place for theatre. You can make theatre political by portraying a resistance fighter at a protest. If animals are being killed in a shelter, performing outside that shelter can become a political act. You can become political by performing in the midst of conflict, among tear gas canisters in France or in Kurdistan today.




Demanding peace is the greatest political demand in this country today. Defending animal rights and demanding that women be able to walk freely through the streets in the middle of the night are among the most political acts. It is not simply about opposing someone. You must have a vision and the means to realize it.




Theatre is the only thing in this life that I believe I can do, the only thing I have proven to myself that I can accomplish. We are trying to keep alive the culture of a people whose language has been banned, or to tell the stories of women who have been confined to their homes at night. We tell the stories of those who have been made invisible and subjected to treatment we believe they do not deserve. We bring these stories to the stage and to the people, recognizing no limits of space, time, place or borders. That is when we are producing political theatre."




'Theatre in Turkey portrays the other through the dominant ideology'




Uysal also addressed the representation of marginalized communities in theatre, emphasizing that peoples must be able to tell their own stories.




Uysal said: "Theatre in Turkey actually looks at the other exactly as it is expected to. There is a saying I particularly like: 'Hunters write the history of lions. Only when lions write their own history will we come face to face with real history.'




Because of the restrictions imposed by Turkey's existing political structures, particularly those concerning mother tongues, Turks today describe these communities as 'disadvantaged groups.' Yet these are the peoples of this land: Kurds, Armenians, Laz, Circassians and Abkhazians. Political restrictions have been imposed on their ability to work in their mother tongues and establish their own organizations. As a result, Turks once again attempt to tell their stories. This reflects the official ideology of the Turkish Republic and its perception of the other.




They need to create this 'other' in their narratives, and art provides the most effective means of packaging and selling that representation. Yet the reality is different. That same Kurd is their neighbor, and that same Armenian is the craftsman living downstairs. This is precisely why the representation of the other in Turkey's official ideological artistic sphere is that of a marginal character, confined to the place assigned to them. There is no contradiction here. It would be meaningless to pretend that the Turkish Republic has always been democratic or that, since its establishment, it has not carried out a comprehensive assault on other peoples, beliefs and ways of life. The representation of the other in Turkish theatre therefore runs parallel to the ideology of the Turkish state. The fundamental problem lies in that ideology and what it produces.




What matters, then, is the emergence of theatre groups that can express their own existence through independent organization, in their own languages and cultures, and according to their own ideological perspectives. Are there examples of this in Turkey? Yes. Has it been done before? Yes. From the Theatre of Action for Revolution to various traditions of political theatre, the dialogue these traditions established with the working class has been extremely important. But what is the situation of the peoples we describe as belonging to other ethnic backgrounds, such as Kurds, Armenians, Abkhazians and Circassians? That is a highly contested issue. Organization, producing art collectively and making art itself a means of organizing are extremely important. Unless you create your own art in your own language and culture, those in power will come and fill that vacuum. And we will have no right to complain about it.''




Uysal continued: "People have paid a price for this in Turkey. The first Kurdish-language theatre productions faced bans and arrests. Singing in Kurdish was likewise prohibited. Today, Kurdish music is somewhat more prominent than our other artistic fields. It has visibility and has established itself. But if we look back about 50 years, there was a period when many melodies from Kurdistan were appropriated, translated into Turkish and marketed as supposedly authentic cultural performances, such as traditional musical gatherings or wedding-style entertainment. Kurdish musical culture has reached its present position through the struggles of hundreds of our institutions and tens of thousands of fellow musicians, including our martyrs, from Ozan Hogir to Delila and many other martyred comrades.




The same can be said of theatre and the theatrical traditions of other peoples. The more productions they create and the more effectively they organize, the more they can break free from being reduced to marginal figures portrayed as ignorant, unclean, backward or associated with the darkest aspects of life. Kurdish life will then find its rightful expression both in society and on stage."




Abdullah Uysal also discussed the role of art in the struggle for peace in the context of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Uysal said: "Democratization is one of Turkey's greatest challenges. Art has a responsibility to help build a world in which we can express ourselves, sustain our own cultural spaces, produce our own art, understand one another and empathize with those who are different from us. We can achieve this through art.




Art has the power to unite. It appeals to emotions. Politics appeals to reason, but art speaks to conscience and feelings. If we have never personally witnessed a guerrilla fighter's mother standing alongside the mother of a Turkish soldier, the only way to understand what that moment feels like is through art. We can convey that experience to both Kurds and Turks through a song or perhaps a theatre performance.




If peace is to come, perhaps it will come through logic, reason and the negotiating table. That is all well and good. But if we are going to discuss how peace between peoples can be achieved, art must fulfill its unifying and healing role and its responsibility to preserve collective memory. This is not simply about saying, 'Let us love one another.' Art is also a way of writing history. We must document what we are experiencing today so that future generations can understand it.




Art has the capacity to heal, empower and preserve collective memory within the Peace and Democratic Society Process. I believe it can make an enormous contribution to the process, provided it is allowed to operate freely."

title: New book documents unique plant diversity in the Hevsel Gardens in Amed
content:
A new scientific book exploring the plant life and ecological diversity of the historic Hevsel Gardens has been presented in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). Titled 

“Species and Habitats – Flora of Hevsel”

(

Türler ve Habitatlar Florası: Hevsel

), the publication is based on years of field research and aims to help document and preserve the city’s natural heritage.




The book launch took place at the Çand Amed Culture and Congress Center. It was organized by the Amed Metropolitan Municipality and the local coordination board of the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB). Attendees included Co-Mayor Emin Ay, City Council Co-Chair Dilan Aydın, scientists and representatives of TMMOB.







Years of research into the plant life of the Hevsel Gardens




The Hevsel Gardens stretch between Amed’s historic city walls and the Tigris River. As part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Diyarbakır Fortress and Hevsel Gardens Cultural Landscape,” they hold both cultural, historical and ecological significance.




The new book examines the vegetation and botanical diversity of this cultural landscape. Prof. Dr. A. Selçuk Ertekin and Dr. Zeki Kanay played particularly important roles in the scientific research. title: Gülengül: The state protects capital and considers it its duty to do so
content:
The explosion that occurred on Monday at the HABAŞ Iron and Steel Factory in İzmir’s Aliağa district, killing 19 workers and injuring 11 others, has once again brought workplace deaths in Turkey into the spotlight. According to the monthly report published by the Workers’ Health and Work Safety Assembly (İSİG), 193 workers lost their lives in work-related incidents in October alone.




İSİG’s periodic reports indicate that at least six workers die in workplace incidents every day in Turkey on average. Despite these deaths, the government continues to ignore warnings rather than ensure workers’ health and safe working conditions.




Seyfettin Gülengül, a member of the Labor Commission of the DEM Party’s Istanbul Provincial Organization, spoke to ANF about the underlying causes of workplace deaths, which have once again come to public attention following the deadly incident at the HABAŞ factory.




‘An average of six workers die every day’




Gülengül stated: “First of all, it must be pointed out that an average of six workers die in workplace incidents every day in Turkey. Let us look at the fatal workplace accidents that have occurred at the HABAŞ Iron and Steel Factory and its port facilities in İzmir’s Aliağa district over the years.




November 16, 2007:

 İlyas Kırdı was killed and ten others were injured when an artillery shell exploded during scrap sorting operations.




August 24, 2008:

 Kutbettin Özkaya lost his life after being crushed beneath a 2.5-ton iron block that slipped from a crane.




2013:

 Two separate accidents occurred within a month, claiming the lives of Olgar Öner, who was killed when a cable snapped, and Engin Solmaz, who was electrocuted.




April 27, 2017 (Kocaeli):

 Nail Demirci was killed in an explosion involving an LPG tanker.




July 26, 2018:

 Evren Erik was seriously injured in an explosion at a steel furnace and died on August 3.




2018:

 Hasan Bostancı lost his life after falling from a dust collection chimney.




August 14, 2020:

 Subcontracted worker Şaban Karaca was killed after becoming trapped between steel blocks.




October 7, 2020:

 Kadir Özdemir fell to his death while working at height without a safety line.




November 6, 2020:

 Port worker Raif Çatan, who was not equipped with a life jacket, fell into the sea and drowned.




August 28, 2022:

 Oktay Eryılmaz died in hospital after falling from a crane.




January 11, 2024:

 Kemal Özdemir was killed when a metal coil fell on him.




October 21, 2026:

 Hakan Doğan fell to his death from a height of eight meters while working on a ladder.




November 5, 2026:

 Eyüp Eğinli lost his life when a tire on a piece of heavy machinery exploded.




November 9, 2026:

 Eighteen workers were killed and 15 others injured when an overhead crane broke loose, triggering an explosion.




So, are all these factories not inspected? They are. In fact, reports are prepared on many of them. However, there is a fundamental problem: Occupational health and safety specialists are paid by the employers receiving their services, meaning the companies or institutions themselves. That is how the law works.”




‘The state protects capital’




Gülengül stated that the government protects capital, saying, “The state protects capital and considers it its duty to do so. It sides with the powerful under the pretext that investors create employment.”




Referring to the Labor Minister’s remarks, Gülengül continued: “Why did the minister speak this way? Let us recall that statements such as ‘Death is inherent in the nature of this work’ or ‘Accidents are inherent in its nature’ were made by the then Prime Minister following the mining disaster on May 13, 2014, in the Soma district of Manisa, which claimed the lives of 301 miners. The same mentality and the same government are still in power today. That is how I interpret the minister’s remarks.”




‘We must have a greater say in the democratization of the country’




Seyfettin Gülengül stated that the DEM Party has been working on the issue of workplace deaths for years: “As the DEM Party, we have stood in solidarity with the families of workers who have lost their lives for years, just as we have in many other areas, and we have stood alongside them on the ground. Our parliamentary representatives also raise these problems, legal shortcomings and injustices in parliament. However, as I have said, correcting certain laws, regulations and similar issues requires the democratization of the country and greater participation in decision-making on our part.”

title: Telling life stories, preserving names in Qandil - III
content:
Martyr Taylan left behind seven or eight notebooks and numerous poems. In one of his notebooks, he had also written a note addressed to whoever might one day edit his writings: “I just write. I write without any particular order. I hope the person who edits this later won't be upset with me. This was all I could do. I could have chosen not to write anything at all. But I felt it was my duty, and that is why I wrote.”




Munzur Diyar, a member of the Martyrs' Studies Committee whom we met in Qandil, said that he came across these lines when Taylan's diaries reached the committee. Diyar and his comrades collect notebooks, letters, photographs and testimonies left behind by guerrillas, preparing some of them for publication as books. However, not every completed work reaches readers.




“Tell our child’s story too”




Families have repeatedly criticized the committee’s television programs. Diyar recounts how relatives pointed out that while the programs featured the life stories of certain guerrilla fighters, their own family members, who had lost their lives many years earlier, were overlooked. They asked: “Our children also lost their lives years ago. Why aren’t there any programs about them?”




In response to this criticism, the committee changed its approach. Whereas individuals had previously been selected for the broadcasts, the committee decided to present the life stories of martyrs in chronological order from then on.













Documenting the lives of 700 martyrs




The idea for this program came from a young guerrilla who had never known his father. His father had joined the PKK (Kurdistan Workers' Party) six months before he was born. When the young man was around 21 or 22, he proposed preparing a program documenting the lives of martyrs individually. He continued this work for approximately ten years, producing programs about the lives of nearly 700 martyrs.




The program covered the lives of those who died in 2012, beginning with the first month of the year and proceeding chronologically. Diyar said that once they completed 2012, they moved on to 2013 and planned to continue with subsequent years. Rather than selecting particular individuals for programs, they aim to document as many lives as possible.




Diyar said that the committee also prepares radio broadcasts and written works alongside its television programs. However, the committee places particular importance on diaries written by guerrillas themselves and memoirs they wrote about one another. These account for a significant proportion of the texts the committee is working to publish as books.













Preparing biographies




Diyar said that the committee holds approximately 1,700 diaries that could be published as books. Some are only 20 or 30 pages long and are being prepared for publication alongside the diaries of other martyrs. Others are long enough to fill several volumes on their own. Taylan's notebooks are among these works.




The committee also began preparing biographies of guerrillas who fell after 2020. According to Diyar, their latest plans involve expanding this work to cover everyone, with the aim of documenting each person's life story as far as their research resources allow.




Building a digital archive




Publishing the diaries requires a considerable amount of work. Diyar explained that the writings cannot simply be printed as they are. They must first be edited and organized into a readable format. Yet even when the texts are ready for publication, their distribution is not guaranteed. The committee has been able to publish some of the works in Europe, while obstacles have prevented their publication in Turkey.




For this reason, committee members have begun building a digital archive intended to be accessible to anyone interested. They plan to publish both the books and other materials from their collection on a website that has not yet been launched. However, disagreements have arisen with publishers who insist that the books should be printed before being made available digitally.




“Publishers may want to print and sell books. But that is not what matters to us. Our primary goal is for the people to learn about the martyrs. Once the texts are published, anyone who wishes to print them is welcome to do so.”




Memorials for those without graves




The graves in the cemeteries of Qandil and other areas account for only a small proportion of those who have lost their lives in the course of the armed struggle. “We are talking about 27,000 martyrs. If we count all the graves in our cemeteries, the total comes to around 2,000.” The figures cited by Diyar are based on the committee’s own records. The burial sites of some of the others are known, but their remains have not yet been repatriated. Others have never been found. There are also those buried in mass graves, such as Newala Qesaba.




The committee therefore plans to establish dedicated memorial areas in the cemeteries for those whose graves either do not exist or are inaccessible. Space for these memorials has already been allocated in the cemetery designs. At the center, there will be a collective monument dedicated to all those who have fallen. Around it, committee members intend to erect smaller memorial stones bearing the names and personal details of each person. Photographs will also be displayed where available.




Before the project can be implemented, however, the committee must determine which individuals already have known graves, whose remains can still be recovered and transferred, and whose burial sites remain permanently untraceable.




“We are going through each area one by one, documenting who lost their lives there. We are trying to establish precisely who has a grave and who does not, and whose remains we can recover and transfer. After that, we want to build a memorial, as we have already done for Comrade Dorşîn.”













Dorşîn is among the martyrs whose remains could not be recovered. During a visit to the cemetery, her family planted a tree in her memory. The committee later erected a symbolic grave marker for Dorşîn beside the tree her mother had planted.




Öcalan spoke not of their deaths, but of their lives




The committee also compiles speeches and reflections by Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan concerning the martyrs. According to Diyar, this material has already been compiled into a two-volume publication, with work underway on further volumes. To explain Öcalan’s approach to commemorating the martyrs, Diyar looks back to the years in Ankara when the PKK first began taking shape as a political group. He noted that Öcalan linked the struggle to the remembrance of martyrs from the very beginning.




This account begins with Fevzi Aslansoy, a student from Suruç. In Öcalan’s narrative, subsequent milestones in the PKK’s organizational development are also linked to the commemoration of martyrs. The transformation into a political party is associated with Haki Karer, the establishment of a guerrilla army with Mahsum Korkmaz, and the emergence of the free women’s movement with the memories of Zîlan and Berîtan.




“Leader Öcalan guided the PKK as a party of the martyrs. When families asked in the early years where the bodies of their loved ones were, he told them: ‘Do not believe that they are dead. They live on in the PKK.’




“From the very beginning, the leader never placed the deaths of martyrs at the center of its narrative. Instead, he always spoke about how they had lived. How did they struggle? What distinguished their struggle? What did they hope to achieve? These were the questions the leader explored, seeking to make their dreams a reality.”













“We must preserve their memory across generations”




Diyar also referred to a statement by Öcalan in notes received from the prison island of Imrali. “He says: ‘How I wish I could memorize the names of every single martyr and keep them all in my memory.’ Through these words, the leader expresses his desire to keep the martyrs alive in his memory.” For the committee members, these words have become a mission: “We must preserve the memory of all martyrs. Not just today, but across generations. We must give them a place in Kurdistan’s collective memory.”




Turning grief into strength for the struggle




As our conversation draws to a close, we return once again to the deaths announced most recently. These losses, which some families learned about only years later, are by no means a thing of the past for the committee members either. Diyar connects the grief of losing comrades with the responsibility to continue pursuing their goals.




“Losing someone is painful. The grief of losing someone you have struggled alongside runs very deep. But we try to turn the pain of losing each and every person into strength for the struggle. Drawing strength from them, we strive to fulfill their goals.” Diyar addresses these words not only to the committee members. He believes that everyone, particularly the families and loved ones of the martyrs, has a role to play.




“The slogan ‘Şehîd namirin’ – ‘The martyrs are immortal’ – does not, in itself, make them immortal. Their immortality lies in the creation of an organized and free society. To the extent that we build such a society, we keep their memory alive. And to the extent that we organize a democratic society based on the legacy of the martyrs and in accordance with the leader’s paradigm, we fulfill our responsibility toward them.”













To the families in the mourning houses




About two months ago, I spoke with families in the mourning houses of Batman, Amed (Diyarbakır) and Şırnak. During these visits, I encountered many questions. The mothers I spoke with wanted to know why they had received no news for years. They wondered what their children had experienced in the final days of their lives, where and with whom they had lost their lives, and whether they had a grave.




This series emerged from those encounters in the mourning houses, from the families’ accounts and from the questions that continued to weigh on their minds. Across its three parts, we have tried to find answers to some of these questions and understand why others remain unanswered to this day.




At the end of the interview, my thoughts return once again to those mothers. What I have heard in Qandil has shown me how far back the history behind the questions raised in the mourning houses extends, and how difficult the search for answers can be. I conclude this investigation reflecting on the challenging conditions under which people are searching for the answers these families await, and on how difficult it can be not only to wait for those answers, but also, ultimately, to hear them.




The undocumented deaths during the self-governance period




To this day, there are no comprehensive records of all those who lost their lives during the fighting that followed the declarations of self-governance, particularly in Cizre, Silopi and Sur. Diyar speaks of families searching for the names of relatives who died during that period. However, the committee itself does not have complete information either.




He explicitly emphasizes that not everyone involved in the fighting was a member of the guerrilla forces. They included members of the youth movement, as well as civilians and people who lost their lives in their own neighborhoods or homes. Because the committee had no direct presence in these areas, documenting their identities and personal details proved particularly difficult.













“We were unable to establish a properly organized archive. We did not have a complete picture of who had lost their lives and who had survived,” Diyar said. Subsequent investigations identified numerous people whose names were then made public. A website was also established to commemorate those who lost their lives during this period. It includes not only guerrilla fighters but also children and elderly people.




Nevertheless, not all those who died could be identified. Diyar referred particularly to those who lost their lives in collapsed buildings and basements that were set on fire. The committee is working to complete its existing records using information it receives and inquiries from relatives. However, Diyar believes that some names are still missing.




Apê Hesen’s garden




Among those involved in selecting the current location of the cemetery in Qandil was Apê (Uncle) Hesen. A father of ten from Siverek, he had come into contact with the PKK in 1979 during the clashes between Hilvan and Siverek. Two of his children later lost their lives in the fighting.




Hesen lived in Istanbul for many years before moving to Russia. At the age of 56, he joined the PKK and arrived in Qandil in the early 2000s. Due to his age, he mostly stayed in one place, where he could look after arriving guests. When discussions began in 2006 about where to establish a new cemetery for the martyrs, Hesen was among those who proposed the present site. Once the decision had been made, however, he did not simply point out the location. He also took part in the construction work himself.




Diyar recalls that Hesen was already over seventy at the time. During the day, he worked alongside his younger comrades, and in the evenings, he sang songs for them. He paid attention to the well-being of those working at the construction site and made sure they were in good spirits.




Hesen carried a camera with him. He photographed the guerrilla fighters involved in building the cemetery and tried to interview them. He wanted to know what they thought and felt, and how they would later remember the days they had spent at that place.













“He also wanted the people who worked here to have a place in history. He tried to capture the feelings of the guerrillas. He had never attended school, but he had a remarkable understanding of people. He asked questions like someone who had been working as a journalist for seventy years.”




Hesen also created a garden near the cemetery. He planted trees and grew roses. Sometimes, he would get up as early as three in the morning to water the flowers. He tended his garden himself and never neglected the flowers in the cemetery either.




In the final years of his life, Hesen underwent treatment for cancer. He had told his comrades that he wanted to be buried in his own garden after his death. When Hesen died in 2010, they initially decided to bury him in the cemetery. They began digging a grave but encountered solid rock beneath the ground. They tried again in another location, only to find rock beneath the soil there as well.




After several unsuccessful attempts, they remembered Hesen’s final wish. In the end, they buried Apê Hesen in his own garden.




This report by Rengin Azizoğlu was originally published in the newspaper Yeni Özgür Politika.

title: Women in Arzoxlî protest against delivery of solar panels
content:
The dispute over the construction of two solar power plants is escalating in the village of Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır). Although an administrative court has temporarily suspended the implementation of the Zenkar-2 project, preparations for the neighboring Zenkar-1 project are continuing. On the 23rd day of a protest vigil against the construction work, trucks delivered solar panels intended for the project to the site.




In response to the delivery, women from Arzoxlî gathered in the village square and marched together toward the construction site. Chanting slogans such as “Excavator operators, get off our grazing land,” “Axa me ava me hebûna me ye” (Our land and water are our existence), “Resistance leads to victory” and “No to companies in Arzoxlî,” they protested against the continuation of the project.













Soldiers block access to construction site




On their way to the project site, the villagers were stopped by Turkish gendarmerie. The soldiers blocked their access and prevented them from proceeding any further. The protesters expressed their anger at the soldiers’ actions.

title: Three ISIS members killed in Pirde
content:
Iraqi security forces killed three suspected members of the Islamic State (ISIS) and arrested another suspect during a military operation in Pirde, in Kirkuk province, on Friday evening. The Iraqi Security Media Cell announced the operation, citing the Armed Forces High Command.




The operation took place at around 8 p.m. local time, based on intelligence gathered by military intelligence. After detecting the movements of a suspected ISIS group, Iraqi army aviation units carried out an airstrike on the group’s location. The operation was conducted within the area of responsibility of the 32nd Infantry Brigade of the 8th Division.




Before the airstrike, security forces had blocked access roads to Pirde and deployed additional military vehicles to the area. Gunfire and explosions were reported in the surrounding area. According to Iraqi authorities, a man suspected of transporting the three people who were killed was also arrested. Searches of the operation area initially continued.




The operation is part of a series of Iraqi military operations targeting remaining ISIS networks in Kirkuk province. As recently as November 9, Iraqi fighter jets struck suspected ISIS positions in the Zaytun Valley, destroying an underground hideout. title: TJK-E: We will stop femicide and wars through organised struggle
content:
The Coordination of the Kurdish Women's Movement in Europe (TJK-E) released a statement on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.




Calling for stronger organizing and collective political resistance, TJK-E warned of increasing violence against women, criticized the militarization of European societies and called for a determined confrontation with patriarchal power structures. It also urged women’s organizations and anti-war movements to actively support the peace and democratic society process. The full statement by TJK-E Coordination reads as follows:




Violence against women is increasing worldwide




“We are living through a historic moment marked by profound transformations and multiple crises. We stand at a crossroads where the old order is collapsing and the new has yet to emerge. At such historic turning points, politics and organized action take on far greater meaning and importance. With this awareness, as we mark November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, we must strengthen our organization and make our political power more effective.




Violence against women, which we regard as the longest war in history, is not decreasing but continues to intensify. Worldwide, 840 million women and girls are affected by male violence. According to official figures, at least 83,000 women and girls were killed by men in 2024. We know that the actual number is significantly higher. In countries such as Germany, France and Italy, a woman is killed by her partner or former partner every three days. In France, 61 percent of the women murdered last year had previously contacted the police and sought help. In Germany, a woman experiences violence at the hands of her partner every four minutes. Violence against women occurs predominantly not on the streets or in the workplace, but within their own homes.




Statistics on sexual and digital violence, as well as misogynistic attacks, also show a worrying increase. At the same time, there is a growing number of cases in which men drug their wives and hand them over to other men to be raped, as in the Pelicot case in France. These cases reveal the horrifying extent of rape culture. As TJK-E, we too declare: Shame must change sides! It is not the survivors who should feel ashamed, but the perpetrators. They must be held publicly accountable, their crimes exposed and punished. Every form of violence against women must have consequences!




Combating patriarchal violence within Kurdish society as well




Violence against women within Kurdish society in Europe has also reached a level that we must describe as femicide. In Germany alone, three Kurdish women have been deliberately murdered in the past two months by men from whom they had separated. This selfish, ruthless and murderous mentality, which regards women as property, refuses to recognize their independent will and does not even hesitate to deprive its own children of their mothers, poses a threat to society as a whole.




There can be no justification for violence against women, especially femicide. The fundamental problem is the culture of male domination. We will intensify our efforts to combat this life-destroying culture, which produces perpetrators and takes human lives, and to foster a culture of equal and free coexistence, as well as a democratic family culture.




Both in our homeland of Kurdistan and in Europe, where we live today, we feel the profound social upheavals arising from the multiple crises of capitalist modernity. The global hegemonic powers are once again attempting to dismantle the old order through war and destruction and establish a new one. At no point since the Second World War has so much been invested in wars or so much money spent on weapons. Never before have European governments so openly diverted public funds into the pockets of the arms industry and paved the way for militarism in order to prepare their societies for war.




Women must actively shape the peace process




As Kurdish people, we know very well what war means. For 200 years, we have been fighting for our existence and freedom against the genocidal regime of capitalist modernity. Today, we are striving to pave the way for a transition from armed conflict to democratic and legal struggle. At a time when sabers are rattling across the world, Abdullah Öcalan has initiated a historic process through his Call for Peace and Democratic Society, aimed at permanently eliminating the underlying causes of war and armed conflict.




Both his manifesto and his theory of democratic integration offer not only a roadmap for a peaceful, political and just resolution of the Kurdish question, but also a society-centered alternative for overcoming the current systemic crisis. While the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1325, which aims to ensure women’s active participation in peace processes, continues to fall far short of its objectives, Abdullah Öcalan places women’s freedom at the heart of his philosophy of peace and regards women as independent actors in negotiations.




On the occasion of November 25, we, as TJK-E, call on all women’s organizations and anti-war movements in Europe to embrace and actively support the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Let us, as women, express our collective determination to achieve genuine and just peace. Let us not allow war, genocide or policies of occupation!




Patriarchal domination as the common root of violence and war




War is the most extreme form of male-dominated state violence. It is directed against life, nature and society. Violence against women, wars and genocides share the same roots. The concept of the “caste-based social murderer,” developed by Abdullah Öcalan, highlights this connection. Drawing on Buddha’s metaphor of the “dagger in the back,” he emphasizes that defending life and society requires a radical struggle against this murderous structure of domination embedded in society.




This “dagger in the back” represents the unresolved question of women’s liberation and hegemonic masculinity. As long as it remains, none of the other fundamental problems facing society can be resolved. The struggle against violence against women must therefore place the mentality and system of this murderous patriarchal domination at its center. It must address the social and historical roots of violence and adopt a holistic perspective.




In this spirit, we call on governments to fully meet their legal and practical obligations. At the same time, as a women’s movement, we reaffirm our commitment to actively driving social change and transformation. We also call on all organized men to free themselves from sexist and patriarchal patterns of thought and actively work toward relationships based on equality and freedom. The transformation of men must be recognized as a fundamental question of freedom and made the focus of a conscious political struggle.




Attacks on the women’s revolution in Kurdistan




Violence against women must not be viewed merely as a series of isolated assaults. We are confronting a systematic war of aggression driven by patriarchal mindsets and structures of domination. In our homeland of Kurdistan, which has become a source of inspiration for women and oppressed peoples worldwide through the women-led revolutionary struggle of recent years, hegemonic masculinity has launched a comprehensive and organized counteroffensive.




The attacks on the achievements of the women’s revolution in Rojava and northeastern Syria, the continued captivity of 2,700 Yazidi women from Shengal who were abducted and enslaved by the so-called Islamic State (ISIS) in 2014, and the threats of execution against women who led the uprising under the slogan “Jin Jiyan Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom] in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan are concrete manifestations of this same global war.




No woman should face violence alone




Every attack on Kurdish women, their collective achievements and their political will is a reason for us to continue the struggle. On the occasion of November 25, we call on all organized women in Europe to strengthen solidarity and collective resistance on the basis of “Jin Jiyan Azadî.” Let us fight together against femicide and systematic violence against women!




The only way to stop all forms of patriarchal and state violence is to strengthen women’s organizing and political power. The more organized we are as women, the more we can develop our awareness, forge a common will, take a collective stand against patriarchal mindsets and create solutions together.




As TJK-E, we therefore call on all Kurdish women in Europe to organize and confront male violence collectively, on a communalist basis.




Now is the time for women




No woman whose life is under threat should have to face her struggles alone. As women, we must above all act with care and a sense of responsibility toward one another. We must never turn a blind eye, remain silent or stand idly by in the face of violence.




As women’s movements, we also have a responsibility to make our struggle against the daily rise in femicide and patriarchal violence more effective at both the social and political levels. By developing and putting into practice a politics of women’s liberation, we must confront every form of attack on women’s existence. At the same time, we must gradually shape and build the free life we seek to achieve.




At a time when the patriarchal and state-centered order is plunging societies into destruction, violence and war, we therefore declare: Now is the time for women! Let us build a free life, a dignified peace and a democratic social order!”

title: Women Defend Rojava launches new campaign phase in Germany
content:
At a meeting last weekend, the Women Defend Rojava campaign discussed its future activities in Germany and launched a new phase of its work. In light of political developments in Syria and the growing threats to the achievements of the women’s revolution in Rojava, the activists intend to expand their information and solidarity efforts. Their first major initiative will be a month of action dedicated to feminist self-defense, centered around the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.




According to the campaign, the discussions were based on a comprehensive assessment of the political and social situation in northeastern Syria. The activists pointed to the increasing impoverishment of the population and the persistent threat posed by Islamist groups, including the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS). Under these circumstances, they stressed, international efforts to defend the women’s revolution are particularly important.




Bringing the experiences of Rojava to wider society
