title: The Third World War, the Middle East and the Kurds
content:
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, Britain, the United States and Israel developed a strategy under the concept of the “New World Order,” aimed at restructuring the international system in the interests of global capital. The conflict that began with the war against Iraq in the 1990s continues to this day and has grown increasingly intense, widespread and complex through successive phases. One of the central objectives of this Third World War was to dismantle the Kurdish freedom movement, resolve the Palestinian question in line with hegemonic interests, and reorganize the Middle East under Israeli dominance and the control of the principal hegemonic power.




To prevent the expansion and further development of the Kurdish freedom movement and ultimately bring about its destruction, a federal Kurdish entity was established in Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq). In doing so, the powers involved relied on both local collaborationist forces and the states among which Kurdistan has been divided. However, despite all the plots directed against the freedom movement and Abdullah Öcalan, they failed to achieve the objectives pursued through this war.




The geopolitical pressures behind Turkey’s strategic reorientation




The failure of the strategy aimed at dismantling the Kurdish freedom movement was not the only factor that prompted the Turkish state to seek new political options. Other developments following Hamas’s attack on Israel on October 7 also played a role: Israeli military operations in the Gaza Strip and Lebanon, the resulting weakening of Hamas and Hezbollah, the escalation of tensions with Iran into open warfare, and the restructuring of international energy and trade routes, which saw Cyprus included in relevant agreements while Turkey was left out. These developments forced the Turkish state to reconsider its previous strategic orientation.




Another significant factor was the resistance developed by the Kurdish freedom movement under Abdullah Öcalan’s leadership, characterized by a far-reaching willingness to make sacrifices. Without this resistance, the changing regional balance of power alone would not have prompted the Turkish state to undertake such a strategic shift. It was only the combination of geopolitical developments and the struggle waged in Kurdistan that compelled the Turkish leadership to respond to Abdullah Öcalan’s approach to initiating a new political process and to issue a corresponding appeal to him.




The nation-state order in the Middle East is being shaken




The military and political upheavals in the region also caused considerable concern within the Turkish leadership. These include the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran, the change of power in Syria that saw Baathist rule replaced by a Sunni-dominated government, and the resulting weakening of the so-called Shia Crescent. At the same time, the nation-state order in the Middle East, rooted in the Sykes-Picot Agreement, became increasingly unstable and was called into question even by the dominant powers themselves. These uncertainties were further heightened by the perception that the hegemonic actors were considering partly divergent approaches to resolving the Kurdish question.




With Israel’s growing hegemonic influence, its increasing capacity for military intervention across the region and the extensive support it receives from the United States, these developments came to be perceived by Turkey as an existential threat to the survival of the state. Against this backdrop, the fact that the political resolution process continues to this day and that Abdullah Öcalan remains recognized as a negotiating partner can largely be attributed to the Turkish leadership’s security concerns and fears for the state’s very existence.




The Third World War, which began in the Middle East and particularly in Kurdistan, has gradually spread to other regions of the world. The collapse of the Soviet Union brought an end to the bipolar world order, prompting the United States to develop a strategy aimed at controlling the Middle East and establishing its unchallenged global hegemony. Despite various crises, the US largely succeeded in securing its dominant position through the support and involvement of cooperating governments. In recent years, however, the People’s Republic of China and Russia have steadily expanded their international influence. Their rise as major economic and military hegemonic powers, along with their growing presence in the Middle East, Latin America and Africa, has significantly intensified the contradictions and tensions within the capitalist hegemonic system.




Trade and energy corridors as instruments of hegemonic competition




These confrontations gained further momentum with the Belt and Road Initiative launched by China, also known as the New Silk Road. The project aims to establish extensive energy and trade links stretching from the Far East through Central Asia, the Middle East, the Caucasus and Ukraine to Eastern Europe, and from there to other parts of Europe. One of the objectives pursued by bringing about the war between Russia and Ukraine was to undermine this Chinese infrastructure and trade project and permanently destabilize the transport routes involved. At the same time, drawing Russia into a protracted war was intended to weaken it militarily and economically.




As a geopolitical counterproject to China’s Silk Road Initiative, the United States launched the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC). This economic and infrastructure corridor is intended to facilitate trade and energy connections from India through the Arab states and Israel, and then via Cyprus and Greece to Europe. Turkey is not included in either project. Iran, too, is excluded from IMEC under the current political circumstances. Against this backdrop, Hamas’s attack on Israel on October 7 must also be viewed in the context of the geopolitical interests of Iran and Turkey, as well as the competing international trade and energy corridors.




The global struggle for resources and spheres of influence




Another manifestation of this Third World War can be seen in developments in Venezuela, which exports a substantial share of its oil to China. In disregard of all norms of international law, Nicolás Maduro was abducted during a military operation and taken to the United States. The new government was subordinated to American interests, while control was seized over the country’s energy and raw material resources. Through these actions, the United States sought to weaken China economically, expand its own trade opportunities and bring international energy markets under its control. Efforts to bring about regime change in Iran and establish a government dependent on Washington, as well as attempts to control the strategically important Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, are also part of this hegemonic power struggle. The Abraham Accords concluded between Israel and several Arab states must be understood within the same geopolitical context. At the same time, regional powers such as Turkey are attempting to exploit the contradictions within the existing system to advance their own interests and gain political advantages from the shifting balance of power.




Although the underlying causes of these developments are by no means new, current political, economic and diplomatic relations, as well as existing contradictions, conflicts and wars, continue to unfold on this basis. The interconnected global conflicts understood as the Third World War therefore cannot be examined independently of the continued failure to resolve the Palestinian and Kurdish questions, the change of power in Syria, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, the political crises and civil wars in numerous African countries, or interventions across the American continent. Rather, these developments must be understood as interconnected manifestations of a global struggle for hegemony.




The Mecca Agreement in NATO’s strategic calculations




The so-called Mecca Agreement between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia must also be viewed as an expression of the alliance-building that has become necessary in the context of the Third World War. It can be assumed that this agreement was reached with NATO’s knowledge and in accordance with its strategic requirements. Otherwise, it would be difficult to imagine the United States accepting the emergence and strengthening of such a military-political alliance in a region as geopolitically significant as the Middle East without objection. Rather, the United States will seek to use this alliance to advance its own interests against the Shia power bloc led by Iran, as well as against the growing influence of Russia and China in the region. In this way, it aims to shape existing regional contradictions in favor of American hegemonic interests. If necessary, the alliance could also serve as a political and military instrument for advancing these interests. Particularly in light of the escalating tensions between Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which are now also affecting trade routes in the Red Sea, there are indications of an intention to involve this alliance more extensively in military confrontations.




Turkey, for its part, will seek to derive its own advantages from this situation and safeguard its security position. Its strategic calculations will be largely shaped by the repeatedly invoked concern over the survival of the state. On this basis, Turkey is also likely to seek an understanding with Israel in order to expand and consolidate its position as a regional power over the long term.




Elections in the US and Israel: Public takes a stand against war policies




The crises and wars generated by the global hegemonic system in its pursuit of maximum profits have now reached a scale where their consequences are increasingly affecting the populations of the hegemonic states themselves. The economic burdens resulting from these wars, along with the accompanying anti-democratic practices, have fueled public discontent, intensified opposition to military conflicts and sparked resistance to authoritarian governance. These developments have found political expression in both the United States and Israel. In Israel’s parliamentary elections on October 27, the governing bloc led by Benjamin Netanyahu suffered significant losses. Its parliamentary representation fell from 64 seats in the 2022 election to 53, leaving it well short of the 61 seats required for a governing majority. The election results have thus made it considerably more difficult for Netanyahu to form another government.




The results of the elections held in the United States on November 3 also reflect this social development. The public has taken a stand against war policies while making it clear that it will not accept an authoritarian approach to governance that disregards its interests and needs. Following his electoral defeat, Donald Trump will no longer be able to push through his political agenda in Congress, particularly in the House of Representatives, to the same extent as before.




The social consequences of the war economy




Before the elections, Trump had promised the American people that he would not start any new wars and would bring existing military conflicts to an end. Instead of fulfilling these promises, however, the United States joined Israel in attacks against Iran, triggering a war that has now been ongoing for months. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the sanctions imposed on Russia have led to a worldwide increase in energy prices. Both European industry and the American population have been significantly affected. Inflationary pressures have intensified in the United States. At the same time, Europe’s share of NATO expenditures has been increased, placing additional strain on the economic and social living conditions of the European population.




While the ongoing wars have boosted the profits of arms manufacturers, they have also further accelerated the international arms race. Trump’s arbitrary handling of tariffs and his policies toward the United States’ traditional allies have also drawn growing criticism within American society. This dissatisfaction was reflected in substantial losses of votes in the elections. The Republican Party’s losses in Congress, particularly in the House of Representatives, will inevitably restrict Trump’s political room for maneuver. As a result of the election results, he is increasingly being perceived as a so-called lame duck, a politically weakened president. Although the American president holds extensive powers, particularly in foreign policy, Trump will no longer be able to exercise them with the same degree of political independence as before.




Trump will also no longer be able to pursue his previous policy toward Europe, which largely disregards European states and is characterized by a patronizing and coercive approach, with the same degree of ruthlessness. However, this does not necessarily mean that these developments will lead to democratic progress or that American policy is on the verge of fundamental change. Nevertheless, there is a discernible opposition among the population to the policies of the capitalist system, which, if effectively organized, could bring about far-reaching political changes. Peace-oriented social forces and democratic movements also exist in Israel.




Democratic counter-movements and social opposition in Europe




In Europe, meanwhile, efforts to fuel nationalist attitudes and anti-immigrant sentiment have been accompanied by the emergence of social counter-movements. At the same time, resistance is growing against the economic and political crises caused by the ongoing wars. Recent developments in various countries thus demonstrate that new social conditions conducive to strengthening democratic movements are emerging worldwide. The end of Orbán’s government in Hungary, the significant electoral successes of the student movement in Serbia, and the growing protest movements in European countries such as France, Germany and Italy are all expressions of this development. In particular, democratic mobilizations, protests by students and workers, and the struggles of environmental and feminist movements demonstrate that the anti-democratic practices and war policies of the capitalist system continue to face sustained social resistance.




These developments also make it clear that the emergence of a broad political movement capable of bringing about far-reaching democratic change is by no means an unrealistic prospect. This would require the various opposition forces, student and women’s movements, as well as left-wing, socialist and social democratic currents, to unite in a common struggle. The social potential for democratic change in Europe is therefore far from exhausted. People remain capable of voicing democratic demands and fighting for their rights. If sustainable organizational structures can be established on the basis of a democratic understanding of society, and existing discontent can be transformed into collective political action, there is a real possibility of developing an effective and sustained movement of social resistance. It is precisely the prospect of such an organized democratic counterforce that causes concern among Europe’s ruling powers.




From armed struggle to a democratic-political strategy




Against the backdrop of these global and regional developments, the ongoing wars, Israel’s growing cooperation with Greece and the Republic of Cyprus in the Mediterranean, and Israeli interventions in Palestine, Lebanon, Iran and Syria, MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli concluded that Turkey, too, was facing an existential threat to its national security and survival. Following Bahçeli’s appeal in the Turkish parliament in October 2024, Abdullah Öcalan took the initiative, formulated his Call for Peace and Democratic Society, published in February 2025, and thereby ushered in a new phase of political struggle.




In developing this new strategy, Abdullah Öcalan took into account both the dangers posed by the current geopolitical situation and the outcomes of a struggle spanning 52 years. In his assessment, the existence of the Kurdish people had by then been secured, while a point had also been reached where continuing the armed struggle could no longer yield fundamentally new achievements. From this, he concluded that a strategic reorientation was necessary. Since then, the central conviction has been that national and social freedom can be achieved through a determined democratic-political struggle and the organization of society on a communal basis. Through this strategic approach, Öcalan also seeks to overcome the recurring patterns of political and military action that have persisted since 1993.




The Turkish state and the AKP government also came to recognize that a military defeat of the Kurdish freedom movement was unattainable and that the current regional and international balance of power was not conducive to such a strategy. They therefore regarded the initiation of a new political process at this juncture as necessary to serve their own interests. Despite their efforts to delay the process, weaken the Kurdish freedom movement and render it politically ineffective by prolonging the process, as well as their continued intention to dismantle it when a more favorable opportunity arises, Abdullah Öcalan remains committed to his approach. His efforts are aimed at thwarting the strategies of pro-war forces and paving the way for a political solution in the interests of the peoples.




Democratic integration as the foundation of a democratic society




In this context, the approach of democratic integration developed by Abdullah Öcalan must be understood as a strategic vision for a solution aimed at freeing humanity from the constraints imposed by the hegemonic power struggles of the capitalist system. It also reflects an effort to enable peoples to reconnect with their own historically rooted and socially embedded values and, on this basis, create the conditions for democratic coexistence.




Despite the policies of isolation, denial of his existence, erasure of collective identities and imposition of various forms of genocidal violence directed against him, Abdullah Öcalan has developed a vision of social liberation for the Kurdish people and the oppressed sections of humanity through the paradigm of a democratic-communal society. In doing so, he has also outlined a possible way out of the current social and political crises. The attacks on Rojava, which target Öcalan’s concept of the democratic nation and the democratic confederal system, must also be viewed against this backdrop. While the concept of the democratic nation offers an alternative to the nation-state order, which has turned the world into an arena of perpetual violence and destruction, the democratic confederal system is intended to enable all peoples and religious communities living in the region to freely express their collective identities and social ways of life. The deliberate targeting of these approaches in Rojava as part of the strategic plans of the capitalist hegemonic powers must therefore be understood as part of a broader struggle over the social and political order of the region.




Rojava and the struggle over alternative models of society




The continued provocative attacks on the alternative social order that still exists in Rojava, despite its now considerably reduced territorial extent, the refusal to shape the integration process on a democratic basis, and the ongoing occupation of civilian residential areas by armed groups are all manifestations of the continuation of this policy. The aim is to reinforce the notion that peaceful coexistence among different peoples and religious communities is impossible and that security and social stability can only be guaranteed by a centralized nation-state. At the same time, various forms of political and military violence are being employed to strengthen nationalist currents within Kurdish society and undermine confidence in the social paradigm developed by Abdullah Öcalan.




The political obstruction of the peace process




A similar strategy is also being directed against the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish freedom movement seek to advance in Northern Kurdistan and Turkey. A wide range of methods are being employed to undermine coexistence among peoples who have shared a common social history for centuries and to destroy the foundations of their peaceful coexistence. At the same time, deliberate provocations are being used to destabilize the political process and ultimately bring about its failure. The capitalist hegemonic system and those who uphold the mentality of domination underpinning it continually resort to methods of special warfare to prevent Abdullah Öcalan’s efforts to build a democratic society from producing tangible results.




The political stance of the Turkish state and its government is particularly evident in the deliberate promotion of nationalist attitudes, the prioritization of short-term electoral interests, and the continued refusal to take substantive measures of their own, despite all the steps and initiatives undertaken by the Kurdish freedom movement over the past two years. Added to this is the attempt to reduce Abdullah Öcalan’s political role to organizing and overseeing disarmament, rather than recognizing his role in coordinating the transition to a democratic political struggle. This approach reveals the political objectives of the state actors and their underlying understanding of power and governance. Against this backdrop, it also becomes clear that Abdullah Öcalan is engaged in a comprehensive political struggle despite the numerous obstacles he faces. He responds to attempts to obstruct the process with flexible and creative political approaches aimed at expanding the available scope for political action and further advancing the path he has embarked upon.




We are currently in a phase in which the state is attempting to strip the political process of its substantive meaning through systematic delays and reduce it to the issue of disarmament. At the same time, it is preparing for further military confrontations both domestically and internationally, continuing its policies of cultural assimilation and genocidal oppression, and intensifying environmental destruction. Rather than initiating democratic reforms, it is escalating political repression, attempting to silence opposition media and reshape political parties in accordance with its own interests. As a result, increasingly authoritarian practices of governance are emerging, reminiscent of the political order under one-party rule.




The nation-state as an instrument of social domination




Under these conditions, the Kurdish freedom movement, democratic and left-wing forces, oppressed social groups and all opposition movements bear a particular responsibility. By its very nature, the state is an organization of domination that can resort to a wide range of means to maintain and perpetuate its power while ensuring the strength and effectiveness of its civilian and military bureaucracy. This is the fundamental purpose of the state apparatus and its political institutions. To expect such a structure of domination to democratize itself and abandon its repressive practices of its own accord is therefore to place hopes for overcoming existing relations of domination in the very institution that creates and sustains them.




The state, particularly in its nation-state form, is an instrument of exploitation and oppression. It can consolidate its rule to the extent that it succeeds in dismantling social bonds and alienating people from their communal and ethical values. Against this backdrop, asking why the state fails to introduce democratic reforms, restricts freedom of expression, degrades women and young people within society, tolerates organized crime, drug trafficking and corruption, or perpetuates social injustice reflects an inadequate understanding of its structural nature. For state power is inherently geared toward destroying social bonds, weakening society’s capacity for autonomous self-defense and creating the conditions for its exploitation. To achieve these objectives, it fundamentally regards any means it considers expedient as legitimate.




Communal self-organization as the foundation of social emancipation




If the state, in accordance with its structural nature, secures its existence by dismantling social bonds, it can only be countered through the establishment and strengthening of autonomous forms of social organization. Contemporary social reality is often characterized by people’s alienation from their own values, the restriction of their intellectual and critical capacities, and the loss of their ability to govern themselves collectively. This is accompanied by an increasing transfer of social decision-making powers to external authorities. Overcoming these conditions requires reconstituting society on the basis of its own values, organizing it within democratic, egalitarian and libertarian structures, and developing a social system capable of independently resolving collective problems and shaping communal life through self-determination.




This gives rise to the need to build a comprehensive network of communal organizational structures from the grassroots up. Central to this is the establishment of democratic associations in which people can independently identify their own problems and needs, discuss them collectively, develop appropriate solutions and take responsibility for putting them into practice.




Organized society as the only viable foundation




To expect change from the state is to leave one’s fate at its mercy. The only reliable foundation for social emancipation, therefore, can be organized society itself. It encompasses diverse ethnic communities, religious beliefs and ideological currents. It includes women, who form the foundation of social coexistence while being particularly subjected to oppression and exploitation. It also includes young people whose future prospects are restricted by existing conditions, workers who are alienated from the products and conditions of their own labor, and numerous other social groups, individuals and intellectuals who are critical of or opposed to the current system. Reaching a common understanding of shared interests and objectives among these diverse social forces, together with their collective organization, can create the conditions for the emergence of a new form of social organization.




The Democratic Republic as a vision for collective self-determination




It is against this backdrop that Abdullah Öcalan’s repeated calls to build a movement for a Democratic Republic must be understood. Given the existing political and social conditions, it is more necessary than ever to bring together the various opposition forces and those social groups that are denied fundamental freedoms and subjected to state oppression in a common political struggle. Communes, civil society organizations and other forms of social self-organization can create spaces in which democratic consciousness can emerge and the capacity for collective political action can develop. What is crucial is that people no longer remain passive victims of circumstances but become autonomous political actors capable of articulating their interests, shaping social change and securing tangible achievements. Expanding and strengthening a united democratic movement has therefore become a more urgent task than ever. Only on this basis can the Peace and Democratic Society Process move forward.

title: Hatimoğulları: Now is the time to expand the ecological struggle
content:
Tülay Hatimoğulları, co-chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), criticized the UN Climate Summit COP31 in Antalya as a platform serving the interests of governments and major corporations. At a press conference with representatives of the ecology movement, she accused those responsible of using climate protection as a pretext to legitimize an economic system based on limitless growth, exploitation and the destruction of the natural foundations of life.




Hatimoğulları spoke during protests against the official climate conference. Alongside COP31, ecological and civil society organizations in Antalya are organizing an alternative People’s Climate Summit. The DEM Party politician welcomed activists who had traveled from various regions and paid particular tribute to the resistance of women, farmers, young people and workers against the destruction of their living environments.




“COP31 is nothing but exploitation”




The DEM Party co-chair fundamentally questioned whether the very governments and corporations whose economic and energy policies have significantly contributed to worsening the climate crisis could be expected to develop solutions to it. “COP31, jointly organized by the state and capital, represents the domination of capital over life, the exercise of power over society and the plundering of nature. It is nothing but exploitation itself,” Hatimoğulları declared.




The climate crisis, she said, is not merely an ecological problem but a reflection of social power relations. “The climate crisis is a question of class exploitation and justice. Its root cause is the insatiable greed for profit.”




In this context, she also recalled the deaths of 19 workers at HABAŞ in Izmir. Hatimoğulları blamed the disregard for occupational safety regulations and the profit-driven interests of company management for the deadly working conditions. She noted that workers who sought to protest against these conditions had reportedly been attacked by the gendarmerie. She stressed that the DEM Party stands alongside the workers and supports their struggle for decent working conditions.













Ecological destruction in Kurdistan is increasing




A particular focus of Hatimoğulları’s speech was the expansion of mining and energy projects in Kurdistan. She warned that the economic exploitation of the Kurdish provinces was accelerating precisely at a time when peace and a democratic solution to the Kurdish question were being discussed. “Today, as we discuss the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the guns have fallen silent, we are witnessing capitalism and capital rapidly advancing into the Kurdish provinces,” she said.




The DEM Party co-chair noted that the government and major corporations have already carried out extensive interventions in nature in the Aegean, Black Sea and Mediterranean regions, and are now increasingly targeting the Kurdish provinces with similar projects.




“This is not merely about exploiting natural resources, but also about destroying long-established social environments and ways of life,” she underlined.




“The village where we were born, the summer pastures we migrate to, and the fields where we earn our livelihoods are living environments. For the people who live there, this land, these trees and natural resources are neither objects nor commodities.” Hatimoğulları pointed to protests against controversial energy and mining projects in Sur in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), Varto and Diyadin, as well as ecological resistance movements in Artvin, Gümüşhane, Uşak and the highlands of the Black Sea region.




She described these struggles as manifestations of a common conflict between the livelihoods and well-being of local communities and an economic policy that subordinates natural resources to corporate exploitation. She sharply criticized Law No. 7554, which ecological initiatives have described as the “Plunder Law.” Remarking that the legislation was passed despite resistance from social movements and the parliamentary opposition, she said: “We do not recognize Law No. 7554. As far as we are concerned, it is null and void.”




Oil discoveries in Gabar and contradictory climate policies




As an example of the contradictions between official climate pledges and actual government policies, Hatimoğulları cited the announcement of new oil discoveries in Gabar during the first days of COP31. “While the entire world is expecting concrete steps toward phasing out fossil fuels, Turkey continues to present new oil discoveries as good news for society,” she stated. In Antalya, she said, the government promises to uphold the Paris Climate Agreement’s 1.5-degree target and act as a mediator between the Global North and Global South. At the same time, she added, it continues to expand fossil fuel production and the industrial exploitation of natural resources.




Hatimoğulları referred to climate data from the World Meteorological Organization, according to which global warming, ocean warming and sea-level rise have reached new record highs. Between January and September 2026, the global average temperature was approximately 1.47 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Turkey’s climate policies also lag behind in international comparisons. According to the Climate Change Performance Index, Turkey ranks 53rd out of 64 countries assessed, based on its climate measures and greenhouse gas emissions trends.













Turkey has become an open-air dumping ground




Hatimoğulları pointed to waste imports from Europe as another example of the consequences of these policies: “While the Turkish government promotes its Zero Waste strategy internationally, large quantities of foreign waste are brought into the country and disposed of, particularly in economically disadvantaged regions. Those who promote their Zero Waste rhetoric on the international stage have turned Turkey into an open-air dumping ground.”




According to figures cited by the DEM Party co-chair, Turkey imported approximately 650,000 tonnes of waste in 2025, including 510,000 tonnes from the European Union and 140,000 tonnes from the United Kingdom. Around 60 percent of this waste is disposed of in the predominantly agricultural region of Adana. According to Hatimoğulları, the economically disadvantaged neighborhood of Küçük Dikili is particularly affected. The government, she argued, is attempting to attribute the waste problem to individual habits and a lack of environmental awareness. In reality, however, it is a structural problem rooted in capitalist relations of production and consumption, she underlined.




Limak and the destruction of Akbelen’s olive groves




Hatimoğulları was particularly critical of the Turkish conglomerate Limak, which organized an event at COP31 on the role of women in shaping the climate economy. The company presents itself as a champion of a sustainable economy while simultaneously being associated with controversial energy projects and the destruction of natural habitats. The DEM Party co-chair referred to the resistance against coal mining in the Akbelen area near Milas, where villagers have been fighting for years against the expansion of mining operations, deforestation and the destruction of agricultural land.




Hatimoğulları referred to 88-year-old Zehra, who drew public attention when she desperately clung to a tree to prevent it from being cut down. She also cited the repression of activists Necla Işık and her daughter Esra Işık as an example of how the authorities treat protesting communities. She noted that Esra Işık was imprisoned for a period before being released following public protests. “While olive trees in Milas are being uprooted to supply coal-fired power plants, the same economic actors are portraying themselves as environmental protectors at the climate summit through symbolic tree-planting ceremonies,” she said.













Corporations at the negotiating table, affected communities excluded




Hatimoğulları also criticized the composition of the climate summit, stating: “Companies such as Cengiz, Limak, Rönesans and Sinpaş, whose projects have been linked to ecological conflicts and legal proceedings, are granted access to the events. Meanwhile, those directly affected by environmental destruction and organizing resistance against it are excluded.” She pointed to protest movements in Varto, on the Perşembe Plateau and in Çambaşı, as well as in Akbelen, Cerattepe, the Ida Mountains and Akseki. She also cited resistance against the destruction of olive groves in Antakya, struggles over natural habitats in Diyadin, and protests against deforestation in Siirt.




“The very companies that should be held accountable for the climate crisis are sitting at the negotiating table. But the villagers defending their land, water and living environments have no seat at that table. To put it in a single word, this is a summit of oppressors,” she declared.




Hatimoğulları also described the discussions at COP31 on developing resilient cities as contradictory in light of Turkey’s construction and urban development policies. She noted that riverbeds are being encased in concrete, natural floodplains are being destroyed, and essential protective measures are being neglected. She recalled the floods in Istanbul, Kocaeli and Antalya, as well as the consequences of the February 2023 earthquakes in the Maraş and Antakya regions. “Despite the devastating destruction, many people in Adıyaman and Hatay are still forced to live in container settlements,” she added.




“We must also make peace with our trees”




Hatimoğulları drew a direct connection between the Peace and Democratic Society Process and ecological destruction in Kurdistan. She pointed out that decades of militarization, military exclusion zones and security measures have destroyed forests, pastures and entire ecosystems. As an example, she cited deforestation in Besta in Şırnak, where the DEM Party co-chair had participated in a protest vigil against the ongoing clearing of forests. The felled trees are transported away and their trunks sold, while local communities struggle to protect the remaining forest areas.




The DEM Party co-chair said she had been particularly moved by an encounter with a Kurdish mother who spoke in her native language about the importance of peace during the protest vigil. “We have been struggling for peace in Turkey for 50 years. We are working for peace in this country and for a peaceful and democratic solution to the Kurdish question. When we make peace, the guns will fall silent, yes. But we must also learn to make peace with our trees,” Hatimoğulları quoted the woman as saying.




In this context, she called for ecocide to be recognized as a crime under international law. “Funds must be allocated to the ecological restoration of destroyed ecosystems. Social peace also means making peace with nature,” she emphasized.




“We do not expect solutions from COP31”




Hatimoğulları contrasted the official climate negotiations with the self-organization of social movements. The solution to the ecological crisis, she argued, cannot be left to the governments and corporations that profit from the exploitation of natural resources. “We do not expect solutions from COP31. We are looking for solutions within ourselves. We see the solution in those who defend nature. Now is precisely the time to expand the ecological struggle,” she declared.




The real driving forces of social change, she emphasized, are people defending their living environments, workers fighting for their rights, women, young people, Indigenous communities and organized ecological movements. Hatimoğulları pointed to the international protests and alternative events held alongside previous UN climate conferences, including COP26 in Glasgow in 2021 and COP30 in Belém, Brazil, in 2025. In Antalya, she said, this resistance would continue and be linked to the struggles of communities in Turkey and Kurdistan.




“The DEM Party rejects an economic model that treats forests, soil, water and air as inexhaustible sources of raw materials while simultaneously viewing the planet as a dumping ground.”




Call for a united international movement




Concluding her speech, Hatimoğulları called for the unification of social, ecological and political struggles that have often been waged separately: “Water, food and energy must be defended as common foundations of life rather than subjected to the laws of the market. Such a movement must not be confined to Turkey but should emerge from local resistance struggles and unite at the international level.”




She continued: “We will defend the right to life of all living beings to the very end, whatever the cost – the rights of birds, insects, trees and leaves. Rivers and streams will flow freely, and we will defend their rights. The power of the existing economic system is not insurmountable. What matters is that the social forces opposing exploitation and destruction develop a shared vision.




If we, as the peoples of the world, as workers, laborers, women, young people, and defenders of nature and human rights, unite our struggles, stand together and act with a shared vision, we can change this system. We will change this system. We will succeed.”

title: Tayip Temel says new developments could emerge in the peace process
content:
DEM Party Deputy Co-Chair Tayip Temel stated that new developments could emerge in the Peace and Democratic Society Process in the foreseeable future. Temel said that the latest talks had been positive and had raised hopes that existing obstacles could be overcome. At the same time, he emphasized that a political solution to the Kurdish question should not be reduced to the laying down of arms. Rather, he argued, the priority should be to establish the legal and social conditions necessary for democratic restructuring.




Temel spoke during a panel discussion organized by the Southeastern Anatolia Journalists’ Association (GGC) in Cologne. The event, titled “The Memory of the Media in the Peace Process: A European Perspective,” focused on prospects for resolving the Kurdish question and the role of the media in the current political process. Moderated by Hozan Adar, the discussion featured simultaneous interpretation between Kurdish and Turkish.




At the beginning of his remarks, Temel highlighted the distinctive role of the Kurdish press, which, he said, unlike other media, had always also served as a platform for political resistance. He commemorated Musa Anter, known as Apê Musa, and the journalists who had been killed in the struggle for press freedom.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/4e4469df_20261114130309_2026-11-14-koln-tayip-temel-dem-parti-es-genel-baskan-yardimcisi-panel-demokratik-toplum-ve-baris-sureci-1.mp4













Peace process enters a decisive phase




Temel outlined the current state of the peace process in terms of four successive stages. He explained that the first stage involved ending the armed conflict, thereby creating the conditions necessary for political dialogue. This was followed by the initiation of talks between Abdullah Öcalan, the Kurdish movement and the Turkish state. According to Temel, Öcalan involved leading political figures from other parts of Kurdistan from the very beginning. Temel referred to contacts with Masoud Barzani, Bafel Talabani and Mazlum Abdi. He said that Öcalan had sent letters to these figures and numerous Kurdish institutions, seeking their views on the process. As a result, the process did not remain confined solely to relations between the Kurdish movement and Ankara.




Temel identified the establishment of a legal and political framework as the third stage. He noted that important steps had been taken with the formation of a parliamentary commission on the Kurdish question and the passage of a law, despite existing shortcomings. In his view, the fact that the Kurdish question was being addressed in the Turkish parliament represented a historic turning point.




“The real challenge, however, lies in the fourth phase, which the process is currently undergoing: opening up the legal and social space for democratic politics,” Temel said. He noted that Kurdish political activities had been criminalized for decades and that large sections of the Kurdish movement had been excluded from legal political life. The necessary conditions must now be established to enable those affected to represent their social and political interests without facing repression, he said. These will include, in particular, legal recognition and protection of Kurdish identity, recognition of fundamental rights and freedoms, and the removal of obstacles to democratic political participation. Without these changes, he argued, the fourth phase could not be completed.




Positive talks despite political obstacles




According to Temel, discussions are currently taking place between Imrali and the Kurdish movement on how to continue the peace process on a solid legal foundation. Although difficulties and delays have recently emerged, he said the latest talks yielded positive results. In this context, Temel expressed hope that the Turkish National Security Council (MGK) would expedite its decisions. The framework law adopted on August 10 and brought into force on August 18 provides legal provisions for disarmament and the reintegration of former PKK members into civilian life. However, the implementation of key provisions is conditional upon confirmation that the PKK has dissolved and disarmed, as well as a corresponding decision by the MGK.




The DEM Party politician also identified political tensions between Hewlêr (Erbil) and Sulaymaniyah in Southern Kurdistan as a potential source of strain. He warned that the ongoing conflicts between political forces in the region could also affect the further development of the peace process. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that the political momentum achieved so far could no longer be fundamentally reversed. He argued that no actor was now in a position to completely derail the process or withdraw from it. According to Temel, the positive outcomes of the latest talks had strengthened expectations that existing obstacles could be overcome and the next legal steps initiated.




“It is not just about laying down arms”




Temel also placed the current developments in the context of shifting political power dynamics in the Middle East. “The Kurdish question has historically been shaped by the division of Kurdistan among four states. However, decades of attempts to suppress Kurdish identity and political demands through repression, assimilation and military force have failed to produce a solution.”




He argued that Turkey’s policies in particular had not resolved the Kurdish question but had instead increasingly intensified its social and political repercussions. These developments, he said, were compounded by emerging regional power dynamics, particularly changes in relations between Israel and Iran. Under these circumstances, he maintained, it had become clear that a political solution could no longer be postponed.




“Against this backdrop, Abdullah Öcalan’s initiative of February 27, 2025, should be understood as an effort aimed not merely at ending the armed conflict but also at overcoming its historical and political causes. After 50 years of war, it has become necessary to end this war and establish peace. But this is not just about laying down arms. An approach that reduces the entire process to disarmament is misguided. This debate is being deliberately pursued, even though it fails to address the heart of the matter,” Temel underlined.




According to Temel, Öcalan’s appeal had outlined a vision based on the recognition of Kurdish identity, the restoration of Kurdish rights and a democratic solution. He noted that ending the armed conflict was therefore a prerequisite, rather than the ultimate political objective of the process. According to Temel, this also meant that the Kurdish question could not be treated solely as a domestic issue of Turkey. He argued that developments in Rojava, Southern Kurdistan and Eastern Kurdistan, along with political changes across the wider region, were inseparably linked to the prospects for a democratic solution.




Integration requires changes on both sides




Temel placed particular emphasis on the debate surrounding democratic integration. He argued that the term was frequently misunderstood or deliberately equated with submission and the abandonment of Kurdish demands. “Such an interpretation, however, is incompatible with the political approach underpinning the current process. Integration can only succeed if both the forms of Kurdish political engagement and the attitude of the Turkish state undergo fundamental changes. While the Kurds should increasingly pursue their struggle through political, democratic and social means, the state must abandon its longstanding policy of denying Kurdish identity,” he stated.




According to Temel, this would not mean abandoning existing political objectives, but rather changing the means and conditions under which they were pursued. “This is not about the Kurds abandoning their struggle. On the contrary, the struggle is being reshaped under new conditions. It is a new phase of resistance in which the struggle is carried out through political, democratic and social means.”




Temel emphasized that integration therefore meant neither capitulation nor the abandonment of identity and rights. Rather, he stressed, it should be understood as a process of transformation that would enable Kurds to participate in democratic political life on an equal footing while preserving their own identity and rights.

title: KJAR: Society cannot be liberated without women’s freedom
content:
The Free Women’s Society of Eastern Kurdistan (KJAR) called for resistance against state repression, patriarchal violence and the systematic deprivation of women’s rights in Iran. In a statement on the occasion of November 25, International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, KJAR painted a picture of escalating violence, ranging from executions and enforced disappearances of politically persecuted individuals to femicides, economic dependence and social discrimination. At the same time, it paid tribute to the resistance of political prisoners and called for the various social struggles to be united through collective organization. November 25, it said, must not remain merely a symbolic day of remembrance but should become an expression of everyday resistance against violence and oppression.




The full statement by KJAR reads as follows:




State repression in the shadow of war




“As November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, approaches, the political situation in the region is being shaped by profound crises and conflicts, including the war between the United States, Israel and the Iranian regime. In such a tense situation, the greatest danger is that the war the regime is waging against society within the country, particularly the structural violence against women, will be overlooked. Historical experience shows that repressive systems of rule exploit external crises to consolidate their power domestically.




Over the past year, repression by the security forces and judiciary has intensified at an unprecedented scale and pace. Reports have documented a wave of enforced disappearances in Kurdistan, Balochistan and other parts of the country. People are being arrested without any information being provided about their whereabouts, prisoners are being transferred to secret detention facilities run by the security services, and death sentences continue to be handed down and carried out without interruption. According to the organization Iran Human Rights, at least 528 people were executed in the first eight months of 2026 alone. This alarming figure demonstrates that spreading fear has become a central instrument of the government in its efforts to keep all forms of opposition under control.




Femicides and patriarchal impunity




While state violence continues, society is also facing an unprecedented scale of femicides and killings within families and tribal communities. According to available data, this violence claims the life of a woman in Iran every day, or at least every few days. Gaps in legal protections, a judiciary that facilitates crimes committed under the pretext of so-called honor, and the patriarchal ideology perpetuated by the structures of power grant perpetrators widespread impunity.




One harrowing example is the murder of 28-year-old Meryem Yarmohammedi on Qeshm Island. She was tortured and mutilated by her brother and killed with the involvement of her husband. Rallies were subsequently held in support of the perpetrator. This case demonstrates the extent to which violence legitimized by reactionary traditions and laws has escalated. The victims of this violence also include 21-year-old Soraya, a mother of three who was beaten to death with a hammer, and Ayda Haydariyan from Sine. A society that fails to protect women’s right to life and freedom is condemned to remain trapped in a complex cycle of violence.




The invisible forms of violence




In 2026, less visible forms of violence against women also continued in Iran, including systematic economic disadvantage, unjustified legal discrimination, and psychological and cultural pressure imposed under the pretext of protecting honor, as well as the practice of blaming victims themselves. These invisible forms of violence are further exacerbated by economic and social crises and the absence of effective laws for protection and prevention. They normalize the subordination of women in everyday life, undermine their independence and create fertile ground for overt, often deadly violence.




Prisons have become centers of resistance




Despite these various forms of oppression, the country’s prisons have become centers of resistance, the struggle for justice and political awareness. The resistance of women such as Zeynab Jalalian, Varisheh Moradi and Pakhshan Azizi, along with the ongoing struggle of those subjected to enforced disappearance and state persecution, including Zehra Pirdehqan, Parvin Raseq Qezelbash and Sara Rashidi, demonstrate that prison walls cannot silence voices demanding equality. This steadfastness has transformed prisons into bastions where political and social resistance converges with the struggle for justice.




United struggle against all forms of oppression




Years of struggle and sacrifice by women have now brought about achievements that can no longer be reversed. These gains place key responsibilities upon us:




- The demands of the women’s movement must be united with the struggles of workers, teachers, students and oppressed minorities to collectively confront structural and economic violence, as well as violence committed in the name of so-called honor.




- Enforced disappearances, executions and cases of femicide must remain continuously on the social and political agenda. We must not allow reports of state repression to be forgotten amid military and political crises.




- The resistance of political prisoners must be brought to public attention, and their demands must be supported as a foundation for broader social protest movements.




November 25 is not just a single day




Therefore, as KJAR, we declare that November 25 represents a renewal of our commitment to equality and human dignity. We firmly believe that society can only be liberated from all forms of violence when women’s rights and freedoms are fully and unconditionally realized and guaranteed.




November 25 is not just a single day. Violence against women is far from over. It continues every day – in homes, on the streets, in detention centers and prisons. Therefore, the struggle against this violence must not be confined to a single day on the calendar.




We stand against this violence every day of the year and call on everyone to join our resistance until no woman is ever again victimized because of her identity.”

title: Peoples march for climate justice against ecological destruction in Antalya
content:
The Antalya Labor and Democracy Forces gathered at Aydın Kanza Park to protest the COP31 negotiations, ecological deception and environmental destruction. The demonstrators then marched to Cumhuriyet Square. The gathering brought together environmental organizations, trade unions, political parties and thousands of citizens from across Turkey and Kurdistan, as well as hundreds of participants from 90 different countries. Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), and DEM Party members of parliament also attended the demonstration.







Hundreds of participants in the international procession chanted slogans against the climate crisis and Israel’s attacks on Palestine, while also singing protest songs. Some participants from different countries joined the march wearing traditional clothing. The international procession featured colorful scenes, with puppet performances, musical instruments and effigies expressing opposition to Trump. Delegations from various countries marched with banners highlighting their demands concerning the ecological destruction taking place in their respective countries.







At Cumhuriyet Square, Çağrı Sert and Erol Malçok read out a joint statement on behalf of the demonstrators. The statement expressed skepticism and distrust towards the COP31 negotiations, emphasized the participants’ demand to have a say in the process, and accused governments of continuing their hypocrisy. The statement stressed that COP31 meetings were dominated by government officials and representatives of fossil fuel companies and other major corporations.







“For 31 years, this pattern has remained unchanged, and unfortunately, they have never surprised us. The vast majority of countries participating in these summits have not only avoided putting concrete proposals capable of providing genuine solutions to the climate crisis on their agendas, but have also failed to make progress toward ensuring that the decisions adopted are legally binding. Meanwhile, the desperate cries of Pacific island nations, whose lands and living spaces will be submerged in the very near future, have gone unanswered. The demands for justice from the peoples of countries that have contributed the least to polluting the planet have been met with attempts by major polluters to buy them off through the establishment of carbon markets.







Yet what peoples demand is genuine climate justice based on lasting, structural solutions, not hush money or superficial approaches involving ‘greenwashing.’ Children, young people, farmers, workers, the unemployed, retirees, caregivers, refugees, women and LGBTI+ individuals, who are among those most affected by the climate crisis, demand justice, not oppression and marginalization.”







The statement recalled that Turkey, as the host country, had paved over large areas of agricultural land in Aksu to facilitate transportation for international delegations arriving to discuss the climate crisis. It continued:




“The government is spending billions of liras in public funds on cosmetic improvements to the city rather than addressing its structural problems. While promoting its ‘zero waste’ campaign, the government is simultaneously turning the country into a dumping ground for Europe’s plastic waste. It also deliberately avoids making any commitments to phase out fossil fuels.







Like all other capitalist countries, host countries such as Turkey and Australia continue their hypocrisy by holding climate summits while simultaneously destroying and poisoning nature and all living beings through mining, hydroelectric power plants, thermal and nuclear power stations, massive fossil fuel consumption, speciesist practices of domination and exploitation that deprive animals of their lives and freedom, and wars.”







Emphasizing that war constitutes a crime against humanity and an act of ecocide, the statement further said the following:




“For giant corporations and states whose sole concern is selling weapons, the lives of humans, animals and natural vegetation are of no importance. For them, the only thing that matters is money, and more money.







In the war between Russia and Ukraine, which has been ongoing for years, tens of thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of soldiers have been killed or injured. More than 3,000 people were killed in the war between the United States and Iran, including at least 254 children.







As a result of Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip since October 7, 2023—including starvation, preventing births, destroying civilian infrastructure, bombing healthcare facilities, killing healthcare workers and aid volunteers, shooting journalists, carrying out widespread forced displacement, committing sexual assaults, and destroying cultural sites and educational facilities—more than 70,000 people have been killed and approximately 170,000 injured in Gaza.







The devastation caused by this almost entirely one-sided war is a stain of shame on the conscience of every country and humanity as a whole. Yet alongside this mass slaughter and the crime of genocide, the ecological destruction caused by wars is rarely discussed at COP summits.







The statement noted that the capitalist system disregards the planet’s finite resources, saying:




“It is also poisoning the water, air, soil and food on which all living beings depend. It is destroying biodiversity at an alarming rate. Clean and fairly produced food can only be produced on a small scale by a limited number of producers, while impoverished communities cannot afford to access it. As a result of the enormous income inequality worldwide, billions of people are unable even to meet their basic nutritional needs, let alone access food produced under fair conditions.







Access to healthy food and drinking water is a fundamental right of every living being and must be guaranteed. However, no state operating within the capitalist system, driven by the motto ‘grow or die,’ will be willing to create these conditions.




Agroecological farming has the potential to feed the entire world, safeguard the planet and ensure that everyone has access to healthy food. All that is needed is the political will and fair distribution.







Our call goes out to all defenders of life across the world: From Glasgow to Dubai, from Belém to local resistance movements in every corner of the globe, climate justice movements have been proclaiming the same truth for years: Climate justice!”




The rally continued with a concert by Luxus.

title: Saturday Mothers demand answers over the disappearance of Bekir Demir
content:
For more than three decades, Bekir Demir’s family has been trying to find out what happened to him after he was detained by Turkish soldiers at the age of 29. Although numerous witnesses saw him being taken away during a military operation in October 1993, his fate remains unknown. Investigations were closed on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired, while military records remained classified. At their 1,129th vigil in Istanbul’s Galatasaray Square, the Saturday Mothers therefore called for the case to be reopened and the military archives to be made public.




The Saturday Mothers initiative, which has been fighting for decades to uncover the truth about enforced disappearances in Turkey, commemorated Demir alongside human rights defenders. Participants carried photographs of the disappeared and those who had been killed, as well as red carnations. The statement issued by the Commission Against Enforced Disappearances in Custody of the Human Rights Association (IHD) was read out by Zeynep Yıldız.




Taken away by soldiers in front of his family




Bekir Demir was originally from Batman, lived with his family in Adana and earned his living as a taxi driver at the bus terminal. In October 1993, the father of four traveled with his wife and their 18-month-old child to the hamlet of Badi, part of Alacakepir village in the district of Kulp in Amed. A colleague had invited him there to buy honey, walnuts and other winter provisions from his father-in-law.




At the time, the Turkish army was conducting extensive military operations in the region under the command of General Yavuz Ertürk. On October 13, 1993, the second day of the family’s visit, soldiers also entered Badi. Around 30 residents were rounded up in the village square, where their identity documents were checked.




Because Demir was not from the village, he was singled out. Under the pretext that the commander wanted to see him, soldiers took him to a military helicopter and flew him away. His wife and numerous villagers witnessed the incident. Demir has not been seen or heard from since that day. The family subsequently appealed to the provincial authorities, the gendarmerie and various public prosecutors’ offices. However, their appeals yielded no results. Although eyewitnesses described his detention, the authorities initially claimed that there was insufficient evidence.




Military archives allegedly submerged in water




Further criminal complaints filed by the family in 1995 and 2002 also failed to shed light on Demir’s fate. Instead, the authorities claimed that no military operation had taken place in the area at the time of his disappearance. However, official documents that later came to light confirmed that units of the 2nd Commando Brigade from Bolu had been deployed there.




The handling of military operational records is particularly troubling for the family. On November 6, 2011, the military prosecutor’s office had requested that the Commando Brigade in Bolu disclose the identities of the officers and non-commissioned officers who had participated in the operation in Alacakepir. The requested information was not provided. The explanation given was that the building housing the archives had been flooded, making the documents inaccessible.




As a result, the identities of the military personnel responsible remained unknown. On November 3, 2014, the public prosecutor’s office in Kulp ultimately closed the investigation on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired. An appeal filed by the family was rejected on March 5, 2015, by a court in Amed (Diyarbakır). An application to the Turkish Constitutional Court also failed to shed light on the case. The complaint alleging a violation of the right to life was declared inadmissible on the grounds that the application deadline had been missed. The family subsequently turned to the European Court of Human Rights.




The Saturday Mothers criticized the failure to thoroughly examine either the detailed eyewitness testimonies or the military operational records. They argued that an effective investigation could have helped establish the truth about the case years ago. “The response to Bekir Demir’s family’s 33-year search for justice cannot consist of decisions based on statutes of limitations and explanations about missing archives,” Zeynep Yıldız said. She emphasized that the authorities must fulfill their international obligations to investigate enforced disappearances and bring those responsible to justice.




“A family’s life slipped away between these desks”




Demir’s son Osman gave a particularly moving account of the consequences of his father’s unresolved disappearance. In a letter addressed to the vigil, which was read aloud by IHD member Nazım Dikbaş, he recalled that he was just six years old when his father was taken away. “I was the eldest of four siblings. At the time, I was too young to understand what had happened. But with every passing year, as I grew older, I felt more painfully what it means for a child to have their father taken away.”




Osman said that the entire family had been waiting for an answer for 33 years. He said the case file had been passed back and forth between various authorities for decades, without any court substantively addressing the central question. “For years, the case file moved from one desk to another. Between those desks, a family’s life slipped away. For more than thirty years, no court has addressed the question ‘Where is Bekir Demir?’ on its merits.”




Osman Demir also questioned the accountability of state institutions. How could a person disappear without a trace after being detained by state security forces, and how could a state not know which members of its own armed forces had participated in such an operation? In his letter, he called on the Ministry of Justice and public prosecutors’ offices to reopen the investigation, question witnesses again and stop dismissing the case on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired.




He called on the Ministry of Defense, the gendarmerie command and the military judiciary to disclose all records concerning the units deployed in the region in 1993 and their commanders. “We want to know what happened to our father, who took him away and where he was taken. We want those responsible to be held accountable before a court. This is our most fundamental human right.”




Osman Demir concluded his letter with an appeal to state institutions: “A state’s commitment to justice is measured not by where it demonstrates its power, but by where it accepts accountability. In this case, the sincerity of the state will be measured not by its words, but by its actions.”

title: YRK: Iranian attacks caused extensive damage in Merîwan
content:
The East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) released a statement announcing the aftermath of Iranian attacks on several villages in the Merîwan (Marivan) region. According to the YRK Command, troops of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards targeted the villages of Qamîşele, Henarşêxan and Gagal with drones and heavy weapons on Wednesday.




According to the statement, the attacks caused extensive damage to numerous residential buildings, as well as gardens, vineyards and agricultural land belonging to the villagers. The YRK forces suffered no casualties in the attacks, the statement added.
